title: Book of Jasher — Restored Names Edition
front_matter:
The Book of Jasher

Restored Names Edition

With Complete Nazarite Commentary, Cross-References, and Restored Divine
Names

By Yoshi

More Than Milk Ministries

Introduction

This is not another reprint of the 1840 Moses Samuel translation. This
is a restored-names edition with full Nazarite commentary, built for the
awakening remnant.

Why does Jasher matter? The Spirit named it. Joshua 10:13 cites the book
of Jasher as the record of the sun standing still over Gibeon. 2 Samuel
1:18 cites it again for the lament of David over Jonathan. No other book
outside the canon is named by name in the canonical scripture — not the
book of the wars of YAHUAH, not the chronicles of the kings, not any
ancient work. Only Jasher. The very volume now in your hand is cited by
name in the inspired text.

What makes this edition different from every other Jasher on Amazon?
First, restored divine names — YAHUAH, Elohim, YAHUSHA — in place of the
generic the Lord and God that hide the covenant identity. Second,
modernized language: the archaic thou/thee/hath/saith/unto of 1840 has
been rendered into readable modern English without stripping the
reverent register. Third, section-by-section commentary from a
Torah-observant covenant framework that connects every passage to
Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, the Prophets, the
Writings, and the testimony of the Messiah. And fourth, a
cross-reference line at the close of every commentary, naming the
canonical passages that illuminate that chapter, so the reader can move
from Jasher to Scripture and back without losing the thread.

The competitors sell cheap reprints of the archaic 1840 text without
commentary, without restored names, without the covenant lens. The Ken
Johnson edition at least cross-references Joshua, 2 Samuel, and 2
Timothy, but it reads Jasher through an evangelical frame that misses
the covenant heart of the book. The Cepher edition embeds Jasher inside
a proprietary name-scheme that cannot be replicated. Nobody is doing
what this volume does: restored names, modern readable English, and a
Nazarite commentary that traces the seed of promise from Adam to Joshua,
naming the tares in every generation and proclaiming the gathering of
the scattered house at the end.

If YAHUAH has opened your eyes to His Torah, if you have begun to see
that your fathers inherited lies (Jeremiah 16:19), if you are watching
the removal of the wicked and the restoration of the righteous in real
time — this commentary was written for you. Not to make you proud. Not
to make you feel special. But to anchor your feet in the Word, to show
you that you are not alone, and to prepare you for what is coming.

Before You Begin

This book combines three elements into one integrated study.

First, the full scripture text of the Book of Jasher, chapter by
chapter. This is the 1840 Moses Samuel translation (public domain) with
restored divine names and modernized English (you instead of thou, has
instead of hath). The scripture text is the foundation. Everything else
exists to help you understand it.

Second, section-by-section commentary from a modern Nazarite
perspective. The commentary is Torah-observant and covenant-aware. It
connects every major passage to the full counsel of Scripture — from the
books of Moses through the Prophets and Writings to the testimony of the
Messiah. It is written for the remnant who has awakened to the truth
that YAHUAH’s commandments are still the fixed order of creation, and
that every religious system — Christian, Jewish, and Hebrew roots — has
inherited deceptions that must be named and dismantled by the Word.

Third, a cross-reference line at the close of every commentary. Every
major passage cited in the commentary is named in context as the
argument is made, and then listed again at the end of the chapter for
quick reference. The aim is that the reader can move from Jasher to
Scripture and back without losing the thread, and can return to a
chapter months later and reconstruct the connections at a glance.

Each chapter follows the same structure: the scripture text appears
first, followed by a visual divider, followed by the commentary. At the
end of every commentary is a Cross-references line listing the primary
passages cited in that chapter’s commentary.

The commentary names three deceived groups with equal care:
institutional Christianity, Judaism, and the Torah-observant / Hebrew
roots movement. None of them is the enemy. All of them have inherited
framework errors — the church from the antinomian reading of Paul,
Judaism from the rabbinic wall against the plain reading of the
prophets, and the Torah-observant community from the False Inclusion
Gospel and from its inherited Replacement Theology in Hebrew-roots
dress. The tone throughout is patience, not condescension. The people
still inside these systems are the lost sheep, not the adversary. The
purpose of the commentary is to dismantle lies with the Word, not to
attack the misled.

Two interpretive keys recur throughout the commentary and should be
named at the outset:

The 1234 of Truth — 1 John 2:3–4 — is the master filter. And hereby we
do know that we know Him, if we keep His commandments. He that says, I
know Him, and keeps not His commandments, is a liar, and the truth is
not in him. If any reading of any scripture requires 1 John 2:3–4 to be
false, that reading is false. YAHUAH does not lie. The filter is not one
interpretation among many. It is the standard the Word itself provides.

The Methodological Sequence for Reading Paul — when Paul is cited, two
steps are always followed. First, establish what Paul was drawing FROM:
he was a Pharisee trained in the Torah and the prophets, and every
argument he makes is sourced there. Second, identify what Paul was
arguing AGAINST: his letters are one side of a conversation, and the
distortion he was rebutting must be named before his answer is read.
This sequence is the antidote to both failures — the church that misuses
Paul for antinomianism and the Torah community that drops Paul entirely.

A Note on the Translation

This edition is built on the 1840 English translation of the Sefer
HaYashar (Book of the Upright) by Moses Samuel, a Jewish translator
working in Liverpool. The Samuel translation is in the public domain. It
is the most complete and accessible English version of Jasher available,
translated directly from the Hebrew edition printed at Venice in 1625,
which itself reproduces an older manuscript tradition preserved in
Jewish communities since the medieval period.

Divine name restoration. The 1840 text uses the familiar English
conventions of its era: the Lord for the covenant name, and God for the
plural majesty. This edition restores YAHUAH where the Samuel
translation has the Lord, and Elohim where it has God. The first
occurrence of each restored name in each chapter includes the original
English term in parentheses so the reader can see what was rendered. El
Shaddai (the Almighty) is preserved where the Samuel text uses it
explicitly. Lowercase elohim is used for the gods of the nations, as in
the canonical Torah.

Divine names are the only restoration. Patriarch names and place names
are kept in their familiar English forms — Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses,
Joseph — rather than being swapped for their Hebrew equivalents. This
matches the Enoch volume of the Restored Names series and keeps the
restored-Name signal sharp for readers new to the walk. The goal is not
novelty. The goal is to recover what was buried — and what was buried is
the covenant name.

Readability modernization. Archaic language (thou, thee, thy, thine, ye,
hath, saith, doth, wilt, didst, unto) has been modernized to you, your,
has, says, does, will, did, to. Adverbs and connectors (wherefore,
thereof, therein, whereby, thence, hither) have been rendered into
modern equivalents. Behold is retained as an elevated but not archaic
word. No verse was cut. No verse was added. The content of the 1840 text
is preserved in full — 91 chapters, 3,913 verse-numbered passages.

Parenthetical content. Samuel’s 1840 translation is exceptionally clean.
It contains no critical apparatus, no bracketed editorial insertions,
and almost no translator glosses. A single narrative aside at Jasher
12:33 has been retained because it belongs to the 1625 Hebrew text
Samuel was translating.

The result is a text that honors Samuel’s scholarship while restoring
the covenant name and opening the prose to a modern reader. What you
have in your hand is as close to what the Spirit cited by name in Joshua
10:13 and 2 Samuel 1:18 as any English-speaking reader has ever held.

How to Read This Book

You are about to read a book the Spirit named.

That sentence is the whole orientation. If you can sit with it for a
moment before you open Chapter 1 — let it press on you, let it ask what
it is asking — you will read this volume in a way that the usual habits
of reading scripture will never deliver. You are not holding a
curiosity. You are not holding a devotional supplement. You are not
holding a lost secret. You are holding a text that the inspired Word of
YAHUAH (God) cited by name in two separate places, a text that was read
and known by the covenant community Joshua led across the Jordan, a text
that was still being taught to the children of Yahudah (Judah) in the
days of King David, and a text that the Restorer of the scattered seed
has now placed in your hand after seventeen centuries of suppression.

That is what you are holding. And because that is what you are holding,
it cannot be read the way you have been taught to read scripture. The
habits you picked up in whichever of the four houses you are walking out
of will trip on this book. The habits your parents taught you will trip
on it. The habits your pastor or your rabbi or your imam or your teacher
at the Hebrew Roots study group taught you will trip on it. You need a
different posture to read this well. That is what this piece is for.

What This Book Is Not

Before anything else, name what this book is not, so that the wrong
expectations do not set the reading on the wrong foot from the first
paragraph of Chapter 1.

This book is not scripture-grade canonical Torah. The five books that
Moses wrote at the direction of YAHUAH (God), the prophets YAHUAH (God)
raised up and whose words the covenant community received as the word of
YAHUAH (God) Himself, the writings the covenant community preserved as
inspired — those stand in their own category, and Jasher does not join
them. The Book of Jasher is a supplementary witness, a cited source, a
volume the Spirit knew and named but did not gather into the covenant
deposit of the Torah, the Prophets, and the Writings. To read it as if
it were Leviticus or Isaiah is to give it more weight than the Spirit
gave it. The book's own witness is higher than that.

This book is not a devotional. A devotional is a short daily piece
designed to produce an emotional lift and a next-day return, usually
organized around a single verse lifted from its context and given a
modern-life application. Jasher was not written for that. The 1840 Moses
Samuel translation preserved it as a continuous narrative running from
the creation of Adam to the death of Joshua — ninety-one chapters, three
thousand nine hundred and thirteen verses. The commentary that follows
each chapter is built to be read alongside the chapter's full narrative,
not extracted for a morning thought. If you read this book in
devotional-sized bites, you will lose the arc of what the text is doing.
Read it slowly. Read it in passages the length the text itself organizes
into. Let the chapter end be the chapter end.

This book is not a concordance. You are not meant to open it to look
something up and close it. That is how the pulpit has trained the last
several centuries of readers to read scripture — as a search engine for
the answer to the question you arrived with. Jasher is not that kind of
book. You will read things in Jasher that the Spirit recorded without
telling you what to do with them. You will read things in Jasher that
expand what Genesis tells you without resolving every question you
bring. This is not a flaw in the text. This is the text asking you to
come as a listener, not as a seeker of a verdict.

This book is not a secret-knowledge text. There is a tradition — in some
of the more esoteric Hebrew-roots corners, and in the broader
gnostic/mystic genre that has always trailed the Christian mainstream —
of receiving books like Jasher and Enoch as the hidden lore the church
suppressed so it could keep you ignorant. That framing is wrong on both
sides. The church did suppress these books, and that suppression was a
specific act of the fourth beast of Daniel 7:25 changing times and laws.
But what was suppressed was not secret knowledge in the gnostic sense.
It was the plain covenant record of what YAHUAH (God) did with the line
of Adam through the line of Noah through the line of Abraham. It was not
coded. It was not hidden in symbols only the initiated could read. It
was the family history of a people whose identity the horn needed to
erase so its replacement could stand. The recovery of Jasher is not the
reader becoming an initiate. It is the reader becoming a family member
again.

This book is not a historical novel. It is not an imaginative filling-in
of the gaps Genesis leaves. The 1625 Venice Hebrew edition that Moses
Samuel translated preserved a manuscript tradition that traces back into
Second Temple memory — the same memory that produced Josephus, the Dead
Sea Scrolls, and the writings the apostles quoted. Whether every
sentence in Jasher corresponds to an event as the narrative describes,
whether certain details reflect later interpretive overlay, whether the
compiler of the Hebrew text you read in English through Samuel's work
added any storyteller's seasoning — all of that belongs to a careful
historical conversation you are welcome to have elsewhere. What it is
not is made up. It is an ancient text preserved by a covenant community
across centuries, containing material the inspired scripture assumes its
readers know.

So — not Torah, not devotional, not concordance, not secret knowledge,
not novel. That is what this book is not. Now what it is.

What This Book Is

This book is a recovered witness. It is the same witness Joshua was
citing when he recorded the sun standing still over Gibeon — and the sun
stood still, and the moon stayed, until the people had avenged
themselves upon their enemies. Is not this written in the book of
Jasher? — Joshua 10:13. It is the same witness the second book of
Shemu'el (Samuel) was citing when David's lament over Sha'ul (Saul) and
Jonathan was being taught to the children of Yahudah (Judah) — also he
bade them teach the children of Judah the use of the bow: behold, it is
written in the book of Jasher — 2 Samuel 1:18. It is the book the
inspired writers expected their readers to know and to be able to
consult. The reader across whose shoulder you are now reading — the
reader whom Joshua and the compiler of Samuel were writing for — is the
reader you are being invited to become again.

This book is a restored text. The 1840 Samuel translation was the first
and has remained the most faithful English rendering of the Hebrew Sefer
HaYashar. What this edition has added is the restoration of the divine
name YAHUAH (God) where Samuel rendered it the Lord, the restoration of
the title Elohim (God) where Samuel rendered it God, and the
modernization of Samuel's archaic English so the text reads as a living
prose. No verse was cut. No verse was added. The content of the 1840
text is preserved in full. What has changed is that the covenant name is
now audible on the page where the earlier English obscured it, and the
language no longer presents a nineteenth-century filter between the
reader and the word. That is a small set of changes, deliberately small.
The text's own weight is what you are meant to encounter. The edition
gets out of the way.

This book is a commented text. The commentary that follows each chapter
is the reason this edition exists. There are cheaper reprints of the
1840 text. There are compendium editions that embed Jasher inside larger
projects. What none of those editions provides is a section-by-section
Nazarite commentary that reads the text through the covenant framework
the text itself assumes. The commentary is not decoration. The
commentary is the lens that lets you see what the text is doing. Without
the lens, Jasher becomes a trivia-supplement to Genesis. With the lens,
Jasher becomes the deepening of Genesis the Spirit intended when He
named the book in the canonical record. You are holding the scripture
text and the commentary as one integrated reading.

This book is a Series volume. It is the second volume of the Restored
Names work, following the Book of Enoch and preceding other volumes in
various stages of preparation. The Series is not a numbered box set. The
Series is a body of work restoring, one volume at a time, the witnesses
the horn dropped. Enoch was first because Enoch is the pre-flood
witness. Jasher is second because Jasher carries the covenant story from
Adam through the death of Joshua in a single narrative thread that
Genesis through Joshua in the canonical deposit preserves with less
connective tissue. What comes next the Father will show in its time. The
reader who wants to know how many more volumes is asking the wrong
question. The right question is — what is on the page in front of me,
and what is the Father saying through it?

That is what this book is: a recovered witness, a restored text, a
commented text, a volume in an ongoing body of work. Now — how does the
reader who is walking out of one of the four houses read a book like
this well?

Four Reading Postures, and Why Three of Them Will Fail Here

Every reader of this book is arriving with a reading posture they did
not choose. You picked it up from the house you grew up in. You picked
it up from the pulpit you sat under for twenty years. You picked it up
from the Shabbat table where the parashah was discussed after the meal.
You picked it up from the Sunday morning children's class, from the
afternoon madrasa, from the Hebrew Roots podcast. The posture is
invisible to you because it is the water you have always swum in. It is
exactly what has to be named before this book will read well.

Three postures are common among the readers who arrive here. All three
will fail this text. A fourth posture — the one the remnant is learning
— will receive what is on the page.

The first is the Christian devotional posture. This is the posture that
says: open the text, find a verse, find the application, apply it to my
life, close the book until tomorrow. The frame is pietistic. The frame
is anthropocentric — what does this mean for me? The frame is atomistic
— verses lifted, applications extracted. The frame is anti-narrative —
the story's shape does not matter; only the nugget inside it matters. If
you read Jasher this way, you will leave ninety percent of the book on
the floor. You will pick out the lines that sound like something you
already believe, you will apply them to a Tuesday-afternoon situation,
and you will miss the covenant architecture the book is trying to put in
front of you. Jasher is not a nugget dispenser. Jasher is a narrative
witness. You have to let the narrative carry you, not mine it for
takeaways.

The second is the rabbinic harmonization posture. This is the posture
that says: when the text seems to say something that contradicts another
text, layer a midrash on it that reconciles both. The frame is
protective of the tradition. The frame assumes that the written text
plus the oral tradition together equal the revelation, and that any
surface contradiction is actually a deeper harmony waiting to be
expounded. This is an honorable posture in its place — it has preserved
Judahite covenant memory across exile and diaspora for two thousand
years — but it will fail you here if you import it wholesale. Jasher
will sometimes say something that does not harmonize with a later
midrashic overlay. That is not Jasher being wrong. That is the midrashic
overlay being later. The Judahite reader walking out of the synagogue
tradition into the remnant needs to let Jasher speak in its own voice,
not through the filter of Rashi or the tosafot. You will find Jasher a
closer ally of the prophets than of the medieval sages; and that is the
recovery the Spirit is doing in you.

The third is the Torah-observant practice posture. This is the posture
that says: open the text, find the commandment, work out exactly how to
keep it this week, make the to-do list, check the box. The frame is
performative. The frame assumes that reading is for doing, and that
doing is the goal of reading. This is not entirely wrong — YAHUAH (God)
did say that the Torah is given that we might do it, not just know it —
but as a reading posture for Jasher it will strip the book of its voice.
Jasher is not a how-to. Jasher does not tell you how to keep the Sabbath
or how to prepare a Passover lamb. Jasher tells you what your fathers
did when they stood at Mount Horeb, what Avraham (Abraham) did when he
confronted Nimrod, what Yosef (Joseph) did when he refused Zelicah, what
Moshe did when he stood before Paroh the second time. If you read Jasher
looking for what do I do now, you will miss what your fathers did then.
And the doing-now you are looking for grows out of the knowing-then
Jasher is offering. Let the narrative teach you first. The practice,
when it comes, will come more rooted than any to-do list could root it.

The fourth is the Islamic replacement posture. This posture is quieter —
most readers of Jasher will not be coming from the Muslim tradition, but
some will — and it needs to be named because it will filter the text in
a specific way. The posture says: the Torah and the earlier scriptures
are corrupted, but this passage may preserve a fragment of the original
revelation that was given to the prophets, and what matters is whether
this book confirms or contradicts the final messenger's recitation. If
you read Jasher with that filter, you will miss that the covenant runs
through Yitschaq (Isaac) and Ya'aqov (Jacob), not through Yishma'el
(Ishmael), and that Jasher maintains that distinction with the same
clarity the Torah maintains it. You do not have to abandon your love of
the prophets or your respect for the Arabic scholarly tradition to read
Jasher well. You do have to let Jasher's own family-line claim stand —
that the seed of promise was in Isaac and not in Ishmael — and walk into
the implications of that with your heart honest before YAHUAH (God).

Those are the three failure postures. Every one of them has inside it
some element that was once alive and is being preserved by the Father in
the very reader who walks out of that house. The Christian's love of
scripture. The Jew's careful preservation. The Torah-observant reader's
heart to do what the Father said. The Muslim's conviction that
revelation matters and that the earlier prophets spoke truly. None of
that is being discarded. All of it is being reoriented.

The fourth posture — the remnant posture — is the one the reader of this
book is being invited to take. Simply stated: hear the text, honor the
voice, let the Spirit restore what was scattered, do not demand that the
text answer the question inherited from the house you are walking out
of. The remnant reader arrives at Jasher without a grid pre-loaded. The
remnant reader opens Chapter 1 and reads the creation account as Jasher
tells it, and lets Jasher's telling stand next to Genesis's telling
without needing to harmonize them in the first pass. The remnant reader
comes to Chapter 6 and reads the flood narrative and lets Jasher's
detail of the door shut by YAHUAH (God) Himself press on the reader
without needing to lift a rule out of it. The remnant reader reads the
long Joseph cycle across chapters 41 through 54 and lets the weight of
Yosef's (Joseph's) slow arc through the pit and the prison and the
throne fall on the reader's own heart without needing to map every beat
onto a personal circumstance. The remnant reader finishes the book and
sits with it.

That is what the fourth posture looks like. The remnant reader listens
first. The remnant reader receives before responding. The remnant reader
trusts that YAHUAH (God) is the one who will produce the response when
He is ready to produce it.

Two Sequencing Rules

If the posture is right, the sequencing does most of the rest of the
work. Two rules govern how to read each chapter of this book, and if you
hold them, the commentary will serve the text rather than the other way
around.

The first rule is: read the scripture first. The chapter text of Jasher
runs at the top of every chapter. It is set apart with a small visual
divider from the commentary that follows. Read the scripture all the way
through before you touch the commentary. Let Jasher speak to you before
any other voice speaks over Jasher. There will be places in the
scripture text where you do not know what to do with what you just read.
Let that discomfort sit for a moment. Do not rush to the commentary to
resolve it. The commentary is there for you when you are ready. The
scripture's voice is what the Spirit named.

This rule is harder than it sounds, for a reader trained in the
Christian study-Bible tradition, where the commentary is printed in
columns alongside the text and the eye drifts across before the text has
had a chance to finish speaking. Your eye will want to run to the
commentary. Train it to stop. Read the scripture to the bottom of the
chapter. Close your eyes for a moment if you have to. Let the chapter be
a chapter.

The second rule is: read the commentary only after the scripture has had
its full voice. The commentary will address the passage you just read.
It will name the cross-references in the Torah, the prophets, the
writings, and the apostolic record that bear on what Jasher is saying.
It will flag the Christian distortion, the rabbinic distortion, the
Torah-observant distortion, the Islamic distortion that the passage
usually gets filtered through. It will present the covenant reading —
the reading that flows from the framework the prophets themselves laid
down. But it will do all of this after Jasher has spoken. The order
matters. The order is the same order the Spirit used when He put Jasher
in Joshua's hand and then gave Joshua's record to us: the earlier voice
first, the later reading of that voice after.

If you hold these two rules, you will find the book opens. If you break
them — if you read the commentary first, or if you skim the scripture
looking for the next commentary bolt-on — you will find yourself reading
a book of opinions instead of a book of witnesses. That is not what this
volume is for.

The 1234 Filter — How to Use It When You Read

You were introduced to the 1234 filter in the Before You Begin piece.
Here it is named again as a working tool, because it is going to matter
to you as you read.

And hereby we do know that we know Him, if we keep His commandments. He
that says, I know Him, and keeps not His commandments, is a liar, and
the truth is not in him. — 1 John 2:3–4.

That is the filter. YAHUAH (God) does not lie. Any reading of any
scripture that requires 1 John 2:3–4 to be false is a wrong reading. The
filter is not one interpretation among many. It is the standard the Word
itself provides.

Here is how you actually use it while reading Jasher.

When a passage in Jasher seems to contradict a commandment in the Torah,
pause. The contradiction is not in the text. The contradiction is in
your reading. Either the Jasher passage is saying something different
than you first thought, or the Torah commandment is saying something
different than you first thought. Go back and read both. Let the
commandment set the floor. If the plain sense of Jasher actually does
violate a commandment — if the book seems to approve what the Torah
forbids — you now have evidence to weigh the passage. Does it pass 1
John 2:3–4? If not, receive the chapter's testimony as you receive any
uninspired witness: useful where it aligns, discardable where it fails.
Most of the time you will find, as you read carefully, that the apparent
contradiction dissolves. Jasher was preserved by a covenant community
for a reason; it tracks the Torah far more closely than its Christian
reputation would suggest.

When a passage in Jasher seems to contradict the prophets' restoration
promises, pause again. The Spirit's restoration timeline — the gathering
of the paternal blood remnant of all twelve tribes of Yashar'el
(Israel), the second recovery now underway, the coming reunion of the
two houses under one Davidic king — is set in the prophetic corpus and
cannot be moved. If a passage in Jasher seems to argue against that
timeline, read the passage again. The restoration is the covenant's
load-bearing promise. Jasher does not contradict the prophets when
Jasher is read in its own voice; it tends to ground them. If you find
yourself reading Jasher against the prophets, you are reading Jasher
through one of the four-house filters that flattens the twelve tribes
into a binary. Reset.

When a passage in Jasher seems to contradict a commentary note, test
both. The commentary in this volume is not inerrant. Yoshi is a son of
Adam who has walked out of the horn's reading and into the covenant
reading, and who is writing to assist you in the same walk. The
commentary has been written with care and reviewed against the
yoshi-voice framework More Than Milk Ministries has developed over
years. It is still the work of a man. When a commentary note seems to
contradict the plain sense of what Jasher is saying, put the note under
1 John 2:3–4. If the note passes, the disagreement is in the reader, and
the reader should sit longer with the note. If the note fails, the
disagreement is in the note, and the reader should set the note aside
and read the passage on its own terms.

You are not asked to agree with every commentary note in this book. You
are asked to test what you read. The remnant does not breed a new
priesthood of commentary-receivers. The remnant reads the Word, tests
everything against the Word, and walks.

The Methodological Sequence for Reading Paul — Deepened Here

When Paul — Sha'ul (Saul) of Tarsus — is cited in this commentary, he
will be read by a two-step sequence the Before You Begin piece already
introduced. The sequence is worth restating because this book cites Paul
often, and the pulpit's reading of Paul is the specific reading this
commentary exists to dismantle.

Step one: establish what Paul was drawing from. Paul was a
Torah-observant Israelite of the tribe of Benjamin, trained under
Gamaliel, set apart for the gospel of the Messiah (Christ). He kept the
Sabbath. He kept the feasts. He took Nazarite vows. He paid the Temple
offering for four men in Acts 21 specifically to refute the slander that
he taught Israel to forsake Moses. Every argument he makes in every
letter is drawn from the Torah and the prophets. Find the source in the
Hebrew scriptures, and you know what Paul meant.

Step two: identify what Paul was arguing against. Paul's letters are one
side of a conversation. Once you have his Torah foundation clear, the
distortion he is rebutting becomes identifiable. In Galatians: the
circumcision party's false gospel of become-a-Yahudi (Jew)-to-be-saved.
In Romans: both antinomian drift among the Gentile-seeming scattered
Yashar'el (Israel) and synagogue pride among Judahite believers. In
Corinth: antinomian overreach. In Colossae: Gnostic shadow. Identify the
target, and the argument's shape becomes clear.

Why this matters for your reading of Jasher. Jasher is a Torah-framed
book. It records the patriarchs as they lived the covenant. When the
commentary cites Paul as agreeing with what Jasher is showing — and it

The Restored Names Project — Why the Name, Why the Text, Why the 1840
Samuel Translation

The short note on the translation that you read a few pages ago covered
what this edition restored and what it modernized. This longer piece
covers why. Why the name is load-bearing. Why the suppression of the
name was not an accident. Why YAHUAH (God) and not Yahweh or Jehovah.
Why Yahusha (Jesus) and not Yeshua or Yahushua. Why Moses Samuel's 1840
translation was chosen out of every possible English text. Why the
restoration scope was limited to divine names and a specific set of
covenant people-names. And why Jasher sits where it sits in a body of
work — the Restored Names Series — that is still being written.

If you are walking out of the horn's seventeen centuries of suppression,
you have not been taught any of this. You have been taught that the Lord
is a respectful English equivalent of the divine name, that the
pronunciation of the name is a mystery only scholars can debate, that
restoring the name is a novelty some Hebrew Roots people chase, that the
Christian canon came down from the apostles intact and the books outside
of it are the leftovers. Every one of those teachings is false, and
every one of them is part of the same mechanism. This piece names the
mechanism and explains the decisions behind this edition.

The Name Was Spoken

Start here, because this is where the fence-building begins and where
the recovery begins. The name YAHUAH (God) was spoken aloud in the
covenant community. It was not a secret. It was not a mystery only
whispered by the high priest once a year. It was on the lips of the
patriarchs, on the lips of the prophets, on the lips of the mothers in
Yashar'el (Israel) when they named their children — Yahu-chanan, YAHUAH
(God) has given grace; Yesha'-yahu, YAHUAH (God) saves; Yirme-yahu,
YAHUAH (God) lifts up; Yechezq-el, Elohim (God) strengthens. Half the
names in the canonical scripture carry pieces of the tetragrammaton
because the Name was a spoken, used, living part of covenant life.

Three converging lines of evidence establish this, and any one of them
would be sufficient.

The first is Josephus. Flavius Josephus was a first-century Yahudi
(Jewish) priest and historian. He served in the Temple before the Temple
fell in 70 AD. He knew the name — he had heard it pronounced in the
Temple by the priests who served there. In Wars of the Jews 5.5.7,
describing the high priest's mitre and the golden plate inscribed with
the name, Josephus writes that the plate bore the holy name in four
vowels. Four vowels. Not three consonants and two inferred vowels, as
the later Masoretic tradition reshaped the pronunciation. Four vowel
sounds. That is the exact shape of YAH-U-AH when it is said aloud — four
sounds, all vowels, pronounced at the open throat: Ee-Ah-Oo-Ah. Josephus
is describing the name as the priests said it.

The second is the Samaritan tradition. The Samaritans — the community
descended from the mixed population that settled in the land after the
Assyrian scattering of 722 BCE and that preserved its own version of the
Torah and its own priesthood — have preserved a continuous oral
tradition of the pronunciation of the name. They did not accept the
later rabbinic fence that forbade pronouncing it. To this day, the
Samaritan priestly tradition pronounces the name in a form close to
Yahwe or Yahuah, with the four-vowel shape, not the Masoretic hybrid.
The Samaritan preservation matters because it is independent of the
rabbinic fence-building; it reflects what the name sounded like in the
centuries before the third-century BCE fence went up.

The third is the Dead Sea Scrolls. The Qumran community — the ascetic
covenant community that hid its library in the Judean desert around the
turn of the first century — preserved scripture texts that include the
tetragrammaton written in paleo-Hebrew script even in manuscripts that
are otherwise in the square Aramaic script. That is a deliberate
retention, on the page, of the ancient written form of the name, even
when the surrounding text was being copied in the newer script. The
Qumran scribes were preserving the name as it had always been. They were
not burying it.

Those three lines converge. The name was known. The name was spoken. The
name was preserved. That is the starting point. The suppression came
later, and the suppression is what produced the English translation
tradition you were handed.

The Suppression — Three Waves

The burial of the name happened in three waves across about eighteen
hundred years. Each wave had a different rationale. Each one was done by
people doing what they thought was faithful. None of them was intended
maliciously. All of them, taken together, produced the result that the
covenant name has been hidden from most English-speaking readers of the
scripture for the whole of their lives.

The first wave was the rabbinic fence. Beginning roughly in the third
century BCE — the period between the closing of the Tanakh and the
coming of the Messiah (Christ) — the developing rabbinic tradition began
to teach that the name YAHUAH (God) was too holy to be pronounced
casually, and that to say it in everyday reading would risk violating
the third commandment — you shall not take the name of YAHUAH (God) your
Elohim (God) in vain, Exodus 20:7. The fence was: do not say the name
aloud; substitute Adonai (my Lord). The intent was honorable — protect
the name from being misused. The effect, compounded across centuries,
was that the name's pronunciation gradually passed out of common usage
among Yahudim (Jews). By the time the Temple fell in 70 AD, only the
priesthood still pronounced it in the Temple liturgy. With the fall of
the Temple, the priesthood's public pronunciation ended. The fence had,
over four centuries, accomplished what it set out to prevent: the name
became inaccessible.

The second wave was the Masoretic vowel-pointing. Around the eighth to
tenth centuries AD, the Masoretes — the Yahudi (Jewish) scribal
tradition that preserved the consonantal Hebrew text with meticulous
care and developed the system of vowel-points that let the unpointed
text be read correctly — faced a specific problem. The Torah manuscripts
they were preserving contained the tetragrammaton thousands of times,
and the oral reading tradition already substituted Adonai at every
occurrence. To cue the reader to say Adonai instead of attempting to
pronounce the name, the Masoretes placed the vowels of Adonai onto the
consonants of the tetragrammaton. The result, on the page, was the
hybrid form Ye-Ho-Wah — the consonants YHWH with the vowels e-o-a from
Adonai. This hybrid never existed as a name in any Yahudi (Jewish)
community. It was a reading-cue. No one in the Masoretic tradition
thought they were preserving the pronunciation; they were preserving the
rule that the pronunciation be suppressed.

The hybrid form, however, had an unintended consequence. Christian
scholars who later learned Hebrew did not know the convention. They read
the pointed text and saw the vowels pointed onto the tetragrammaton and
concluded — incorrectly — that the vowels belonged to the name. They
transliterated the hybrid as Jehovah, and the word entered the Christian
tradition as if it were a genuine pronunciation. It was not. It was a
reading-cue fossilized into a name by scholars who did not know what
they were looking at.

The third wave was Reformation-era translation politics. The sixteenth
and seventeenth centuries produced the great vernacular translations of
the scripture — Luther's German, Tyndale's and the Geneva and the King
James in English, and several others. The Reformers had the Hebrew. They
had the Masoretic tradition. Some of them had sufficient Hebrew
scholarship to recognize the vowel-pointing issue and the hybrid
Jehovah. What they did not have, institutionally, was the freedom to
break with the Septuagint-derived Christian tradition of rendering the
tetragrammaton as a title rather than a name. The Septuagint — the Greek
translation of the Hebrew scriptures made in the third and second
centuries BCE and used by the first-century Greek-speaking synagogue and
the early church — had generally rendered the tetragrammaton as Kyrios
(Lord). The entire Christian liturgical tradition had been built on that
substitution for fifteen hundred years. The Reformers, even when they
knew better, chose continuity over restoration. They rendered the
tetragrammaton as the LORD in small capitals, signaling to the informed
reader that the underlying Hebrew was the tetragrammaton while keeping
the word as the pulpit and the liturgy already used it. That choice
cemented the suppression into every English translation that followed —
the King James, the Revised Version, the American Standard Version
(which briefly experimented with Jehovah), the Revised Standard Version,
the New International Version, the English Standard Version, every
version the Protestant Christian world has used.

Three waves. Each one honorable in intent. All three together producing
a situation in which the reader of the English scripture in the
twenty-first century opens the Bible and reads the LORD several thousand
times across the Torah and the prophets and does not know that the
Hebrew behind every one of those occurrences is the spoken name of
YAHUAH (God). The reader has met the Lord. The reader has not met YAHUAH
(God).

This edition of Jasher is a direct response to that situation. Not a
protest — the Reformers are honored for their scholarship and their
courage; the Masoretes are honored for the consonantal text they
preserved; the rabbinic fence-builders are honored for the care with
which they tried to protect the name. A restoration, not a protest. The
name was buried. The name is being lifted.

The Third-Commandment Weight

You shall not take the name of YAHUAH (God) your Elohim (God) in vain;
for YAHUAH (God) will not hold him guiltless that takes his name in
vain. — Exodus 20:7.

The third commandment has always been read, in the Christian tradition,
as a prohibition on using the word God as an expletive. That reading is
not wrong; casual profane use of the name is included in what the
commandment forbids. But that reading is also shallow. The Hebrew verb
under take is nasa — to bear, to lift, to carry. The commandment is not
only do not say my name lightly. It is more deeply do not bear my name
emptily, do not carry my name for nothing, do not wear my name without
meaning it.

Read that way, the commandment cuts further than profanity. It cuts into
every use of a substitute for the name. To bear the name of YAHUAH (God)
is to speak the name. To call the name by something else — the Lord,
God, Adonai, HaShem, Hashem — is to bear a substitute, not the name
itself. That is not profanity, but it is also not fulfillment of the
commandment's positive call. The positive call of the third commandment
is to lift the name. To know the name. To say the name. To teach the
name to your children. The third commandment is the single command that,
above all the others, has been reduced to a prohibition and stripped of
its positive voice.

Extol him that rides upon the heavens by his name YAH, and rejoice
before him. — Psalm 68:4.

The psalmist is doing what the third commandment commands. He is
extolling the Father by his name. Not by a substitute. By the name. And
the short form of the name — YAH — is the form the psalmist chose, the
form that appears in Halelu-YAH (praise ye YAH) in every praise psalm,
the form the covenant community spoke in worship.

I am YAHUAH (God): that is my name: and my glory will I not give to
another, neither my praise to graven images. — Isaiah 42:8.

YAHUAH (God) Himself, through the prophet, asserts the name and refuses
to give His glory to another. To render the name as the Lord is to give
part of His own self-revelation to the Canaanite term Ba'al — which
means lord — and the parallel is not invented. The Philistines and the
Canaanites called their gods Ba'al. The Christian English tradition, by
substituting the Lord, has accidentally handed the Father's glory into
the vocabulary of the nations. That is not malicious. It is what happens
when three waves of suppression compound across eighteen centuries
without anyone seriously asking whether the substitution is faithful.

How long shall this be in the heart of the prophets that prophesy lies?
yea, they are prophets of the deceit of their own heart; who think to
cause my people to forget my name by their dreams, which they tell every
man to his neighbour, as their fathers have forgotten my name for Ba'al.
— Jeremiah 23:26–27.

Jeremiah names the mechanism directly. The forgetting of the name is not
accidental. There is an active spiritual pressure — Jeremiah calls it
prophets of the deceit of their own heart — that works toward the
forgetting. The Father through Jeremiah names the end state plainly:
their fathers have forgotten my name for Ba'al. Ba'al — which, again,
means lord. The substitution of Ba'al for YAHUAH (God) was the exact
covenant offense that brought the scattering down on the northern house
in the first place. The later Christian substitution of the Lord for
YAHUAH (God) is the same offense in English dress.

That is the weight of the third commandment as it bears on the Restored
Names Project. The name was given to be borne. Bearing is saying. Saying
is restoration. The Restored Names edition of Jasher — and the Restored
Names edition of Enoch, and every volume of the Series that follows — is
built around that weight. The reader who picks up these volumes is being
handed back something the Father through the prophets said He was not
willing to permanently lose: my name.

Why YAHUAH (God) — Not Yahweh, Not Jehovah, Not Yehovah

The informed reader arriving at this Series will have seen other
renderings of the tetragrammaton. Yahweh is the most common in scholarly
writing. Jehovah appears in older English translations and in a few
specific traditions (the Jehovah's Witnesses most visibly). Yehovah
appears in some Hebrew Roots material that accepts the Masoretic
vowel-points as a preserved pronunciation. Why does this Series use
YAHUAH (God)?

Yahweh is a nineteenth-century German scholarly reconstruction. The
academic Hebraists of that era — Gesenius, Ewald, and their successors —
worked from the consonantal text and from certain transliterations in
early patristic sources (especially the Greek Iaōue found in Theodoret
and Clement of Alexandria) and concluded that the original pronunciation
was Yah-weh. The reconstruction became standard in academic and seminary
circles and has dominated scholarly writing ever since. But the
reconstruction has a specific weakness. It derives the pronunciation
from Greek transliterations made by Hellenized Christian writers who
were themselves working with Greek phonology that does not reliably
preserve Hebrew back-vowels. Yah-weh has lost the third vowel sound —
the U of the four-vowel name Josephus described. Yah-weh is two
syllables. The Josephus description is four vowels. That is not a match.

Jehovah, as the section above explained, is the Masoretic hybrid
fossilized into a Christian proper noun by scholars who did not
understand that they were reading a vowel-pointing convention rather
than a preserved pronunciation. Jehovah is not a name. It is an
accidental transliteration of a reading-cue. The J is an English
consonantal approximation of the Hebrew yod; the e is the shewa of
Adonai; the o is the cholem of Adonai; the a is the qamats of Adonai.
Every vowel in Jehovah is from the word Adonai. The consonants YHV (or
YHW) are from the tetragrammaton. The two were never meant to be
combined as a name. The combination is a scribal artifact made into a
proper noun by historical accident.

Yehovah is a more recent variant — often championed in Hebrew Roots
circles — that accepts the Masoretic vowel-points as a preserved
pronunciation and treats Ye-Ho-Vah as a genuine name. It has the
advantage of keeping the Masoretic signal closer to its original form.
It has the disadvantage that the Masoretes themselves did not believe
they were recording the pronunciation; they believed they were recording
a reading-cue to say Adonai. To accept the Masoretic points as a
pronunciation is to accept the fence-builders' vowels as the Father's
name, which the fence-builders themselves would have denied.

YAHUAH (God) is chosen because it reconstructs the four-vowel shape
Josephus described, drawing on the Samaritan tradition and on the
internal evidence of theophoric Hebrew names. The covenant community's
children were named with pieces of the tetragrammaton, and those names
preserve vowels — Yeshu'a, Yirmi-yah, Yesha'-yahu, Eli-yahu. The YAH and
the YAHU elements appear consistently; the long-U sound is preserved
repeatedly. The full name, reconstructed from the theophoric evidence
and aligned with Josephus's four-vowel description, produces YA-HU-AH,
spoken at the open throat with the breath riding through each vowel.
That is the form this edition uses, and it matches the pronunciation
Yoshi grew up hearing from his father.

This is not offered as a competitive correction of Yahweh or Jehovah or
Yehovah readers. The Father who knows the heart knows the heart. A
reader who calls on the Father as Jehovah in sincerity is calling on the
right Father. The point of the Restored Names Project is not to gate
salvation behind a pronunciation. The point is to lift the name out of
the substitution that buried it — to restore what the three waves of
suppression rendered inaccessible — and to let the reader meet the name
afresh. YAHUAH (God) is the form the Project uses because it most
honestly reconstructs what the Father's covenant community heard when
the name was spoken before the fence went up.

Why Yahusha (Jesus) — Not Yeshua, Not Yahshua, Not Yahushua

The same logic governs the choice of Yahusha (Jesus) for the Messiah
(Christ)'s name. The name the angel gave to Miryam (Mary) in Luke 1:31 —
thou shalt call his name JESUS — is the Greek Iēsous, which is the
Hellenization of the Hebrew Yehoshua / Yeshua, meaning YAHUAH (God)
saves. That meaning is not incidental. It is the reason the angel
specified the name. For he shall save his people from their sins —
Matthew 1:21. The name carries the verb. The name is the statement.

Yeshua is the short form that has survived in rabbinic Hebrew and in
modern Messianic Yahudi (Jewish) usage. It is a legitimate short form —
it is how the name was abbreviated in later Hebrew usage — but it has a
specific weakness: it drops the YAH prefix. In the longer form Yehoshua
(which is the form of the name of Yehoshua (Joshua) son of Nun), the
YAHU element is visible; the name is YAHUAH (God)-saves. In the short
form Yeshua, the YAHU element has been truncated to the initial Ye, and
the theophoric weight is no longer audible. That is a loss, for a name
whose entire point is the Father's name combined with the salvation
verb.

Yahshua is a form that appears in some Hebrew Roots material,
constructed by moving the YAH prefix directly against the shua verb stem
without the connecting vowel. It has the advantage of making the YAH
explicit. It has the disadvantage of being a construction that does not
appear in the ancient Hebrew record; no manuscript, no inscription, no
extant tradition preserves the name as Yah-shua. It is an internal
Hebrew Roots reconstruction.

Yahushua is a fuller form that appears in some Sacred Name movement
material. It preserves the YAHU prefix and adds an extra syllable —
Yah-u-shu-a — that lengthens the name beyond what the Second Temple
evidence supports. The Dead Sea Scrolls, the first-century ossuaries,
and the Greek transliterations all point to a three-syllable or
four-syllable name Yahusha (Jesus) or Yehoshua, not a five-syllable
Yahushua.

Yahusha (Jesus) is the form this Series uses because it preserves the
YAH prefix audibly, tracks closely to the ancient Hebrew shape, aligns
with the first-century pronunciation that produced the Greek Iēsous, and
remains the form Yoshi's own community has used for decades. It is the
Name combined with the verb: YAH-USHA. YAHUAH (God) saves. That is who
He is. That is what His name records.

Again, no gatekeeping. A reader who has called on Yeshua in sincerity
has called on the right Messiah (Christ). A reader who has called on
Jesus in sincerity has called on the right Messiah (Christ). The
Restored Names Project does not make pronunciation a salvation test.
What the Project does is restore the audible weight of the name so the
reader can hear what the name says. YAHUAH (God) saves. Read Jasher with
that in your mouth, and the entire arc of the covenant story — from Adam
to the death of Yehoshua (Joshua) — rises up out of the text.

Why Moses Samuel's 1840 Translation

There is more than one English version of the Book of Jasher on the
market. Some are cheap reprints of Samuel's 1840 work with no
restoration and no commentary. Some are sincere evangelical efforts that
cross-reference Jasher with the canonical scripture but read the book
through a Christian doctrinal frame. One major compendium — the Cepher —
embeds Jasher inside a larger proprietary project with its own name
conventions. Why did the Restored Names Project build its Jasher on
Samuel's 1840 rather than starting from one of the alternatives or from
scratch?

Four grounds converged.

First, Moses Samuel was a Yahudi (Jewish) scholar, not a Christian
missionary. He was born in Liverpool in 1795, trained in Hebrew from his
Yahudi (Jewish) community's tradition, and spent his working life as a
translator of Hebrew texts into English. He rendered Jasher out of the
1625 Venice Hebrew edition with no Christian theological filter imposed
on the text. When the Hebrew said something the Christian reading
tradition would have found awkward, Samuel preserved the plain sense;
when the Hebrew made a covenant claim that the Christian reading
tradition would have wanted to spiritualize, Samuel let the covenant
claim stand. His was the honest rendering of a covenant insider, not the
filtered rendering of an outside apologist.

Second, the source text Samuel worked from was itself the most reliable
extant Hebrew Jasher. The 1625 Venice edition of the Sefer HaYashar —
the Hebrew book of the upright — was published by Yosef ben Shemuel
ha-Kohen in Venice, drawn from medieval Yahudi (Jewish) manuscripts that
themselves preserved a textual tradition reaching back into Second
Temple memory. The 1625 Venice edition is not the oldest Jasher
manuscript — older fragments exist — but it is the most complete and the
most carefully prepared of the available Hebrew base texts. By choosing
Samuel's 1840 translation, the Restored Names edition inherits that
base-text scholarship.

Third, Samuel's 1840 is exceptionally clean of editorial apparatus.
There are no bracketed insertions. There are no critical footnotes
crowding the margin. There is almost nothing Samuel added to the Hebrew
he was rendering — a single narrative aside at Jasher 12:33 is the only
one flagged, and even it belongs to the 1625 Hebrew. Compared to R. H.
Charles's 1912 Enoch — which is laced with Charles's own editorial
overlays — Samuel's Jasher arrives almost without mediation. The
translator got out of the way. That makes the restoration work far
easier and far more honest.

Fourth, the 1840 Samuel translation is in the public domain. No
licensing politics stand between the text and the reader. No estate can
demand royalties. No publisher can claim exclusive rights to a specific
rendering of the Hebrew. The text is free, which means the restoration
can be done fully and the result can be made available to every reader
who wants it. That is not a minor consideration. The horn's suppression
of the text for seventeen centuries has finally broken down partly
because the text is now free. Keeping it free is part of keeping it
restored.

Those four grounds — Yahudi (Jewish) scholarship, reliable source text,
minimal editorial overlay, public domain — converged to make Samuel's
1840 translation the obvious foundation for the Restored Names Jasher.
The edition does not pretend to have produced a new translation from the
Hebrew; that would have required a translation team and years of work,
and the result would not have been as clean as what Samuel already gave.
The edition restores the divine names, modernizes the English, adds the
Nazarite commentary, and presents the whole as a reading volume for the
awakening remnant. The underlying translation is Samuel's. The honor is
his.

Why the Restoration Scope Was Limited

A reader coming from some Hebrew Roots or Sacred Name traditions will
notice that this edition restores only divine names and a specific set
of covenant people-names. The patriarchs appear in their familiar
English forms — Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Joseph — not in their
Hebrew transliterations Avraham, Yitschaq, Ya'aqov, Mosheh, Yosef.
Cities appear in their familiar forms — Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Hebron —
not Yerushalayim, Beit-Lechem, Chevron. The apostle appears as John, not
Yochanan. Why this scope, and not more?

The scope was chosen deliberately, and it matches the scope of the Book
of Enoch volume that precedes this one in the Series. Three reasons hold
it in place.

First, the retention mechanism. The restored-names signal works best
when it is sharp — when the name YAHUAH (God) and the name Yahusha
(Jesus) and the name Yashar'el (Israel) stand out against a background
of familiar English. If every patriarch's name is also transliterated —
Avraham, Yitschaq, Ya'aqov — the restoration signal dissolves into a
general Hebraization of the text. The Christian reader who opens the
page is now parsing not just the covenant name but every proper noun,
and the entry cost has risen sharply. The load-bearing restoration — the
name of YAHUAH (God), the name of Yahusha (Jesus), the name of the
covenant people — gets buried under the secondary transliterations.
Keeping the scope narrow keeps the restoration signal clear.

Second, the third-commandment weight. The names YAHUAH (God) and Yahusha
(Jesus) and Elohim (God) carry specific covenant weight that Exodus 20:7
addresses directly. The names Yashar'el (Israel), Yahudah (Judah),
Yahudim (Jews), and Yahudi (Jew / Jewish) carry the specific covenant
weight of identifying the people YAHUAH (God) formed and the particular
house that retained covenant identity through exile. These carry
commandment-level weight. The names of the patriarchs do not carry the
same weight. Abraham is a name the patriarch himself received in Hebrew
— Avraham, father of a multitude — but it is a covenant promise, not a
covenant name in the third-commandment sense. Keeping the patriarchs in
their familiar English forms does not breach any commandment.

Third, the welcome to the new reader. Many of the readers of this book
are Christians meeting these concepts for the first time, or awakening
remnant who are walking out of the institutional Church and have not yet
made friends with Hebrew transliteration. To hand them a text in which
every proper noun has been changed is to make the reading cost
prohibitive. Keeping the patriarchs and cities and apostles in their
familiar English forms honors the welcome posture that governs every
volume of the Series. The restored names that appear are load-bearing
and they are explained with parentheticals on every mention. The other
names stay as the reader already knows them.

If a later volume in the Series has a specific reason to restore a
patriarch's name or a city's name — a chapter that hinges on the meaning
of the Hebrew form, a prophetic passage whose weight turns on the
theophoric element in a name — that restoration will be made where it is
load-bearing. What will not happen is a blanket Hebraization of the
entire proper-noun inventory. The restoration is surgical. The welcome
is continuous.

Where Jasher Sits in the Restored Names Series

The Restored Names Series is a body of work. It is not a boxed set with
a predetermined number of volumes. It is the ongoing restoration of the
witnesses the horn dropped from the Christian inheritance. The first two
volumes — Enoch and Jasher — are both out. Further volumes are in
various stages of preparation; when a volume is ready the Father will
bring it forward.

This is worth stating plainly because the reader coming from the
institutional Christian world is trained to think of book series in
finite numeric terms — the Chronicles of Narnia (seven volumes), the
Lord of the Rings (three), the Complete Works of Shakespeare (a fixed
canon). The Restored Names Series is not that kind of thing. It is a
restoration project that continues for as long as there is material to
restore and a remnant to receive it. To name it by count — to say "the
n-volume Restored Names Series" — would be to impose a finality that the
Father has not imposed. The work is open-ended.

Where Jasher specifically sits: Jasher is the second volume because
Jasher carries the covenant narrative from the creation of Adam through
the death of Yehoshua (Joshua) in a single continuous thread, filling
the gaps in Genesis through the canonical Joshua with the level of
detail the inspired writers assumed their audiences already knew. Jasher
is what the author of Genesis assumed you had read. Jasher is what the
compiler of the canonical Joshua cited by name because it was already on
the shelf of every covenant-literate household. Restoring Jasher second
in the Series, after Enoch, makes the book available to the reader who
needs to understand what Genesis was resting on.

Enoch was first because Enoch is the pre-flood witness. Enoch records
what happened to the Watchers, what the antediluvian righteous saw in
their visions, what the Parables disclosed about the Elect One who was
named before the sun and the stars were created. Enoch is foundational
in a specific way: the entire seed-war architecture that runs through
the rest of the covenant scripture needs Enoch's pre-flood witness to
stand fully. Putting Enoch first, Jasher second, tracks the chronology
of the covenant story itself. The Father has always taught His remnant
in order.

What comes after Jasher the reader will meet when the Father brings it.
Some of the candidate material is well known — the book of Jubilees, 2
Esdras / 4 Ezra, the Apocalypse of Baruch. Some of it is less well
known. The Father knows which volumes are next, and when, and the Series
will bring them forward at His pace. What matters for the reader of
Jasher, right now, is that Jasher is in your hand and that Enoch is
available as a companion. That is enough. That is the reading for this
season.

You have held the history, now you hold the text. The three waves of
suppression produced the English-speaking church of the last several
centuries; the restoration is undoing what those waves did. YAHUAH (God)
gave the name. The prophets called people to lift the name. The
Masoretes and the Reformers and the rabbinic fence-builders, each in
their own way, acted to preserve the covenant community through their
specific hour and in doing so buried the name deeper than they intended.
Now the name is being lifted. That is what this edition is. That is why
the page in front of you reads YAHUAH (God), Yahusha (Jesus), Elohim
(God), Yashar'el (Israel), Yahudah (Judah), Yahudim (Jews), Ruach
HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) — every mention, every time. The name is out of
the tomb.

Now — read on. The orientation is complete. The name is on your tongue.
The book the Spirit cited by name is in front of you. Open to Chapter 1.
Let Jasher speak.

chapters.title: The Creation, the First Disobedience, and the First Blood on

verses.text: And Elohim (God) said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness, and Elohim created man in his own image.
And Elohim formed man from the ground, and he blew into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living soul endowed with speech.
And YAHUAH (the Lord) said, It is not good for man to be alone; I will make to him a helpmeet.

And YAHUAH caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept, and he took away one of his ribs, and he built flesh upon it, and formed it and brought it to Adam, and Adam awoke from his sleep, and behold a woman was standing before him.
And he said, This is a bone of my bones and it shall be called woman, for this has been taken from man; and Adam called her name Eve, for she was the mother of all living.
And Elohim blessed them and called their names Adam and Eve in the day that he created them, and YAHUAH Elohim (the Lord God) said, Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.

And YAHUAH Elohim took Adam and his wife, and he placed them in the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it; and he commanded them and said to them, From every tree of the garden you may eat, but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die.
And when Elohim had blessed and commanded them, he went from them, and Adam and his wife dwelt in the garden according to the command which YAHUAH had commanded them.
And the serpent, which Elohim had created with them in the earth, came to them to incite them to transgress the command of Elohim which he had commanded them.

And the serpent enticed and persuaded the woman to eat from the tree of knowledge, and the woman hearkened to the voice of the serpent, and she transgressed the word of Elohim, and took from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and she ate, and she took from it and gave also to her husband and he ate.
And Adam and his wife transgressed the command of Elohim which he commanded them, and Elohim knew it, and his anger was kindled against them and he cursed them.

And YAHUAH Elohim drove them that day from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from which they were taken, and they went and dwelt at the east of the garden of Eden; and Adam knew his wife Eve and she bore two sons and three daughters.

And she called the name of the first born Cain, saying, I have obtained a man from the YAHUAH, and the name of the other she called Abel, for she said, In vanity we came into the earth, and in vanity we shall be taken from it.
And the boys grew up and their father gave them a possession in the land; and Cain was a tiller of the ground, and Abel a keeper of sheep.

And it was at the expiration of a few years, that they brought an approximating offering to YAHUAH, and Cain brought from the fruit of the ground, and Abel brought from the firstlings of his flock from the fat of it, and Elohim turned and inclined to Abel and his offering, and a fire came down from YAHUAH from heaven and consumed it.

And to Cain and his offering YAHUAH did not turn, and he did not incline to it, for he had brought from the inferior fruit of the ground before YAHUAH, and Cain was jealous against his brother Abel on account of this, and he sought a pretext to slay him.

And in some time after, Cain and Abel his brother, went one day into the field to do their work; and they were both in the field, Cain tilling and ploughing his ground, and Abel feeding his flock; and the flock passed that part which Cain had ploughed in the ground, and it sorely grieved Cain on this account.
And Cain approached his brother Abel in anger, and he said to him, What is there between me and you, that you come to dwell and bring your flock to feed in my land?
And Abel answered his brother Cain and said to him, What is there between me and you, that you shall eat the flesh of my flock and clothe thyself with their wool?

And now therefore, put off the wool of my sheep with which you have clothed thyself, and recompense me for their fruit and flesh which you have eaten, and when you shall have done this, I will then go from your land as you have said?
And Cain said to his brother Abel, Surely if I slay you this day, who will require your blood from me?

And Abel answered Cain, saying, Surely Elohim who has made us in the earth, he will avenge my cause, and he will require my blood from you should you slay me, for YAHUAH is the judge and arbiter, and it is he who will requite man according to his evil, and the wicked man according to the wickedness that he may do upon earth.
And now, if you should slay me here, surely Elohim knows your secret views, and will judge you for the evil which you did declare to do to me this day.
And when Cain heard the words which Abel his brother had spoken, behold the anger of Cain was kindled against his brother Abel for declaring this thing.

And Cain hastened and rose up, and took the iron part of his ploughing instrument, with which he suddenly smote his brother and he slew him, and Cain spilt the blood of his brother Abel upon the earth, and the blood of Abel streamed upon the earth before the flock.
And after this Cain repented having slain his brother, and he was sadly grieved, and he wept over him and it vexed him exceedingly.
And Cain rose up and dug a hole in the field, wherein he put his brother’s body, and he turned the dust over it.
And YAHUAH knew what Cain had done to his brother, and YAHUAH appeared to Cain and said to him, Where is Abel your brother that was with you?

And Cain dissembled, and said, I do not know, am I my brother’s keeper? And YAHUAH said to him, What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground where you have slain him.
For you have slain your brother and have dissembled before me, and did imagine in your heart that I saw you not, nor knew all your actions.

But you did this thing and did slay your brother for naught and because he spoke rightly to you, and now, therefore, cursed be you from the ground which opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand, and wherein you did bury him.

And it shall be when you shall till it, it shall no more give you its strength as in the beginning, for thorns and thistles shall the ground produce, and you shall be moving and wandering in the earth until the day of your death.
And at that time Cain went out from the presence of YAHUAH, from the place where he was, and he went moving and wandering in the land toward the east of Eden, he and all belonging to him.
And Cain knew his wife in those days, and she conceived and bare a son, and he called his name Enoch, saying, In that time YAHUAH began to give him rest and quiet in the earth.

And at that time Cain also began to build a city: and he built the city and he called the name of the city Enoch, according to the name of his son; for in those days YAHUAH had given him rest upon the earth, and he did not move about and wander as in the beginning.

And Irad was born to Enoch, and Irad begat Mechuyael and Mechuyael begat Methusael. • • • Jasher opens not with a cosmology or a theological treatise but with an action — Elohim said. The speaking Elohim of Genesis 1 is the Expressed Word, the Formed One through whom all things were made. The Ethiopic Enoch called Him the Holy Great One who treads upon the earth. The Tanakh calls Him YAHUAH when He walks and speaks, and Elohim when His creative power is in view. Jasher uses both names in the first verse — Elohim said… Elohim created — and by the third verse is already calling Him YAHUAH. This is not two gods, and it is not a problem to be solved. It is the Formless Father expressing Himself through the Formed Word, both fully one in essence and distinguishable only in manifestation. The same Word who said Let us make man is the same Word who in John 1:14 was made flesh. Keep that identification in mind across the whole narrative — every time Jasher says YAHUAH walks, appears, speaks face to face, wrestles, eats, it is the Formed One doing the walking. Man is made endowed with speech. This is a Jasher detail Genesis does not explicitly include, and it is more than flourish. Speech is the image of YAHUAH in man. The Elohim who said made a creature who could say. Every word we speak either builds up the image or corrupts it. By verse 11 Adam has already used his speech to transgress a command — and from that point forward, every sin of the seed will have a spoken word somewhere near its center. Cain’s angry words before the killing. Lamech’s song to his wives. The builders at Babel plotting in one tongue. Abraham speaking truth to Nimrod. The contest for the seed is always in part a contest over the tongue (James 3:9–10 is not a new doctrine — it is as old as Eden). Cain’s offering was rejected not because grain was the wrong commodity (Torah later accepts grain offerings — Leviticus 2) but because the offering was inferior. Jasher names it: “he had brought from the inferior fruit of the ground.” This is the first appearance of what the New Testament writers call the way of Cain (Jude 1:11). It is not that Cain picked the wrong ritual. It is that Cain picked the cheapest version of the right ritual and expected heaven to be impressed anyway. Every subsequent generation will produce worshipers like this. They honor YAHUAH with their lips while their hearts keep back the firstfruits (Isaiah 29:13). The 1234 applies: if any reading of any text lets a person claim to know YAHUAH while holding back obedience and still be counted faithful, that reading is false. Cain’s own story proves it. The iron ploughing instrument is another Jasher detail. It tells us something about Cain that Genesis compresses. Cain was a cultivator of the ground, and his tool became his weapon. The very instrument that was supposed to bring forth food from the cursed earth became the instrument that put the first righteous blood into that same earth. There is a pattern here that repeats all through scripture: whatever a man is given for blessing becomes, in the hand of a rebellious heart, an instrument of destruction. The priesthood becomes the means of selling animal sacrifices in the temple court. The Torah becomes the means of walling out the scattered sheep. The name of the Messiah becomes the means of replacing His people. Every holy thing can be turned to an unholy use by an unregenerate heart. Abel is the first righteous man to die. He is a type of every righteous martyr who will come after him, and ultimately a type of the Messiah Himself, whose innocent blood also cried from the ground — but whose blood, Hebrews 12:24 says, speaks a better word than the blood of Abel. Abel’s blood cried for judgment. The Messiah’s blood cries for mercy on all who return. This is the pattern of the seed of promise: righteous blood will fall in every generation, and every drop of it is heard (Revelation 6:9–10). The saints of every era are united in a long cry from the ground that YAHUAH will answer on the day He treads the winepress. And it begins here. On page one. Cross-references: Genesis 1:26–27; Genesis 2:7; Genesis 3:1–24; Genesis 4:1–16; John 1:1–14; Hebrews 11:4; Hebrews 12:24; 1 John 3:12; Jude 1:11; Matthew 23:35; Revelation 6:9–11; James 3:9–10; Isaiah 29:13.

verses.text: And it was in the hundred and thirtieth year of the life of Adam upon the earth, that he again knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bare a son in his likeness and in his image, and she called his name Seth, saying, Because Elohim (God) has appointed me another seed in the place of Abel, for Cain has slain him.

And Seth lived one hundred and five years, and he begat a son; and Seth called the name of his son Enosh, saying, Because in that time the sons of men began to multiply, and to afflict their souls and hearts by transgressing and rebelling against Elohim.
And it was in the days of Enosh that the sons of men continued to rebel and transgress against Elohim, to increase the anger of YAHUAH (the Lord) against the sons of men.

And the sons of men went and they served other gods, and they forgot YAHUAH who had created them in the earth: and in those days the sons of men made images of brass and iron, wood and stone, and they bowed down and served them.

And every man made his god and they bowed down to them, and the sons of men forsook YAHUAH all the days of Enosh and his children; and the anger of YAHUAH was kindled on account of their works and abominations which they did in the earth.

And YAHUAH caused the waters of the river Gihon to overwhelm them, and he destroyed and consumed them, and he destroyed the third part of the earth, and notwithstanding this, the sons of men did not turn from their evil ways, and their hands were yet extended to do evil in the sight of YAHUAH.
And in those days there was neither sowing nor reaping in the earth; and there was no food for the sons of men and the famine was very great in those days.

And the seed which they sowed in those days in the ground became thorns, thistles and briers; for from the days of Adam was this declaration concerning the earth, of the curse of Elohim, which he cursed the earth, on account of the sin which Adam sinned before YAHUAH.
And it was when men continued to rebel and transgress against Elohim, and to corrupt their ways, that the earth also became corrupt.
And Enosh lived ninety years and he begat Cainan;

And Cainan grew up and he was forty years old, and he became wise and had knowledge and skill in all wisdom, and he reigned over all the sons of men, and he led the sons of men to wisdom and knowledge; for Cainan was a very wise man and had understanding in all wisdom, and with his wisdom he ruled over spirits and demons;
And Cainan knew by his wisdom that Elohim would destroy the sons of men for having sinned upon earth, and that YAHUAH would in the latter days bring upon them the waters of the flood.
And in those days Cainan wrote upon tablets of stone, what was to take place in time to come, and he put them in his treasures.
And Cainan reigned over the whole earth, and he turned some of the sons of men to the service of Elohim.
And when Cainan was seventy years old, he begat three sons and two daughters.

And these are the names of the children of Cainan; the name of the first born Mahlallel, the second Enan, and the third Mered, and their sisters were Adah and Zillah; these are the five children of Cainan that were born to him.
And Lamech, the son of Methusael, became related to Cainan by marriage, and he took his two daughters for his wives, and Adah conceived and bare a son to Lamech, and she called his name Jabal.
And she again conceived and bare a son, and called his name Jubal; and Zillah, her sister, was barren in those days and had no offspring.
For in those days the sons of men began to trespass against Elohim, and to transgress the commandments which he had commanded to Adam, to be fruitful and multiply in the earth.
And some of the sons of men caused their wives to drink a draught that would render them barren, in order that they might retain their figures and by which their beautiful appearance might not fade.
And when the sons of men caused some of their wives to drink, Zillah drank with them.
And the child-bearing women appeared abominable in the sight of their husbands as widows, whilst their husbands lived, for to the barren ones only they were attached.
And in the end of days and years, when Zillah became old, YAHUAH opened her womb.
And she conceived and bare a son and she called his name Tubal Cain, saying, After I had withered away have I obtained him from the El Shaddai (Almighty God).
And she conceived again and bare a daughter, and she called her name Naamah, for she said, After I had withered away have I obtained pleasure and delight.
