Dost you not know, or have you not heard, that this evil which you do, our ancestors sinned in it in days of old, and the eternal Elohim brought the waters of the flood upon them and destroyed them all, and also destroyed the whole earth on their account? And will you and your people rise up now and do like to this work, in order to bring down the anger of the YAHUAH Elohim (Lord God) of the universe, and to bring evil upon you and the whole earth?
Now therefore put away this evil deed which you do, and serve the Elohim of the universe, as your soul is in his hands, and then it will be well with you.

And if your wicked heart will not hearken to my words to cause you to forsake your evil ways, and to serve the eternal Elohim, then will you die in shame in the latter days, you, your people and all who are connected with you, hearing your words or walking in your evil ways.

And when Abram had ceased speaking before the king and princes, Abram lifted up his eyes to the heavens, and he said, YAHUAH sees all the wicked, and he will judge them. « • • • Jasher 11 is where Abram becomes Abram the idol-breaker. He enters his father’s house and sees twelve large wooden gods and a chamber full of smaller ones. He challenges them with food. They do not eat. He breaks them. He puts the hatchet in the hand of the largest one. When his father confronts him, he mocks the idols to his father’s face by blaming the largest idol — and in so doing he forces his father to confess, aloud, that the idols have no power. This is a model for every faithful son who grows up inside a religious system built on idols. Abram’s father Terah was not a wicked man in the simple sense. He was a sincere man inside a deeply compromised system. He was Nimrod’s chief of staff. He had twelve idols in his house, one for each month. He performed the rites. He taught his children. And his son looked past the whole system and asked the only question that mattered: where is the Elohim who actually made heaven and earth? If these carved things did not make anything, who did? That is the awakening question. It is the question that started the whole covenant line. It is the question that is waking up Christians today who have begun to ask “who actually gave us Sunday and Christmas and Easter and the trinity formula — and does any of this look like what the Torah actually says?” It is the question that is waking up Torah observant believers who have begun to ask “who taught me that Paul cancels the Sabbath, and does Paul actually say that when I read him in context?” Every awakening in scripture begins with a son of Terah refusing to bow to the twelve idols in his father’s house. Notice something carefully. Abram does not disown his father. He does not attack his father personally. He argues. He reasons. He weeps. He pleads. “Now therefore my father refrain from this, and bring not evil upon your soul and the souls of your household” (verse 48). This is the posture — the posture of the awakened one toward those still inside the system. They are not the enemy. They are victims of an inherited deception. Abram loved Terah. Abram grieved over Terah’s idolatry. Abram wanted Terah out. This is exactly the posture the remnant in our day must carry toward Christian parents, Jewish grandparents, Messianic mentors, pastor friends, pew-mates. Not contempt — covenant grief. Not superiority — the concern of a son for a father still sitting in a room full of images. And then the confrontation with Nimrod in verses 52–61. Abram stands before the most powerful king on the earth and says (verse 57), “I thought you would teach your servants the upright way, but you have not done this, but have filled the whole earth with your sins.” That is the voice of a prophet. That is the voice of a man who is not afraid of the throne. That is a line that could be spoken today to every teacher, every celebrity, every technocrat, every religious hierarch who has been given a platform and has used it to lead the multitudes astray. You were given a platform to teach the upright way. You did not. Abram is the pattern of Elijah before Ahab, of John the Baptist before Herod, of Peter and John before the Sanhedrin, of YAHUSHA before Pilate. Truth stands and speaks in the king’s court, and the king is judged. But notice the gentleness even in the confrontation. Abram does not curse Nimrod personally. He warns him. He lays out the alternative. He ends with “Now therefore put away this evil deed which you do, and serve the Elohim of the universe… it will be well with you” (verse 59). Even to Nimrod. Even to Nimrod, there is an invitation to come home. Abram is not writing off Nimrod’s soul. He is giving him a chance. The invitation is always open, until it is not. This is the posture of the true witness: fearless, direct, scriptural — and still merciful, still calling the deceived home. The awakening son inside a Nimrodic system A final word on Abram smashing the idols in his father's house, because the posture of that scene is the posture this commentary has been pressing from its opening page. Abram did not hate his father. Abram did not denounce his father's generation. Abram did not stand in the marketplace with a sign listing Terah's sins. He argued, he reasoned, he mocked the idols until his father was forced to name their weakness aloud, and he wept over his father's unwillingness to hear. "Now therefore my father refrain from this, and bring not evil upon your soul and the souls of your household" (Jasher 11:48). That is the awakening son's prayer over an idolater father. Not contempt. Covenant grief. This distinction is the whole difference between the witness Yahuah (God) asked Abram to be and the witness the flesh would have made him into. The flesh, awakened to how deep Terah's system ran, would have attacked Terah. It would have severed the relationship, disowned the father, publicly shamed the household, and gone on with the march of truth unencumbered by family ties. That is not Abram. Abram stayed. Abram pleaded. Abram went with Terah when Terah finally left Ur and walked as far as Haran with his father before Yahuah (God) called him farther. Terah died in Haran still holding a compromise, and Abram buried him. This is the awakening son's task through every generation. Plead. Stay. Weep. Go as far with your father as your father can go, and then go farther alone when you must. Never despise the man who loved you even while he served the twelve carved images in the corner of his house. The Catholic grandfather who hung the crucifix he believed would bless the home. The Protestant mother who kept the Sunday fast and sent her children to the church picnic every Easter. The Hebrew roots teacher who assembled a library of Torah scholarship and raised his daughters to love the feasts and never once felt that his Galatians reading was the horn's reading. The imam who memorized the Quran in his youth and believes he is serving the Elohim (God) of Abraham. Every one of these is a Terah somewhere. Every one of these is loved by an awakening son or daughter whose eyes have been opened by the Father to the deeper architecture. The awakening son does not attack the father. The awakening son pleads with the father. The awakening son names the idols for what they are without calling the father an idolater — because the architecture taught the father to call the idols by the name of Yahuah (God), and the father did what he was taught. And Yahuah (God) knew Terah. The same Yahuah (God) who called Abram out of Ur knew the man Abram had to leave. The Father does not lose sight of the father. Terah is named in Genesis 11. Terah is named in the Acts 7 sermon of Stephen. Terah is in the ledger. The Father remembers him. Whatever mercy the Father has for Terah at the judgment is the Father's to give. The son's task was to plead while pleading was possible, to go farther when going farther was required, and to trust that the Father's dealings with the father are not frustrated by the son's departure from the father's house. Joshua 24:2 says "Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor: and they served other gods." Stephen in Acts 7 confirms the same thing. And yet the father of the faithful still went back into the ledger with a son whose prayers had included him to the end. The awakening reader who is carrying grief over parents, grandparents, siblings, congregations of origin — the grief is honored. The grief is right. The pleading is to continue as long as the pleading is possible. The trust is that the Father who called you out of that house is the Father who is still dealing with everyone in it. Your job is not to save them. Your job is to walk the walk in front of them, to name the lies without naming them as liars, to love them without capitulating to the system they serve, and to let the Shepherd call whom He will call. Many more are being drawn out than any of us yet see. The pleading matters. Keep pleading. Cross-references: Genesis 26:5; Psalm 115:4–8; Isaiah 44:9–20; Jeremiah 10:1–16; Acts 7:2–3; Joshua 24:2; Hebrews 11:8; Revelation 18:4 (“come out of her, my people”); 2 Corinthians 6:14–18; James 4:4; Joshua 24:2–3; Acts 7:2–4; Genesis 11:27–32; Genesis 12:1–5; Matthew 10:34–39; Luke 14:26 (properly read in its family-preference context, not as actual hatred); 1 Corinthians 7:12–16; 2 Corinthians 6:14–18 (read as come-out-of-Babylon's-system, not estrangement-from-loved-ones).

chapters.title: The Furnace, the Dream, and the Flight

verses.text: And when the king heard the words of Abram he ordered him to be put into prison; and Abram was ten days in prison.

And at the end of those days the king ordered that all the kings, princes and governors of different provinces and the sages should come before him, and they sat before him, and Abram was still in the house of confinement.

And the king said to the princes and sages, Have you heard what Abram, the son of Terah, has done to his father? Thus has he done to him, and I ordered him to be brought before me, and thus has he spoken; his heart did not misgive him, neither did he stir in my presence, and behold now he is confined in the prison.
And therefore decide what judgment is due to this man who reviled the king; who spoke and did all the things that you heard.

And they all answered the king saying, The man who reviles the king should be hanged upon a tree; but having done all the things that he said, and having despised our gods, he must therefore be burned to death, for this is the law in this matter.

If it pleases the king to do this, let him order his servants to kindle a fire both night and day in your brick furnace, and then we will cast this man into it. And the king did so, and he commanded his servants that they should prepare a fire for three days and three nights in the king’s furnace, that is in Casdim; and the king ordered them to take Abram from prison and bring him out to be burned.
And all the king’s servants, princes, lords, governors, and judges, and all the inhabitants of the land, about nine hundred thousand men, stood opposite the furnace to see Abram.

And all the women and little ones crowded upon the roofs and towers to see what was doing with Abram, and they all stood together at a distance; and there was not a man left that did not come on that day to behold the scene.

And when Abram was come, the conjurors of the king and the sages saw Abram, and they cried out to the king, saying, Our sovereign lord, surely this is the man whom we know to have been the child at whose birth the great star swallowed the four stars, which we declared to the king now fifty years since.
And behold now his father has also transgressed your commands, and mocked you by bringing you another child, which you did kill.
And when the king heard their words, he was exceedingly wroth, and he ordered Terah to be brought before him.
And the king said, Have you heard what the conjurors have spoken? Now tell me truly, how did you; and if you shall speak truth you shall be acquitted.

And seeing that the king’s anger was so much kindled, Terah said to the king, My Lord and king, you have heard the truth, and what the sages have spoken is right. And the king said, How could you do this thing, to transgress my orders and to give me a child that you did not beget, and to take value for him?
And Terah answered the king, Because my tender feelings were excited for my son, at that time, and I took a son of my handmaid, and I brought him to the king.
And the king said Who advised you to this? Tell me, do not hide aught from me, and then you shall not die.

And Terah was greatly terrified in the king’s presence, and he said to the king, It was Haran my eldest son who advised me to this; and Haran was in those days that Abram was born, two and thirty years old.

But Haran did not advise his father to anything, for Terah said this to the king in order to deliver his soul from the king, for he feared greatly; and the king said to Terah, Haran your son who advised you to this shall die through fire with Abram; for the sentence of death is upon him for having rebelled against the king’s desire in doing this thing.
And Haran at that time felt inclined to follow the ways of Abram, but he kept it within himself.

And Haran said in his heart, Behold now the king has seized Abram on account of these things which Abram did, and it shall come to pass, that if Abram prevail over the king I will follow him, but if the king prevail I will go after the king.
And when Terah had spoken this to the king concerning Haran his son, the king ordered Haran to be seized with Abram.

And they brought them both, Abram and Haran his brother, to cast them into the fire; and all the inhabitants of the land and the king’s servants and princes and all the women and little ones were there, standing that day over them.
And the king’s servants took Abram and his brother, and they stripped them of all their clothes excepting their lower garments which were upon them.
And they bound their hands and feet with linen cords, and the servants of the king lifted them up and cast them both into the furnace.
And YAHUAH (the Lord) loved Abram and he had compassion over him, and YAHUAH came down and delivered Abram from the fire and he was not burned.
But all the cords with which they bound him were burned, while Abram remained and walked about in the fire.

And Haran died when they had cast him into the fire, and he was burned to ashes, for his heart was not perfect with YAHUAH; and those men who cast him into the fire, the flame of the fire spread over them, and they were burned, and twelve men of them died.

And Abram walked in the midst of the fire three days and three nights, and all the servants of the king saw him walking in the fire, and they came and told the king, saying, Behold we have seen Abram walking about in the midst of the fire, and even the lower garments which are upon him are not burned, but the cord with which he was bound is burned.

And when the king heard their words his heart fainted and he would not believe them; so he sent other faithful princes to see this matter, and they went and saw it and told it to the king; and the king rose to go and see it, and he saw Abram walking to and fro in the midst of the fire, and he saw Haran’s body burned, and the king wondered greatly.

And the king ordered Abram to be taken out from the fire; and his servants approached to take him out and they could not, for the fire was round about and the flame ascending toward them from the furnace.
And the king’s servants fled from it, and the king rebuked them, saying, Make haste and bring Abram out of the fire that you shall not die.
And the servants of the king again approached to bring Abram out, and the flames came upon them and burned their faces so that eight of them died.

And when the king saw that his servants could not approach the fire lest they should be burned, the king called to Abram, O servant of the Elohim (God) who is in heaven, go forth from amidst the fire and come here before me; and Abram hearkened to the voice of the king, and he went forth from the fire and came and stood before the king.
And when Abram came out the king and all his servants saw Abram coming before the king, with his lower garments upon him, for they were not burned, but the cord with which he was bound was burned.
And the king said to Abram, How is it that you were not burned in the fire?
And Abram said to the king, The Elohim of heaven in whom I trust and who has all in his power, he delivered me from the fire into which you did cast me.
And Haran the brother of Abram was burned to ashes, and they sought for his body, and they found it consumed.

And Haran was eighty-two years old when he died in the fire of Casdim. And the king, princes, and inhabitants of the land, seeing that Abram was delivered from the fire, they came and bowed down to Abram.

And Abram said to them, Do not bow down to me, but bow down to the Elohim of the world who made you, and serve him, and go in his ways for it is he who delivered me from out of this fire, and it is he who created the souls and spirits of all men, and formed man in his mother’s womb, and brought him forth into the world, and it is he who will deliver those who trust in him from all pain.

And this thing seemed very wonderful in the eyes of the king and princes, that Abram was saved from the fire and that Haran was burned; and the king gave Abram many presents and he gave him his two head servants from the king’s house; the name of one was Oni and the name of the other was Eliezer.
And all the kings, princes and servants gave Abram many gifts of silver and gold and pearl, and the king and his princes sent him away, and he went in peace.
And Abram went forth from the king in peace, and many of the king’s servants followed him, and about three hundred men joined him.

And Abram returned on that day and went to his father’s house, he and the men that followed him, and Abram served YAHUAH his Elohim (the Lord his God) all the days of his life, and he walked in his ways and followed his law.
And from that day forward Abram inclined the hearts of the sons of men to serve YAHUAH.

And at that time Nahor and Abram took to themselves wives, the daughters of their brother Haran; the wife of Nahor was Milca and the name of Abram’s wife was Sarai. And Sarai, wife of Abram, was barren; she had no offspring in those days.

And at the expiration of two years from Abram’s going out of the fire, that is in the fifty-second year of his life, behold king Nimrod sat in Babel upon the throne, and the king fell asleep and dreamed that he was standing with his troops and hosts in a valley opposite the king’s furnace.

And he lifted up his eyes and saw a man in the likeness of Abram coming forth from the furnace, and that he came and stood before the king with his drawn sword, and then sprang to the king with his sword, when the king fled from the man, for he was afraid; and while he was running, the man threw an egg upon the king’s head, and the egg became a great river.
And the king dreamed that all his troops sank in that river and died, and the king took flight with three men who were before him and he escaped.
And the king looked at these men and they were clothed in princely dresses as the garments of kings, and had the appearance and majesty of kings.

And while they were running, the river again turned to an egg before the king, and there came forth from the egg a young bird which came before the king, and flew at his head and plucked out the king’s eye.
And the king was grieved at the sight, and he awoke out of his sleep and his spirit was agitated; and he felt a great terror.
And in the morning the king rose from his couch in fear, and he ordered all the wise men and magicians to come before him, when the king related his dream to them.

And a wise servant of the king, whose name was Anuki, answered the king, saying, This is nothing else but the evil of Abram and his seed which will spring up against my Lord and king in the latter days.
And behold the day will come when Abram and his seed and the children of his household will war with my king, and they will smite all the king’s hosts and his troops.

And as to what you have said concerning three men which you did see like to thyself, and which did escape, this means that only you will escape with three kings from the kings of the earth who will be with you in battle.

And that which you saw of the river which turned to an egg as at first, and the young bird plucking out your eye, this means nothing else but the seed of Abram which will slay the king in latter days.
This is my king’s dream, and this is its interpretation, and the dream is true, and the interpretation which your servant has given you is right.

Now therefore my king, surely you know that it is now fifty-two years since your sages saw this at the birth of Abram, and if my king will suffer Abram to live in the earth it will be to the injury of my Lord and king, for all the days that Abram lives neither you nor your kingdom will be established, for this was known formerly at his birth; and why will not my king slay him, that his evil may be kept from you in latter days?
And Nimrod hearkened to the voice of Anuki, and he sent some of his servants in secret to go and seize Abram, and bring him before the king to suffer death.

And Eliezer, Abram’s servant whom the king had given him, was at that time in the presence of the king, and he heard what Anuki had advised the king, and what the king had said to cause Abram’s death.

And Eliezer said to Abram, Hasten, rise up and save your soul, that you may not die through the hands of the king, for thus did he see in a dream concerning you, and thus did Anuki interpret it, and thus also did Anuki advise the king concerning you.

And Abram hearkened to the voice of Eliezer, and Abram hastened and ran for safety to the house of Noah and his son Shem, and he concealed himself there and found a place of safety; and the king’s servants came to Abram’s house to seek him, but they could not find him, and they searched through out the country and he was not to be found, and they went and searched in every direction and he was not to be met with.

And when the king’s servants could not find Abram they returned to the king, but the king’s anger against Abram was stilled, as they did not find him, and the king drove from his mind this matter concerning Abram.

And Abram was concealed in Noah’s house for one month, until the king had forgotten this matter, but Abram was still afraid of the king; and Terah came to see Abram his son secretly in the house of Noah, and Terah was very great in the eyes of the king.
And Abram said to his father, Dost you not know that the king thinks to slay me, and to annihilate my name from the earth by the advice of his wicked counsellors?
Now whom have you here and what have you in this land? Arise, let us go together to the land of Canaan, that we may be delivered from his hand, lest you perish also through him in the latter days.
Dost you not know or have you not heard, that it is not through love that Nimrod gives you all this honor, but it is only for his benefit that he bestows all this good upon you?
And if he do to you greater good than this, surely these are only vanities of the world, for wealth and riches cannot avail in the day of wrath and anger.

Now therefore hearken to my voice, and let us arise and go to the land of Canaan, out of the reach of injury from Nimrod; and serve you YAHUAH who created you in the earth and it will be well with you; and cast away all the vain things which you pursue.
And Abram ceased to speak, when Noah and his son Shem answered Terah, saying, True is the word which Abram has said to you.

And Terah hearkened to the voice of his son Abram, and Terah did all that Abram said, for this was from YAHUAH, that the king should not cause Abram’s death. « • • • Chapter 12 is the famous passage of Abram in the fiery furnace — the first martyrdom-attempt in scripture, the first time a king of the earth passed an explicit sentence of death by fire on a worshiper of YAHUAH. And it is not an accident that the pattern repeats in Daniel 3 with Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-Nego in Babylon. What Abram endured in Babel, his descendants would one day endure back in Babel. The pattern is fixed: the servants of the covenant God are cast into the fire by the kings of the earth, and the covenant God walks with them in the flames. The fourth man in the fire of Daniel 3 is the same one who walked with Abram in the furnace of Casdim. He is the pre-incarnate YAHUSHA, the Expressed Word, the one who treads the earth in every age on behalf of His people. Notice verse 26: Haran died when they had cast him into the fire, and he was burned to ashes, for his heart was not perfect with YAHUAH. Abram’s brother went into the same furnace and did not come out. Two men, same fire, different outcome — because one’s heart was perfect with YAHUAH and the other’s was not. This is worth sitting with. It is easy to assume that whoever is standing next to a believer during the trial will share the believer’s deliverance. Jasher says no. The fire tests each heart. Haran had hedged — “if Abram prevails over the king, I will follow him; if the king prevails, I will go after the king” (verse 19). The double-minded heart is not preserved in the fire. James 1:6–8 says the same thing: “a double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.” Only the heart that has fully committed to YAHUAH — not the hedged heart, not the waiting-to-see heart, not the both-sides heart — comes through the furnace alive. The awakening remnant is being called to this kind of undivided heart. The days are coming — they may already be here — when neutrality will not be an option. The faithful and the hedged will both be in the fire. Only the faithful will come out. Verses 45–56 give us Nimrod’s dream and its interpretation. Nimrod dreams that a man like Abram comes out of the furnace with a sword and puts his troops into a river. The interpretation: Abram’s seed will destroy Nimrod’s kingdom, and only three kings will escape with him. This is the first of many royal dreams in scripture — Pharaoh’s seven cows, Nebuchadnezzar’s statue, Belshazzar’s writing, Herod’s dream about the wise men. Every great anti-covenant king is at some point given a dream that tells him his kingdom will fall to the covenant seed. Every one of them receives the warning. Every one of them ignores it or fights it. None of them succeed. Nimrod’s response — to send secret assassins — is defeated by a man named Eliezer, Abram’s own servant, who had once been Nimrod’s servant. Eliezer overhears the plot and warns Abram, who flees to the house of Noah and Shem. This is a detail worth noting: Abram was preserved by a servant who had defected from Nimrod’s system. The faithful witness in Nimrod’s court. Obadiah in Ahab’s house. Daniel in Nebuchadnezzar’s court. There is always a hidden Eliezer in the enemy’s system. There is always someone inside the system who hears what is said and protects the saints. Never assume that the system is solid on the inside. YAHUAH has His people there too. The flight of Abram to the house of Noah and Shem for one full month (verse 63), followed by the speech in which Abram urges his father to come out of Nimrod’s kingdom entirely (verses 64–68), is the first explicit “come out from among them” exhortation in scripture. “Dost you not know that the king thinks to slay me… Arise, let us go together to the land of Canaan, that we may be delivered from his hand.” Noah and Shem endorse the exhortation. Terah, finally, listens. The whole family prepares to leave Babylon. The gospel of the remnant has always been this gospel. Come out of her, my people. Every covenant awakening in scripture has as its first action a physical or spiritual exodus from Babylon. Abram comes out of Ur. Israel comes out of Egypt. Judah comes out of Babylon under Zerubbabel. The disciples come out of temple Judaism. The early saints come out of pagan Rome. The Reformation comes out of corrupted Catholicism. The Restoration movements come out of dead Protestantism. And the last call of Revelation 18 is the same call: “Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues” (Revelation 18:4). The pattern started with Abram. It will complete with the last-days remnant. It is the same pattern, the same voice, the same Shepherd. The fourth man in the furnace and the Come-out-of-her thread One more pattern to name before we leave the Ur narrative. The furnace at Casdim is the first cast-into-the-fire episode in covenant history, and it opens a thread that runs all the way to Revelation 20. Every time a covenant-hostile king has cast a witness of Yahuah (God) into a fire, the Formed One has walked in that fire with the witness. Jasher calls it "Yahuah (the Lord) came down and delivered Abram from the fire." The text does not say Yahuah (God) sent an angel. The text says Yahuah (God) came down — the same verb used at Babel, the same verb used at Sinai, the same verb used when the Messiah (Christ) stepped into Galilean flesh. The Formed of the Formless descends into the furnace of the witness. This is a specific grammar, and it is maintained across the whole canon. The same Formed One is the Fourth Man in the furnace of Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 3:25: "And the form of the fourth is like the Son of Elohim (God)." Nebuchadnezzar did not know whom he was seeing, but he knew that the figure in the fire was of a kind he had not ordered thrown in. The Fourth Man is the same one who came down at Casdim. The same one who walked with Enoch. The same one who ate bread at Mamre. The same one who sat on the crystal throne Ezekiel saw. The same one who addressed John in Revelation 1 in a voice that sounded as many waters. Every age has a furnace. Every furnace has the same Visitor. Do not import Nicene grammar into this. The Fourth Man in the fire is not the second person of a philosophical triad. He is the Expressed Word, the visible Form of the Formless, the Elohim (God) who walks. The Father — the Formless from whom the Formed proceeds — has never been visible, because He is beyond the category of visibility. "No man hath seen Elohim (God) at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him" (John 1:18). The Son is the declaration. The Father is the source of the declaration. When the Son walks into a fire, the Formless is declaring Himself into that specific furnace — and the witness is not alone. The declaration has come down with the declaration's object. This is worth saying because the institutional church has so thoroughly colonized the grammar of the Son's divinity with Greek philosophical vocabulary that many awakening readers, upon encountering the Messiah's (Christ's) deity, assume they must speak Nicene grammar to affirm it. They must not. The Christology of the prophets is not the Christology of the creeds. The prophets saw the throne and the one on it (Isaiah 6:1; Ezekiel 1:26–28; Daniel 7:9; Revelation 4:2–3). The one on the throne is the Formed of the Formless. The Father is the Formless from whom the Formed proceeds. The Shema holds because the Elohim (God) on the throne and the Formless behind the throne are not two gods but one Elohim (God) in two modes. Yahusha (Jesus) is the Son. The Father has a Son because the Formless has a Form — the one consecration of Himself into a voice that speaks, a face that is seen, a Word through which all things were made. Deny the Son's divinity to protect the Father's uniqueness and you have torn the declaration off the Formless. Insist on Greek metaphysics to defend the Son's divinity and you have imported a grammar the prophets did not use. The honest reading is Yoshi's reading. The Formed of the Formless. One Elohim (God) in two modes. A Son who is God, and a Father who is not another god because the Father is beyond the category being. The verse that closes this chapter — Abram's flight to the house of Noah and Shem, and then his urging Terah and the household to leave Ur entirely — is the first Come out of her, My people in scripture. Every covenant movement is at its root this movement. Abram came out of Ur. Yashar'el (Israel) came out of Egypt. Yahudah (Judah) came out of Babylon. The disciples came out of a second-temple Yahudaism (Judaism) that had rejected its own Messiah (Christ). The early saints came out of Rome's civic religion. The Reformation came out of corrupted institutional Catholicism. The Restoration movements came out of dead Protestantism. The Hebrew roots movement of the last half-century came out of the dead Sabbath and the dead feasts of the institutional church. The awakening of this moment is coming out of all of it — not in defiance of the sincere believers still inside any of those houses, but in the simple obedience of the call: "Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues" (Revelation 18:4). The her in Revelation 18 is Babylon the great — the final rebuilt tower, the composite beast, the last Babel. She includes inside her costume every system that has made merchandise of the Word and the souls of men. She includes the institutional church trading in indulgences and celebrity pastors. She includes the Judaic tradition that has walled out the regathering of its own brothers. She includes the Hebrew roots teachers who have turned Torah into a pedigree ladder. She includes every imam whose loyalty is to a successor claim that re-writes the covenant promise around Ishmael. Every one of these systems is inside her. Every one of their inhabitants is loved by the Father who is still calling. The call of Revelation 18 is the same call Abram heard in Jasher 12. Come out. Not in fear. In obedience. Not with contempt for the ones you love still inside. With pleading for them, and with the faith that pleads. The Shepherd has pulled His people out of every Babel that has ever risen. The last Babel is no different. The walking has already begun. The door is still open. The Formed One walks in the fire of the last furnace just as He walked in the first. The ones who hear the call and walk out will find the same Visitor waiting on the other side of the wall of the city He has destined to fall. Cross-references: Daniel 3:1–30; 1 Peter 1:6–7; James 1:5–8; Revelation 18:1–24; Genesis 12:1–5; Hebrews 11:8; 2 Corinthians 6:17; Acts 7:2–4; Isaiah 52:11; Jeremiah 51:6, 45; Daniel 3:24–25; John 1:18; Exodus 3:6–14; Matthew 27:51 (temple veil rent — the Formed One made accessible); Revelation 1:8, 1:13–18; Revelation 18:4; Revelation 19:11–16; Hebrews 1:1–3; Colossians 1:15–19; 1 Timothy 6:15–16.

chapters.title: The Call, the Covenant, and the Land

verses.text: And Terah took his son Abram and his grandson Lot, the son of Haran, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, the wife of his son Abram, and all the souls of his household and went with them from Ur Casdim to go to the land of Canaan. And when they came as far as the land of Haran they remained there, for it was exceedingly good land for pasture, and of sufficient extent for those who accompanied them.

And the people of the land of Haran saw that Abram was good and upright with Elohim (God) and men, and that YAHUAH his Elohim (the Lord his God) was with him, and some of the people of the land of Haran came and joined Abram, and he taught them the instruction of YAHUAH (the Lord) and his ways; and these men remained with Abram in his house and they adhered to him.

And Abram remained in the land three years, and at the expiration of three years YAHUAH appeared to Abram and said to him; I am YAHUAH who brought you forth from Ur Casdim, and delivered you from the hands of all your enemies.

And now therefore if you will hearken to my voice and keep my commandments, my statutes and my laws, then will I cause your enemies to fall before you, and I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven, and I will send my blessing upon all the works of your hands, and you shall lack nothing.

Arise now, take your wife and all belonging to you and go to the land of Canaan and remain there, and I will there be to you for a Elohim, and I will bless you. And Abram rose and took his wife and all belonging to him, and he went to the land of Canaan as YAHUAH had told him; and Abram was fifty years old when he went from Haran.
And Abram came to the land of Canaan and dwelt in the midst of the city, and he there pitched his tent amongst the children of Canaan, inhabitants of the land.

And YAHUAH appeared to Abram when he came to the land of Canaan, and said to him, This is the land which I gave to you and to your seed after you forever, and I will make your seed like the stars of heaven, and I will give to your seed for an inheritance all the lands which you see.
And Abram built an altar in the place where Elohim had spoken to him, and Abram there called upon the name of YAHUAH.

At that time, at the end of three years of Abram’s dwelling in the land of Canaan, in that year Noah died, which was the fifty-eighth year of the life of Abram; and all the days that Noah lived were nine hundred and fifty years and he died.

And Abram dwelt in the land of Canaan, he, his wife, and all belonging to him, and all those that accompanied him, together with those that joined him from the people of the land; but Nahor, Abram’s brother, and Terah his father, and Lot the son of Haran and all belonging to them dwelt in Haran.

In the fifth year of Abram’s dwelling in the land of Canaan the people of Sodom and Gomorrah and all the cities of the plain revolted from the power of Chedorlaomer, king of Elam; for all the kings of the cities of the plain had served Chedorlaomer for twelve years, and given him a yearly tax, but in those days in the thirteenth year, they rebelled against him.

And in the tenth year of Abram’s dwelling in the land of Canaan there was war between Nimrod king of Shinar and Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Nimrod came to fight with Chedorlaomer and to subdue him.

For Chedorlaomer was at that time one of the princes of the hosts of Nimrod, and when all the people at the tower were dispersed and those that remained were also scattered upon the face of the earth, Chedorlaomer went to the land of Elam and reigned over it and rebelled against his Lord.

And in those days when Nimrod saw that the cities of the plain had rebelled, he came with pride and anger to war with Chedorlaomer, and Nimrod assembled all his princes and subjects, about seven hundred thousand men, and went against Chedorlaomer, and Chedorlaomer went out to meet him with five thousand men, and they prepared for battle in the valley of Babel which is between Elam and Shinar.

And all those kings fought there, and Nimrod and his people were smitten before the people of Chedorlaomer, and there fell from Nimrod’s men about six hundred thousand, and Mardon the king’s son fell amongst them.

And Nimrod fled and returned in shame and disgrace to his land, and he was under subjection to Chedorlaomer for a long time, and Chedorlaomer returned to his land and sent princes of his host to the kings that dwelt around him, to Arioch king of Elasar, and to Tidal king of Goyim, and made a covenant with them, and they were all obedient to his commands.

And it was in the fifteenth year of Abram’s dwelling in the land of Canaan, which is the seventieth year of the life of Abram, and YAHUAH appeared to Abram in that year and he said to him, I am YAHUAH who brought you out from Ur Casdim to give you this land for an inheritance.
Now therefore walk before me and be perfect and keep my commands, for to you and to your seed I will give this land for an inheritance, from the river Mitzraim to the great river Euphrates.

And you shall come to your fathers in peace and in good age, and the fourth generation shall return here in this land and shall inherit it forever; and Abram built an altar, and he called upon the name of YAHUAH who appeared to him, and he brought up sacrifices upon the altar to YAHUAH.

At that time Abram returned and went to Haran to see his father and mother, and his father’s household, and Abram and his wife and all belonging to him returned to Haran, and Abram dwelt in Haran five years.
And many of the people of Haran, about seventy-two men, followed Abram and Abram taught them the instruction of YAHUAH and his ways, and he taught them to know YAHUAH.
In those days YAHUAH appeared to Abram in Haran, and he said to him, Behold, I spoke to you these twenty years back saying,

Go forth from your land, from your birth-place and from your father’s house, to the land which I have shown you to give it to you and to your children, for there in that land will I bless you, and make you a great nation, and make your name great, and in you shall the families of the earth be blessed.

Now therefore arise, go forth from this place, you, your wife, and all belonging to you, also every one born in your house and all the souls you have made in Haran, and bring them out with you from here, and rise to return to the land of Canaan.
And Abram arose and took his wife Sarai and all belonging to him and all that were born to him in his house and the souls which they had made in Haran, and they came out to go to the land of Canaan.

And Abram went and returned to the land of Canaan, according to the word of YAHUAH. And Lot the son of his brother Haran went with him, and Abram was seventy-five years old when he went forth from Haran to return to the land of Canaan.

And he came to the land of Canaan according to the word of YAHUAH to Abram, and he pitched his tent and he dwelt in the plain of Mamre, and with him was Lot his brother’s son, and all belonging to him.

And YAHUAH again appeared to Abram and said, To your seed will I give this land; and he there built an altar to YAHUAH who appeared to him, which is still to this day in the plains of Mamre. « • • • The covenant call to Abram in Jasher 13:3–5 is framed in unmistakably Torah language: “hearken to my voice and keep my commandments, my statutes and my laws.” This is the language of Sinai, spoken to Abram four hundred years before Sinai. This is the same language that will be used in Genesis 26:5 to describe why YAHUAH blessed Isaac: “because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.” There was a Torah before Sinai. It was oral. It was carried by the patriarchs. Abraham knew it. Isaac knew it. Jacob knew it. Joseph knew it. The written codification at Sinai was a gift to a people Israel had just become. But the commandments themselves are as old as Abram’s call. This is a total refutation of the antinomian reading of Paul. Paul, in Galatians, is not contrasting “faith-era Abraham” with “law-era Moses.” He is contrasting the true covenant — faith that issues in obedience — with the false covenant — circumcision-as-entry-ticket-without-heart. Paul quotes Genesis 15:6 (Abraham believed, and it was counted to him for righteousness) not to prove that Abraham never kept commandments, but to prove that Abraham’s faith came first and his commandment-keeping flowed out of it. Jasher confirms this reading perfectly. Abram first reasoned his way to YAHUAH (chapter 9). Then YAHUAH appeared and made covenant (chapter 13 here). Then obedience followed. Faith, then obedience. Both together. Never one without the other. The 1234 of truth again: “He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him.” Applying the Methodological Sequence for Reading Paul to Galatians 3:16 (“he saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is the Messiah”): Step one — what is Paul drawing from? Paul is quoting Genesis 12:7, 13:15, 17:7, 24:7 — passages where YAHUAH promises the land to Abraham’s seed. Paul notes that the Hebrew word zera (seed) can be singular or collective, and applies it singularly to the Messiah as the ultimate Heir. Step two — what is Paul arguing against? The Judaizers in Galatia were teaching that Gentile believers had to undergo physical circumcision to be counted as heirs of Abraham. Paul’s response is that Abraham’s inheritance flows first to the Messiah (the singular zera) and then to all who are in the Messiah by faith — a faith which, as Abraham’s own example shows, produces obedience. Paul is not denying that Abraham obeyed; he is denying that Gentile believers need to become ethnic Jews to share in the promise. Read this way, Galatians 3 is not a cancellation of Torah. It is a defense of the correct order: faith first, obedience second, never reversed. Verse 7 — “This is the land which I gave to you and to your seed after you forever” — is one of the most important covenant land-promises in scripture. Forever means forever. The land of Israel is deeded to the seed of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in perpetuity. No supersessionist theology, Christian or otherwise, can wash that “forever” away. Jasher preserves the covenant’s enduring weight. This is not land given to anyone who happens to identify with the covenant. It is land given to a specific seed. The scattered twelve tribes are the inheritors. Every prophecy of the regathering — Ezekiel 36, 37, Isaiah 11, Jeremiah 31 — is a prophecy about the return of those specific people to that specific land. Cross-references: Genesis 12:1–8; Genesis 15:1–21; Genesis 17:1–27; Genesis 26:5; Hebrews 11:8–10; Galatians 3:6–29; Romans 4:1–25; Ezekiel 36:22–38; Ezekiel 37:15–28; Jeremiah 31:31–37; Isaiah 11:11–12.

chapters.title: The Origin of Pharaoh — A Kingdom Built on a Lie About Death

verses.text: In those days there was in the land of Shinar a wise man who had understanding in all wisdom, and of a beautiful appearance, but he was poor and indigent; his name was Rikayon and he was hard set to support himself.

And he resolved to go to Egypt, to Oswiris the son of Anom king of Egypt, to show the king his wisdom; for perhaps he might find grace in his sight, to raise him up and give him maintenance; and Rikayon did so.

And when Rikayon came to Egypt he asked the inhabitants of Egypt concerning the king, and the inhabitants of Egypt told him the custom of the king of Egypt, for it was then the custom of the king of Egypt that he went from his royal palace and was seen abroad only one day in the year, and after that the king would return to his palace to remain there.
And on the day when the king went forth he passed judgment in the land, and every one having a suit came before the king that day to obtain his request.
And when Rikayon heard of the custom in Egypt and that he could not come into the presence of the king, he grieved greatly and was very sorrowful.

And in the evening Rikayon went out and found a house in ruins, formerly a bake house in Egypt, and he abode there all night in bitterness of soul and pinched with hunger, and sleep was removed from his eyes.
And Rikayon considered within himself what he should do in the town until the king made his appearance, and how he might maintain himself there.
And he rose in the morning and walked about, and met in his way those who sold vegetables and various sorts of seed with which they supplied the inhabitants.
And Rikayon wished to do the same in order to get a maintenance in the city, but he was unacquainted with the custom of the people, and he was like a blind man among them.
And he went and obtained vegetables to sell them for his support, and the rabble assembled about him and ridiculed him, and took his vegetables from him and left him nothing.
And he rose up from there in bitterness of soul, and went sighing to the bake house in which he had remained all the night before, and he slept there the second night.
And on that night again he reasoned within himself how he could save himself from starvation, and he devised a scheme how to act.

And he rose up in the morning and acted ingeniously, and went and hired thirty strong men of the rabble, carrying their war instruments in their hands, and he led them to the top of the Egyptian sepulchre, and he placed them there.

And he commanded them, saying, Thus says the king, Strengthen yourselves and be valiant men, and let no man be buried here until two hundred pieces of silver be given, and then he may be buried; and those men did according to the order of Rikayon to the people of Egypt the whole of that year.

And in eight months time Rikayon and his men gathered great riches of silver and gold, and Rikayon took a great quantity of horses and other animals, and he hired more men, and he gave them horses and they remained with him.
And when the year came round, at the time the king went forth into the town, all the inhabitants of Egypt assembled together to speak to him concerning the work of Rikayon and his men.
And the king went forth on the appointed day, and all the Egyptians came before him and cried to him, saying,

May the king live forever. What is this thing you do in the town to your servants, not to suffer a dead body to be buried until so much silver and gold be given? Was there ever the like to this done in the whole earth, from the days of former kings yea even from the days of Adam, to this day, that the dead should not be buried only for a set price?
We know it to be the custom of kings to take a yearly tax from the living, but you dost not only do this, but from the dead also you exact a tax day by day.
Now, O king, we can no more bear this, for the whole city is ruined on this account, and dost you not know it?
And when the king heard all that they had spoken he was very wroth, and his anger burned within him at this affair, for he had known nothing of it.
And the king said, Who and where is he that dares to do this wicked thing in my land without my command? Surely you will tell me.
And they told him all the works of Rikayon and his men, and the king’s anger was aroused, and he ordered Rikayon and his men to be brought before him.

And Rikayon took about a thousand children, sons and daughters, and clothed them in silk and embroidery, and he set them upon horses and sent them to the king by means of his men, and he also took a great quantity of silver and gold and precious stones, and a strong and beautiful horse, as a present for the king, with which he came before the king and bowed down to the earth before him; and the king, his servants and all the inhabitants of Egypt wondered at the work of Rikayon, and they saw his riches and the present that he had brought to the king.

And it greatly pleased the king and he wondered at it; and when Rikayon sat before him the king asked him concerning all his works, and Rikayon spoke all his words wisely before the king, his servants and all the inhabitants of Egypt.

And when the king heard the words of Rikayon and his wisdom, Rikayon found grace in his sight, and he met with grace and kindness from all the servants of the king and from all the inhabitants of Egypt, on account of his wisdom and excellent speeches, and from that time they loved him exceedingly.
And the king answered and said to Rikayon, Your name shall no more be called Rikayon but Pharaoh shall be your name, since you did exact a tax from the dead; and he called his name Pharaoh.
And the king and his subjects loved Rikayon for his wisdom, and they consulted with all the inhabitants of Egypt to make him prefect under the king.
And all the inhabitants of Egypt and its wise men did so, and it was made a law in Egypt.

And they made Rikayon Pharaoh prefect under Oswiris king of Egypt, and Rikayon Pharaoh governed over Egypt, daily administering justice to the whole city, but Oswiris the king would judge the people of the land one day in the year, when he went out to make his appearance.
And Rikayon Pharaoh cunningly usurped the government of Egypt, and he exacted a tax from all the inhabitants of Egypt.
And all the inhabitants of Egypt greatly loved Rikayon Pharaoh, and they made a decree to call every king that should reign over them and their seed in Egypt, Pharaoh.

Therefore all the kings that reigned in Egypt from that time forward were called Pharaoh to this day. « • • • Jasher chapter 14 is one of the strangest and most revealing chapters in the book, because it tells us where the title Pharaoh actually came from. A clever but starving man named Rikayon came to Egypt, saw he had no way to meet the king, and schemed up a new tax: he hired thugs to stand at the city’s cemetery and refuse burial to anyone who would not pay silver. In one year he made himself wealthy. When the city complained to the king, Rikayon appeared in royal robes with a thousand children dressed in embroidery and a present of gold, and by sheer pageantry and wit, won the king over. The king renamed him Pharaoh — “since you did exact a tax from the dead” — and appointed him second ruler. From that day, every king of Egypt was called Pharaoh. The title Pharaoh comes from a tax on corpses. Every Pharaoh who ever lived — every Pharaoh of the Exodus, every Pharaoh of Joseph’s day, every Pharaoh down the long corridor of Egyptian dynasties — bore a title whose origin was the monetization of grief. This is one of the most symbolically heavy moments in all of Jasher, and it speaks directly into the spiritual architecture of every worldly kingdom that builds its wealth on death. Every Babylonian system is ultimately a Rikayon system. It profits from death — from the death of the unborn, from the death of the martyrs, from the slow death of the soul under oppression, from the literal funeral tax on the grieving. Modern pharmaceutical empires that profit from chronic illness. Modern military empires that profit from perpetual war. Modern media empires that profit from the broken mental health of a generation. Modern religious empires that sell indulgences for the souls of the departed. All of them are wearing Rikayon’s robes. All of them are Pharaohs by heritage, because the tax on the dead is the oldest scheme in the book. And this is the Egypt into which Abraham is about to step in the next chapter. Not a harmless, ancient civilization. A system founded, at its core, on the exploitation of death. Abraham does not know Rikayon’s backstory — but YAHUAH does. Every step Abraham takes into Egypt is a step into a system that YAHUAH already knows the founding lie of. This will become important in chapter 15. Cross-references: Exodus 1:8–14; Ezekiel 29:3; Isaiah 30:1–3; Hosea 8:13; Revelation 18:11–17; 1 Timothy 6:10; Ecclesiastes 5:8–9.

chapters.title: Sarai in Pharaoh’s House, and the Separation from Lot

verses.text: And in that year there was a heavy famine throughout the land of Canaan, and the inhabitants of the land could not remain on account of the famine for it was very grievous.
And Abram and all belonging to him rose and went down to Egypt on account of the famine, and when they were at the brook Mitzraim they remained there some time to rest from the fatigue of the road.
And Abram and Sarai were walking at the border of the brook Mitzraim, and Abram beheld his wife Sarai that she was very beautiful.

And Abram said to his wife Sarai, Since Elohim (God) has created you with such a beautiful countenance, I am afraid of the Egyptians lest they should slay me and take you away, for the fear of Elohim is not in these places.
Surely then you shall do this, Say you are my sister to all that may ask you, in order that it may be well with me, and that we may live and not be put to death.

And Abram commanded the same to all those that came with him to Egypt on account of the famine; also his nephew Lot he commanded, saying, If the Egyptians ask you concerning Sarai say she is the sister of Abram.

And yet with all these orders Abram did not put confidence in them, but he took Sarai and placed her in a chest and concealed it amongst their vessels, for Abram was greatly concerned about Sarai on account of the wickedness of the Egyptians.

And Abram and all belonging to him rose up from the brook Mitzraim and came to Egypt; and they had scarcely entered the gates of the city when the guards stood up to them saying, Give tithe to the king from what you have, and then you may come into the town; and Abram and those that were with him did so.
And Abram with the people that were with him came to Egypt, and when they came they brought the chest in which Sarai was concealed and the Egyptians saw the chest.
And the king’s servants approached Abram, saying, What have you here in this chest which we have not seen? Now open you the chest and give tithe to the king of all that it contains.
And Abram said, This chest I will not open, but all you demand upon it I will give. And Pharaoh’s officers answered Abram, saying, It is a chest of precious stones, give us the tenth of it.
Abram said, All that you desire I will give, but you must not open the chest.
And the king’s officers pressed Abram, and they reached the chest and opened it with force, and they saw, and behold a beautiful woman was in the chest.

And when the officers of the king beheld Sarai they were struck with admiration at her beauty, and all the princes and servants of Pharaoh assembled to see Sarai, for she was very beautiful. And the king’s officers ran and told Pharaoh all that they had seen, and they praised Sarai to the king; and Pharaoh ordered her to be brought, and the woman came before the king.

And Pharaoh beheld Sarai and she pleased him exceedingly, and he was struck with her beauty, and the king rejoiced greatly on her account, and made presents to those who brought him the tidings concerning her.
And the woman was then brought to Pharaoh’s house, and Abram grieved on account of his wife, and he prayed to YAHUAH (the Lord) to deliver her from the hands of Pharaoh.

And Sarai also prayed at that time and said, O YAHUAH Elohim (O Lord God) you did tell my Lord Abram to go from his land and from his father’s house to the land of Canaan, and you did promise to do well with him if he would perform your commands; now behold we have done that which you did command us, and we left our land and our families, and we went to a strange land and to a people whom we have not known before.

And we came to this land to avoid the famine, and this evil accident has befallen me; now therefore, O YAHUAH Elohim, deliver us and save us from the hand of this oppressor, and do well with me for the sake of your mercy.
And YAHUAH hearkened to the voice of Sarai, and YAHUAH sent an angel to deliver Sarai from the power of Pharaoh.
And the king came and sat before Sarai and behold an angel of YAHUAH was standing over them, and he appeared to Sarai and said to her, Do not fear, for YAHUAH has heard your prayer.
And the king approached Sarai and said to her, What is that man to you who brought you here? and she said, He is my brother.

And the king said, It is incumbent upon us to make him great, to elevate him and to do to him all the good which you shall command us; and at that time the king sent to Abram silver and gold and precious stones in abundance, together with cattle, men servants and maid servants; and the king ordered Abram to be brought, and he sat in the court of the king’s house, and the king greatly exalted Abram on that night.
And the king approached to speak to Sarai, and he reached out his hand to touch her, when the angel smote him heavily, and he was terrified and he refrained from reaching to her.
And when the king came near to Sarai, the angel smote him to the ground, and acted thus to him the whole night, and the king was terrified.

And the angel on that night smote heavily all the servants of the king, and his whole household, on account of Sarai, and there was a great lamentation that night amongst the people of Pharaoh’s house.
And Pharaoh, seeing the evil that befell him, said, Surely on account of this woman has this thing happened to me, and he removed himself at some distance from her and spoke pleasing words to her.

And the king said to Sarai, Tell me I pray you concerning the man with whom you came here; and Sarai said, This man is my husband, and I said to you that he was my brother for I was afraid, lest you should put him to death through wickedness.

And the king kept away from Sarai, and the plagues of the angel of YAHUAH ceased from him and his household; and Pharaoh knew that he was smitten on account of Sarai, and the king was greatly astonished at this.

And in the morning the king called for Abram and said to him, What is this you have done to me? Why did you say, She is my sister, owing to which I took her to me for a wife, and this heavy plague has therefore come upon me and my household.

Now therefore here is your wife, take her and go from our land lest we all die on her account. And Pharaoh took more cattle, men servants and maid servants, and silver and gold, to give to Abram, and he returned to him Sarai his wife.
And the king took a maiden whom he begat by his concubines, and he gave her to Sarai for a handmaid.

And the king said to his daughter, It is better for you my daughter to be a handmaid in this man’s house than to be mistress in my house, after we have beheld the evil that befell us on account of this woman.
And Abram arose, and he and all belonging to him went away from Egypt; and Pharaoh ordered some of his men to accompany him and all that went with him.
And Abram returned to the land of Canaan, to the place where he had made the altar, where he at first had pitched his tent.
And Lot the son of Haran, Abram’s brother, had a heavy stock of cattle, flocks and herds and tents, for YAHUAH was bountiful to them on account of Abram.

And when Abram was dwelling in the land the herdsmen of Lot quarrelled with the herdsmen of Abram, for their property was too great for them to remain together in the land, and the land could not bear them on account of their cattle.

And when Abram’s herdsmen went to feed their flock they would not go into the fields of the people of the land, but the cattle of Lot’s herdsmen did otherwise, for they were suffered to feed in the fields of the people of the land.
And the people of the land saw this occurrence daily, and they came to Abram and quarrelled with him on account of Lot’s herdsmen.

And Abram said to Lot, What is this you are doing to me, to make me despicable to the inhabitants of the land, that you order your herdsman to feed your cattle in the fields of other people? Dost you not know that I am a stranger in this land amongst the children of Canaan, and why will you do this to me?
And Abram quarrelled daily with Lot on account of this, but Lot would not listen to Abram, and he continued to do the same and the inhabitants of the land came and told Abram.
And Abram said to Lot, How long will you be to me for a stumbling block with the inhabitants of the land? Now I beseech you let there be no more quarrelling between us, for we are kinsmen.
But I pray you separate from me, go and choose a place where you may dwell with your cattle and all belonging to you, but Keep thyself at a distance from me, you and your household.
And be not afraid in going from me, for if any one do an injury to you, let me know and I will avenge your cause from him, only remove from me.
And when Abram had spoken all these words to Lot, then Lot arose and lifted up his eyes toward the plain of Jordan.
And he saw that the whole of this place was well watered, and good for man as well as affording pasture for the cattle.
And Lot went from Abram to that place, and he there pitched his tent and he dwelt in Sodom, and they were separated from each other.

And Abram dwelt in the plain of Mamre, which is in Hebron, and he pitched his tent there, and Abram remained in that place many years. « • • • Jasher gives us the Sarai-in-a-chest detail that Genesis 12 does not include. Abram, trying to protect his wife in the first encounter with Egypt, physically hides her. This detail is sometimes read as a failure of faith. It is better read as the first human attempt to protect the covenant seed — an attempt that is insufficient, as all human protection is insufficient. YAHUAH’s angel is the one who actually protects Sarai. Abram’s chest is uncovered in a moment. The angel’s intervention is what keeps Pharaoh’s hand from her womb. This is the pattern of every protection the seed has ever had. Every ark Noah built was insufficient by itself; YAHUAH shut the door. Every basket Jochebed wove for Moses was insufficient by itself; Pharaoh’s daughter drew him out. Every attempt of modern believers to shield their children from the spiritual pollutions of the age is insufficient by itself; only YAHUAH’s angels keep the covering effective. The practical implication is not that we stop trying. Abram tried. The implication is that we understand the limits of our effort and cry out to the One who actually does the shielding. Unless YAHUAH build the house, they labor in vain that build it (Psalm 127:1). The scene in verse 22 is almost comic in its awful detail. Pharaoh reaches for Sarai, and the angel smites him heavily. Pharaoh keeps trying. The angel keeps smiting. “And the angel on that night smote heavily all the servants of the king, and his whole household” (verse 25). The message from heaven is clear and physical. When Pharaoh finally realizes what is happening and sends Sarai back to Abram with gold, silver, cattle, and a handmaid (Hagar — verse 31, who will become enormously important later), he has learned a lesson that every emperor and every institution eventually learns: do not touch My anointed. Psalm 105:14–15, reflecting on this exact moment, says “He suffered no man to do them wrong: yea, he reproved kings for their sakes; Saying, Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.” Every time a covenant-hostile king or institution has reached for the covenant seed and been smitten mid-reach, the Psalm 105 pattern is being enacted. Notice the handmaid given to Sarai by Pharaoh — Hagar. Jasher verse 32 gives us a remarkable detail: “The king said to his daughter, It is better for you my daughter to be a handmaid in this man’s house than to be mistress in my house.” Hagar is Pharaoh’s own daughter, given to Sarai because Pharaoh now sees that the house of Abram is under a protection his house cannot match. This adds tragic depth to Hagar’s later story. She will be the mother of Ishmael, and her son will be the progenitor of nations (the Arab peoples). She was a princess of Egypt who became a handmaid of Sarai, and through her son has come forth a people whose destiny is still being worked out in our own day. Paul will use her allegorically in Galatians 4; the allegory is not a dismissal of Hagar’s real humanity or of Ishmael’s real line — it is a pastoral teaching about the contrast between the slave covenant (works-for-status) and the free covenant (faith that produces obedience). Hagar the person is not the enemy. She was, like Sarai, a woman in a difficult situation trying to survive. Her descendants, in our day, are also not the enemy. They are also invited to the promise through faith — the same promise Abram had. The separation of Abram and Lot in verses 36–46 is the first of several times in Jasher where two related men must part ways because their flocks have grown too large to share the land. This is never just economics. It is always a parable. Lot chose Sodom because Sodom was well-watered and looked prosperous. Abram chose the harder land of Hebron because it was where YAHUAH had appeared to him. Every generation of believers has a Lot-choice and an Abram-choice in front of it. The well-watered plains of the world’s system. The rocky hills of the covenant walk. One leads to Sodom. The other leads to the oaks of Mamre and a visitation from YAHUAH Himself. Both men were righteous in some sense — 2 Peter 2:7 calls Lot “righteous” — but only one of them made the choice that positioned him to receive the deeper revelation. Lot survives Sodom’s fire; Abram inherits the covenant. The difference is what they chose when the two roads diverged. Cross-references: Genesis 12:10–20; Genesis 13:1–18; Psalm 105:14–15; Psalm 127:1; 2 Peter 2:7–8; Galatians 4:21–31; Hebrews 11:8–10; Revelation 18:4; Matthew 7:13–14.

chapters.title: The War of the Kings, Melchizedek, and Hagar

verses.text: At that time Chedorlaomer king of Elam sent to all the neighboring kings, to Nimrod, king of Shinar who was then under his power, and to Tidal, king of Goyim, and to Arioch, king of Elasar, with whom he made a covenant, saying, Come up to me and assist me, that we may smite all the towns of Sodom and its inhabitants, for they have rebelled against me these thirteen years.
And these four kings went up with all their camps, about eight hundred thousand men, and they went as they were, and smote every man they found in their road.

And the five kings of Sodom and Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, Shemeber king of Zeboyim, Bera king of Sodom, Bersha king of Gomorrah, and Bela king of Zoar, went out to meet them, and they all joined together in the valley of Siddim.
And these nine kings made war in the valley of Siddim; and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah were smitten before the kings of Elam.

And the valley of Siddim was full of lime pits and the kings of Elam pursued the kings of Sodom, and the kings of Sodom with their camps fled and fell into the lime pits, and all that remained went to the mountain for safety, and the five kings of Elam came after them and pursued them to the gates of Sodom, and they took all that there was in Sodom.

And they plundered all the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, and they also took Lot, Abram’s brother’s son, and his property, and they seized all the goods of the cities of Sodom, and they went away; and Unic, Abram’s servant, who was in the battle, saw this, and told Abram all that the kings had done to the cities of Sodom, and that Lot was taken captive by them.

And Abram heard this, and he rose up with about three hundred and eighteen men that were with him, and he that night pursued these kings and smote them, and they all fell before Abram and his men, and there was none remaining but the four kings who fled, and they went each his own road.
And Abram recovered all the property of Sodom, and he also recovered Lot and his property, his wives and little ones and all belonging to him, so that Lot lacked nothing.
And when he returned from smiting these kings, he and his men passed the valley of Siddim where the kings had made war together.
And Bera king of Sodom, and the rest of his men that were with him, went out from the lime pits into which they had fallen, to meet Abram and his men.
And Adonizedek king of Jerusalem, the same was Shem, went out with his men to meet Abram and his people, with bread and wine, and they remained together in the valley of Melech.
And Adonizedek blessed Abram, and Abram gave him a tenth from all that he had brought from the spoil of his enemies, for Adonizedek was a priest before Elohim (God).

And all the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah who were there, with their servants, approached Abram and begged of him to return them their servants whom he had made captive, and to take to himself all the property.

And Abram answered the kings of Sodom, saying, As YAHUAH (the Lord) lives who created heaven and earth, and who redeemed my soul from all affliction, and who delivered me this day from my enemies, and gave them into my hand, I will not take anything belonging to you, that you may not boast tomorrow, saying, Abram became rich from our property that he saved.
For YAHUAH my Elohim (the Lord my God) in whom I trust said to me, You shall lack nothing, for I will bless you in all the works of your hands.

And now therefore behold, here is all belonging to you, take it and go; as YAHUAH lives I will not take from you from a living soul down to a shoetie or thread, excepting the expense of the food of those who went out with me to battle, as also the portions of the men who went with me, Anar, Ashcol, and Mamre, they and their men, as well as those also who had remained to watch the baggage, they shall take their portion of the spoil.
And the kings of Sodom gave Abram according to all that he had said, and they pressed him to take of whatever he chose, but he would not.
And he sent away the kings of Sodom and the remainder of their men, and he gave them orders about Lot, and they went to their respective places.

And Lot, his brother’s son, he also sent away with his property, and he went with them, and Lot returned to his home, to Sodom, and Abram and his people returned to their home to the plains of Mamre, which is in Hebron.

At that time YAHUAH again appeared to Abram in Hebron, and he said to him, Do not fear, your reward is very great before me, for I will not leave you, until I shall have multiplied you, and blessed you and made your seed like the stars in heaven, which cannot be measured nor numbered.
And I will give to your seed all these lands that you see with your eyes, to them will I give them for an inheritance forever, only be strong and do not fear, walk before me and be perfect.
And in the seventy-eighth year of the life of Abram, in that year died Reu, the son of Peleg, and all the days of Reu were two hundred and thirty-nine years, and he died.
And Sarai, the daughter of Haran, Abram’s wife, was still barren in those days; she did not bear to Abram either son or daughter.
And when she saw that she bare no children she took her handmaid Hagar, whom Pharaoh had given her, and she gave her to Abram her husband for a wife.
For Hagar learned all the ways of Sarai as Sarai taught her, she was not in any way deficient in following her good ways.
And Sarai said to Abram, Behold here is my handmaid Hagar, go to her that she may bring forth upon my knees, that I may also obtain children through her.
And at the end of ten years of Abram’s dwelling in the land of Canaan, which is the eighty-fifth year of Abram’s life, Sarai gave Hagar to him.
And Abram hearkened to the voice of his wife Sarai, and he took his handmaid Hagar and Abram came to her and she conceived.

And when Hagar saw that she had conceived she rejoiced greatly, and her mistress was despised in her eyes, and she said within herself, This can only be that I am better before Elohim than Sarai my mistress, for all the days that my mistress has been with my Lord, she did not conceive, but me YAHUAH has caused in so short a time to conceive by him.
And when Sarai saw that Hagar had conceived by Abram, Sarai was jealous of her handmaid, and Sarai said within herself, This is surely nothing else but that she must be better than I am.
And Sarai said to Abram, My wrong be upon you, for at the time when you did pray before YAHUAH for children why did you not pray on my account, that YAHUAH should give me seed from you?
And when I speak to Hagar in your presence, she despises my words, because she has conceived, and you will say nothing to her; may YAHUAH judge between me and you for what you have done to me.
And Abram said to Sarai, Behold your handmaid is in your hand, do to her as it may seem good in your eyes; and Sarai afflicted her, and Hagar fled from her to the wilderness.

And an angel of YAHUAH found her in the place where she had fled, by a well, and he said to her, Do not fear, for I will multiply your seed, for you shall bear a son and you shall call his name Ishmael; now then return to Sarai your mistress, and submit thyself under her hands.
And Hagar called the place of that well Beer-lahai-roi, it is between Kadesh and the wilderness of Bered.

And Hagar at that time returned to her master’s house, and at the end of days Hagar bare a son to Abram, and Abram called his name Ishmael; and Abram was eighty-six years old when he begat him. « • • • Jasher 16:11 gives us one of the most important identifications in all of the apocryphal literature: “Adonizedek king of Jerusalem, the same was Shem.” Melchizedek — called Adonizedek here — is Shem, the son of Noah, still alive in the time of Abraham. Shem outlived every one of his immediate descendants except the last few, and according to the biblical genealogies he was still alive when Abraham was alive. Jasher makes the identification that centuries of rabbinic tradition preserved. Melchizedek is not a mysterious heavenly being. Melchizedek is Shem. He is the patriarch of the covenant line, two generations removed from Abram by descent, who had been preserved through the flood and who functioned as priest of YAHUAH in the land while Abram was being called. This changes how we read Hebrews 7. The author of Hebrews notes that Melchizedek is introduced in Genesis “without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life” — meaning, in the Hebrews 7 argument, that his priesthood is not traced through descent the way Aaron’s was. Hebrews 7 is making a literary argument about how Melchizedek appears in the Genesis text, not a metaphysical argument that Melchizedek was some pre-incarnate Messiah or angel. The Messiah is a priest after the order of Melchizedek because the Messiah’s priesthood is not traced through the Aaronic line — it is traced through a royal, pre-Aaronic line that predates Sinai. Melchizedek (Shem) was the first righteous priest-king in the covenant land. YAHUSHA is the final righteous priest-king in the covenant land. The order runs from Shem to Yeshua. It does not require Melchizedek to be divine; it requires Melchizedek to be outside the Aaronic line. This is important because the institutional church, especially in its Catholic and high-liturgical expressions, has often turned Melchizedek into a mystical pre-incarnate figure in order to support certain eucharistic doctrines. The simpler, rabbinic, Jasher-confirmed reading is that Melchizedek is Shem, functioning as priest in Salem (Jerusalem), blessing Abram with bread and wine in a covenant meal. The bread and wine are not a sacrament — they are the ordinary elements of a covenant meal in the ancient world, the same elements YAHUSHA would later use to institute the memorial of His own covenant-blood. The typology holds without needing to deify Melchizedek. Abram pays tithes to Melchizedek because the priest of the true Elohim is due the firstfruits of every victory. This is before the Levitical priesthood, before Aaron, before the written Torah. The principle of tithing to the priesthood of YAHUAH was already in effect in Abram’s day — and the author of Hebrews uses this in chapter 7 to argue that the Messiah’s priesthood (Melchizedek’s order) takes precedence over the Levitical (Aaron’s order). Both are legitimate within their seasons. Aaron’s priesthood was for the wilderness and the temple. Melchizedek’s priesthood — royal, universal, not tied to a specific temple — is the priesthood of the Messiah in the age to come and forever. Verses 23–36 give us the Hagar episode. Sarai has not borne children. She gives Hagar to Abram. Hagar conceives and becomes contemptuous of her barren mistress. Sarai afflicts Hagar. Hagar flees. The angel of YAHUAH meets her at a well and tells her to return. Ishmael is born. Abram is eighty-six years old. Read from the victims-not-enemies posture: every person in this chapter is behaving from a place of pain, and every person is still loved by YAHUAH. Sarai is barren and carries the pain of barrenness in a culture where a woman’s worth was measured in children.
