Now therefore hear my words that I have this day spoken to you, and send our brother that he may go away lest you and the people of your land die by the sword, for you cannot all prevail over me.

And Joseph answered Judah, saying, Why have you opened wide your mouth and why dost you boast over us, saying, Strength is with you? as Pharaoh lives, if I command all my valiant men to fight with you, surely you and these your brethren would sink in the mire.

And Judah said to Joseph, Surely it becomes you and your people to fear me; as the YAHUAH (the Lord) lives if I once draw my sword I shall not sheathe it again until I shall this day have slain all Egypt, and I will commence with you and finish with Pharaoh your master.

And Joseph answered and said to him, Surely strength belongs not alone to you; I am stronger and mightier than you, surely if you draw your sword I will put it to your neck and the necks of all your brethren.

And Judah said to him, Surely if I this day open my mouth against you I would swallow you up that you be destroyed from off the earth and perish this day from your kingdom. And Joseph said, Surely if you open your mouth I have power and might to close your mouth with a stone until you shall not be able to utter a word; see how many stones are before us, truly I can take a stone, and force it into your mouth and break your jaws.

And Judah said, Elohim is witness between us, that we have not hitherto desired to battle with you, only give us our brother and we will go from you; and Joseph answered and said, As Pharaoh lives, if all the kings of Canaan came together with you, you should not take him from my hand.

Now therefore go your way to your father, and your brother shall be to me for a slave, for he has robbed the king’s house. And Judah said, What is it to you or to the character of the king, surely the king sends forth from his house, throughout the land, silver and gold either in gifts or expenses, and you still talk about your cup which you did place in our brother’s bag and say that he has stolen it from you?
Elohim forbid that our brother Benjamin or any of the seed of Abraham should do this thing to steal from you, or from any one else, whether king, prince, or any man.
Now therefore cease this accusation lest the whole earth hear your words, saying, For a little silver the king of Egypt wrangled with the men, and he accused them and took their brother for a slave.
And Joseph answered and said, Take to you this cup and go from me and leave your brother for a slave, for it is the judgment of a thief to be a slave.

And Judah said, Why are you not ashamed of your words, to leave our brother and to take your cup? Surely if you give us your cup, or a thousand times as much, we will not leave our brother for the silver which is found in the hand of any man, that we will not die over him.
And Joseph answered, And why did you forsake your brother and sell him for twenty pieces of silver to this day, and why then will you not do the same to this your brother?
And Judah said, YAHUAH is witness between me and you that we desire not your battles; now therefore give us our brother and we will go from you without quarreling.

And Joseph answered and said, If all the kings of the land should assemble they will not be able to take your brother from my hand; and Judah said, What shall we say to our father, when he sees that our brother comes not with us, and will grieve over him?
And Joseph answered and said, This is the thing which you shall tell to your father, saying, The rope has gone after the bucket.
And Judah said, Surely you are a king, and why speak you these things, giving a false judgment? woe to the king who is like to you.

And Joseph answered and said, There is no false judgment in the word that I spoke on account of your brother Joseph, for all of you sold him to the Midianites for twenty pieces of silver, and you all denied it to your father and said to him, An evil beast has devoured him, Joseph has been torn to pieces.

And Judah said, Behold the fire of Shem burns in my heart, now I will burn all your land with fire; and Joseph answered and said, Surely your sister-in-law Tamar, who killed your sons, extinguished the fire of Shechem.
And Judah said, If I pluck out a single hair from my flesh, I will fill all Egypt with its blood.

And Joseph answered and said, Such is your custom to do as you did to your brother whom you sold, and you dipped his coat in blood and brought it to your father in order that he might say an evil beast devoured him and here is his blood.

And when Judah heard this thing he was exceedingly wroth and his anger burned within him, and there was before him in that place a stone, the weight of which was about four hundred shekels, and Judah’s anger was kindled and he took the stone in one hand and cast it to the heavens and caught it with his left hand.
And he placed it afterward under his legs, and he sat upon it with all his strength and the stone was turned into dust from the force of Judah.

And Joseph saw the act of Judah and he was very much afraid, but he commanded Manassah his son and he also did with another stone like to the act of Judah, and Judah said to his brethren, Let not any of you say, this man is an Egyptian, but by his doing this thing he is of our father’s family.

And Joseph said, Not to you only is strength given, for we are also powerful men, and why will you boast over us all? and Judah said to Joseph, Send I pray you our brother and ruin not your country this day.
And Joseph answered and said to them, Go and tell your father, an evil beast has devoured him as you said concerning your brother Joseph.

And Judah spoke to his brother Naphtali, and he said to him, Make haste, go now and number all the streets of Egypt and come and tell me; and Simeon said to him, Let not this thing be a trouble to you; now I will go to the mount and take up one large stone from the mount and level it at every one in Egypt, and kill all that are in it.
And Joseph heard all these words that his brethren spoke before him, and they did not know that Joseph understood them, for they imagined that he knew not to speak Hebrew.

And Joseph was greatly afraid at the words of his brethren lest they should destroy Egypt, and he commanded his son Manasseh, saying, Go now make haste and gather to me all the inhabitants of Egypt, and all the valiant men together, and let them come to me now upon horseback and on foot and with all sorts of musical instruments, and Manasseh went and did so.
And Naphtali went as Judah had commanded him, for Naphtali was lightfooted as one of the swift stags, and he would go upon the ears of corn and they would not break under him.

And he went and numbered all the streets of Egypt, and found them to be twelve, and he came hastily and told Judah, and Judah said to his brethren, Hasten you and put on every man his sword upon his loins and we will come over Egypt, and smite them all, and let not a remnant remain.

And Judah said, Behold, I will destroy three of the streets with my strength, and you shall each destroy one street; and when Judah was speaking this thing, behold the inhabitants of Egypt and all the mighty men came toward them with all sorts of musical instruments and with loud shouting.
And their number was five hundred cavalry and ten thousand infantry, and four hundred men who could fight without sword or spear, only with their hands and strength.
And all the mighty men came with great storming and shouting, and they all surrounded the sons of Jacob and terrified them, and the ground quaked at the sound of their shouting.
And when the sons of Jacob saw these troops they were greatly afraid of their lives, and Joseph did so in order to terrify the sons of Jacob to become tranquilized.

And Judah, seeing some of his brethren terrified, said to them, Why are you afraid whilst the grace of Elohim is with us? and when Judah saw all the people of Egypt surrounding them at the command of Joseph to terrify them, only Joseph commanded them, saying, Do not touch any of them.
Then Judah hastened and drew his sword, and uttered a loud and bitter scream, and he smote with his sword, and he sprang upon the ground and he still continued to shout against all the people.
And when he did this thing YAHUAH caused the terror of Judah and his brethren to fall upon the valiant men and all the people that surrounded them.

And they all fled at the sound of the shouting, and they were terrified and fell one upon the other, and many of them died as they fell, and they all fled from before Judah and his brethren and from before Joseph.

And whilst they were fleeing, Judah and his brethren pursued them to the house of Pharaoh, and they all escaped, and Judah again sat before Joseph and roared at him like a lion, and gave a great and tremendous shriek at him.

And the shriek was heard at a distance, and all the inhabitants of Succoth heard it, and all Egypt quaked at the sound of the shriek, and also the walls of Egypt and of the land of Goshen fell in from the shaking of the earth, and Pharaoh also fell from his throne upon the ground, and also all the pregnant women of Egypt and Goshen miscarried when they heard the noise of the shaking, for they were terribly afraid.

And Pharaoh sent word, saying, What is this thing that has this day happened in the land of Egypt? and they came and told him all the things from beginning to end, and Pharaoh was alarmed and he wondered and was greatly afraid.

And his fright increased when he heard all these things, and he sent to Joseph, saying, You have brought to me the Hebrews to destroy all Egypt; what will you do with that thievish slave? send him away and let him go with his brethren, and let us not perish through their evil, even we, you and all Egypt.

And if you desire not to do this thing, cast off from you all my valuable things, and go with them to their land, if you delight in it, for they will this day destroy my whole country and slay all my people; even all the women of Egypt have miscarried through their screams; see what they have done merely by their shouting and speaking, moreover if they fight with the sword, they will destroy the land; now therefore choose that which you desire, whether me or the Hebrews, whether Egypt or the land of the Hebrews.

And they came and told Joseph all the words of Pharaoh that he had said concerning him, and Joseph was greatly afraid at the words of Pharaoh and Judah and his brethren were still standing before Joseph indignant and enraged, and all the sons of Jacob roared at Joseph, like the roaring of the sea and its waves.
And Joseph was greatly afraid of his brethren and on account of Pharaoh, and Joseph sought a pretext to make himself known to his brethren, lest they should destroy all Egypt.
And Joseph commanded his son Manasseh, and Manasseh went and approached Judah, and placed his hand upon his shoulder, and the anger of Judah was stilled.
And Judah said to his brethren, Let no one of you say that this is the act of an Egyptian youth for this is the work of my father’s house.
And Joseph seeing and knowing that Judah’s anger was stilled, he approached to speak to Judah in the language of mildness.

And Joseph said to Judah, Surely you speak truth and have this day verified your assertions concerning your strength, and may your Elohim who delights in you, increase your welfare; but tell me truly why from amongst all your brethren dost you wrangle with me on account of the lad, as none of them have spoken one word to me concerning him.
And Judah answered Joseph, saying, Surely you must know that I was security for the lad to his father, saying, If I brought him not to him I should bear his blame forever.

Therefore have I approached you from amongst all my brethren, for I saw that you were unwilling to suffer him to go from you; now therefore may I find grace in your sight that you shall send him to go with us, and behold I will remain as a substitute for him, to serve you in whatever you desire, for wheresoever you shall send me I will go to serve you with great energy.

Send me now to a mighty king who has rebelled against you, and you shall know what I will do to him and to his land; although he may have cavalry and infantry or an exceeding mighty people, I will slay them all and bring the king’s head before you.

Dost you not know or have you not heard that our father Abraham with his servant Eliezer smote all the kings of Elam with their hosts in one night, they left not one remaining? and ever since that day our father’s strength was given to us for an inheritance, for us and our seed forever.

And Joseph answered and said, You speak truth, and falsehood is not in your mouth, for it was also told to us that the Hebrews have power and that YAHUAH their Elohim (the Lord their God) delights much in them, and who then can stand before them?

However, on this condition will I send your brother, if you will bring before me his brother the son of his mother, of whom you said that he had gone from you down to Egypt; and it shall come to pass when you bring to me his brother I will take him in his stead, because not one of you was security for him to your father, and when he shall come to me, I will then send with you his brother for whom you have been security.

And Judah’s anger was kindled against Joseph when he spoke this thing, and his eyes dropped blood with anger, and he said to his brethren, How does this man this day seek his own destruction and that of all Egypt!

And Simeon answered Joseph, saying, Did we not tell you at first that we knew not the particular spot to which he went, and whether he be dead or alive, and therefore speaks my Lord like to these things?
And Joseph observing the countenance of Judah discerned that his anger began to kindle when he spoke to him, saying, Bring to me your other brother instead of this brother.

And Joseph said to his brethren, Surely you said that your brother was either dead or lost, now if I should call him this day and he should come before you, would you give him to me instead of his brother?
And Joseph began to speak and call out, Joseph, Joseph, come this day before me, and appear to your brethren and sit before them.
And when Joseph spoke this thing before them, they looked each a different way to see from whence Joseph would come before them.

And Joseph observed all their acts, and said to them, Why do you look here and there? I am Joseph whom you sold to Egypt, now therefore let it not grieve you that you sold me, for as a support during the famine did Elohim send me before you.
And his brethren were terrified at him when they heard the words of Joseph, and Judah was exceedingly terrified at him.
And when Benjamin heard the words of Joseph he was before them in the inner part of the house, and Benjamin ran to Joseph his brother, and embraced him and fell upon his neck, and they wept.
And when Joseph’s brethren saw that Benjamin had fallen upon his brother’s neck and wept with him, they also fell upon Joseph and embraced him, and they wept a great weeping with Joseph.
And the voice was heard in the house of Joseph that they were Joseph’s brethren, and it pleased Pharaoh exceedingly, for he was afraid of them lest they should destroy Egypt.

And Pharaoh sent his servants to Joseph to congratulate him concerning his brethren who had come to him, and all the captains of the armies and troops that were in Egypt came to rejoice with Joseph, and all Egypt rejoiced greatly about Joseph’s brethren.

And Pharaoh sent his servants to Joseph, saying, Tell your brethren to fetch all belonging to them and let them come to me, and I will place them in the best part of the land of Egypt, and they did so.

And Joseph commanded him that was set over his house to bring out to his brethren gifts and garments, and he brought out to them many garments being robes of royalty and many gifts, and Joseph divided them amongst his brethren.

And he gave to each of his brethren a change of garments of gold and silver, and three hundred pieces of silver, and Joseph commanded them all to be dressed in these garments, and to be brought before Pharaoh.
And Pharaoh seeing that all Joseph’s brethren were valiant men, and of beautiful appearance, he greatly rejoiced.
And they afterward went out from the presence of Pharaoh to go to the land of Canaan, to their father, and their brother Benjamin was with them.

And Joseph rose up and gave to them eleven chariots from Pharaoh, and Joseph gave to them his chariot, upon which he rode on the day of his being crowned in Egypt, to fetch his father to Egypt; and Joseph sent to all his brothers’ children, garments according to their numbers, and a hundred pieces of silver to each of them, and he also sent garments to the wives of his brethren from the garments of the king’s wives, and he sent them.
And he gave to each of his brethren ten men to go with them to the land of Canaan to serve them, to serve their children and all belonging to them in coming to Egypt.
And Joseph sent by the hand of his brother Benjamin ten suits of garments for his ten sons, a portion above the rest of the children of the sons of Jacob.

And he sent to each fifty pieces of silver, and ten chariots on the account of Pharaoh, and he sent to his father ten asses laden with all the luxuries of Egypt, and ten she asses laden with corn and bread and nourishment for his father, and to all that were with him as provisions for the road.

And he sent to his sister Dinah garments of silver and gold, and frankincense and myrrh, and aloes and women’s ornaments in great plenty, and he sent the same from the wives of Pharaoh to the wives of Benjamin.

And he gave to all his brethren, also to their wives, all sorts of onyx stones and bdellium, and from all the valuable things amongst the great people of Egypt, nothing of all the costly things was left but what Joseph sent of to his father’s household.
And he sent his brethren away, and they went, and he sent his brother Benjamin with them.
And Joseph went out with them to accompany them on the road to the borders of Egypt, and he commanded them concerning his father and his household, to come to Egypt.
And he said to them, Do not quarrel on the road, for this thing was from YAHUAH to keep a great people from starvation, for there will be yet five years of famine in the land.
And he commanded them, saying, When you come to the land of Canaan, do not come suddenly before my father in this affair, but act in your wisdom.
And Joseph ceased to command them, and he turned and went back to Egypt, and the sons of Jacob went to the land of Canaan with joy and cheerfulness to their father Jacob.

And they came to the borders of the land, and they said to each other, What shall we do in this matter before our father, for if we come suddenly to him and tell him the matter, he will be greatly alarmed at our words and will not believe us.

And they went along until they came nigh to their houses, and they found Serach, the daughter of Asher, going forth to meet them, and the damsel was very good and subtle, and knew how to play upon the harp.

And they called to her and she came before them, and she kissed them, and they took her and gave to her a harp, saying, Go now before our father, and sit before him, and strike upon the harp, and speak these words.
And they commanded her to go to their house, and she took the harp and hastened before them, and she came and sat near Jacob.
And she played well and sang, and uttered in the sweetness of her words, Joseph my uncle is living, and he rules throughout the land of Egypt, and is not dead.
And she continued to repeat and utter these words, and Jacob heard her words and they were agreeable to him.
He listened whilst she repeated them twice and thrice, and joy entered the heart of Jacob at the sweetness of her words, and the spirit of Elohim was upon him, and he knew all her words to be true.

And Jacob blessed Serach when she spoke these words before him, and he said to her, My daughter, may death never prevail over you, for you have revived my spirit; only speak yet before me as you have spoken, for you have gladdened me with all your words.
And she continued to sing these words, and Jacob listened and it pleased him, and he rejoiced, and the spirit of Elohim was upon him.
Whilst he was yet speaking with her, behold his sons came to him with horses and chariots and royal garments and servants running before them.
And Jacob rose up to meet them, and saw his sons dressed in royal garments and he saw all the treasures that Joseph had sent to them.
And they said to him, Be informed that our brother Joseph is living, and it is he who rules throughout the land of Egypt, and it is he who spoke to us as we told you.

And Jacob heard all the words of his sons, and his heart palpitated at their words, for he could not believe them until he saw all that Joseph had given them and what he had sent him, and all the signs which Joseph had spoken to them.

And they opened out before him, and showed him all that Joseph had sent, they gave to each what Joseph had sent him, and he knew that they had spoken the truth, and he rejoiced exceedingly an account of his son.
And Jacob said, It is enough for me that my son Joseph is still living, I will go and see him before I die.
And his sons told him all that had befallen them, and Jacob said, I will go down to Egypt to see my son and his offspring.
And Jacob rose up and put on the garments which Joseph had sent him, and after he had washed, and shaved his hair, he put upon his head the turban which Joseph had sent him.
And all the people of Jacob’s house and their wives put on the garments which Joseph had sent to them, and they greatly rejoiced at Joseph that he was still living and that he was ruling in Egypt,
And all the inhabitants of Canaan heard of this thing, and they came and rejoiced much with Jacob that he was still living.

And Jacob made a feast for them for three days, and all the kings of Canaan and nobles of the land ate and drank and rejoiced in the house of Jacob. « • • • Chapter 54 is the climax of the whole cycle. It contains two linked scenes. Judah’s speech before the vizier, and Joseph’s revelation to his brothers. We will walk both. Jasher’s version of Judah’s confrontation is more belligerent than Genesis 44. In Genesis, Judah’s speech is the measured, beautiful petition that ends in the offer of his own life: let your servant abide instead of the lad, a bondsman to my lord, and let the lad go up with his brethren. Jasher preserves a more heated exchange. Judah is angry. He threatens to destroy Egypt. He lifts a stone that weighs four hundred shekels and crushes it under him into dust. Joseph’s son Manasseh lifts a similar stone in response. Judah roars like a lion, and Jasher says the walls of Egypt and Goshen shake and Pharaoh falls off his throne and the pregnant women of Egypt miscarry at the sound. Jasher is preserving, we think, the family memory that when Judah stood up to the vizier on behalf of Benjamin, the room was charged with the power of the covenant. The Spirit on Judah in that moment was not the Spirit of the man who had priced Joseph at twenty pieces of silver. It was the Spirit of the man from whose loins the scepter would not depart. Whether the stones were actually crushed is not the point. The point is the shift in Judah. This is a man who had been willing to sell a brother. He is standing, now, in front of the most powerful man in the world, threatening to destroy that man’s entire country, on behalf of his brother. Read the arc. It has taken twenty-two years. It has gone through Tamar. It has gone through the famine. It has gone through the long journeys down to Egypt. And Judah is now on the other side of the transformation. And then Joseph reveals himself. The language is worth catching. Joseph has to ask his Egyptian officers to leave the room. No man stood with him while he made himself known to his brothers. He weeps so loudly that the Egyptians outside the chamber hear him and it is reported to Pharaoh. He says, I am Joseph. Then he says, does my father yet live? And Jasher notes that his brothers cannot answer him, they are so troubled at his presence. He says then the words that are the theological heart of the entire Joseph cycle. Now therefore be not grieved nor angry with yourselves that you sold me here, for Elohim did send me before you to preserve life. It was not you who sent me here, but Elohim. Let these words sit. This is not cheap forgiveness. This is not Joseph pretending nothing happened. He had twelve years in prison to reckon with what they had done, and nothing in his life before this moment had excused them. What Joseph is doing at the moment of revelation is the thing the Messiah will do at the cross. He is naming the sin accurately and also naming the larger providence that has ridden on top of the sin without excusing it. It was their evil. It was the Father’s rescue. Both are true. The fact that YAHUAH brought good out of evil does not diminish the evil. The fact that the evil was real does not diminish the good. Joseph holds both, and he holds them for his brothers’ sake, not for his own. His brothers could not come into full reconciliation while they still believed he was going to avenge himself. He releases them from that fear. This is the clearest place in the Torah where the central doctrine of atonement is pre-written. The one who was betrayed says, it was not finally you. It was the Father working through you. The betrayer is not excused. The betrayer is not exonerated. The betrayer is reconciled. The work of reconciliation is done by the offended party at his own cost. He does not demand restitution. He opens his own stores. He feeds them. He settles them in the best of the land. He treats their children as his children. He forgives without being asked. And they did not ask. That is the hardest piece to sit with. Scripture, as far as any text records, does not show the brothers asking Joseph for forgiveness at this moment. They are too terrified to speak. Joseph forgives before they ask. This is the gospel pattern. We love Him because He first loved us. While we were yet sinners, the Messiah died for us. He reconciled us before we thought to reconcile. The offended party made the first move. Now, the Messiah typology we have been developing across this whole chapter reaches its fullest point here. A favorite son is sent from the father to the brothers. The brothers take counsel and sell him for silver. He is handed over to the Gentiles. He goes into an imprisonment that reads like death. He is raised up and given authority over the kingdom of the world and given a bride from outside the covenant people. A famine comes. The brothers come seeking bread. They do not recognize him the first time. They come a second time. At the second coming, he makes himself known. He weeps with them. He provides for them. He tells them that what they intended for evil, YAHUAH intended for good, to save much people alive. He does not destroy them. He feeds them. And the land is preserved through his hand. Every element of that paragraph is the Joseph cycle and every element of that paragraph is the ministry of Yahusha (Jesus). The first coming is rejection by His own. The imprisonment is the grave. The exaltation is the resurrection and the seating at the right hand. The bride is from outside. The famine is the judgment on the earth. The brothers coming down is the scattered house being driven by need to come home. The first audience is the initial encounter. The second audience, where the eyes are opened, is the day He will make Himself known to His own. The brothers’ repentance is the repentance of Jacob’s sons at the last day. The weeping is Zechariah 12:10: they shall look upon Me whom they have pierced and shall mourn for Him as one mourns for his only son. The reconciliation is the in-gathering of the twelve tribes into the city of Jerusalem under the King. None of this is a stretch. None of this is allegory imposed on the text. The pattern is in the Torah first and in the Gospels second because the Father wrote the pattern first in Joseph so that when it came in Yahusha (Jesus), His people would know Him. That many of them did not know Him at the first coming is the tragedy. That the pattern is in Torah for all to see is the mercy. Before we close this chapter, one more thing has to be said about what Joseph does not do. He does not say, let us now establish the rule that you are no longer my brothers. He does not say, the covenant has now passed to me and my Egyptian sons and you are excluded. He says, come home, come all of you home, bring the father, bring the children, bring your wives, bring your herds. He settles them in the best of the land. He counts them family. He adopts no replacement. This is the part of the chapter that has the most direct thing to say to institutional Christianity. The reader who has been taught replacement theology — the reading in which the church inherits the covenant and Israel is set aside — has been taught a reading that the Joseph cycle refutes. When the exalted brother sees his family coming to him in famine, he does not declare that the family is set aside in favor of his Egyptian household. He brings his Egyptian household and his Canaanite brothers and his aged father and his nephew’s wives all into one room and calls them the one family. He includes, he does not replace. The widening of the covenant under the exalted brother is always a widening that keeps the original family. The gospel the New Testament preached, before centuries of Gentile-majority interpretation distorted it, was the gospel in which the Gentiles were brought in alongside and not instead of. Paul said this in Romans 11 in exactly so many words. The natural branches are not cast out. The wild branches are grafted in. Both bear fruit of the same root. And to the Torah observant reader who has dropped Paul over the replacement reading, the same Joseph cycle has something to say in the other direction. Paul did not teach replacement. Step 1 of the Methodological Sequence: where did Paul draw from. Paul drew from the Joseph pattern, from the Isaiah pattern, from the Ezekiel pattern. When he wrote that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, he meant that the social boundary that had been built between them was finished, not that their distinct covenant callings were abolished. Step 2: what did he argue against. He argued against a first-century school that was teaching Gentile believers that they had to become formal proselytes to Judaism — circumcision under the hand of the rabbis, formal submission to the oral law then being codified — in order to belong to the Messiah. Paul said no. The graft is already done. You do not need to be re-grafted by human hands. And he would have said, had he stood in a Torah observant room today, exactly the same thing he said then: hold the substance, drop the inherited lies, welcome the brother, welcome the stranger, do not build up the walls the Messiah has broken down. Drop the flattened Paul you were given by the institutional church. Do not drop Paul himself. The man wrote out of the Torah and the Prophets. Read him in their light and he comes back to you whole. The 1234 of Truth one more time, because it applies to the revelation scene. If any reading of what Joseph did at the reconciliation requires the conclusion that the commandments are no longer in force — that the covenant has dissolved, that the family has been replaced, that the Torah is cancelled, that any person can receive the feeding without walking in the commandment — then that reading has 1 John 2:3–4 against it. Joseph fed his brothers in the context of the covenant family he was still calling family. He did not dissolve the family. He did not dissolve the commandments. He dissolved the distance. Any gospel that dissolves the commandments in the name of grace has, by its own logic, dissolved the feeding. The feeding is a covenant feeding. The bread Joseph gave was his father’s bread, stored in his father’s land, preserved for his father’s sons. Grace is the feeding of a covenant family. Grace is not the dissolution of the family. The chapter closes with the brothers going back to Canaan to bring Jacob. They meet Serach, the daughter of Asher, a detail Jasher preserves that Genesis does not, and they commission her to play the harp before Jacob and sing to him that Joseph is still alive. Jacob hears the song and the spirit of Elohim comes upon him and he knows it is true. Then the sons arrive with the royal garments and the chariots and the treasures Joseph has sent. Jacob sees and believes. He says, it is enough; my son Joseph is still living; I will go and see him before I die. The cycle ends where it began in chapter 43, with a father being told something about a son. In chapter 43 he was told his son was dead, by a bloody coat, and he believed the lie for twenty-two years. In chapter 54 he is told his son is alive, first by a girl’s song and then by his own sons’ testimony and then by the gifts sent from the son’s own hand. And the spirit of Elohim that fell on him as he listened to the song was the witness that ratified the testimony. This is the order: the Spirit witnesses, the testimony is corroborated by the works (the gifts, the chariots, the robes), the father believes. It is the pattern the Father above uses to bring His children to the knowledge that the Son He sent is alive. The Spirit witnesses. The testimony of the Scriptures is corroborated by the visible works. The heart of the father — the heart of His people — is made alive to the news. I will go and see my son before I die. Every believer who has ever heard the Spirit and felt the old mourning break open has said the same thing in some form. My son is alive. I will go to Him. Chapter 54 closes here, with Jacob rising to put on the garments Joseph has sent and the whole house of Canaan rejoicing that Joseph is still alive. The actual descent into Egypt, the settlement in Goshen, the blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh with crossed hands, and Jacob’s prophetic blessings over the twelve sons belong to the next stretch of Jasher. Jasher locates them from chapter 55 forward, interwoven with the beginning of the oppression. We will take them up in the chapters that follow. A Pauline Coda: 1 Corinthians 10 and the Joseph Seed Before we close, one more Pauline passage belongs here, because the cycle we have just read is the root of a typology that Paul later draws on explicitly. In 1 Corinthians 10, Paul writes that all the fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink, for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them, and that Rock was the Messiah. Paul is treating the wilderness generation as a typological community, and he is saying that the provision they received in the wilderness was the provision of the Messiah Himself operating before His incarnation. Step 1 of the Methodological Sequence. Where was Paul drawing from. He was drawing from the exodus narrative, which begins in Joseph. The seed that multiplies into the nation that walks through the sea and eats the manna is the seed that Joseph planted when he brought the house of Jacob into Goshen at the end of the cycle we have just read. The spiritual food in the wilderness is the late echo of the physical food in Egypt that Joseph stored up. The Rock that followed the people in the wilderness is the same One who had led Joseph to Dothan so that the pit would receive him and the providence would begin. Paul is not spiritualizing the exodus. He is saying that the exodus was, from beginning to end, the operation of the Messiah through the seed of the Hebrews. That is exactly the reading the Joseph cycle bears when it is read straight. The Messiah is there from the pit to the throne to the famine to the feeding. Step 2 of the Methodological Sequence. What was Paul arguing against. He was arguing against a congregation in Corinth that had begun to treat the ordinances of the faith as magical covers for immorality, assuming that because they had been baptized and taken the supper they were safe regardless of how they were living. Paul pointed back at the wilderness generation to make the point with overwhelming clarity. They all ate. They all drank. They all had the Rock. And yet, Paul says, with many of them YAHUAH was not well pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness. Now these things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things. Read as our examples. This is the 1234 of Truth in Pauline form, and it is a rebuke to the same institutional reading of Paul that the Joseph cycle already rebukes. If eating of the bread Joseph stored up did not protect the wilderness generation from destruction when they lusted and committed fornication and murmured, the claim that any modern believer is protected from the consequences of unrepented sin by the mere fact of religious participation is exposed as a lie. Paul learned this lesson from Joseph’s household. We should learn it from Paul. Grace feeds the repentant. Grace does not cover the unrepentant. And a word to the Torah observant reader who may have, over the last years, dropped Paul because of the centuries of abuse of his letters. This is the Paul we are defending in the yoshi-voice framework. This is the Paul who said, let every man that names the name of the Messiah depart from iniquity. This is the Paul who said, shall we continue in sin that grace may abound? Elohim forbid. This is the Paul who wrote the book of Hebrews or inspired whoever wrote it, the book that holds up Joseph’s bones as a witness of patient covenant faith. This Paul is not the enemy of Torah. This Paul is the friend of Torah. When the twisted reading of Paul is set aside and the Pharisee who was trained at the feet of Gamaliel is allowed to speak in his own Torah voice, he becomes a witness for the very things the Hebrew roots community has rightly loved. Drop the lie about Paul. Do not drop Paul. The Joseph cycle is the Torah’s first complete rehearsal of the shape of the gospel. We have handled it carefully, tracing Joseph as the type of the Messiah, Judah as the type of the repentant man through whom the messianic line carries forward, the descent into Egypt as the first great furnace of covenant refinement, and the family as the physical seed of the scattered-Israel promise. We have named, through the chapters, the errors that inherited teaching has layered on top of this cycle. We have named the institutional reading that turned Joseph into a nice story about perseverance and stripped the Messiah pattern out of him. We have named the replacement reading that treated the reconciliation scene as the moment when the old family was finished, when in fact the reconciliation scene is the moment when the old family is preserved and widened. We have named the Hebrew roots replacement reading that treats the grafting-in passages as invitations for anyone to become Israel on their own terms, and we have held that against the specific physical fact of Manasseh and Ephraim being adopted in by the patriarch himself, not by their own initiative. We have named the false inclusion gospel and held the line that the covenant remains a covenant with a specific physical seed, and that the Father Himself adopts — we do not adopt ourselves. We have named the 1234 of Truth at the moment Joseph refused Potiphar’s wife, and at the moment of reconciliation where any reading that dissolves the commandments has been refuted by the passage itself. We have walked Step 1 and Step 2 of the Methodological Sequence for Paul at Hebrews 11 and at the reconciliation scene, establishing what Paul was drawing from in the Torah and what he was arguing against in the first-century distortion. And we have held, throughout, the victims-not-enemies posture. The brothers who sold Joseph were wrong. They were also not beyond mercy. Judah, who named the price for his brother, was wrong. He also became the forefather of the Messiah. Zelicah, who lied, was wrong. She was also, in the Jasher account, a specific woman in a specific moral collapse and not a stock figure usable against women as a class. Potiphar, who imprisoned an innocent man, was wrong. He was also a man, not a caricature of Egypt. The brothers who searched the harlot quarters for their brother were wrong in what their guess revealed about them. They were also still loved by the brother they had sold. Every single person in this cycle who sinned was loved through the sinning by someone whose love was not finished by the sin. That is the Father’s heart, and it is the heart of the entire More Than Milk Ministries series. The seed has been planted in Egypt. The household is about to go down. The next great movement in scripture is the oppression and the deliverance. We go there next. Sola YAHUAH. Sola the Torah and the Prophets. Sola the Messiah who walked them both. The scene in Jasher 54 and Genesis 45 is one of the longest sustained emotional passages in the Hebrew scriptures, and the details deserve slow reading because the pattern they trace is the pattern of the gathering the prophets promised. Joseph could not contain himself. "Then Joseph could not refrain himself before all them that stood by him; and he cried, Cause every man to go out from me. And there stood no man with him, while Joseph made himself known unto his brethren. And he wept aloud: and the Egyptians and the house of Pharaoh heard" (Genesis 45:1–2). The first movement is the removing of every witness. The reconciliation between the betrayed brother and the betrayers happens without an audience. The cosmic reconciliation between the two houses of Yashar'el, when it comes in its fullness, will have the same privacy — the Father's own hand, the Son's own face, the Spirit's own moving, without the pundits and the commentators and the systems that have made their living off the separation being allowed to manage the moment. Joseph insisted three times that the brothers come near. "And Joseph said unto his brethren, Come near to me, I pray you. And they came near. And he said, I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt. Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for Elohim did send me before you to preserve life" (Genesis 45:4–5). "Come near." The betrayed brother summons the betrayers out of their fear. The closer-than-they-could-have-imagined welcome — the man they sold now feeds them, provides for them, weeps over them — is the pattern Yahusha will extend to the whole covenant people in the final gathering. "Come near." No distance kept for punishment. No probationary distance imposed for their guilt to finish working its shame. "Come near." The brothers could not speak. "And his brethren could not answer him; for they were troubled at his presence" (Genesis 45:3). The stunning silence of men who know what they did and now stand before the one they did it to is part of every reconciliation. The Judahite reader who has missed the Messiah for two millennia will stand in that silence when the Messiah who came through Judah's line is revealed as the one Judah had missed. The Christian reader who has been told "the church replaced Israel" and who stands before the prophet-Messiah who identifies as the King of the Yahudim (Jews) at His return will stand in that silence. The Torah-observant reader who has claimed Ephraim identity on terms Paul did not grant and who will see what Paul actually wrote will stand in that silence. Every house has its version of the brothers-cannot-answer moment. The reconciliation requires the silence. Joseph's reframing of the whole history is the covenant word. "But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but Elohim meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive. Now therefore fear ye not: I will nourish you, and your little ones. And he comforted them, and spake kindly unto them" (Genesis 50:20–21). Twenty years of separation summarized in two sentences. The brothers' intent and the Father's purpose were running in opposite directions, and the Father's purpose was stronger. The evil they had done was real. The Father had not dissolved the history; He had turned it inside out. The brothers' betrayal became the mechanism by which the family was fed through the famine. The Father's good was larger than the brothers' evil. Romans 11:25–26 reads through this lens with new weight. "For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in. And so all Israel shall be saved." The fulness of the nations coming in is Joseph's Egyptian storehouse filling the world. The partial blindness of Yashar'el lifting is the brothers' eyes opening to the brother they had sold. All Israel saved is the whole family gathered at Joseph's table in the land of Goshen — the two-stick reunion that Ezekiel saw. The pattern is the pattern. The reader who puts this book down and looks up at the current moment — at the awakening movement running through Christianity, Judaism, Hebrew Roots, even Islam; at the scattered seed waking up in places the horn never expected; at the Yahudi (Jewish) scholars beginning to read the prophets with fresh eyes; at the Messiah Yahudah (Judah) had rejected being increasingly recognized as the one the prophets announced — is standing inside the pattern Joseph wrote for the Father twelve centuries before. The wagons are rolling toward Egypt. The storehouse is open. The betrayed brother weeps. The Father nourishes. The family reunites. The tears shed at great reconciliations in the covenant scriptures deserve to be counted together. Jacob and Esau at the ford of Jabbok — "and Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept" (Genesis 33:4). The prodigal son with his father — "his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). The disciples on the road to Emmaus when the risen Messiah broke bread and their eyes were opened (Luke 24:30–32) — unstated tears, but the "burning hearts" imply them. Every great scene of covenant reconciliation in the scriptures has the grammar of the fallen-on-the-neck embrace, the weeping, the words the parties could not manage before the Father's presence broke the silence. Joseph with his brothers is the first and the longest of these scenes. The Messiah's return in Revelation 1:7 — "and every eye shall see him, and they also which pierced him: and all kindreds of the earth shall wail because of him" — is the same grammar projected onto the cosmic scale. The fallen-on-the-neck embrace becomes the wail of every kindred seeing the face they had pierced. And yet the promise is not only the wail; the promise is that the piercers He came to save are gathered even as they mourn. "And so all Israel shall be saved" (Romans 11:26). The tears become the homecoming. The reader's own tears are part of this pattern. If the reader has wept over a broken family, a betraying brother, a father who died before reconciliation was made, a community that walked away, a spouse who left, a child who rebelled — the tears are not outside the covenant. The tears are the covenant's own language. The Father has been keeping every tear in His bottle (Psalm 56:8) and will empty the bottle back as joy when the gathering completes. Joseph's tears over his brothers, Rachel's tears for her children, Jacob's tears over the bloody coat, the Messiah's tears at Lazarus' grave and over Jerusalem's unresponsive heart — all are held in the same Father's hand, and all are being answered. The reconciliation is not a theological doctrine. It is a scene that has been rehearsed in the scriptures for the reader's specific comfort. The Father knows exactly how to close a broken family's story. The question is not whether He can. The question is whether the reader will come near when the call comes. Come near. Cross-references: Genesis 44; Genesis 45; Genesis 46:1–7; Zechariah 12:10; Romans 11:17–24; Ephesians 2:11–22; 1 John 4:19; Romans 5:8; 1 John 2:3–4.

chapters.title: The Descent into Goshen and the Storehouse of the Seed

verses.text: And it came to pass after this that Jacob said, I will go and see my son in Egypt and will then come back to the land of Canaan of which Elohim (God) had spoken to Abraham, for I cannot leave the land of my birth-place.
Behold the word of YAHUAH (the Lord) came to him, saying, Go down to Egypt with all your household and remain there, fear not to go down to Egypt for I will there make you a great nation.
And Jacob said within himself, I will go and see my son whether the fear of his Elohim is yet in his heart amidst all the inhabitants of Egypt.
And YAHUAH said to Jacob, Fear not about Joseph, for he still retains his integrity to serve me, as will seem good in your sight, and Jacob rejoiced exceedingly concerning his son.

At that time Jacob commanded his sons and household to go to Egypt according to the word of YAHUAH to him, and Jacob rose up with his sons and all his household, and he went out from the land of Canaan from Beersheba, with joy and gladness of heart, and they went to the land of Egypt.

And it came to pass when they came near Egypt, Jacob sent Judah before him to Joseph that he might show him a situation in Egypt, and Judah did according to the word of his father, and he hastened and ran and came to Joseph, and they assigned for them a place in the land of Goshen for all his household, and Judah returned and came along the road to his father.

And Joseph harnessed the chariot, and he assembled all his mighty men and his servants and all the officers of Egypt in order to go and meet his father Jacob, and Joseph’s mandate was proclaimed in Egypt, saying, All that do not go to meet Jacob shall die.

And on the next day Joseph went forth with all Egypt a great and mighty host, all dressed in garments of fine linen and purple and with instruments of silver and gold and with their instruments of war with them.

And they all went to meet Jacob with all sorts of musical instruments, with drums and timbrels, strewing myrrh and aloes all along the road, and they all went after this fashion, and the earth shook at their shouting.

And all the women of Egypt went upon the roofs of Egypt and upon the walls to meet Jacob, and upon the head of Joseph was Pharaoh’s regal crown, for Pharaoh had sent it to him to put on at the time of his going to meet his father.

And when Joseph came within fifty cubits of his father, he alighted from the chariot and he walked toward his father, and when all the officers of Egypt and her nobles saw that Joseph had gone on foot toward his father, they also alighted and walked on foot toward Jacob.
And when Jacob approached the camp of Joseph, Jacob observed the camp that was coming toward him with Joseph, and it gratified him and Jacob was astonished at it.

And Jacob said to Judah, Who is that man whom I see in the camp of Egypt dressed in kingly robes with a very red garment upon him and a royal crown upon his head, who has alighted from his chariot and is coming toward us? and Judah answered his father, saying, He is your son Joseph the king; and Jacob rejoiced in seeing the glory of his son.
And Joseph came nigh to his father and he bowed to his father, and all the men of the camp bowed to the ground with him before Jacob.

And behold Jacob ran and hastened to his son Joseph and fell upon his neck and kissed him, and they wept, and Joseph also embraced his father and kissed him, and they wept and all the people of Egypt wept with them.
And Jacob said to Joseph, Now I will die cheerfully after I have seen your face, that you are still living and with glory.
And the sons of Jacob and their wives and their children and their servants, and all the household of Jacob wept exceedingly with Joseph, and they kissed him and wept greatly with him.

And Joseph and all his people returned afterward home to Egypt, and Jacob and his sons and all the children of his household came with Joseph to Egypt, and Joseph placed them in the best part of Egypt, in the land of Goshen.

And Joseph said to his father and to his brethren, I will go up and tell Pharaoh, saying, My brethren and my father’s household and all belonging to them have come to me, and behold they are in the land of Goshen.
And Joseph did so and took from his brethren Reuben, Issachar Zebulun and his brother Benjamin and he placed them before Pharaoh.

And Joseph spoke to Pharaoh, saying, My brethren and my father’s household and all belonging to them, together with their flocks and cattle have come to me from the land of Canaan, to sojourn in Egypt; for the famine was sore upon them.
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, Place your father and brethren in the best part of the land, withhold not from them all that is good, and cause them to eat of the fat of the land.
And Joseph answered, saying, Behold I have stationed them in the land of Goshen, for they are shepherds, therefore let them remain in Goshen to feed their flocks apart from the Egyptians.

And Pharaoh said to Joseph, Do with your brethren all that they shall say to you; and the sons of Jacob bowed down to Pharaoh, and they went forth from him in peace, and Joseph afterward brought his father before Pharaoh.
And Jacob came and bowed down to Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh, and he then went out; and Jacob and all his sons, and all his household dwelt in the land of Goshen.

In the second year, that is in the hundred and thirtieth year of the life of Jacob, Joseph maintained his father and his brethren, and all his father’s household, with bread according to their little ones, all the days of the famine; they lacked nothing.

And Joseph gave to them the best part of the whole land; the best of Egypt had they all the days of Joseph; and Joseph also gave to them and to the whole of his father’s household, clothes and garments year by year; and the sons of Jacob remained securely in Egypt all the days of their brother.
And Jacob always ate at Joseph’s table, Jacob and his sons did not leave Joseph’s table day or night, besides what Jacob’s children consumed in their houses.
And all Egypt ate bread during the days of the famine from the house of Joseph, for all the Egyptians sold all belonging to them on account of the famine.

And Joseph purchased all the lands and fields of Egypt for bread on the account of Pharaoh, and Joseph supplied all Egypt with bread all the days of the famine, and Joseph collected all the silver and gold that came to him for the corn which they bought throughout the land, and he accumulated much gold and silver, besides an immense quantity of onyx stones, bdellium and valuable garments which they brought to Joseph from every part of the land when their money was spent.

And Joseph took all the silver and gold that came into his hand, about seventy two talents of gold and silver, and also onyx stones and bdellium in great abundance, and Joseph went and concealed them in four parts, and he concealed one part in the wilderness near the Red sea, and one part by the river Perath, and the third and fourth part he concealed in the desert opposite to the wilderness of Persia and Media.

And he took part of the gold and silver that was left, and gave it to all his brothers and to all his father’s household, and to all the women of his father’s household, and the rest he brought to the house of Pharaoh, about twenty talents of gold and silver.

And Joseph gave all the gold and silver that was left to Pharaoh, and Pharaoh placed it in the treasury, and the days of the famine ceased after that in the land, and they sowed and reaped in the whole land, and they obtained their usual quantity year by year; they lacked nothing.
And Joseph dwelt securely in Egypt, and the whole land was under his advice, and his father and all his brethren dwelt in the land of Goshen and took possession of it.

And Joseph was very aged, advanced in days, and his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, remained constantly in the house of Jacob, together with the children of the sons of Jacob their brethren, to learn the ways of YAHUAH and his law.

And Jacob and his sons dwelt in the land of Egypt in the land of Goshen, and they took possession in it, and they were fruitful and multiplied in it. « • • • Chapter 55 is the seam between the Joseph cycle and the Egypt cycle. The patriarch is still alive; the deliverer has not been born; the covenant family is about to take up residence in the land where it will be both preserved and nearly destroyed. Jasher gives us the entry scene in full color, and almost every detail matters. The first verse to sit with is verse 2. YAHUAH speaks to Jacob before he goes down. Fear not to go down to Egypt, for I will there make you a great nation. This is the verse that separates the Torah reader from the institutional reader. The institutional reading treats the descent into Egypt as an almost incidental piece of geography, a stage on the way to the real action at Sinai. The Torah reading treats it as a covenant act. YAHUAH is not merely permitting the descent. He is authoring it. The nation will be forged in Egypt. The promise to Abraham that his seed would be strangers in a land that was not theirs and would be afflicted there four hundred years is being fulfilled in the moment that Jacob loads his wagons. This is one of the Father’s most consistent patterns and one of the hardest to sit with. He leads His own people into the furnace because only a people tested in a furnace can be trusted with the land. Isaiah 48:10 later names this pattern explicitly: I have refined you, but not as silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of affliction. The furnace is the method. Egypt is the first one. Verse 7 is Joseph’s order: All that do not go to meet Jacob shall die. Jasher gives us a Joseph who is not simply the Pharaoh-appointed vizier but a man now exercising royal authority on behalf of his own father. The whole host of Egypt goes out in procession. Fine linen, purple, silver and gold instruments, drums and timbrels, myrrh and aloes strewn along the road. The pagan court of a pagan empire is called out to honor one aged Hebrew shepherd because the man ruling the empire knows who that shepherd is. This is the first picture in scripture of a pattern that will later reach its climax in Revelation: the kings of the nations bringing their glory into the city of the covenant God. It is Joseph-shaped because the gospel pattern is Joseph-shaped. The exalted brother brings the nations to meet the father. Jacob sees the camp coming and he asks Judah a question. Who is that man dressed in kingly robes with a royal crown upon his head, who has alighted from his chariot and is coming toward us? Judah answers: he is your son Joseph the king. The moment is small but it is luminous. Jacob cannot tell from the distance that the man in royal garments is his son. The son has been remade in the eyes of the world; only the eyes of those who already know him can name him. This is how every exalted messianic figure in scripture is identified. The outsider sees the robes and the crown. The insider sees the face. When the Messiah returns, the nations will see a king in glory. His own will see Him as the son they have loved. Verse 15 is the embrace. The text is explicit: Jacob ran. The old man ran. The patriarch who walked with a limp from Peniel, the man whose days of life were already one hundred and thirty years, ran. He did not stand on dignity. He did not wait for his son to come the final cubits. He hurried out to meet him. This is the hinge detail that the Messiah himself will later place inside the parable of the prodigal. When the son was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran. The father runs. The son has been away twenty-two years. The father runs. Hold this in the back of the mind every time any religious system tries to teach that the Father is reluctant, begrudging, slow, or quick to anger. The Father runs toward the returning son. He always has. Verses 18 through 25 place the family in Goshen. Goshen is geographically the best pasturage in the delta of the Nile. Theologically it is deliberately set apart. Joseph himself requests it from Pharaoh so that the Hebrews may remain shepherds apart from the Egyptians, for every shepherd is an abomination unto the Egyptians. The seed in the storehouse is to be kept distinct from the Egyptians even as it grows in the middle of Egypt. Paul’s later instruction in 2 Corinthians 6 that believers not be unequally yoked with unbelievers is not a new invention. It is a Goshen instinct. The covenant people dwell among the nations but do not merge with them. They take from Egypt the bread Egypt has stored; they do not take from Egypt their wives and their worship. The first step of the deliverance at the end is that the Hebrews do in fact carry out a substantial amount of Egypt’s wealth with them (Exodus 12:35–36). They do not carry out Egypt’s gods. A Goshen discipline preserved the seed. Verses 26 through 34 are the years of Joseph’s feeding of Egypt and the world. Jasher notes that Joseph gathered about seventy-two talents of gold and silver and a great abundance of onyx stones and bdellium and costly garments, and that he hid them in four places — near the Red Sea, by the river Perath, and two parts in the desert opposite the wilderness of Persia and Media. Then he gave part to his brothers and their households, gave twenty talents to Pharaoh, and retained the rest for later use. This is one of those Jasher details that institutional histories have rarely known what to do with. It matters theologically. The accumulated wealth of the famine was not spent and forgotten. It was stored. Some of it Joseph poured into his own household. Some of it went to Pharaoh. Much of it was hidden in the four corners where the seed of Israel would later walk, and some rabbinic traditions link the hidden stores to later figures and to the spoils of the Exodus itself. The framework does not stand or fall on the tradition. What it stands on is the pattern: what the exalted Hebrew stores up in the days of famine is not lost even when the famine ends. The wealth Joseph stored will continue to ripple through scripture, a reminder that the Father’s providence is never wasted, never fully spent, never lost. Verse 35 is the last note of the chapter and the most important for what follows. Joseph’s two sons Ephraim and Manasseh remained constantly in the house of Jacob, together with the children of the sons of Jacob their brethren, to learn the ways of YAHUAH and his law. Here is the sentence that makes the whole two-house framework go. Ephraim and Manasseh are not being absorbed into Egypt. They are being trained in the patriarch’s house in the ways of YAHUAH and His Torah. They are Hebrew boys learning Hebrew faith. The patriarch himself is discipling them. When Jacob adopts them formally in chapter 56, he is not adopting strangers. He is adopting the sons his own house has raised in the covenant. This matters for every later passage about the scattered house. Ephraim is not a generic name for everyone who reads the Torah. Ephraim is a specific tribe born into Joseph’s house in Egypt and raised under Jacob’s teaching. The scattered house of Israel that the prophets keep addressing is a physical people with a physical line, and Jasher is careful to plant that line’s covenant formation here at the beginning. Cross-references: Genesis 46:1–34; Genesis 47:1–12, 27–28; Genesis 15:13–16; Isaiah 48:10; Hebrews 11:13–16; Luke 15:20; 2 Corinthians 6:14–18; Revelation 21:24–26; 1 Peter 1:6–7.

chapters.title: The Death of Jacob, the Blessing of Judah, and the Funeral

verses.text: And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years, and the days of Jacob, and the years of his life were a hundred and forty seven years.
At that time Jacob was attacked with that illness of which he died and he sent and called for his son Joseph from Egypt, and Joseph his son came from Egypt and Joseph came to his father.

And Jacob said to Joseph and to his sons, Behold I die, and the Elohim (God) of your ancestors will visit you, and bring you back to the land, which YAHUAH (the Lord) sware to give to you and to your children after you, now therefore when I am dead, bury me in the cave which is in Machpelah in Hebron in the land of Canaan, near my ancestors.
And Jacob made his sons swear to bury him in Machpelah, in Hebron, and his sons swore to him concerning this thing.
And he commanded them, saying, Serve YAHUAH your Elohim (the Lord your God), for he who delivered your fathers will also deliver you from all trouble.

And Jacob said, Call all your children to me, and all the children of Jacob’s sons came and sat before him, and Jacob blessed them, and he said to them, YAHUAH Elohim (the Lord God) of your fathers shall grant you a thousand times as much and bless you, and may he give you the blessing of your father Abraham; and all the children of Jacob’s sons went forth on that day after he had blessed them.

And on the next day Jacob again called for his sons, and they all assembled and came to him and sat before him, and Jacob on that day blessed his sons before his death, each man did he bless according to his blessing; behold it is written in the book of the law of YAHUAH appertaining to Israel.
And Jacob said to Judah, I know my son that you are a mighty man for your brethren; reign over them, and your sons shall reign over their sons forever.
Only teach your sons the bow and all the weapons of war, in order that they may fight the battles of their brother who will rule over his enemies.
And Jacob again commanded his sons on that day, saying, Behold I shall be this day gathered to my people; carry me up from Egypt, and bury me in the cave of Machpelah as I have commanded you.
Howbeit take heed I pray you that none of your sons carry me, only yourselves, and this is the manner you shall do to me, when you carry my body to go with it to the land of Canaan to bury me,
Judah, Issachar and Zebulun shall carry my bier at the eastern side; Reuben, Simeon and Gad at the south, Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin at the west, Dan, Asher and Naphtali at the north.

Let not Levi carry with you, for he and his sons will carry the ark of the covenant of the YAHUAH with the Israelites in the camp, neither let Joseph my son carry, for as a king so let his glory be; howbeit, Ephraim and Manasseh shall be in their stead.

Thus shall you do to me when you carry me away; do not neglect any thing of all that I command you; and it shall come to pass when you do this to me, that YAHUAH will remember you favorably and your children after you forever.
And you my sons, honor each his brother and his relative, and command your children and your children’s children after you to serve YAHUAH Elohim of your ancestors all the days.

In order that you may prolong your days in the land, you and your children and your children’s children for ever, when you do what is good and upright in the sight of YAHUAH your Elohim, to go in all his ways.
And you, Joseph my son, forgive I pray you the prongs of your brethren and all their misdeeds in the injury that they heaped upon you, for Elohim intended it for your and your children’s benefit.

And O my son leave not your brethren to the inhabitants of Egypt, neither hurt their feelings, for behold I consign them to the hand of Elohim and in your hand to guard them from the Egyptians; and the sons of Jacob answered their father saying, O, our father, all that you have commanded us, so will we do; may Elohim only be with us.
And Jacob said to his sons, So may Elohim be with you when you keep all his ways; turn not from his ways either to the right or the left in performing what is good and upright in his sight.
For I know that many and grievous troubles will befall you in the latter days in the land, yea your children and children’s children, only serve YAHUAH and he will save you from all trouble.

And it shall come to pass when you shall go after Elohim to serve him and will teach your children after you, and your children’s children, to know YAHUAH, then will YAHUAH raise up to you and your children a servant from amongst your children, and YAHUAH will deliver you through his hand from all affliction, and bring you out of Egypt and bring you back to the land of your fathers to inherit it securely.
And Jacob ceased commanding his sons, and he drew his feet into the bed, he died and was gathered to his people.
And Joseph fell upon his father and he cried out and wept over him and he kissed him, and he called out in a bitter voice, and he said, O my father, my father.
And his son’s wives and all his household came and fell upon Jacob, and they wept over him, and cried in a very loud voice concerning Jacob.

And all the sons of Jacob rose up together, and they tore their garments, and they all put sackcloth upon their loins, and they fell upon their faces, and they cast dust upon their heads toward the heavens.
And the thing was told to Osnath Joseph’s wife, and she rose up and put on a sack and she with all the Egyptian women with her came and mourned and wept for Jacob.
And also all the people of Egypt who knew Jacob came all on that day when they heard this thing, and all Egypt wept for many days.
And also from the land of Canaan did the women come to Egypt when they heard that Jacob was dead, and they wept for him in Egypt for seventy days.

And it came to pass after this that Joseph commanded his servants the doctors to embalm his father with myrrh and frankincense and all manner of incense and perfume, and the doctors embalmed Jacob as Joseph had commanded them.

And all the people of Egypt and the elders and all the inhabitants of the land of Goshen wept and mourned over Jacob, and all his sons and the children of his household lamented and mourned over their father Jacob many days.

And after the days of his weeping had passed away, at the end of seventy days, Joseph said to Pharaoh, I will go up and bury my father in the land of Canaan as he made me swear, and then I will return.

And Pharaoh sent Joseph, saying, Go up and bury your father as he said, and as he made you swear; and Joseph rose up with all his brethren to go to the land of Canaan to bury their father Jacob as he had commanded them.
And Pharaoh commanded that it should be proclaimed throughout Egypt, saying, Whoever goes not up with Joseph and his brethren to the land of Canaan to bury Jacob, shall die.

And all Egypt heard of Pharaoh’s proclamation, and they all rose up together, and all the servants of Pharaoh, and the elders of his house, and all the elders of the land of Egypt went up with Joseph, and all the officers and nobles of Pharaoh went up as the servants of Joseph, and they went to bury Jacob in the land of Canaan.
And the sons of Jacob carried the bier upon which he lay; according to all that their father commanded them, so did his sons to him.

And the bier was of pure gold, and it was inlaid round about with onyx stones and bdellium; and the covering of the bier was gold woven work, joined with threads, and over them were hooks of onyx stones and bdellium.
And Joseph placed upon the head of his father Jacob a large golden crown, and he put a golden scepter in his hand, and they surrounded the bier as was the custom of kings during their lives.

And all the troops of Egypt went before him in this array, at first all the mighty men of Pharaoh, and the mighty men of Joseph, and after them the rest of the inhabitants of Egypt, and they were all girded with swords and equipped with coats of mail, and the trappings of war were upon them.
And all the weepers and mourners went at a distance opposite to the bier, going and weeping and lamenting, and the rest of the people went after the bier.

And Joseph and his household went together near the bier barefooted and weeping, and the rest of Joseph’s servants went around him; each man had his ornaments upon him, and they were all armed with their weapons of war.

And fifty of Jacob’s servants went in front of the bier, and they strewed along the road myrrh and aloes, and all manner of perfume, and all the sons of Jacob that carried the bier walked upon the perfumery, and the servants of Jacob went before them strewing the perfume along the road.

And Joseph went up with a heavy camp, and they did after this manner every day until they reached the land of Canaan, and they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which was on the other side of Jordan, and they mourned an exceeding great and heavy mourning in that place.
And all the kings of Canaan heard of this thing and they all went forth, each man from his house, thirty-one kings of Canaan, and they all came with their men to mourn and weep over Jacob.
And all these kings beheld Jacob’s bier, and behold Joseph’s crown was upon it, and they also put their crowns upon the bier, and encircled it with crowns.
And all these kings made in that place a great and heavy mourning with the sons of Jacob and Egypt over Jacob, for all the kings of Canaan knew the valor of Jacob and his sons.
And the report reached Esau, saying, Jacob died in Egypt, and his sons and all Egypt are conveying him to the land of Canaan to bury him.

And Esau heard this thing, and he was dwelling in mount Seir, and he rose up with his sons and all his people and all his household, a people exceedingly great, and they came to mourn and weep over Jacob.
And it came to pass, when Esau came he mourned for his brother Jacob, and all Egypt and all Canaan again rose up and mourned a great mourning with Esau over Jacob in that place
And Joseph and his brethren brought their father Jacob from that place, and they went to Hebron to bury Jacob in the cave by his fathers.

And they came to Kireath-arba, to the cave, and as they came Esau stood with his sons against Joseph and his brethren as a hindrance in the cave, saying, Jacob shall not be buried in it, for it belongs to us and to our father.

And Joseph and his brethren heard the words of Esau’s sons, and they were exceedingly wroth, and Joseph approached to Esau, saying, What is this thing which they have spoken? surely my father Jacob bought it from you for great riches after the death of Isaac, now five and twenty years ago, and also all the land of Canaan he bought from you and from your sons, and your seed after you.
And Jacob bought it for his sons and his seed after him for an inheritance for ever, and why speak you these things this day?
And Esau answered, saying, You speak falsely and utter lies, for I sold not anything belonging to me in all this land, as you say, neither did my brother Jacob buy aught belonging to me in this land.
And Esau spoke these things in order to deceive Joseph with his words, for Esau knew that Joseph was not present in those days when Esau sold all belonging to him in the land of Canaan to Jacob.
And Joseph said to Esau, Surely my father inserted these things with you in the record of purchase, and testified the record with witnesses, and behold it is with us in Egypt.
And Esau answered, saying to him, Bring the record, all that you will find in the record, so will we do.

And Joseph called to Naphtali his brother, and he said, Hasten quickly, stay not, and run I pray you to Egypt and bring all the records; the record of the purchase, the sealed record and the open record, and also all the first records in which all the transactions of the birth-right are written, fetch you.
And you shall bring them to us here, that we may know from them all the words of Esau and his sons which they spoke this day.

And Naphtali hearkened to the voice of Joseph and he hastened and ran to go down to Egypt, and Naphtali was lighter on foot than any of the stags that were upon the wilderness, for he would go upon ears of corn without crushing them.

And when Esau saw that Naphtali had gone to fetch the records, he and his sons increased their resistance against the cave, and Esau and all his people rose up against Joseph and his brethren to battle.

And all the sons of Jacob and the people of Egypt fought with Esau and his men, and the sons of Esau and his people were smitten before the sons of Jacob, and the sons of Jacob slew of Esau’s people forty men.

And Chushim the son of Dan, the son of Jacob, was at that time with Jacob’s sons, but he was about a hundred cubits distant from the place of battle, for he remained with the children of Jacob’s sons by Jacob’s bier to guard it.
And Chushim was dumb and deaf, still he understood the voice of consternation amongst men.

And he asked, saying, Why do you not bury the dead, and what is this great consternation? and they answered him the words of Esau and his sons; and he ran to Esau in the midst of the battle, and he slew Esau with a sword, and he cut off his head, and it sprang to a distance, and Esau fell amongst the people of the battle.
And when Chushim did this thing the sons of Jacob prevailed over the sons of Esau, and the sons of Jacob buried their father Jacob by force in the cave, and the sons of Esau beheld it.
And Jacob was buried in Hebron, in the cave of Machpelah which Abraham had bought from the sons of Heth for the possession of a burial place, and he was buried in very costly garments.
And no king had such honor paid him as Joseph paid to his father at his death, for he buried him with great honor like to the burial of kings.

And Joseph and his brethren made a mourning of seven days for their father. « • • • Jasher’s account of Jacob’s death is shorter and more compressed than Genesis 49. Where Genesis preserves the long poetic prophecies over each of the twelve sons — the Shiloh passage, Issachar as the strong ass, Dan as a serpent, Joseph the fruitful bough, Benjamin the ravenous wolf — Jasher preserves only the summary of the blessings and then gives its distinctive attention to the funeral procession. This is not a defect in Jasher. It is a deliberate division of labor: Jasher tells us what the Torah does not, and assumes we have the Torah in our hand for what the Torah already does. This is the place to slow down and hold the Genesis 49 blessings in view, because even though Jasher compresses them the theology they carry is load-bearing for everything that follows in scripture. Reuben loses his preeminence because of his defilement of his father’s bed — the firstborn who is not firstborn because the covenant does not transmit by birth-order alone but by character in the fear of YAHUAH. Simeon and Levi are scattered in Israel because of their violence at Shechem — a prophecy that will come partly to bitter fulfillment in Simeon’s absorption into Judah’s allotment and partly to glorious fulfillment in Levi’s scattering through the land as the priests who own no tribal territory but teach in every city. Judah receives the scepter. The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be. This is the deepest messianic prophecy in the Torah outside of Genesis 3:15 and Numbers 24:17. The scepter is the royal authority. Shiloh is the One to whom it truly belongs. The gathering of the people is the regathering at the end.
