Every reading of scripture that says the Sabbath was for the Jews under the old covenant and is now abolished has already failed at Genesis 2. The Sabbath belongs to every human made in the image of the Father who rested. The Torah command simply names for the redeemed community what the Father has already rested in from the foundation of the world. Colossians 2:16–17 is not abolishing the Sabbath; it is telling the gentile believers in Colossae not to let anyone judge them in the matter of holy days, because the body of Messiah — not the opinion of outside judges — is what sets the standard. Hebrews 4:9 says plainly there remaineth therefore a rest to the people of Elohim. The Sabbath stands. Cross-references: Exodus 4:10–17; 1 Corinthians 2:1–5; 2 Corinthians 12:9–10; Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 20:8–11; Isaiah 56:1–8; Isaiah 58:13–14; Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:1–11.

chapters.title: Moses at Eighteen, the Egyptian Struck Down, and the Angel

verses.text: And when Moses was eighteen years old, he desired to see his father and mother and he went to them to Goshen, and when Moses had come near Goshen, he came to the place where the children of Israel were engaged in work, and he observed their burdens, and he saw an Egyptian smiting one of his Hebrew brethren.

And when the man who was beaten saw Moses he ran to him for help, for the man Moses was greatly respected in the house of Pharaoh, and he said to him, My Lord attend to me, this Egyptian came to my house in the night, bound me, and came to my wife in my presence, and now he seeks to take my life away.

And when Moses heard this wicked thing, his anger was kindled against the Egyptian, and he turned this way and the other, and when he saw there was no man there he smote the Egyptian and hid him in the sand, and delivered the Hebrew from the hand of him that smote him.
And the Hebrew went to his house, and Moses returned to his home, and went forth and came back to the king’s house.
And when the man had returned home, he thought of repudiating his wife, for it was not right in the house of Jacob, for any man to come to his wife after she had been defiled.
And the woman went and told her brothers, and the woman’s brothers sought to slay him, and he fled to his house and escaped.
And on the second day Moses went forth to his brethren, and saw, and behold two men were quarreling, and he said to the wicked one, Why dost you smite your neighbor?

And he answered him and said to him, Who has set you for a prince and judge over us? dost you think to slay me as you did slay the Egyptian? and Moses was afraid and he said, Surely the thing is known?
And Pharaoh heard of this affair, and he ordered Moses to be slain, so Elohim (God) sent his angel, and he appeared to Pharaoh in the likeness of a captain of the guard.

And the angel of YAHUAH (the Lord) took the sword from the hand of the captain of the guard, and took his head off with it, for the likeness of the captain of the guard was turned into the likeness of Moses.
And the angel of YAHUAH took hold of the right hand of Moses, and brought him forth from Egypt, and placed him from without the borders of Egypt, a distance of forty days’ journey.
And Aaron his brother alone remained in the land of Egypt, and he prophesied to the children of Israel, saying,
Thus says YAHUAH Elohim (the Lord God) of your ancestors, Throw away, each man, the abominations of his eyes, and do not defile yourselves with the idols of Egypt.
And the children of Israel rebelled and would not hearken to Aaron at that time.
And YAHUAH thought to destroy them, were it not that YAHUAH remembered the covenant which he had made with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

In those days the hand of Pharaoh continued to be severe against the children of Israel, and he crushed and oppressed them until the time when Elohim sent forth his word and took notice of them. « • • • Chapter 71 gives us Moses as a young man. He goes out among his brethren. He sees an Egyptian taskmaster smiting a Hebrew. He looks this way and that way, and he kills the Egyptian and hides him in the sand. The next day he comes out again and sees two Hebrews striving together. He rebukes the one who is in the wrong. The Hebrew says to him, who made thee a prince and a judge over us? intendest thou to kill me as thou killedst the Egyptian? Moses realizes the matter is known. Word reaches Pharaoh. Pharaoh sends to have Moses executed. Moses flees. Jasher preserves a curious detail. When Pharaoh’s men came to strike off Moses’ head, the angel of YAHUAH descended, assumed the likeness of Moses, and took his place. The executioner struck, but the one struck was not Moses. Moses himself had already been taken away by the Father to a place of safety. Hold this loosely. Whether it is literally what happened or whether it is a theological way of saying the Father preserved Moses when the executioner came, the doctrine beneath is sound. The Father hides His servants when the executioner’s sword is raised before their time. He hid Elijah at Cherith. He hid Jeremiah in the pit. He hid David in the cave. He hid Athanasius in the desert. He hid the woman of Revelation 12 in the wilderness for one thousand two hundred and sixty days. He hides the believers of every age when their time is not yet, and He brings them out again when the hour is right. The specific mechanism of an angel’s body-swap is not doctrine. The pattern of divine preservation is. What is not in dispute from the canonical text is that Moses killed an Egyptian. Acts 7:24–25 gives us Stephen’s reading: Moses, seeing one of them suffer wrong, defended him, and avenged him that was oppressed, and smote the Egyptian; for he supposed his brethren would have understood how that Elohim by his hand would deliver them, but they understood not. Stephen reads this as Moses moving prematurely. Moses was right about what he was for. He was a deliverer. He was wrong about the timing. He was not yet forty. The people were not ready. The Father had not yet called him. Moses tried to start the deliverance forty years early and it cost him forty years of exile in Midian. Every zealous young believer should hear this carefully. The call to deliverance is real, but the timing is not yours. Moses had the right anointing and the wrong day. He had to spend forty years in Midian being broken of the timing of the palace before he could be entrusted with the timing of the burning bush. Exodus 3 comes after Exodus 2 for a reason. The bush does not burn until the man is empty enough to see it. The zealous killing of the Egyptian is evidence of the calling. It is not the execution of it. The deliverer must be prepared in the wilderness before he is sent back to the palace. And the rejection by the Hebrew on the second day — who made thee a prince and a judge over us? — is the first rejection of Moses by the people he came to save. It foreshadows the rejection of Yahusha by the same people. John 1:11 says He came unto his own, and his own received him not. Moses was rejected first. Stephen will make this connection explicit in Acts 7:35: this Moses whom they refused, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge? the same did Elohim send to be a ruler and a deliverer by the hand of the angel which appeared to him in the bush. The rejected one is the sent one. The one the people refused becomes the one YAHUAH uses. Cross-references: Exodus 2:11–15; Acts 7:23–29, 35; Hebrews 11:24–27; John 1:11; Luke 4:24; 1 Samuel 30:6; Galatians 6:9.

chapters.title: Moses in the Camp of Kikianus, the Siege of Cush, and the

verses.text: And it was in those days that there was a great war between the children of Cush and the children of the east and Aram, and they rebelled against the king of Cush in whose hands they were.
So Kikianus king of Cush went forth with all the children of Cush, a people numerous as the sand, and he went to fight against Aram and the children of the east, to bring them under subjection.
And when Kikianus went out, he left Balaam the magician, with his two sons, to guard the city, and the lowest sort of the people of the land.
So Kikianus went forth to Aram and the children of the east, and he fought against them and smote them, and they all fell down wounded before Kikianus and his people.
And he took many of them captives and he brought them under subjection as at first, and he encamped upon their land to take tribute from them as usual.

And Balaam the son of Beor, when the king of Cush had left him to guard the city and the poor of the city, he rose up and advised with the people of the land to rebel against king Kikianus, not to let him enter the city when he should come home.
And the people of the land hearkened to him, and they swore to him and made him king over them, and his two sons for captains of the army.
So they rose up and raised the walls of the city at the two corners, and they built an exceeding strong building.
And at the third corner they dug ditches without number, between the city and the river which surrounded the whole land of Cush, and they made the waters of the river burst forth there.
At the fourth corner they collected numerous serpents by their incantations and enchantments, and they fortified the city and dwelt in it, and no one went out or in before them.
And Kikianus fought against Aram and the children of the east and he subdued them as before, and they gave him their usual tribute, and he went and returned to his land.

And when Kikianus the king of Cush approached his city and all the captains of the forces with him, they lifted up their eyes and saw that the walls of the city were built up and greatly elevated, so the men were astonished at this.

And they said one to the other, It is because they saw that we were delayed, in battle, and were greatly afraid of us, therefore have they done this thing and raised the city walls and fortified them so that the kings of Canaan might not come in battle against them.

So the king and the troops approached the city door and they looked up and behold, all the gates of the city were closed, and they called out to the sentinels, saying, Open to us, that we may enter the city.
But the sentinels refused to open to them by the order of Balaam the magician, their king, they suffered them not to enter their city.
So they raised a battle with them opposite the city gate, and one hundred and thirty men of the army at Kikianus fell on that day.
And on the next day they continued to fight and they fought at the side of the river; they endeavored to pass but were not able, so some of them sank in the pits and died.
So the king ordered them to cut down trees to make rafts, upon which they might pass to them, and they did so.
And when they came to the place of the ditches, the waters revolved by mills, and two hundred men upon ten rafts were drowned.

And on the third day they came to fight at the side where the serpents were, but they could not approach there, for the serpents slew of them one hundred and seventy men, and they ceased fighting against Cush, and they besieged Cush for nine years, no person came out or in.
At that time that the war and the siege were against Cush, Moses fled from Egypt from Pharaoh who sought to kill him for having slain the Egyptian.
And Moses was eighteen years old when he fled from Egypt from the presence of Pharaoh, and he fled and escaped to the camp of Kikianus, which at that time was besieging Cush.
And Moses was nine years in the camp of Kikianus king of Cush, all the time that they were besieging Cush, and Moses went out and came in with them.

And the king and princes and all the fighting men loved Moses, for he was great and worthy, his stature was like a noble lion, his face was like the sun, and his strength was like that of a lion, and he was counsellor to the king.
And at the end of nine years, Kikianus was seized with a mortal disease, and his illness prevailed over him, and he died on the seventh day.
So his servants embalmed him and carried him and buried him opposite the city gate to the north of the land of Egypt.
And they built over him an elegant strong and high building, and they placed great stones below.
And the king’s scribes engraved upon those stones all the might of their king Kikianus, and all his battles which he had fought, behold they are written there at this day.
Now after the death of Kikianus king of Cush it grieved his men and troops greatly on account of the war.
So they said one to the other, Give us counsel what we are to do at this time, as we have resided in the wilderness nine years away from our homes.
If we say we will fight against the city many of us will fall wounded or killed, and if we remain here in the siege we shall also die.

For now all the kings of Aram and of the children of the east will hear that our king is dead, and they will attack us suddenly in a hostile manner, and they will fight against us and leave no remnant of us.
Now therefore let us go and make a king over us, and let us remain in the siege until the city is delivered up to us.
And they wished to choose on that day a man for king from the army of Kikianus, and they found no object of their choice like Moses to reign over them.
And they hastened and stripped off each man his garments and cast them upon the ground, and they made a great heap and placed Moses on it.
And they rose up and blew with trumpets and called out before him, and said, May the king live, may the king live!
And all the people and nobles swore to him to give him for a wife Adoniah the queen, the Cushite, wife of Kikianus, and they made Moses king over them on that day.
And all the people of Cush issued a proclamation on that day, saying, Every man must give something to Moses of what is in his possession.
And they spread out a sheet upon the heap, and every man cast into it something of what he had, one a gold earring and the other a coin.
Also of onyx stones, bdellium, pearls and marble did the children of Cush cast to Moses upon the heap, also silver and gold in great abundance.
And Moses took all the silver and gold, all the vessels, and the bdellium and onyx stones, which all the children of Cush had given to him, and he placed them amongst his treasures.

And Moses reigned over the children of Cush on that day, in the place of Kikianus king of Cush. « • • • Chapter 72 is the unique Jasher passage that the canonical Torah compresses to near-invisibility and that Stephen in Acts 7 seems to hint at when he tells us Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was mighty in words and in deeds, and when he counts forty full years in Egypt before Moses’ flight. Jasher gives the content of that forty years’ worth of experience. Moses, after fleeing Pharaoh, does not go directly to Midian. He goes south. He falls in with the army of Kikianus king of Cush, who has been campaigning away from his capital. During Kikianus’ absence his treacherous general Balaam (yes, the same Balaam — Jasher treats him as a single figure whose career spans decades) seized Cush’s capital city. Kikianus cannot retake it. He dies. The army elects Moses as king in Kikianus’ place, because of his wisdom and his skill in war. Moses takes the city by a stratagem involving storks trained to attack the defending snakes on the walls. Balaam flees. Moses reigns over Cush for forty years. He marries the queen Adoniah in a ceremonial sense but never consummates the marriage, because he had not been given to her by the Father and would not defile the wife of another king. After forty years the aging queen rises up in discontent. Moses peacefully steps down, blesses the kingdom, and leaves. Only then does he go to Midian. The historical weight of the passage is not what matters most. What matters is the theological shape. Three things to hold. First, the Hebrew-in-foreign-court pattern is established as a recurring form in the way the Father prepares His servants. Joseph in Pharaoh’s court. Moses in Pharaoh’s court and then in Cush’s court. Daniel in Babylon. Nehemiah in Shushan. Esther in Shushan. Mordecai in Shushan. Paul in the household of Caesar. The covenant servants are repeatedly seasoned in foreign power before they are given the work among the people of YAHUAH. The palace teaches them administration, diplomacy, and the limits of human glory. The wilderness teaches them dependence. Moses had both. Forty years in Pharaoh’s palace. Forty years in Cush’s. Forty years as a shepherd in Midian. One hundred and twenty years of preparation before the forty-year assignment with Israel in the wilderness began. The Father’s schools are thorough. No seminary in the world can match the curriculum of the Spirit. Second, the character of Moses shown in Jasher 72 is already the character of the Moses who will lead Israel. He does not take what has not been given to him. He refuses to consummate a marriage that has been politically arranged but not covenantally blessed. He refuses to hold a throne past the moment when the people he served want another. He leaves peacefully when the transition is offered. These are exactly the virtues of the Moses who in Numbers will beg the Father not to consume Israel in the wilderness, who will not lift himself up when his sister Miriam challenges him, who will refuse to seize the priesthood for his own line even when it would be easier, who will lay down the office at the end and bless Joshua as his successor without struggle. The man who did not grab Adoniah did not grab glory either. Meekness is not a trait Moses grew into late. It was in him from his youth. Numbers 12:3 says now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth. Jasher 72 lets us see the meekness at work in a pagan court before it is recorded in the canonical Torah on a mountain. Third, the continued presence of Balaam here bridges Jasher’s earlier portrait of him with the Balaam of Numbers. Balaam has been the perpetual anti-Moses figure from infancy. He counseled the murder of the Hebrew children. He betrayed the king of Cush. He fled from Moses when Moses took the capital. He will reappear in Numbers with hire in his hands, trying to curse Israel, only to be forced by the Father to bless. His final counsel to Balak — the doctrine of Balaam rebuked in Revelation 2:14 — will be to corrupt Israel through the daughters of Moab at Peor. Balaam will finally be killed by Israel in Numbers 31:8 in a small and unmemorable note. The man whose career was built on counseling destruction against Israel dies at Israel’s hand without a eulogy. The Father disposes of his enemies in time. Hold Jasher 72 loosely as history. Hold it firmly as a theological portrait. Moses the king of Cush is the same Moses who will be the prophet of Israel. The preparation is not wasted. And the Father, who can put a Hebrew on an African throne for forty years without anyone losing count of where the covenant runs, is not troubled by any throne anywhere. He does not need an approved platform to train His servants. He will use whatever throne is available and will take His servant off that throne at exactly the hour the next assignment begins. Cross-references: Acts 7:22–30; Exodus 2:15–22; Numbers 12:1–3; Numbers 22–24; Numbers 31:1–8, 16; Revelation 2:14; Deuteronomy 34:5–8; Daniel 1–6; Esther; Nehemiah 1–2.

chapters.title: The Storks, the Serpents, and the Taking of the City

verses.text: In the fifty-fifth year of the reign of Pharaoh king of Egypt, that is in the hundred and fifty-seventh year of the Israelites going down into Egypt, reigned Moses in Cush.
Moses was twenty-seven years old when he began to reign over Cush, and forty years did he reign.
And YAHUAH (the Lord) granted Moses favor and grace in the eyes of all the children of Cush, and the children of Cush loved him exceedingly, so Moses was favored by YAHUAH and by men.
And in the seventh day of his reign, all the children of Cush assembled and came before Moses and bowed down to him to the ground.
And all the children spoke together in the presence of the king, saying, Give us counsel that we may see what is to be done to this city.
For it is now nine years that we have been besieging round about the city, and have not seen our children and our wives.
So the king answered them, saying, If you will hearken to my voice in all that I shall command you, then will YAHUAH give the city into our hands and we shall subdue it.
For if we fight with them as in the former battle which we had with them before the death of Kikianus, many of us will fall down wounded as before.
Now therefore behold here is counsel for you in this matter; if you will hearken to my voice, then will the city be delivered into our hands.
So all the forces answered the king, saying, All that our Lord shall command that will we do.
And Moses said to them, Pass through and proclaim a voice in the whole camp to all the people, saying,
Thus says the king, Go into the forest and bring with you of the young ones of the stork, each man a young one in his hand.
And any person transgressing the word of the king, who shall not bring his young one, he shall die, and the king will take all belonging to him.
And when you shall bring them they shall be in your keeping, you shall rear them until they grow up, and you shall teach them to dart upon, as is the way of the young ones of the hawk.
So all the children of Cush heard the words of Moses, and they rose up and caused a proclamation to be issued throughout the camp, saying,
To you, all the children of Cush, the king’s order is, that you go all together to the forest, and catch there the young storks each man his young one in his hand, and you shall bring them home.
And any person violating the order of the king shall die, and the king will take all that belongs to him.

And all the people did so, and they went out to the wood and they climbed the fir trees and caught, each man a young one in his hand, all the young of the storks, and they brought them into the desert and reared them by order of the king, and they taught them to dart upon, similar to the young hawks.
And after the young storks were reared, the king ordered them to be hungered for three days, and all the people did so.

And on the third day, the king said to them, strengthen yourselves and become valiant men, and put on each man his armor and gird on his sword upon him, and ride each man his horse and take each his young stork in his hand.
And we will rise up and fight against the city at the place where the serpents are; and all the people did as the king had ordered.
And they took each man his young one in his hand, and they went away, and when they came to the place of the serpents the king said to them, Send forth each man his young stork upon the serpents.
And they sent forth each man his young stork at the king’s order, and the young storks ran upon the serpents and they devoured them all and destroyed them out of that place.
And when the king and people had seen that all the serpents were destroyed in that place, all the people set up a great shout.
And they approached and fought against the city and took it and subdued it, and they entered the city.
And there died on that day one thousand and one hundred men of the people of the city, all that inhabited the city, but of the people besieging not one died.
So all the children of Cush went each to his home, to his wife and children and to all belonging to him.
And Balaam the magician, when he saw that the city was taken, he opened the gate and he and his two sons and eight brothers fled and returned to Egypt to Pharaoh king of Egypt.
They are the sorcerers and magicians who are mentioned in the book of the law, standing against Moses when YAHUAH brought the plagues upon Egypt.
So Moses took the city by his wisdom, and the children of Cush placed him on the throne instead of Kikianus king of Cush.
And they placed the royal crown upon his head, and they gave him for a wife Adoniah the Cushite queen, wife of Kikianus.
And Moses feared YAHUAH Elohim (the Lord God) of his fathers, so that he came not to her, nor did he turn his eyes to her.
For Moses remembered how Abraham had made his servant Eliezer swear, saying to him, You shall not take a woman from the daughters of Canaan for my son Isaac.
Also what Isaac did when Jacob had fled from his brother, when he commanded him, saying, You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan, nor make alliance with any of the children of Ham.

For YAHUAH our Elohim (the Lord our God) gave Ham the son of Noah, and his children and all his seed, as slaves to the children of Shem and to the children of Japheth, and to their seed after them for slaves, forever.
Therefore Moses turned not his heart nor his eyes to the wife of Kikianus all the days that he reigned over Cush.

And Moses feared YAHUAH his Elohim (the Lord his God) all his life, and Moses walked before YAHUAH in truth, with all his heart and soul, he turned not from the right way all the days of his life; he declined not from the way either to the right or to the left, in which Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had walked.
And Moses strengthened himself in the kingdom of the children of Cush, and he guided the children of Cush with his usual wisdom, and Moses prospered in his kingdom.
And at that time Aram and the children of the east heard that Kikianus king of Cush had died, so Aram and the children of the east rebelled against Cush in those days.
And Moses gathered all the children of Cush, a people very mighty, about thirty thousand men, and he went forth to fight with Aram and the children of the east.
And they went at first to the children of the east, and when the children of the east heard their report, they went to meet them, and engaged in battle with them.
And the war was severe against the children of the east, so YAHUAH gave all the children of the east into the hand of Moses, and about three hundred men fell down slain.
And all the children of the east turned back and retreated, so Moses and the children of Cush followed them and subdued them, and put a tax upon them, as was their custom.
So Moses and all the people with him passed from there to the land of Aram for battle.
And the people of Aram also went to meet them, and they fought against them, and the YAHUAH delivered them into the hand of Moses, and many of the men of Aram fell down wounded.
And Aram also were subdued by Moses and the people of Cush, and also gave their usual tax.
And Moses brought Aram and the children of the east under subjection to the children of Cush, and Moses and all the people who were with him, turned to the land of Cush.

And Moses strengthened himself in the kingdom of the children of Cush, and YAHUAH was with him, and all the children of Cush were afraid of him. « • • • Chapter 73 opens the Cushite kingship with a military parable. The city has been besieged for nine years. The wall is guarded not by men but by serpents. The usual tactics have already cost the Cushite army too many men. Moses proposes a strange and patient plan. Every man is to go into the forest and take a young stork from the nest. Each family will rear its own stork in the wilderness and train it to dart upon prey the way a hawk does. At the end of the training the birds are kept hungry for three days. Then the army rides to the wall with a hungry trained stork in each man’s hand, and at the king’s word the birds are loosed on the serpents, and the serpents are devoured, and the wall falls. The picture is almost unbearably homely for a story about military conquest. Men in the forest climbing fir trees for nestling storks. Soldiers tending birds in the desert for months. Hungry birds let loose on snakes. And yet this is Jasher’s window onto the way the Father’s man in a foreign court wins his wars. Moses does not storm the wall. He does not out-violence the violence. He assembles the patience and the training and the small obedient instruments of the natural world, and at the word of the king those instruments do what no army could do for nine years. Isaiah will later say that they that wait upon YAHUAH shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles (Isaiah 40:31). The Cushite soldiers mount up with wings as storks. The deliverer is being taught, in a foreign kingdom, that the weapons of the righteous are not the weapons of the empire. Verse 28 is the note that makes this chapter load-bearing for everything ahead. Balaam the magician, when the city falls, opens a gate and escapes. He and his two sons and eight brothers flee to Egypt to Pharaoh’s court. Verse 29 is Jasher’s explicit identification: these are the sorcerers and magicians named in the book of the law who later stand against Moses when YAHUAH brings the plagues upon Egypt. The Balaam of the Cush campaign is the same Balaam who counselled the drowning of the Hebrew sons at Jasher 66. He is the same Balaam who will be summoned later by Balak of Moab to curse Israel at Jasher 85, and who will die by Israel’s sword at Jasher 86:8. Jasher is building one long arc around this man across more than a century of narrative time. The career anti-Moses counselor pops up at every covenant crisis. He advised Pharaoh at the drowning. He flees at the taking of the city. His sons serve as magicians at the plagues. He is hired to curse Israel from the Moabite hills. He survives by counsel at Peor. He dies by the sword. The Father is patient with His enemies, but the Father eventually disposes of them. Revelation 2:14 will name Balaam by name as the teacher whose error endures in the church at Pergamum — there is always a Balaam somewhere, and every age has to name him. Verse 32 is the moral hinge of Moses’ forty years in Cush. The Cushites place the royal crown upon his head and give him Adoniah the Cushite queen, widow of Kikianus, for a wife. Moses feared YAHUAH his Elohim and did not come to her. He did not turn his eyes to her. The footnote in verse 33 is theological. Moses remembered the oath Abraham had required of Eliezer — no daughter of Canaan for the son of the covenant — and the oath Isaac had required of Jacob. Moses is a Hebrew in a foreign kingship. The kingship is a real kingship. The throne is a real throne. The wife is waiting, the kingdom is at his command. Moses refuses the bed. For forty years. This is the discipline that makes the deliverer. Not the sword work. Not the stork trick. The long refusal in a foreign court of an intimacy that would have compromised the line. The Torah record is silent on the Cushite queen; Jasher gives us the moral anatomy of the silence. Joseph refused Zelicah for twelve years in Potiphar’s house. Moses refuses Adoniah for forty years on a throne. Daniel will refuse the king’s meat in Babylon. The pattern is older than all three: a Hebrew of the covenant in a foreign court keeps what must be kept even when keeping it costs him what the empire offers. Verse 37 is the summary Jasher wants read aloud. Moses feared YAHUAH all his life; Moses walked before YAHUAH in truth, with all his heart and soul; he did not turn from the right way all the days of his life; he did not decline either to the right or to the left, in which Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had walked. This is a 1 John 2:3–4 sentence written about a king on a Cushite throne. He knew YAHUAH and he kept His commandments — even the unwritten ones, even the implied ones, even the ones that cost him his bed. Contrast this with what is coming in the golden calf chapter at Jasher 82. Israel, only months out of Egypt, will cry out for a calf to go before them. Moses, forty years in a foreign court surrounded by foreign gods, held. The discipline forged in the furnace of Cush is what lets him stand between YAHUAH and the people at Sinai when the people fail. The deliverer must already have been delivered in himself before he can lead anyone else out. Cross-references: Genesis 24:3–4; Genesis 28:1; Exodus 7:11; Numbers 22–24; Numbers 31:8; Deuteronomy 23:4–5; Joshua 13:22; 2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11; Revelation 2:14; 1 John 2:3–4; Hebrews 11:24–27; Isaiah 40:31; Psalm 1.

chapters.title: The Long Geopolitical Interval

verses.text: In the end of years died Saul king of Edom, and Baal Chanan the son of Achbor reigned in his place.
In the sixteenth year of the reign of Moses over Cush, Baal Chanan the son of Achbor reigned in the land of Edom over all the children of Edom for thirty-eight years.
In his days Moab rebelled against the power of Edom, having been under Edom since the days of Hadad the son of Bedad, who smote them and Midian, and brought Moab under subjection to Edom.
And when Baal Chanan the son of Achbor reigned over Edom, all the children of Moab withdrew their allegiance from Edom.
And Angeas king of Africa died in those days, and Azdrubal his son reigned in his stead.

And in those days died Janeas king of the children of Chittim, and they buried him in his temple which he had built for himself in the plain of Canopia for a residence, and Latinus reigned in his stead.
In the twenty-second year of the reign of Moses over the children of Cush, Latinus reigned over the children of Chittim forty-five years.
And he also built for himself a great and mighty tower, and he built in it an elegant temple for his residence, to conduct his government, as was the custom.
In the third year of his reign he caused a proclamation to be made to all his skilful men, who made many ships for him.

And Latinus assembled all his forces, and they came in ships, and went in it to fight with Azdrubal son of Angeas king of Africa, and they came to Africa and engaged in battle with Azdrubal and his army.

And Latinus prevailed over Azdrubal, and Latinus took from Azdrubal the aqueduct which his father had brought from the children of Chittim, when he took Janiah the daughter of Uzi for a wife, so Latinus overthrew the bridge of the aqueduct, and smote the whole army of Azdrubal a severe blow.
And the remaining strong men of Azdrubal strengthened themselves, and their hearts were filled with envy, and they courted death, and again engaged in battle with Latinus king of Chittim.
And the battle was severe upon all the men of Africa, and they all fell wounded before Latinus and his people, and Azdrubal the king also fell in that battle.

And the king Azdrubal had a very beautiful daughter, whose name was Ushpezena, and all the men of Africa embroidered her likeness on their garments, on account of her great beauty and comely appearance.
And the men of Latinus saw Ushpezena, the daughter of Azdrubal, and praised her to Latinus their king.
And Latinus ordered her to be brought to him, and Latinus took Ushpezena for a wife, and he turned back on his way to Chittim.

And it was after the death of Azdrubal son of Angeas, when Latinus had turned back to his land from the battle, that all the inhabitants of Africa rose up and took Anibal the son of Angeas, the younger brother of Azdrubal, and made him king instead at his brother over the whole land at Africa.
And when he reigned, he resolved to go to Chittim to fight with the children of Chittim, to avenge the cause of Azdrubal his brother, and the cause of the inhabitants of Africa, and he did so.
And he made many ships, and he came in it with his whole army, and he went to Chittim.
So Anibal fought with the children of Chittim, and the children of Chittim fell wounded before Anibal and his army, and Anibal avenged his brother’s cause.
And Anibal continued the war for eighteen years with the children of Chittim, and Anibal dwelt in the land of Chittim and encamped there for a long time.
And Anibal smote the children of Chittim very severely, and he slew their great men and princes, and of the rest of the people he smote about eighty thousand men.

And at the end of days and years, Anibal returned to his land of Africa, and he reigned securely in the place of Azdrubal his brother. « • • • Chapter 74 reads on first glance like Jasher has wandered off into a political almanac. A king dies in Edom and is replaced. A king dies in Chittim and is replaced. Africa and Chittim war with each other. A man named Anibal rises and wars eighteen years with Chittim and kills eighty thousand. The Hebrew eye reading for the main story can be tempted to skim. Do not skim. What Jasher is doing in these interludes — chapter 74 here, earlier the Zepho cycle at Jasher 60 and 61, later the Abianus cycle in chapter 90 — is maintaining the book’s structural commitment to the nations. Jasher is a book of the upright. Its Torah-parallel spine is the seed of promise. But it refuses to forget that the nations are real, that their wars are real, that their kings die in specific years and are buried in specific tombs. This is the same posture the prophets will later take when they pause in the middle of speaking to Israel to deliver long burdens against Egypt, Tyre, Moab, Ammon, and Edom (Isaiah 13 through 23; Jeremiah 46 through 51; Ezekiel 25 through 32). The Father has not stopped watching the nations while He works on Israel. He has never stopped. The Babel-scattered families have kings and battles and deaths and successions, and all of it is held together in His providence even when no prophet is present to narrate it. There is one detail worth pausing on. Verse 5 notes that Angeas king of Africa dies and his son Azdrubal reigns. Verse 17 tells of Anibal son of Angeas — the younger brother — rising to avenge his brother and warring eighteen years in Chittim. These are not random names. Later Gentile history will know an Anibal in Chittim who will be remembered for warring many years against Italian peoples. Jasher is older than Rome by centuries, and Rome’s legends of Hannibal reach back into a family line Jasher already knew. The commentary does not need to stand or fall on the identification, but it does register the pattern. The movements of the nations Jasher is tracing are not isolated; they are the upstream currents of the Gentile histories that will be written in the centuries ahead. For the framework, two small notes. First, the chapter confirms that the length of time Moses reigned over Cush gave the Father time to rearrange the entire Mediterranean basin. Kings rose, kings fell, Africa warred with Chittim, eighty thousand men of Chittim died in a war the Hebrews never saw, and all of it was happening while the Hebrew in the furnace of foreign kingship kept his eyes off of Adoniah. The Father is always doing more than one thing at once. Second, when Anibal avenges his brother Azdrubal with eighteen years of war and eighty thousand dead, Jasher lets the reader see the ordinary human economy of empire: it costs people, it takes decades, and the kings remembered by name are remembered because someone paid for their names in blood. The Father’s economy runs differently. He delivers a whole nation with a lamb and a band of hyssop and a trained stick. Cross-references: Genesis 25:30, 36:31–39; Deuteronomy 2:4–8; Isaiah 13–23; Jeremiah 46–51; Ezekiel 25–32; Amos 1–2; Psalm 2; Acts 17:26.

chapters.title: The Ephraimite False Exodus

verses.text: At that time, in the hundred and eightieth year of the Israelites going down into Egypt, there went forth from Egypt valiant men, thirty thousand on foot, from the children of Israel, who were all of the tribe of Joseph, of the children of Ephraim the son of Joseph.
For they said the period was completed which YAHUAH (the Lord) had appointed to the children of Israel in the times of old, which he had spoken to Abraham.

And these men girded themselves, and they put each man his sword at his side, and every man his armor upon him, and they trusted to their strength, and they went out together from Egypt with a mighty hand.

But they brought no provision for the road, only silver and gold, not even bread for that day did they bring in their hands, for they thought of getting their provision for pay from the Philistines, and if not they would take it by force.
And these men were very mighty and valiant men, one man could pursue a thousand and two could rout ten thousand, so they trusted to their strength and went together as they were.
And they directed their course toward the land of Gath, and they went down and found the shepherds of Gath feeding the cattle of the children of Gath.
And they said to the shepherds, Give us some of the sheep for pay, that we may eat, for we are hungry, for we have eaten no bread this day.
And the shepherds said, Are they our sheep or cattle that we should give them to you even for pay? so the children of Ephraim approached to take them by force.
And the shepherds of Gath shouted over them that their cry was heard at a distance, so all the children of Gath went out to them.

And when the children of Gath saw the evil doings of the children of Ephraim, they returned and assembled the men of Gath, and they put on each man his armor, and came forth to the children of Ephraim for battle.
And they engaged with them in the valley of Gath, and the battle was severe, and they smote from each other a great many on that day.
And on the second day the children of Gath sent to all the cities of the Philistines that they should come to their help, saying,
Come up to us and help us, that we may smite the children of Ephraim who have come forth from Egypt to take our cattle, and to fight against us without cause.

Now the souls of the children of Ephraim were exhausted with hunger and thirst, for they had eaten no bread for three days. And forty thousand men went forth from the cities of the Philistines to the assistance of the men of Gath.
And these men were engaged in battle with the children of Ephraim, and YAHUAH delivered the children of Ephraim into the hands of the Philistines.
And they smote all the children of Ephraim, all who had gone forth from Egypt, none were remaining but ten men who had run away from the engagement.

For this evil was from YAHUAH against the children of Ephraim, for they transgressed the word of YAHUAH in going forth from Egypt, before the period had arrived which YAHUAH in the days of old had appointed to Israel.
And of the Philistines also there fell a great many, about twenty thousand men, and their brethren carried them and buried them in their cities.
And the slain of the children of Ephraim remained forsaken in the valley of Gath for many days and years, and were not brought to burial, and the valley was filled with men’s bones.
And the men who had escaped from the battle came to Egypt, and told all the children of Israel all that had befallen them.
And their father Ephraim mourned over them for many days, and his brethren came to console him.

And he came to his wife and she bare a son, and he called his name Beriah, for she was unfortunate in his house. « • • • Chapter 75 is one of the most load-bearing chapters in Jasher for the framework this commentary is holding, and it is also one of the most routinely skipped by edition-readers who treat Jasher as a curiosity rather than as a covenant narrative. Stay with it. Thirty thousand men of the tribe of Ephraim left Egypt thirty years before the Exodus. They calculated the four hundred years prophesied to Abraham in Genesis 15:13 from a date of their own choosing, armored themselves, took silver and gold but no provisions, and marched out by the coastal road toward Canaan trusting in their own strength. At Gath they demanded food from the Philistine shepherds, and when refused they tried to take the flocks by force. The Philistines mustered, the men of Gath sent for reinforcement to the other Philistine cities, and forty thousand Philistine soldiers met the starved Ephraimites in the valley of Gath. All thirty thousand of the children of Ephraim died. Verse 17 is the explicit Jasher verdict. This evil was from YAHUAH against the children of Ephraim, for they transgressed the word of YAHUAH in going forth from Egypt before the period had arrived which YAHUAH in the days of old had appointed to Israel. Psalm 78:9 reaches back to this moment. The children of Ephraim, being armed and carrying bows, turned back in the day of battle. Whole books of commentary on that verse have been written without the Jasher detail, and the verse sits in the psalm like a mystery. With Jasher in hand, the verse becomes plain. The children of Ephraim went out armed and carrying bows. They turned back — they were routed — in the day of battle. Psalm 78 is naming this exact Jasher event as a cautionary hinge in the long rehearsal of Israel’s failures. The psalmist explicitly contrasts it with the way the Father later delivered Israel in His own timing: He brought them out with His hand stretched out, He divided the sea and made them to pass through, He led them with a cloud by day and all night with a light of fire. The difference between the Ephraimite disaster and the Exodus under Moses is not the reality of the Abrahamic promise. Both groups believed the promise. The difference is timing and obedience. The Ephraimites calculated their own exodus from their own reading of the four hundred years. Moses waited for the word of YAHUAH at the bush. This chapter is the most important early-warning text in Jasher for the two-house framework. Ephraim — the tribe that will become the father of the scattered northern kingdom — is already in chapter 75 getting ahead of YAHUAH’s timing. The tribal character is there three centuries before the tribal politics. Ephraim will later split from Judah at the death of Solomon, set up its own calves at Dan and Bethel, and be scattered among the nations by Assyria. The root of every one of those later acts is visible here. The Father loves Ephraim. The Father is going to bring Ephraim back. Ezekiel 37 is explicit about both. But Ephraim’s besetting sin is always running ahead of the word and then needing to be regathered from the consequences. Jeremiah 31:18–20 is the Father’s mother-heart over Ephraim: is Ephraim my dear son? is he a pleasant child? for since I spoke against him, I do earnestly remember him still; therefore my bowels are troubled for him; I will surely have mercy upon him, says YAHUAH. The same Father who let thirty thousand Ephraimites die in the valley of Gath for moving too soon is the Father weeping over His pleasant child in Jeremiah 31 and promising to regather him in Ezekiel 37. For the awakening believer in the Hebrew roots and Torah observant movements, this chapter carries a specific pastoral word. Ephraim’s name is on the movement. Much of what the movement is recovering is the inheritance of Ephraim. That is a right instinct. It is also a dangerous instinct if it is not disciplined by the lesson of this chapter. The movement is prone to running ahead of YAHUAH’s timing — setting its own dates for regathering, its own ways of calculating return, its own coalitions against Philistine powers, its own silver-and-gold-but-no-provisions departures from the institutional systems. Jasher 75 is the warning shot. Ephraim’s timing is not Ephraim’s to set. The four hundred years are the Father’s to count. The regathering will happen. It will not happen because we calculated it. It will happen because He spoke it. A second pastoral note. Verse 21 says that their father Ephraim mourned over them for many days, and his brethren came to console him. Verse 22 says he came to his wife and she bare a son, and he called his name Beriah, for she was unfortunate in his house. The grief is not hidden. The patriarch Ephraim, already dead in Egypt, is pictured in Jasher as grieving over thirty thousand of his children who ran ahead and died. This is another shape of the Father’s grief over every generation of Ephraim that has run ahead and paid for it. The remedy is not self-flagellation. The remedy is Jeremiah 31:18: turn me, and I shall be turned, for you are YAHUAH my Elohim. The regathering is not earned by the readers of this commentary. It is received when the readers of this commentary let YAHUAH set the time. Refuting the false inclusion gospel here matters. Some readings of Jasher 75 have been used to argue that the Ephraimite disaster proves the scattered-Israel framework is fragile and must be supplemented by a spiritual inclusion of anyone who keeps Torah. That reading inverts the chapter. Jasher 75 does not cast doubt on the physicality of the Ephraimite line; it doubles down on it. These are specific sons of Ephraim, named by tribe, dying in a specific valley. Their error is that they did not wait for YAHUAH to fulfill His word to their specific line. The answer to their error is not to widen the line until anyone can be Ephraim; it is to teach Ephraim to wait for the Father. The chapter is a Two-House text, not an anti-Two-House text. Cross-references: Genesis 15:13–16; Exodus 12:40–41; Numbers 14:25; Psalm 78:9–11, 41–42, 52–53; Jeremiah 31:18–20; Ezekiel 37:15–28; Hosea 11:1–11; 1 Chronicles 7:20–22; Proverbs 19:2; Ecclesiastes 3:1; Habakkuk 2:3; Luke 17:20–21; 2 Peter 3:9.

chapters.title: The Return from Cush and the Sickness of Pharaoh

verses.text: And Moses the son of Amram was still king in the land of Cush in those days, and he prospered in his kingdom, and he conducted the government of the children of Cush in justice, in righteousness, and integrity.
And all the children of Cush loved Moses all the days that he reigned over them, and all the inhabitants of the land of Cush were greatly afraid of him.
And in the fortieth year of the reign of Moses over Cush, Moses was sitting on the royal throne whilst Adoniah the queen was before him, and all the nobles were sitting around him.
And Adoniah the queen said before the king and the princes, What is this thing which you, the children of Cush, have done for this long time?
Surely you know that for forty years that this man has reigned over Cush he has not approached me, nor has he served the gods of the children of Cush.
Now therefore hear, O you children of Cush, and let this man no more reign over you as he is not of our flesh.
Behold Menacrus my son is grown up, let him reign over you, for it is better for you to serve the son of your Lord, than to serve a stranger, slave of the king of Egypt.
And all the people and nobles of the children of Cush heard the words which Adoniah the queen had spoken in their ears.
And all the people were preparing until the evening, and in the morning they rose up early and made Menacrus, son of Kikianus, king over them.

And all the children of Cush were afraid to stretch forth their hand against Moses, for the YAHUAH (the Lord) was with Moses, and the children of Cush remembered the oath which they swore to Moses, therefore they did no harm to him.
But the children of Cush gave many presents to Moses, and sent him from them with great honor.

So Moses went forth from the land of Cush, and went home and ceased to reign over Cush, and Moses was sixty-six years old when he went out of the land of Cush, for the thing was from YAHUAH, for the period had arrived which he had appointed in the days of old, to bring forth Israel from the affliction of the children of Ham.
So Moses went to Midian, for he was afraid to return to Egypt on account of Pharaoh, and he went and sat at a well of water in Midian.
And the seven daughters of Reuel the Midianite went out to feed their father’s flock.
And they came to the well and drew water to water their father’s flock.
So the shepherds of Midian came and drove them away, and Moses rose up and helped them and watered the flock.
And they came home to their father Reuel, and told him what Moses did for them.
And they said, An Egyptian man has delivered us from the hands of the shepherds, he drew up water for us and watered the flock.
And Reuel said to his daughters, And where is he? therefore have you left the man?
And Reuel sent for him and fetched him and brought him home, and he ate bread with him.

And Moses related to Reuel that he had fled from Egypt and that he reigned forty years over Cush, and that they afterward had taken the government from him, and had sent him away in peace with honor and with presents.
And when Reuel had heard the words of Moses, Reuel said within himself, I will put this man into the prison house, by which I shall conciliate the children of Cush, for he has fled from them.

And they took and put him into the prison house, and Moses was in prison ten years, and whilst Moses was in the prison house, Zipporah the daughter of Reuel took pity over him, and supported him with bread and water all the time.
And all the children of Israel were yet in the land of Egypt serving the Egyptians in all manner of hard work, and the hand of Egypt continued in severity over the children of Israel in those days.

At that time YAHUAH smote Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he afflicted with the plague of leprosy from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head; owing to the cruel treatment of the children of Israel was this plague at that time from YAHUAH upon Pharaoh king of Egypt.
For YAHUAH had hearkened to the prayer of his people the children of Israel, and their cry reached him on account of their hard work.

Still his anger did not turn from them, and the hand of Pharaoh was still stretched out against the children of Israel, and Pharaoh hardened his neck before YAHUAH, and he increased his yoke over the children of Israel, and embittered their lives with all manner of hard work.
And when YAHUAH had inflicted the plague upon Pharaoh king of Egypt, he asked his wise men and sorcerers to cure him.
And his wise men and sorcerers said to him, That if the blood of little children were put into the wounds he would be healed.
And Pharaoh hearkened to them, and sent his ministers to Goshen to the children of Israel to take their little children.

And Pharaoh’s ministers went and took the infants of the children of Israel from the bosoms of their mothers by force, and they brought them to Pharaoh daily, a child each day, and the physicians killed them and applied them to the plague; thus did they all the days.
And the number of the children which Pharaoh slew was three hundred and seventy-five.
But YAHUAH hearkened not to the physicians of the king of Egypt, and the plague went on increasing mightily.
And Pharaoh was ten years afflicted with that plague, still the heart of Pharaoh was more hardened against the children of Israel.
And at the end of ten years YAHUAH continued to afflict Pharaoh with destructive plagues.
And YAHUAH smote him with a bad tumor and sickness at the stomach, and that plague turned to a severe boil.

At that time the two ministers of Pharaoh came from the land of Goshen where all the children of Israel were, and went to the house of Pharaoh and said to him, We have seen the children of Israel slacken in their work and negligent in their labor.
And when Pharaoh heard the words of his ministers, his anger was kindled against the children of Israel exceedingly, for he was greatly grieved at his bodily pain.

And he answered and said, Now that the children of Israel know that I am ill, they turn and scoff at us, now therefore harness my chariot for me, and I will betake myself to Goshen and will see the scoff of the children of Israel with which they are deriding me; so his servants harnessed the chariot for him.
And they took and made him ride upon a horse, for he was not able to ride of himself;
And he took with him ten horsemen and ten footmen, and went to the children of Israel to Goshen.

And when they had come to the border of Egypt, the king’s horse passed into a narrow place, elevated in the hollow part of the vineyard, fenced on both sides, the low, plain country being on the other side.
And the horses ran rapidly in that place and pressed each other, and the other horses pressed the king’s horse.

And the king’s horse fell into the low plain whilst the king was riding upon it, and when he fell the chariot turned over the king’s face and the horse lay upon the king, and the king cried out, for his flesh was very sore.

And the flesh of the king was torn from him, and his bones were broken and he could not ride, for this thing was from YAHUAH to him, for YAHUAH had heard the cries of his people the children of Israel and their affliction.
And his servants carried him upon their shoulders, a little at a time, and they brought him back to Egypt, and the horsemen who were with him came also back to Egypt.
And they placed him in his bed, and the king knew that his end was come to die, so Aparanith the queen his wife came and cried before the king, and the king wept a great weeping with her.
And all his nobles and servants came on that day and saw the king in that affliction, and wept a great weeping with him.
And the princes of the king and all his counselors advised the king to cause one to reign in his stead in the land, whomsoever he should choose from his sons.
And the king had three sons and two daughters which Aparanith the queen his wife had borne to him, besides the king’s children of concubines.
And these were their names, the firstborn Othri, the second Adikam, and the third Morion, and their sisters, the name of the elder Bathia and of the other Acuzi.
And Othri the first born of the king was an idiot, precipitate and hurried in his words.
But Adikam was a cunning and wise man and knowing in all the wisdom of Egypt, but of unseemly aspect, thick in flesh, and very short in stature; his height was one cubit.
And when the king saw Adikam his son intelligent and wise in all things, the king resolved that he should be king in his stead after his death.
And he took for him a wife Gedudah daughter of Abilot, and he was ten years old, and she bare to him four sons.
And he afterward went and took three wives and begat eight sons and three daughters.
And the disorder greatly prevailed over the king, and his flesh stank like the flesh of a carcass cast upon the field in summer time, during the heat of the sun.
And when the king saw that his sickness had greatly strengthened itself over him, he ordered his son Adikam to be brought to him, and they made him king over the land in his place.
And at the end of three years, the king died, in shame, disgrace, and disgust, and his servants carried him and buried him in the sepulcher of the kings of Egypt in Zoan Mizraim.
But they embalmed him not as was usual with kings, for his flesh was putrid, and they could not approach to embalm him on account of the stench, so they buried him in haste.
For this evil was from YAHUAH to him, for YAHUAH had requited him evil for the evil which in his days he had done to Israel.

And he died with terror and with shame, and his son Adikam reigned in his place.< « • • • Two stories cross in chapter 76. The fortieth year of Moses’ Cushite reign ends when Adoniah the Cushite queen publicly calls out that for forty years Moses has not approached her and has not served the gods of Cush. The nobles hear it. They wait until morning. They make Menacrus, son of the former king Kikianus, king in his stead. They cannot harm Moses because of the oath they swore to him and because YAHUAH is with him. But they send him away with gifts and honor, and the sixty-six-year-old Moses leaves Cush for the first time in forty years and heads to Midian. Verse 12 is the theological key. The thing was from YAHUAH, for the period had arrived which He had appointed. The forty-year reign in Cush was not dead time. It was sealed time. The deliverer’s hidden decades in a foreign kingship were measured to the day, and when the measure was complete he was released. The same providence that sent Joseph down to Egypt in a caravan of Ishmaelites sends Moses up from Cush in a procession of gifts. The same providence that hid David seven years as a fugitive before enthroning him in Hebron is hiding Moses forty years in Cush before commissioning him at Horeb. Every awakening believer who is in a hidden season can take Jasher 76:12 as personal address. The period is being measured. The release will be on time. The hidden kingship of the Hebrew in a foreign court is part of the preparation, not a distraction from it. Verse 13 to 23 pivot to Reuel’s well. Moses comes to Midian and sits at a well. The seven daughters of Reuel come to water their father’s flock and the shepherds drive them away. Moses rises and helps them and waters the flock. They tell their father, an Egyptian man has delivered us. Reuel sends for him and Moses tells Reuel he fled from Egypt forty years ago, reigned over Cush, and has been dismissed in honor. Reuel’s response in verse 22 is unsettling. He says to himself, I will put this man into prison, by which I shall conciliate the children of Cush, for he has fled from them. He imprisons Moses for ten years. Zipporah Reuel’s daughter supports him secretly with bread and water. Jasher’s Reuel is not the simple priest-of-Midian of Exodus 2. He is a political calculator. He sees a political opportunity in Moses’ arrival and takes it. Ten years of prison. The second man handed to a foreign court in chains, hidden for a stretch, sustained quietly by a woman of the household. The pattern holds with Joseph in Potiphar’s prison, with Moses in Reuel’s prison, and eventually with the greater Son in the tomb. The Father uses the binding, not just the release. Zipporah keeping Moses alive with bread and water is the woman’s quiet covenant faithfulness at work inside the court that has locked up the deliverer. There is more than one Zipporah in scripture whose name is rarely said out loud. Rahab. Ruth. The Shunammite. The unnamed women in the royal houses of Israel and of the nations who knew what to do when the Father’s man needed bread. Jasher remembers this one. Verses 25 through 36 turn to Egypt. YAHUAH smites Pharaoh with leprosy from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. Pharaoh’s magicians advise him that only the blood of little children put into the wounds can heal him. Pharaoh hears them and sends to Goshen and they take infants of the children of Israel from the bosoms of their mothers by force, one child each day, and the physicians kill the child and apply the child to the plague. Three hundred and seventy-five children. Ten years. The plague does not heal. The heart of Pharaoh is hardened further. The hand of Pharaoh is still stretched out against the children of Israel. This is one of the chapters modern readers want to look away from. Do not look away. The Pharaoh of the oppression is sick, and his sickness is the kind of sickness empires give themselves when they build their economy on the labor of the covenant people. The proposed cure is the blood of the very children whose parents are being worked to death. Empire consumes its host. The lie of modern civilization that has inherited the leverage of Pharaoh’s Egypt is still asking the same question in different words. Whose children can we sacrifice to sustain the palace? Whose invisible labor will keep the pyramid rising? The Father’s answer in 76:45 is categorical. The hoofbeats of the king’s horse press upon each other, the king’s horse falls, the chariot turns over the king’s face, the horse lies upon him, and the flesh of the king is torn from him and his bones are broken and he cannot ride. For this thing was from YAHUAH to him, for YAHUAH had heard the cries of His people the children of Israel and their affliction. The empire that tries to cure itself with the blood of the children gets crushed under its own horse. Hold the victims-not-enemies posture here. The Pharaoh of Jasher 76 is a specific man named Melol, the Pharaoh who will die in bitterness and disgrace before the deliverer ever returns to Egypt. His son Adikam will be harder. The Egyptian people of Jasher 76 are not villains in a cartoon. The magicians and physicians who advise the infant murder bear specific guilt. The ministers who carry out the decree bear specific guilt. The palace staff who look the other way bear specific guilt. The working Egyptian people in the fields who never saw what happened in Goshen do not bear that specific guilt. They will still lose their firstborn at the tenth plague, because they lived inside an economy they did not build and could not escape. This is the victims-not-enemies posture held tight. The specific wicked are specifically wicked. The ordinary people are caught. The Father sees both and judges both — the wicked by name, the caught ones by mercy where He can give it. Cross-references: Genesis 12:17; Genesis 20:7, 17–18; Exodus 2:15–22; Exodus 7:11; Job 2:7; Isaiah 14:9–17; Ezekiel 29:3–5; Ezekiel 31; Proverbs 16:18; Proverbs 28:16; Revelation 18:2, 24; Matthew 23:35; Matthew 25:40; 1 John 2:3–4.

chapters.title: Adikam, the Bricks in the Wall, and the Sapphire Stick of

verses.text: Adikam was twenty years old when he reigned over Egypt, he reigned four years.
In the two hundred and sixth year of Israel’s going down to Egypt did Adikam reign over Egypt, but he continued not so long in his reign over Egypt as his fathers had continued their reigns.
For Melol his father reigned ninety-four years in Egypt, but he was ten years sick and died, for he had been wicked before YAHUAH (the Lord).
And all the Egyptians called the name of Adikam Pharaoh like the name of his fathers, as was their custom to do in Egypt.
And all the wise men of Pharaoh called the name of Adikam Ahuz, for short is called Ahuz in the Egyptian language.
And Adikam was exceedingly ugly, and he was a cubit and a span and he had a great beard which reached to the soles of his feet.
And Pharaoh sat upon his father’s throne to reign over Egypt, and he conducted the government of Egypt in his wisdom.
And whilst he reigned he exceeded his father and all the preceding kings in wickedness, and he increased his yoke over the children of Israel.

And he went with his servants to Goshen to the children of Israel, and he strengthened the labor over them and he said to them, Complete your work, each day’s task, and let not your hands slacken from our work from this day forward as you did in the days of my father.
And he placed officers over them from amongst the children of Israel, and over these officers he placed taskmasters from amongst his servants.
And he placed over them a measure of bricks for them to do according to that number, day by day, and he turned back and went to Egypt.
At that time the task-masters of Pharaoh ordered the officers of the children of Israel according to the command of Pharaoh, saying,
Thus says Pharaoh, Do your work each day, and finish your task, and observe the daily measure of bricks; diminish not anything.
And it shall come to pass that if you are deficient in your daily bricks, I will put your young children in their stead.
And the task-masters of Egypt did so in those days as Pharaoh had ordered them.

And whenever any deficiency was found in the children of Israel’s measure of their daily bricks, the task-masters of Pharaoh would go to the wives of the children of Israel and take infants of the children of Israel to the number of bricks deficient, they would take them by force from their mother’s laps, and put them in the building instead of the bricks;
Whilst their fathers and mothers were crying over them and weeping when they heard the weeping voices of their infants in the wall of the building.

And the task-masters prevailed over Israel, that the Israelites should place their children in the building, so that a man placed his son in the wall and put mortar over him, whilst his eyes wept over him, and his tears ran down upon his child.
And the task-masters of Egypt did so to the babes of Israel for many days, and no one pitied or had compassion over the babes of the children of Israel.

And the number of all the children killed in the building was two hundred and seventy, some whom they had built upon instead of the bricks which had been left deficient by their fathers, and some whom they had drawn out dead from the building.
And the labor imposed upon the children of Israel in the days of Adikam exceeded in hardship that which they performed in the days of his father.
And the children of Israel sighed every day on account of their heavy work, for they had said to themselves, Behold when Pharaoh shall die, his son will rise up and lighten our work!
But they increased the latter work more than the former, and the children of Israel sighed at this and their cry ascended to Elohim (God) on account of their labor.
And Elohim heard the voice of the children of Israel and their cry, in those days, and Elohim remembered to them his covenant which he had made with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
And Elohim saw the burden of the children of Israel, and their heavy work in those days, and he determined to deliver them.
And Moses the son of Amram was still confined in the dungeon in those days, in the house of Reuel the Midianite, and Zipporah the daughter of Reuel did support him with food secretly day by day.
And Moses was confined in the dungeon in the house of Reuel for ten years.
And at the end of ten years which was the first year of the reign of Pharaoh over Egypt, in the place of his father,
Zipporah said to her father Reuel, No person inquires or seeks after the Hebrew man, whom you did bind in prison now ten years.
Now therefore, if it seem good in your sight, let us send and see whether he is living or dead, but her father knew not that she had supported him.
And Reuel her father answered and said to her, Has ever such a thing happened that a man should be shut up in a prison without food for ten years, and that he should live?
And Zipporah answered her father, saying, Surely you have heard that the Elohim of the Hebrews is great and awful, and does wonders for them at all times.
He it was who delivered Abraham from Ur of the Chaldeans, and Isaac from the sword of his father, and Jacob from the angel of YAHUAH who wrestled with him at the ford of Jabbuk.

Also with this man has he done many things, he delivered him from the river in Egypt and from the sword of Pharaoh, and from the children of Cush, so also can he deliver him from famine and make him live.
And the thing seemed good in the sight of Reuel, and he did according to the word of his daughter, and sent to the dungeon to ascertain what became of Moses.
And he saw, and behold the man Moses was living in the dungeon, standing upon his feet, praising and praying to the Elohim of his ancestors.
And Reuel commanded Moses to be brought out of the dungeon, so they shaved him and he changed his prison garments and ate bread.
And afterward Moses went into the garden of Reuel which was behind the house, and he there prayed to YAHUAH his Elohim (the Lord his God), who had done mighty wonders for him.
And it was that whilst he prayed he looked opposite to him, and behold a sapphire stick was placed in the ground, which was planted in the midst of the garden.
And he approached the stick and he looked, and behold the name of YAHUAH Elohim (the Lord God) of hosts was engraved on it, written and developed upon the stick.
And he read it and stretched forth his hand and he plucked it like a forest tree from the thicket, and the stick was in his hand.
And this is the stick with which all the works of our Elohim were performed, after he had created heaven and earth, and all the host of them, seas, rivers and all their fishes.
And when Elohim had driven Adam from the garden of Eden, he took the stick in his hand and went and tilled the ground from which he was taken.
And the stick came down to Noah and was given to Shem and his descendants, until it came into the hand of Abraham the Hebrew.
And when Abraham had given all he had to his son Isaac, he also gave to him this stick.
And when Jacob had fled to Padan-aram, he took it into his hand, and when he returned to his father he had not left it behind him.
Also when he went down to Egypt he took it into his hand and gave it to Joseph, one portion above his brethren, for Jacob had taken it by force from his brother Esau.

And after the death of Joseph, the nobles of Egypt came into the house of Joseph, and the stick came into the hand of Reuel the Midianite, and when he went out of Egypt, he took it in his hand and planted it in his garden.
And all the mighty men of the Kinites tried to pluck it when they endeavored to get Zipporah his daughter, but they were unsuccessful.
So that stick remained planted in the garden of Reuel, until he came who had a right to it and took it.

And when Reuel saw the stick in the hand of Moses, he wondered at it, and he gave him his daughter Zipporah for a wife. « • • • Chapter 77 gives the reader two things in sequence that belong together. First the new Pharaoh’s answer to the old Pharaoh’s death. Adikam, the second son of Melol, is twenty years old, exceedingly ugly, a cubit and a span tall with a beard to the soles of his feet. Jasher does not describe him as a caricature for sport. It describes him to remember that the face of an empire is sometimes literally as small as the cruelty it imposes. Adikam increases the yoke. He commands that the daily brick quota must be met to the tile, and if the quota is not met the young children of the deficient families will be put in the wall instead of the bricks. Two hundred and seventy children die in the wall. Some are laid in as substitutes for missing bricks and mortared over while their parents’ tears ran down on them. Some are pulled out dead after having been crushed in the building. This is the detail that the institutional reading of the Exodus routinely softens. The oppression is not abstract economic hardship. The oppression is infants in the wall. And it has a specific theological shape: the empire is devouring its own builders. The house rising in Pithom and Rameses is literally built on the bodies of Hebrew children. When YAHUAH later says that He has heard the cries of His people and has come down to deliver them, He is not describing a paperwork grievance. He is describing the cry of mothers whose sons were ground into the wall of a city the empire thought it needed more than it needed them. This is what the Passover lamb will be purchased to answer. This is what the sea will be opened to answer. The plagues are the exact measure of the bricks. Every blow falls on Egypt because Egypt has been measuring the life of Hebrew children against the count of its own mortar. Verse 23 to 25 pivot. The children of Israel sighed every day on account of their heavy work, and the cry ascended to Elohim, and Elohim heard the voice of the children of Israel, and Elohim remembered to them His covenant which He had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and Elohim saw the burden of the children of Israel, and their heavy work in those days, and He determined to deliver them. The full shape of the formula is right here. Israel cries. Elohim hears. Elohim remembers. Elohim sees. Elohim determines. The covenant name is used carefully: Elohim is the name that binds the covenant; YAHUAH will be the name that comes in the fire at the bush. The cry has already reached heaven. The determination is already made. The deliverer is already cut out of the house of Amram and positioned in a Midianite prison. The chapter lays the stones in the order they will be lifted. Now come to the sapphire stick. Moses has been in Reuel’s dungeon ten years and Zipporah has been feeding him. Reuel finally sends to see whether the Hebrew is still alive. The messenger finds Moses standing on his feet, praising and praying to the Elohim of his ancestors. Reuel orders him brought out, shaved, clothed, fed. Moses goes to the garden behind the house to pray and sees a sapphire stick planted in the ground in the middle of the garden. The name of YAHUAH Elohim of hosts is engraved on it. Moses reads it, stretches out his hand, and plucks it like a forest tree. Then Jasher’s narrator steps forward and tells us what the stick is. This is the stick with which all the works of our Elohim were performed after He created heaven and earth and all the host of them, seas, rivers, and all their fishes. When Elohim drove Adam from the garden of Eden, Adam took the stick in his hand and went and tilled the ground from which he was taken. The stick came down to Noah and was given to Shem and his descendants until it came into the hand of Abraham the Hebrew. Abraham gave it to Isaac. Isaac had it. Jacob took it into his hand when he fled to Padan-aram and when he returned. Jacob took it down to Egypt and gave it to Joseph as one portion above his brethren. After Joseph’s death the stick came into the hand of Reuel the Midianite, who took it out of Egypt and planted it in his garden. The mighty men of the Kinites tried to pluck it when they came to get Zipporah for a wife and could not. It remained planted in the garden until he came who had a right to it and took it. Hold this tradition loosely where it is extrabiblical. Jasher is not the Torah. The sapphire stick of Adam is a midrashic tradition that Jasher preserves, and it does not need to be defended as a historical fact in order for its theological shape to be heard. What it is saying matters. The rod that Moses will stretch over the Nile and the sea and the rock is not a piece of random Midianite wood. It is, in Jasher’s telling, a symbol of the continuity of the covenant from Adam forward. The tool of the deliverer’s hand has been in the house of the seed of promise from the beginning. The Torah reader who has walked through Genesis knows that the covenant is never a novelty. Sinai does not make the covenant. Sinai puts a crown on a covenant that has been running since Genesis 3:15. Moses’ rod is an object lesson of that continuity. Whether or not the sapphire stick is historical, the pattern it represents is Torah-true. The deliverer picks up what has been in the Father’s house since Eden. Verse 50 is the beautiful line. The stick remained planted in the garden until he came who had a right to it and took it. Moses did not steal the rod. He did not earn the rod. The rod was waiting for him. Every deliverer in scripture picks up something that was waiting for him. David picks up the sword of Goliath; Elijah’s mantle falls to Elisha; the Spirit of Yahusha (Jesus) rests on the twelve in the upper room; the Spirit of Yahusha (Jesus) still waits on the stones laid for every believer called to a work in his generation. The rod is waiting. When the season comes, the hand comes. Zipporah is given to Moses as wife in verse 51. The ten years of prison end. The sapphire stick is in his hand. The next chapter will pick up the domestic rhythm. Cross-references: Genesis 3:15, 17–19, 24; Genesis 47:29–31; Exodus 1:13–14; Exodus 2:23–25; Exodus 4:2–5; Exodus 7:10–12, 17, 20; Exodus 14:16; Exodus 17:5–6; Numbers 17:8; Psalm 74:20; Isaiah 11:1; Isaiah 66:1; Proverbs 30:17; Matthew 2:16; Matthew 23:35; James 5:4.

chapters.title: Zipporah, Gershom, and the Weight of the Covenant Sign

verses.text: At that time died Baal Channan son of Achbor, king of Edom, and was buried in his house in the land of Edom.

And after his death the children of Esau sent to the land of Edom, and took from there a man who was in Edom, whose name was Hadad, and they made him king over them in the place of Baal Channan, their king.
And Hadad reigned over the children of Edom forty-eight years.

And when he reigned he resolved to fight against the children of Moab, to bring them under the power of the children of Esau as they were before, but he was not able, because the children of Moab heard this thing, and they rose up and hastened to elect a king over them from amongst their brethren.
And they afterward gathered together a great people, and sent to the children of Ammon their brethren for help to fight against Hadad king of Edom.
