And Hadad heard the thing which the children of Moab had done, and was greatly afraid of them, and refrained from fighting against them.
In those days Moses, the son of Amram, in Midian, took Zipporah, the daughter of Reuel the Midianite, for a wife.
And Zipporah walked in the ways of the daughters of Jacob, she was nothing short of the righteousness of Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel and Leah.
And Zipporah conceived and bare a son and he called his name Gershom, for he said, I was a stranger in a foreign land; but he circumcised not his foreskin, at the command of Reuel his father-in-law.

And she conceived again and bare a son, but circumcised his foreskin, and called his name Eliezer, for Moses said, Because the Elohim (God) of your fathers was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh.
And Pharaoh king of Egypt greatly increased the labor of the children of Israel in those days, and continued to make his yoke heavier upon the children of Israel.
And he ordered a proclamation to be made in Egypt, saying, Give no more straw to the people to make bricks with, let them go and gather themselves straw as they can find it.
Also the tale of bricks which they shall make let them give each day, and diminish nothing from them, for they are idle in their work.
And the children of Israel heard this, and they mourned and sighed, and they cried to YAHUAH (the Lord) on account of the bitterness of their souls.
And YAHUAH heard the cries of the children of Israel, and saw the oppression with which the Egyptians oppressed them.

And YAHUAH was jealous of his people and his inheritance, and heard their voice, and he resolved to take them out of the affliction of Egypt, to give them the land of Canaan for a possession. « • • • Chapter 78 is short. Three things happen in it. Zipporah bears Gershom and then Eliezer. Pharaoh (now Adikam) tightens the brick quota by withdrawing the straw. The children of Israel mourn and cry to YAHUAH. Each detail is freighted. Verse 9 is the detail that will become the incident at the inn in chapter 79. Moses names his first son Gershom — a stranger in a foreign land. Moses circumcises him not. Jasher’s explanation is that Reuel his father-in-law commanded it. This is a delicate detail for the commentary to hold carefully. Reuel is a Midianite priest. Midian is descended from Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:1–4). The Midianite priestly tradition has kept some of Abraham’s covenant inheritance — hence Jethro’s later ministry at Sinai in Exodus 18 and Reuel’s reception of Moses into his household. But Reuel has also inherited or preserved modifications. A prohibition on circumcising the firstborn son is not a Torah command; it is a Midianite modification. And Moses, in the house of his father-in-law, submits to it. This is the small compromise that will almost cost him his life on the road back to Egypt. The pattern is important. The deliverer, even the deliverer, can let a domestic arrangement blunt a covenant sign. The road is long. The compromise is small. The Father will not overlook it. Verse 10 shows the correction beginning. When Zipporah bears Eliezer the second son, Moses does not defer to Reuel’s command. He circumcises the child. The name Eliezer means my Elohim is help, and Moses gives the reason: because the Elohim of my fathers was my help and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh. The second son is a covenant son from the eighth day. The first son was not. This is already a divided house spiritually. The two sons of the deliverer, one marked by the covenant sign and one not, will be the shape of the crisis at the inn in chapter 79. Verses 11 through 13 record Pharaoh Adikam’s escalation. He proclaims that no more straw will be given to the people, that they must gather their own straw, but that the tale of bricks shall not be diminished. This is the Exodus 5 moment. The empire has found a new way to crush the slaves without looking as if it is doing anything. It stops the supply. It keeps the demand. The slaves grind harder and fall further behind and get beaten for falling behind. This has been the preferred late-stage technique of every empire that did not want to look brutal while being brutal. Cut the supply. Keep the quota. Let the people punish themselves for not meeting the unmet-able. Every awakening believer inside a religious or institutional system still using this technique — the doctrinal bar raised without the doctrinal help, the performance demand raised without the pastoral supply — will recognize Adikam’s hand on the lever. It is not new. Verse 14 is one of the plainest lines in Jasher. The children of Israel heard this and they mourned and sighed and they cried to YAHUAH on account of the bitterness of their souls. One sentence. The Exodus narrative repeatedly gives us this formula: the people cry, YAHUAH hears. It is the oldest of all the gospels. The Father hears the cry of His oppressed covenant people. He does not always answer immediately — the timing is His — but He hears. Hebrews 5:7 says the Messiah Himself in the days of His flesh offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears to Him that was able to save Him from death and was heard. The Father hears crying. He heard it in Goshen. He heard it in Gethsemane. He hears it in every bedroom at four in the morning where the prayer is only tears. Hold this across the whole chapter: when the brick quota rises, the cry rises, and the ear of the Father is open. Verse 15 and 16 close the chapter. YAHUAH heard, and saw, and was jealous of His people, and resolved to take them out of the affliction of Egypt to give them the land of Canaan for a possession. The resolution is announced before the bush burns. The Father has decided. All that is left is the sending. Cross-references: Genesis 17:9–14; Genesis 25:1–4; Exodus 2:22; Exodus 4:24–26; Exodus 5:6–21; Exodus 6:5; Exodus 18:1–12; Numbers 12:1; Judges 1:16; Hebrews 5:7; Hebrews 11:24–26; Psalm 34:15–17; Psalm 147:3; James 5:4; 1 Peter 3:12.

chapters.title: The Burning Bush, the Inn, and the First Audience with

verses.text: And in those days Moses was feeding the flock of Reuel the Midianite his father-in-law, beyond the wilderness of Sin, and the stick which he took from his father-in-law was in his hand.
And it came to pass one day that a kid of goats strayed from the flock, and Moses pursued it and it came to the mountain of Elohim (God) to Horeb.
And when he came to Horeb, YAHUAH (the Lord) appeared there to him in the bush, and he found the bush burning with fire, but the fire had no power over the bush to consume it.

And Moses was greatly astonished at this sight, therefore the bush was not consumed, and he approached to see this mighty thing, and YAHUAH called to Moses out of the fire and commanded him to go down to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt, to send the children of Israel from his service.
And YAHUAH said to Moses, Go, return to Egypt, for all those men who sought your life are dead, and you shall speak to Pharaoh to send forth the children of Israel from his land.
And YAHUAH showed him to do signs and wonders in Egypt before the eyes of Pharaoh and the eyes of his subjects, in order that they might believe that YAHUAH had sent him.
And Moses hearkened to all that YAHUAH had commanded him, and he returned to his father-in-law and told him the thing, and Reuel said to him, Go in peace.
And Moses rose up to go to Egypt, and he took his wife and sons with him, and he was at an inn in the road, and an angel of Elohim came down, and sought an occasion against him.
And he wished to kill him on account of his first born son, because he had not circumcised him, and had transgressed the covenant which YAHUAH had made with Abraham.
For Moses had hearkened to the words of his father-in-law which he had spoken to him, not to circumcise his first born son, therefore he circumcised him not.
And Zipporah saw the angel of YAHUAH seeking an occasion against Moses, and she knew that this thing was owing to his not having circumcised her son Gershom.
And Zipporah hastened and took of the sharp rock stones that were there, and she circumcised her son, and delivered her husband and her son from the hand of the angel of YAHUAH.
And Aaron the son of Amram, the brother of Moses, was in Egypt walking at the river side on that day.
And YAHUAH appeared to him in that place, and he said to him, Go now toward Moses in the wilderness, and he went and met him in the mountain of Elohim, and he kissed him.
And Aaron lifted up his eyes, and saw Zipporah the wife of Moses and her children, and he said to Moses, Who are these to you?
And Moses said to him, They are my wife and sons, which Elohim gave to me in Midian; and the thing grieved Aaron on account of the woman and her children.
And Aaron said to Moses, Send away the woman and her children that they may go to her father’s house, and Moses hearkened to the words of Aaron, and did so.

And Zipporah returned with her children, and they went to the house of Reuel, and remained there until the time arrived when YAHUAH had visited his people, and brought them forth from Egypt from the hand at Pharaoh.
And Moses and Aaron came to Egypt to the community of the children of Israel, and they spoke to them all the words of YAHUAH, and the people rejoiced an exceeding great rejoicing.
And Moses and Aaron rose up early on the next day, and they went to the house of Pharaoh, and they took in their hands the stick of Elohim.

And when they came to the king’s gate, two young lions were confined there with iron instruments, and no person went out or came in from before them, unless those whom the king ordered to come, when the conjurors came and withdrew the lions by their incantations, and this brought them to the king.
And Moses hastened and lifted up the stick upon the lions, and he loosed them, and Moses and Aaron came into the king’s house.
The lions also came with them in joy, and they followed them and rejoiced as a dog rejoices over his master when he comes from the field.
And when Pharaoh saw this thing he was astonished at it, and he was greatly terrified at the report, for their appearance was like the appearance of the children of Elohim.
And Pharaoh said to Moses, What do you require? and they answered him, saying, The YAHUAH Elohim (Lord God) of the Hebrews has sent us to you, to say, Send forth my people that they may serve me.
And when Pharaoh heard their words he was greatly terrified before them, and he said to them, Go today and come back to me tomorrow, and they did according to the word of the king.

And when they had gone Pharaoh sent for Balaam the magician and to Jannes and Jambres his sons, and to all the magicians and conjurors and counsellors which belonged to the king, and they all came and sat before the king.

And the king told them all the words which Moses and his brother Aaron had spoken to him, and the magicians said to the king, But how came the men to you, on account of the lions which were confined at the gate?
And the king said, Because they lifted up their rod against the lions and loosed them, and came to me, and the lions also rejoiced at them as a dog rejoices to meet his master.
And Balaam the son of Beor the magician answered the king, saying, These are none else than magicians like ourselves.
Now therefore send for them, and let them come and we will try them, and the king did so.
And in the morning Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron to come before the king, and they took the rod of Elohim, and came to the king and spoke to him, saying,
Thus said YAHUAH Elohim (the Lord God) of the Hebrews, Send my people that they may serve me.
And the king said to them, But who will believe you that you are the messengers of Elohim and that you come to me by his order?
Now therefore give a wonder or sign in this matter, and then the words which you speak will be believed.
And Aaron hastened and threw the rod out of his hand before Pharaoh and before his servants, and the rod turned into a serpent.
And the sorcerers saw this and they cast each man his rod upon the ground and they became serpents.
And the serpent of Aaron’s rod lifted up its head and opened its mouth to swallow the rods of the magicians.
And Balaam the magician answered and said, This thing has been from the days of old, that a serpent should swallow its fellow, and that living things devour each other.

Now therefore restore it to a rod as it was at first, and we will also restore our rods as they were at first, and if your rod shall swallow our rods, then shall we know that the spirit of Elohim is in you, and if not, you are only an artificer like to ourselves.

And Aaron hastened and stretched forth his hand and caught hold of the serpent’s tail and it became a rod in his hand, and the sorcerers did the like with their rods, and they got hold, each man of the tail of his serpent, and they became rods as at first.
And when they were restored to rods, the rod of Aaron swallowed up their rods.

And when the king saw this thing, he ordered the book of records that related to the kings of Egypt, to be brought, and they brought the book of records, the chronicles of the kings of Egypt, in which all the idols of Egypt were inscribed, for they thought of finding in it the name of YAHUAH (Jehovah), but they found it not.
And Pharaoh said to Moses and Aaron, Behold I have not found the name of your Elohim written in this book, and his name I know not.
And the counsellors and wise men answered the king, We have heard that the Elohim of the Hebrews is a son of the wise, the son of ancient kings.
And Pharaoh turned to Moses and Aaron and said to them, I know not YAHUAH whom you have declared, neither will I send his people.

And they answered and said to the king, YAHUAH Elohim of elohim (of Gods) is his name, and he proclaimed his name over us from the days of our ancestors, and sent us, saying, Go to Pharaoh and say to him, Send my people that they may serve me.

Now therefore send us, that we may take a journey for three days in the wilderness, and there may sacrifice to him, for from the days of our going down to Egypt, he has not taken from our hands either burnt offering, oblation or sacrifice, and if you will not send us, his anger will be kindled against you, and he will smite Egypt either with the plague or with the sword.

And Pharaoh said to them, Tell me now his power and his might; and they said to him, He created the heaven and the earth, the seas and all their fishes, he formed the light, created the darkness, caused rain upon the earth and watered it, and made the herbage and grass to sprout, he created man and beast and the animals of the forest, the birds of the air and the fish of the sea, and by his mouth they live and die.

Surely he created you in your mother’s womb, and put into you the breath of life, and reared you and placed you upon the royal throne of Egypt, and he will take your breath and soul from you, and return you to the ground whence you were taken.
And the anger of the king was kindled at their words, and he said to them, But who amongst all the elohim (gods) of the nations can do this? my river is mine own, and I have made it for myself.
And he drove them from him, and he ordered the labor upon Israel to be more severe than it was yesterday and before.
And Moses and Aaron went out from the king’s presence, and they saw the children of Israel in an evil condition for the task-masters had made their labor exceedingly heavy.
And Moses returned to YAHUAH and said, Why have you ill treated your people? for since I came to speak to Pharaoh what you did send me for, he has exceedingly ill used the children of Israel.
And YAHUAH said to Moses, Behold you will see that with an outstretched hand and heavy plagues, Pharaoh will send the children of Israel from his land.
And Moses and Aaron dwelt amongst their brethren the children of Israel in Egypt.

And as for the children of Israel the Egyptians embittered their lives, with the heavy work which they imposed upon them. « • • • Chapter 79 is a hinge chapter for the entire Jasher volume. Three scenes. The burning bush. The incident at the inn. The first audience with Pharaoh. Together they answer the question Exodus 3:14 raises and do not close: who is the Elohim who sends Moses? The bush first. Moses is feeding the flock of Reuel beyond the wilderness of Sin, the sapphire stick in his hand, when a kid strays and Moses follows it to Horeb, the mountain of Elohim. The bush burns with fire but the fire has no power over the bush to consume it. YAHUAH calls to Moses out of the fire and commands him to go down to Egypt to Pharaoh king of Egypt to send the children of Israel from his service. The encounter in Jasher is compressed where Exodus 3 is expansive — Jasher presumes the Torah reader has Exodus 3 open — but the weight is the same. Hold three things. First, the name. Exodus 3:14 is where the Father gives Moses the word Ehyeh asher Ehyeh — I AM that I AM. Jasher does not narrate the name-giving exchange in the same detail, but everything that follows in the chapter presupposes it. YAHUAH is not a new Elohim being introduced to a stranger. He is the Elohim who already has a name, who already has covenants, who already has a people. What the bush does is declare that He is, He has always been, He is not becoming, His being is His own, and His name is His covenant presence with the people He made. When Pharaoh later asks in verse 44 who this YAHUAH is whose name is not written in the Egyptian books, the bush has already answered. He is the One whose name is not found in the records of any kingdom, because He is not a kingdom’s Elohim. He is the Elohim of all kingdoms, under whose hand the kingdoms rise and fall. The Son will pick up the “I AM” with shattering consequence in John 8:58. Before Abraham was, I am. The leaders of Judah understood exactly what He said and took up stones to stone Him. They heard the burning bush in the Messiah’s voice. They were right to hear it there. What they refused to see was that the One speaking out of the bush is the One standing on the temple steps. Hebrews 1:1–3 makes it plain: the Father who spoke in many times and ways by the prophets has spoken in these last days by His Son, through whom He made the worlds, the express image of the invisible one. The “I AM” that spoke in the fire is the “I AM” that stood before the Sanhedrin. One ground. One voice. One Elohim. Second, the bush is not consumed. The fire is in it and on it and yet does not burn it up. This is the paradigmatic shape of the Father’s presence in His people ever afterward. He is a consuming fire (Deuteronomy 4:24, Hebrews 12:29), and yet the bush is not consumed. The pillar of fire will stand over the camp and not consume the camp. The flame will rest on the altar and not consume the sanctuary. The tongues of fire will rest on the heads of the twelve at Pentecost and not consume the twelve. The same pattern. The Father’s fire burns His enemies but does not consume His bush. If you are His bush, the fire you are currently inside is not going to burn you up. It is going to show your neighbors that He is in you. Third, the commissioning. YAHUAH says in verse 5: Go, return to Egypt, for all those men who sought your life are dead. Forty years in Cush plus ten in a Midianite prison plus more in the Midianite fields have emptied Egypt of the men who once hunted Moses. The Father does not send until the way is clear, and when He sends He tells you the way is clear so you will not fear. Go. Return. The commission is brief because the preparation has been long. Now the incident at the inn, verses 8 through 12. Moses takes his wife and sons and heads for Egypt. An angel of Elohim comes down and seeks an occasion against him to kill him, on account of his first born son, because Moses had not circumcised him. Verse 10 is explicit: Moses had hearkened to the words of his father-in-law, who had commanded him not to circumcise his firstborn son, therefore Moses circumcised him not. Zipporah sees that the angel is seeking an occasion against her husband and knows that it is because of Gershom. She takes sharp rock stones, circumcises her son, and delivers her husband and her son from the hand of the angel. This passage has confounded institutional readers of Exodus 4:24–26 for centuries. With Jasher’s explanation in the background, the passage is transparent. Moses has accepted a domestic compromise against a covenant sign. The sign is not optional. The Father has been patient until the commissioning. The commissioning is given. The man sent to demand that Pharaoh let the covenant sons go cannot himself have an uncircumcised covenant son on the wagon. The hypocrisy would have strangled the mission. The angel comes to stop it. Zipporah, the Midianite priest’s daughter, seizes a rock and does what Moses should have done eight days after the boy was born. She saves her husband and her son. The deliverer is delivered by his wife. There is no shame in the deliverer being saved by a woman at a crisis. Zipporah stands in a line with Jael, with Rahab, with Esther, with Mary. When the man has blurred the sign, the Father has often used a woman to sharpen it. The lesson in this for the Torah observant is not a hobby lesson about circumcision. It is a lesson about household compromise. The sign you have been asked to neglect for the sake of a father-in-law, a mother-in-law, a boss, a pastor, a denomination, a congregation, a tribal alliance — is still the sign. It does not stop being the sign because your household has asked you to put it down. The Father is patient. He will be patient a long time. At some crossroads He will stop you on the road to the very work He sent you to do, until the sign is in place. Do not be surprised when that crossroads comes. Take the rock. Aaron meets Moses at the mountain of Elohim, verses 13 through 15, and Zipporah and the sons go back to Reuel’s house. Aaron and Moses come to the community of the children of Israel, and they speak to them all the words of YAHUAH, and the people rejoice an exceeding great rejoicing. That rejoicing is going to last about forty days before the first grumbling. Verses 20 through 23 are the scene at the king’s gate. Two young lions are confined there with iron instruments. The conjurors withdraw the lions by their incantations to let appointed visitors pass. Moses lifts up the rod upon the lions and looses them, and the lions come along with Moses and Aaron into the king’s house, following like a dog rejoices over his master when he comes from the field. Pharaoh is greatly terrified. The detail is Jasher’s and not the Torah’s; hold it loosely. What it is picturing theologically is that the wild beasts Egypt uses to terrify the outsiders recognize the Hebrew with the rod from Eden. Daniel in the lions’ den is a later echo. The creation knows its Maker’s agent when He comes. Verses 25 through 26. Moses and Aaron give the word: YAHUAH Elohim of the Hebrews has sent us to you, to say, Send forth my people that they may serve me. Pharaoh answers, Go today and come back to me tomorrow. He stalls. He sends for Balaam the son of Beor the magician, and for Jannes and Jambres his sons, and for all the magicians and conjurors and counsellors of the kingdom. This is where Balaam finally arrives in Egypt after fleeing Cush in Jasher 73. 2 Timothy 3:8 names Jannes and Jambres as the magicians who withstood Moses — the New Testament has inherited the Jasher-line memory of the names and the fact of the opposition. Hold that. Paul knows there were specific names, specific sons, specific magicians. The tradition is old. Verses 32 through 42 are the rod and the serpent. Aaron casts down the rod and it becomes a serpent. The magicians cast down their rods and they become serpents. Balaam speaks up in verse 39: this is an old thing, that a serpent should swallow its fellow. Let each restore his rod, and if Aaron’s then swallows ours, we will know the Spirit of Elohim is in you, and if not you are only an artificer like ourselves. They restore the rods. Aaron’s rod swallows theirs. The magicians have set the test. The test has been passed. Pharaoh’s pride does not yield. Verses 43 through 46 are one of the most theologically important exchanges in Jasher. Pharaoh orders the book of records, the chronicles of the kings of Egypt, in which all the idols of Egypt were inscribed. They look for the name of YAHUAH. They do not find it. Pharaoh says to Moses and Aaron, Behold I have not found the name of your Elohim written in this book, and his name I know not. Pharaoh’s counselors answer, We have heard that the Elohim of the Hebrews is a son of the wise, the son of ancient kings. Pharaoh responds, I know not YAHUAH whom you have declared, neither will I send his people. This is the 1234 of Truth stated by the pagan empire in its purest form. Pharaoh has an authorized canon of gods. His book of records contains every elohim Egypt recognizes. The name of YAHUAH is not in it. Therefore, by the logic of Pharaoh’s book, YAHUAH does not exist or at least has no standing. This is how every institutional authority has tested claims about the Father ever since. Is the name in our book? Is the name in our canon? Is the name in our creed? If not, we do not know this Elohim, and we will not send His people. The Father’s answer in the chapters ahead is categorical. He will prove His own name in the plagues. He does not need His name to be in Pharaoh’s book in order for Pharaoh’s river to turn to blood. The book does not contain the Father. The Father contains the book. Verse 47 is Moses’ answer. YAHUAH Elohim of elohim is His name, and He proclaimed His name over us from the days of our ancestors, and sent us. The name is older than Egypt’s books. The name has been spoken over the Hebrew people since the Father called Abraham out of Ur. The name has covenant standing because covenant is older than any empire’s archive. Pharaoh’s dismissal in verse 51 seals him. “My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself.” Ezekiel 29:3 will later quote this exact Pharaonic boast back to the Egypt of Nebuchadnezzar’s day. The boast has not changed in any century. The empire says the river is the empire’s. The Father says He made the river, and if the empire does not send His people He will turn the river to blood to prove it. Cross-references: Exodus 3; Exodus 4; Exodus 5; Exodus 7:1–13; Deuteronomy 4:24; Deuteronomy 18:15–18; John 1:1–14; John 8:56–59; 2 Timothy 3:8; Hebrews 1:1–3; Hebrews 11:24–27; Hebrews 12:29; Acts 2:3; Acts 7:30–34; Ezekiel 29:3–5; Isaiah 43:10–13; Revelation 1:8; 1 John 2:3–4.

chapters.title: The Plagues as the Dismantling of the Egyptian Pantheon

verses.text: And at the end of two years, YAHUAH (the Lord) again sent Moses to Pharaoh to bring forth the children of Israel, and to send them out of the land of Egypt.

And Moses went and came to the house of Pharaoh, and he spoke to him the words of the YAHUAH who had sent him, but Pharaoh would not hearken to the voice of YAHUAH, and Elohim (God) roused his might in Egypt upon Pharaoh and his subjects, and Elohim smote Pharaoh and his people with very great and sore plagues.
And YAHUAH sent by the hand of Aaron and turned all the waters of Egypt into blood, with all their streams and rivers.

And when an Egyptian came to drink and draw water, he looked into his pitcher, and behold all the water was turned into blood; and when he came to drink from his cup the water in the cup became blood.
And when a woman kneaded her dough and cooked her victuals, their appearance was turned to that of blood.
And YAHUAH sent again and caused all their waters to bring forth frogs, and all the frogs came into the houses of the Egyptians.
And when the Egyptians drank, their bellies were filled with frogs and they danced in their bellies as they dance when in the river.
And all their drinking water and cooking water turned to frogs, also when they lay in their beds their perspiration bred frogs.
Notwithstanding all this the anger of YAHUAH did not turn from them, and his hand was stretched out against all the Egyptians to smite them with every heavy plague.
And he sent and smote their dust to lice, and the lice became in Egypt to the height of two cubits upon the earth.

The lice were also very numerous, in the flesh of man and beast, in all the inhabitants of Egypt, also upon the king and queen YAHUAH sent the lice, and it grieved Egypt exceedingly on account of the lice.
Notwithstanding this, the anger of YAHUAH did not turn away, and his hand was still stretched out over Egypt.
And YAHUAH sent all kinds of beasts of the field into Egypt, and they came and destroyed all Egypt, man and beast, and trees, and all things that were in Egypt.
And YAHUAH sent fiery serpents, scorpions, mice, weasels, toads, together with others creeping in dust.
Flies, hornets, fleas, bugs and gnats, each swarm according to its kind.
And all reptiles and winged animals according to their kind came to Egypt and grieved the Egyptians exceedingly.
And the fleas and flies came into the eyes and ears of the Egyptians.
And the hornet came upon them and drove them away, and they removed from it into their inner rooms, and it pursued them.
And when the Egyptians hid themselves on account of the swarm of animals, they locked their doors after them, and Elohim ordered the Sulanuth which was in the sea, to come up and go into Egypt.
And she had long arms, ten cubits in length of the cubit of a man.
And she went upon the roofs and uncovered the raftering and flooring and cut them, and stretched forth her arm into the house and removed the lock and the bolt, and opened the houses of Egypt.
Afterward came the swarm of animals into the houses of Egypt, and the swarm of animals destroyed the Egyptians, and it grieved them exceedingly.
Notwithstanding this the anger of YAHUAH did not turn away from the Egyptians, and his hand was yet stretched forth against them.
And Elohim sent the pestilence, and the pestilence pervaded Egypt, in the horses and asses, and in the camels, in herds of oxen and sheep and in man.
And when the Egyptians rose up early in the morning to take their cattle to pasture they found all their cattle dead.
And there remained of the cattle of the Egyptians only one in ten, and of the cattle belonging to Israel in Goshen not one died.

And Elohim sent a burning inflammation in the flesh of the Egyptians, which burst their skins, and it became a severe itch in all the Egyptians from the soles of their feet to the crowns of their heads.
And many boils were in their flesh, that their flesh wasted away until they became rotten and putrid.
Notwithstanding this the anger of YAHUAH did not turn away, and his hand was still stretched out over all Egypt.
And YAHUAH sent a very heavy hail, which smote their vines and broke their fruit trees and dried them up that they fell upon them.
Also every green herb became dry and perished, for a mingling fire descended amidst the hail, therefore the hail and the fire consumed all things.
Also men and beasts that were found abroad perished of the flames of fire and of the hail, and all the young lions were exhausted.
And YAHUAH sent and brought numerous locusts into Egypt, the Chasel, Salom, Chargol, and Chagole, locusts each of its kind, which devoured all that the hail had left remaining.
Then the Egyptians rejoiced at the locusts, although they consumed the produce of the field, and they caught them in abundance and salted them for food.
And YAHUAH turned a mighty wind of the sea which took away all the locusts, even those that were salted, and thrust them into the Red Sea; not one locust remained within the boundaries of Egypt.
And Elohim sent darkness upon Egypt, that the whole land of Egypt and Pathros became dark for three days, so that a man could not see his hand when he lifted it to his mouth.
At that time died many of the people of Israel who had rebelled against YAHUAH and who would not hearken to Moses and Aaron, and believed not in them that Elohim had sent them.
And who had said, We will not go forth from Egypt lest we perish with hunger in a desolate wilderness, and who would not hearken to the voice of Moses.
And YAHUAH plagued them in the three days of darkness, and the Israelites buried them in those days, without the Egyptians knowing of them or rejoicing over them.

And the darkness was very great in Egypt for three days, and any person who was standing when the darkness came, remained standing in his place, and he that was sitting remained sitting, and he that was lying continued lying in the same state, and he that was walking remained sitting upon the ground in the same spot; and this thing happened to all the Egyptians, until the darkness had passed away.

And the days of darkness passed away, and YAHUAH sent Moses and Aaron to the children of Israel, saying, Celebrate your feast and make your Passover, for behold I come in the midst of the night amongst all the Egyptians, and I will smite all their first born, from the first born of a man to the first born of a beast, and when I see your Passover, I will pass over you.
And the children of Israel did according to all that YAHUAH had commanded Moses and Aaron, thus did they in that night.
And it came to pass in the middle of the night, that YAHUAH went forth in the midst of Egypt, and smote all the first born of the Egyptians, from the first born of man to the first born of beast.
And Pharaoh rose up in the night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians, and there was a great cry throughout Egypt in that night, for there was not a house in which there was not a corpse.
Also the likenesses of the first born of Egypt, which were carved in the walls at their houses, were destroyed and fell to the ground.

Even the bones of their first born who had died before this and whom they had buried in their houses, were raked up by the dogs of Egypt on that night and dragged before the Egyptians and cast before them.
And all the Egyptians saw this evil which had suddenly come upon them, and all the Egyptians cried out with a loud voice.
And all the families of Egypt wept upon that night, each man for his son and each man for his daughter, being the first born, and the tumult of Egypt was heard at a distance on that night.

And Bathia the daughter of Pharaoh went forth with the king on that night to seek Moses and Aaron in their houses, and they found them in their houses, eating and drinking and rejoicing with all Israel.
And Bathia said to Moses, Is this the reward for the good which I have done to you, who have reared you and stretched you out, and you have brought this evil upon me and my father’s house?
And Moses said to her, Surely ten plagues did YAHUAH bring upon Egypt; did any evil accrue to you from any of them? did one of them affect you? and she said, No.
And Moses said to her, Although you are the first born to your mother, you shall not die, and no evil shall reach you in the midst of Egypt.
And she said, What advantage is it to me, when I see the king, my brother, and all his household and subjects in this evil, whose first born perish with all the first born of Egypt?
And Moses said to her, Surely your brother and his household, and subjects, the families of Egypt, would not hearken to the words of YAHUAH, therefore did this evil come upon them.
And Pharaoh king of Egypt approached Moses and Aaron, and some of the children of Israel who were with them in that place, and he prayed to them, saying,

Rise up and take your brethren, all the children of Israel who are in the land, with their sheep and oxen, and all belonging to them, they shall leave nothing remaining, only pray for me to YAHUAH your Elohim (the Lord your God).

And Moses said to Pharaoh, Behold though you are your mother’s first born, yet fear not, for you will not die, for YAHUAH has commanded that you shall live, in order to show you his great might and strong stretched out arm.
And Pharaoh ordered the children of Israel to be sent away, and all the Egyptians strengthened themselves to send them, for they said, We are all perishing.
And all the Egyptians sent the Israelites forth, with great riches, sheep and oxen and precious things, according to the oath of YAHUAH between him and our Father Abraham.
And the children of Israel delayed going forth at night, and when the Egyptians came to them to bring them out, they said to them, Are we thieves, that we should go forth at night?
And the children of Israel asked of the Egyptians, vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and garments, and the children of Israel stripped the Egyptians.
And Moses hastened and rose up and went to the river of Egypt, and brought up from from there the coffin of Joseph and took it with him.

The children of Israel also brought up, each man his father’s coffin with him, and each man the coffins of his tribe. « • • • Chapter 80 gives the plagues in compressed Jasher form. The Torah’s Exodus 7 through 12 is the long-form account; Jasher summarizes. Read both together. What Jasher does distinctively is name the sea-creature Sulanuth in the plague of beasts, record that Israelite rebels perished in the three days of darkness, describe Bathia’s confrontation of Moses on the night of the tenth plague, and note Moses personally retrieving the coffin of Joseph from the Nile on the way out. Everything else tracks Exodus. The frame that must be held across the whole chapter is that the plagues are a covenant lawsuit. Exodus 9:16 says, “in very deed for this cause have I raised thee up, for to show in thee my power, and that my name may be declared throughout all the earth.” Exodus 12:12 says, “against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment; I am YAHUAH.” The plagues are not generic punishments. They are targeted judgments against specific gods. Egypt’s pantheon is numerous. Every plague selects at least one of Egypt’s deities and humiliates that deity by overruling the domain it claims. Name them as you go. Plague one, the Nile turned to blood. Hapi was the god of the Nile. Osiris was said to live in the annual flood. Khnum was the guardian of the Nile’s source. The blood in the pitcher and the cup is an indictment of every water god Egypt worshiped. Their water is not their water. YAHUAH owns the river. Jasher verse 5 adds a striking domestic detail: when a woman kneaded her dough and cooked her victuals, their appearance was turned to that of blood. The plague follows the Egyptian home all the way into the kitchen. The empire cannot eat its own bread. The covenant-breaking empire cannot feed itself. Plague two, the frogs. Heqet was the frog-headed goddess of fertility, invoked at childbirth. Verse 7 says the Egyptians drank and their bellies were filled with frogs and the frogs danced in their bellies as they dance in the river. Their fertility goddess is now a plague in the belly. The empire that has been murdering Hebrew children is overrun with the icon of its own fertility. Plague three, the lice. The magicians fail at this plague in Exodus 8:19 and say, this is the finger of Elohim. Jasher compresses the magicians’ concession but the theological note remains. Geb, the Egyptian earth-god, has lost control of his own dust. The first crack in the Egyptian confidence is here. Even the conjurors can name it. Plague four, the mixed swarm. Verse 14 catalogs fiery serpents, scorpions, mice, weasels, toads, and creeping things, together with flies, hornets, fleas, bugs, and gnats, each swarm according to its kind, and all reptiles and winged animals according to their kind. Then Jasher adds its distinctive detail in verse 19. When the Egyptians hid themselves and locked their doors, Elohim ordered the Sulanuth which was in the sea to come up and go into Egypt. The Sulanuth had long arms ten cubits in length. She went upon the roofs, uncovered the raftering, cut the flooring, stretched her arm into the house, and removed the locks and bolts and opened the houses. Hold the Sulanuth loosely where it is extrabiblical. What the detail is saying is that the Egyptians could not hide from the swarm. Whatever hidden creature of the sea the Father used, the result is theological. No lock will shut out a judgment YAHUAH has ordered. Anubis the jackal, Khepri the scarab, and every local guardian-god are all simultaneously overruled. Plague five, the cattle. Hathor the cow-goddess and Apis the bull-god are both deities of livestock. Every Egyptian farmer wakes up to dead herds. The Israelite herds in Goshen do not die. Verse 26: of the cattle of the Egyptians only one in ten remained, and of the cattle belonging to Israel in Goshen not one died. This is a covenant distinction drawn in dead animals. The Father makes a line between the covenant people and the empire that is holding them captive, and He draws the line on the bodies of cows. The two-house framework pays attention to this. The Father has always drawn lines on physical bodies. Circumcision on Hebrew men. Healthy cattle in Goshen. A sign on the doorposts at Passover. This physical distinction is not bigotry. It is covenant. When the prophets later speak of a regathering of a specific scattered people, they are speaking within the logic of a Father who has always drawn distinctions on specific bodies. Plague six, the boils. Isis the health-goddess, Sekhmet the lion-goddess of healing, and the deified physician Imhotep are all overruled. The magicians cannot even stand before Moses because of the boils (Exodus 9:11). The healers cannot heal themselves. Verse 28 says their flesh wasted away until they became rotten and putrid. The physicians who had advised Pharaoh in Jasher 76 to put infant blood into his leprosy wounds are now covered with putrid flesh of their own. Plague seven, the hail with fire mingled. Nut the sky-goddess, Shu the god of air, Set the god of storms, and Horus the falcon-god of the sky are overruled. Every green herb becomes dry and perishes because a mingling fire descends amid the hail. Verse 32 notes that the young lions were exhausted, an echo-phrase suggesting the creation itself is groaning. Plague eight, the locusts. Senehem the locust-protector, Renenutet the harvest-goddess, and Min the fertility-god of vegetation are all overruled. Jasher preserves the four Hebrew species-names: Chasel, Salom, Chargol, Chagole. The Egyptians in verse 34 even rejoice briefly at the locusts and catch them in abundance and salt them for food. Empire’s short-term opportunism. Then the wind from the sea takes them all away, even the salted ones, not one locust remains, and the food stores are gone. Plague nine, the darkness. Ra the sun god is the chief deity of Egypt’s imperial cult. Pharaoh was said to be the son of Ra. The darkness that covers Egypt for three days is a personal indictment of Ra and a personal indictment of Pharaoh. Verse 40 adds the eerie domestic touch: a man standing when the darkness came remained standing, a man sitting remained sitting, a man lying remained lying. The darkness is not a mere absence of light; it is a paralysis. Creation has forgotten how to function because its authorized god has been muted. And the Israelites have light in their dwellings (Exodus 10:23) — the line drawn on the bodies of the cattle is now drawn in candlelight across the whole camp. Jasher verses 37 through 39 preserve a detail the institutional reading has tended to soften. During the three days of darkness many of the people of Israel died — Israelites who had rebelled against YAHUAH and refused to hearken to Moses and Aaron, who said, We will not go forth from Egypt lest we perish with hunger in a desolate wilderness. YAHUAH plagued them in the darkness, and the Israelites buried them without the Egyptians knowing of them or rejoicing over them. Hold this tight. The line the Father draws is not a merely ethnic line. Hebrew by blood who refused to leave Egypt died in the darkness alongside the Egyptian adult who refused to confess. The physical covenant matters. The obedient response to the commandment matters more. 1 John 2:3–4 is on every page of this chapter. The one who says he knows YAHUAH and does not keep His commandment is a liar — even if he is Hebrew by birth, even if he is in Goshen, even if his mother sang him to sleep with the prayers of Abraham. The rebels in Goshen died in the darkness. They were not spared because they were Israelite. They were covenant sons who refused the covenant. The Father was specific with them. Plague ten, the firstborn. Pharaoh himself was considered the incarnate god of Egypt, and his firstborn son the heir of the god. Every Egyptian household line is struck where it lives. Verse 45 adds the Jasher detail that even the likenesses of the first born of Egypt carved in the walls of their houses were destroyed and fell to the ground, and that the bones of the first born who had died before this and whom they had buried in their houses were raked up by the dogs of Egypt and cast before their families. The memorials of the first born fall. The bones of the first born already buried are exhumed by dogs. The empire’s past, present, and future in its first-born line are all struck on the same night. Pharaoh as incarnate god is personally indicted. His household, his subjects, and the walls of his own houses confess the judgment. Verses 49 through 54 are the Bathia scene that the institutional reading almost never treats. Bathia daughter of Pharaoh — who as Jasher 68 recorded drew Moses from the river and raised him — goes forth with the king on that night to seek Moses and Aaron. They find them eating and drinking and rejoicing with all Israel. Bathia asks Moses, is this the reward for the good which I have done to you, who reared you and stretched you out, and you have brought this evil upon me and my father’s house? Moses answers with a piercing kindness. Ten plagues did YAHUAH bring upon Egypt; did any evil accrue to you from any of them? did one of them affect you? She says no. Moses says, although you are the first born to your mother, you shall not die, and no evil shall reach you in the midst of Egypt. She says, what advantage is it to me, when I see the king my brother and all his household and subjects in this evil, whose first born perish with all the first born of Egypt? Hold Bathia carefully. She is the Egyptian princess who disobeyed her own father’s drowning decree. She raised the Hebrew deliverer as her own son. She is a first-born and by the night’s judgment should have died. She does not die, because the Father remembers the ark in the water and the Hebrew mother’s wages from her hand. This is the Father’s mercy on a specific Gentile woman who loved a specific Hebrew child. It is not a pattern for a false inclusion gospel that opens the covenant to anyone who wants it; it is a pattern for the Father’s covenant-faithfulness toward specific acts of mercy shown to His covenant people. Rahab will be treated the same way at Jericho for hiding the spies. Cornelius will be treated the same way in Acts 10 for praying to the Elohim of Israel and giving alms to Israel’s poor. The Father honors specific Gentile mercies toward His people. He does not thereby make those Gentiles into Israel. Bathia is spared; she is not thereby a Hebrew. Rahab is saved; she is grafted into the genealogy through the patience of generations, not by self-declaration. Cornelius receives the Spirit; he is a Gentile with the Spirit, not a new Israelite. Hold this distinction. It is the answer to the false inclusion gospel without any hardness toward the merciful Gentile. Bathia’s line in verse 53 is one of the most haunting lines in Jasher. What advantage is it to me when I see the king, my brother, and all his household perishing? She does not rejoice to be spared alone. Her spared life is spent weeping for a family that the Father has judged. This is the shape of mercy received inside judgment. The saved one does not gloat. The saved one grieves. The Messiah will later weep over Jerusalem when He could see the judgment coming. The judged ones are not enemies of the saved; they are the saved one’s own household. Hold this as the deep texture of the victims-not-enemies posture. Every act of the Father’s deliverance of His covenant people sets the delivered one weeping over those still inside the empire. Verses 55 through 62 close the chapter. Pharaoh comes to Moses and Aaron and prays — the first time in the narrative he uses the language of prayer — and says Rise up and take your brethren, only pray for me to YAHUAH your Elohim. Moses says to Pharaoh, behold though you are your mother’s first born, yet fear not, for you will not die, for YAHUAH has commanded that you shall live in order to show you His great might and strong stretched out arm. This is the Jasher seed of the detail that will flower in chapter 81. Pharaoh will live through the tenth plague. He will pursue into the sea. He will not drown with his army. Jasher has something specific to say about why. Verses 61 and 62. The Israelites strip the Egyptians of silver and gold and garments, fulfilling the word given to Abraham in Genesis 15:14 that his seed would come out with great substance. Moses hastens and goes to the river of Egypt and brings up from there the coffin of Joseph and takes it with him. The children of Israel also bring up each man his father’s coffin with him, and each man the coffins of his tribe. This is the fulfillment of the Jasher 59 oath. Joseph said in his dying words that Elohim would surely visit them and that they must take his bones up from Egypt. Now, four centuries later, Moses personally retrieves the coffin. The oath is kept. Hebrews 11:22 — by faith Joseph, when he died, made mention of the departing of the children of Israel, and gave commandment concerning his bones. Faith across four centuries. The coffin that preached in every Hebrew home during the oppression now rides out with the delivered. And Jasher adds that the coffins of the tribes — the patriarchs’ remains — are also being brought up, which will become crucial at Jasher 90:38–46 when the tribes are buried in the land of their inheritance. The physical bodies of the seed are being carried out to be buried in the physical land of the promise. The covenant is not abstract. It has coffins in it. Cross-references: Exodus 7–12; Exodus 14:30; Exodus 15:11; Deuteronomy 4:32–40; Joshua 2:10; Joshua 24:5–7; Psalm 78, 105, 106, 136; Isaiah 19:1–25; Jeremiah 46; Ezekiel 29–32; Habakkuk 3; Hebrews 11:22, 28; Revelation 15:3; Revelation 16; Romans 9:17; 1 Corinthians 5:7; 1 Corinthians 10:1–13; 1 John 2:3–4; Matthew 23:37.

chapters.title: The Exodus, the Sea, the Song, and Amalek

verses.text: And the children of Israel journeyed from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides the little ones and their wives.
Also a mixed multitude went up with them, and flocks and herds, even much cattle.
And the sojourning of the children of Israel, who dwelt in the land of Egypt in hard labor, was two hundred and ten years.
And at the end of two hundred and ten years, YAHUAH (the Lord) brought forth the children of Israel from Egypt with a strong hand.
And the children of Israel traveled from Egypt and from Goshen and from Rameses, and encamped in Succoth on the fifteenth day of the first month.
And the Egyptians buried all their first born whom YAHUAH had smitten, and all the Egyptians buried their slain for three days.
And the children of Israel traveled from Succoth and encamped in Ethom, at the end of the wilderness.

And on the third day after the Egyptians had buried their first born, many men rose up from Egypt and went after Israel to make them return to Egypt, for they repented that they had sent the Israelites away from their servitude.
And one man said to his neighbor, Surely Moses and Aaron spoke to Pharaoh, saying, We will go a three days’ journey in the wilderness and sacrifice to YAHUAH our Elohim (the Lord our God).

Now therefore let us rise up early in the morning and cause them to return, and it shall be that if they return with us to Egypt to their masters, then shall we know that there is faith in them, but if they will not return, then will we fight with them, and make them come back with great power and a strong hand.

And all the nobles of Pharaoh rose up in the morning, and with them about seven hundred thousand men, and they went forth from Egypt on that day, and came to the place where the children of Israel were.
And all the Egyptians saw and behold Moses and Aaron and all the children of Israel were sitting before Pi-hahiroth, eating and drinking and celebrating the feast of YAHUAH.
And all the Egyptians said to the children of Israel, Surely you said, We will go a journey for three days in the wilderness and sacrifice to our Elohim (God) and return.
Now therefore this day makes five days since you went, why do you not return to your masters?

And Moses and Aaron answered them, saying, Because YAHUAH our Elohim has testified in us, saying, You shall no more return to Egypt, but we will betake ourselves to a land flowing with milk and honey, as YAHUAH our Elohim had sworn to our ancestors to give to us.
And when the nobles of Egypt saw that the children of Israel did not hearken to them, to return to Egypt, they girded themselves to fight with Israel.

And YAHUAH strengthened the hearts of the children of Israel over the Egyptians, that they gave them a severe beating, and the battle was sore upon the Egyptians, and all the Egyptians fled from before the children of Israel, for many of them perished by the hand of Israel.
And the nobles of Pharaoh went to Egypt and told Pharaoh, saying, The children of Israel have fled, and will no more return to Egypt, and in this manner did Moses and Aaron speak to us.

And Pharaoh heard this thing, and his heart and the hearts of all his subjects were turned against Israel, and they repented that they had sent Israel; and all the Egyptians advised Pharaoh to pursue the children of Israel to make them come back to their burdens.
And they said each man to his brother, What is this which we have done, that we have sent Israel from our servitude?
And YAHUAH strengthened the hearts of all the Egyptians to pursue the Israelites, for the YAHUAH desired to overthrow the Egyptians in the Red Sea.
And Pharaoh rose up and harnessed his chariot, and he ordered all the Egyptians to assemble, not one man was left excepting the little ones and the women.
And all the Egyptians went forth with Pharaoh to pursue the children of Israel, and the camp of Egypt was an exceedingly large and heavy camp, about ten hundred thousand men.
And the whole of this camp went and pursued the children of Israel to bring them back to Egypt, and they reached them encamping by the Red Sea.
And the children of Israel lifted up their eyes, and beheld all the Egyptians pursuing them, and the children of Israel were greatly terrified at them, and the children of Israel cried to the YAHUAH.

And on account of the Egyptians, the children of Israel divided themselves into four divisions, and they were divided in their opinions, for they were afraid of the Egyptians, and Moses spoke to each of them.
The first division was of the children of Reuben, Simeon, and Issachar, and they resolved to cast themselves into the sea, for they were exceedingly afraid of the Egyptians.
And Moses said to them, Fear not, stand still and see the salvation of YAHUAH which He will effect this day for you.
The second division was of the children of Zebulun, Benjamin and Naphtali, and they resolved to go back to Egypt with the Egyptians.
And Moses said to them, Fear not, for as you have seen the Egyptians this day, so shall you see them no more for ever.
The third division was of the children of Judah and Joseph, and they resolved to go to meet the Egyptians to fight with them.
And Moses said to them, Stand in your places, for YAHUAH will fight for you, and you shall remain silent.

And the fourth division was of the children of Levi, Gad, and Asher, and they resolved to go into the midst of the Egyptians to confound them, and Moses said to them, Remain in your stations and fear not, only call to YAHUAH that he may save you out of their hands.
After this Moses rose up from amidst the people, and he prayed to YAHUAH and said,
O YAHUAH Elohim (O Lord God) of the whole earth, save now your people whom you did bring forth from Egypt, and let not the Egyptians boast that power and might are theirs.

So YAHUAH said to Moses, Why dost you cry to me? speak to the children of Israel that they shall proceed, and do you stretch out your rod upon the sea and divide it, and the children of Israel shall pass through it.
And Moses did so, and he lifted up his rod upon the sea and divided it.
And the waters of the sea were divided into twelve parts, and the children of Israel passed through on foot, with shoes, as a man would pass through a prepared road.
And YAHUAH manifested to the children of Israel his wonders in Egypt and in the sea by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

And when the children of Israel had entered the sea, the Egyptians came after them, and the waters of the sea resumed upon them, and they all sank in the water, and not one man was left excepting Pharaoh, who gave thanks to YAHUAH and believed in him, therefore the YAHUAH did not cause him to perish at that time with the Egyptians.
And YAHUAH ordered an angel to take him from amongst the Egyptians, who cast him upon the land of Ninevah and he reigned over it for a long time.

And on that day YAHUAH saved Israel from the hand of Egypt, and all the children of Israel saw that the Egyptians had perished, and they beheld the great hand of YAHUAH, in what he had performed in Egypt and in the sea.
Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song to YAHUAH, on the day when the YAHUAH caused the Egyptians to fall before them.
And all Israel sang in concert, saying, I will sing to YAHUAH for He is greatly exalted, the horse and his rider has he cast into the sea; behold it is written in the book of the law of Elohim.

After this the children of Israel proceeded on their journey, and encamped in Marah, and YAHUAH gave to the children of Israel statutes and judgments in that place in Marah, and the YAHUAH commanded the children of Israel to walk in all his ways and to serve him.
And they journeyed from Marah and came to Elim, and in Elim were twelve springs of water and seventy date trees, and the children encamped there by the waters.
And they journeyed from Elim and came to the wilderness of Sin, on the fifteenth day of the second month after their departure from Egypt.
At that time YAHUAH gave the manna to the children of Israel to eat, and YAHUAH caused food to rain from heaven for the children of Israel day by day.
And the children of Israel ate the manna for forty years, all the days that they were in the wilderness, until they came to the land of Canaan to possess it.
And they proceeded from the wilderness of Sin and encamped in Alush.
And they proceeded from Alush and encamped in Rephidim.
And when the children of Israel were in Rephidim, Amalek the son of Eliphaz, the son of Esau, the brother of Zepho, came to fight with Israel.
And he brought with him eight hundred and one thousand men, magicians and conjurers, and he prepared for battle with Israel in Rephidim.

And they carried on a great and severe battle against Israel, and YAHUAH delivered Amalek and his people into the hands of Moses and the children of Israel, and into the hand of Joshua, the son of Nun, the Ephrathite, the servant of Moses.
And the children of Israel smote Amalek and his people at the edge of the sword, but the battle was very sore upon the children of Israel.

And YAHUAH said to Moses, Write this thing as a memorial for you in a book, and place it in the hand of Joshua, the son of Nun, your servant, and you shall command the children of Israel, saying, When you shall come to the land of Canaan, you shall utterly efface the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven.
And Moses did so, and he took the book and wrote upon it these words, saying,
Remember what Amalek has done to you in the road when you went forth from Egypt.
Who met you in the road and smote your rear, even those that were feeble behind you when you were faint and weary.

Therefore it shall be when YAHUAH your Elohim (the Lord your God) shall have given you rest from all your enemies round about in the land which YAHUAH your Elohim gives you for an inheritance, to possess it, that you shall blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven, you shall not forget it.
And the king who shall have pity on Amalek, or upon his memory or upon his seed, behold I will require it of him, and I will cut him off from amongst his people.

And Moses wrote all these things in a book, and he enjoined the children of Israel respecting all these matters. « • • • Chapter 81 covers the Exodus itself, the pursuit, the crossing, the song, and the opening wilderness. It is the chapter with the most theological weight per verse in the entire Jasher middle section. Slow for it. Verse 1. Six hundred thousand men on foot, besides little ones and their wives, journey from Rameses to Succoth. The number is standard Torah-number; Jasher tracks Exodus 12:37. Verse 2. A mixed multitude went up with them. The Hebrew word ereb (mixed multitude) in Exodus 12:38 and Jasher’s corresponding phrase has been weaponized by two opposite misreadings, both of which need to be refused. The institutional Christian misreading treats the mixed multitude as the seed of the later church: here at the Exodus, the misreading claims, the door to the covenant was already being opened to anyone who wanted to come; Israel is therefore already just one more stream among many in a spiritualized people of God; the coming of Messiah will complete what the mixed multitude began. This is replacement theology dressed in a historical garment. The reading ignores what the mixed multitude actually does in the wilderness. Numbers 11:4 names the mixed multitude as the source of the first great wilderness lust: the mixed multitude that was among them fell a lusting, and the children of Israel also wept again and said, Who shall give us flesh to eat? Numbers 11 is YAHUAH’s furious response to a craving that originated in the mixed multitude and spread into the covenant camp. The mixed multitude is not the first church. It is the first case study in what happens when people attach themselves to Israel without being of Israel. The Hebrew roots false inclusion gospel has its own misreading. It treats the mixed multitude as evidence that anyone who obeys Torah is thereby grafted into Israel with full standing. This is Torah observance as the ticket to become Ephraim or Judah at will. The chapter itself refuses this. The mixed multitude is not assigned a tribal allotment. The mixed multitude does not inherit in Canaan. The mixed multitude is the instigator of Numbers 11’s rebellion. Being attached to Israel for the season of the deliverance is real. It is also distinct from being Israel. The covenant is not merely a matter of moral alignment; it is also a matter of whom the Father called, covenanted, and promised to regather. The false inclusion gospel collapses the first into the second and thereby replaces the second with the first. Jasher 81:2 quietly preserves the distinction. Israel came up. A mixed multitude also came up. The two are named in the same sentence, and they are not the same. The pastoral posture toward today’s Gentile believer is unchanged. You are welcome. Your obedience is beautiful. Your love for YAHUAH is honored. If there is Hebrew blood in your line — and in most awakening believers from the nations of the North there is — the Father knows it and the regathering will find you. If there is not, your devotion still matters. You can still be the Rahab hid in the wall, the Ruth gleaning in Boaz’s field, the Bathia drawing a Hebrew child from the river, the Cornelius praying toward Jerusalem. The Father’s commendations of those figures are lavish. He will not call any of them Israel. He will honor every one of them as themselves. Verses 5 through 7 are the departure and the encamping at Succoth and Ethom on the fifteenth day of the first month. The Passover has been eaten. The sixteenth of the first month — first day of unleavened bread — begins the departure. Every subsequent generation of Israel is commanded to rehearse this night (Exodus 12:14 — you shall keep it a feast to YAHUAH throughout your generations; you shall keep it a feast by an ordinance forever). Not until Easter was invented in the fourth century did any part of the people who claim this covenant abandon the ordinance. The institutional replacement of Passover with Easter is the sin of Jeroboam’s calves repeated in a Roman vestment — the worship of YAHUAH by the pattern of the nations, rebranded in Christian language. Hold this firmly. 1 Corinthians 5:7 says the Messiah is our Passover, sacrificed for us. The apostolic church kept the Passover. Acts 12:3 notes that Herod killed James during the days of unleavened bread. Paul calculates his travel plans around Pentecost (Acts 20:16). The feasts are the shape of the apostolic year. They remain the shape of the covenant year for the awakening remnant. Verse 8 through 24 are the Egyptian change of heart and the pursuit. On the third day after burying their first born, many Egyptians rise up and go after Israel to make them return. They reach the camp at Pi-hahiroth and find the Israelites eating and drinking and celebrating the feast of YAHUAH. They confront the Israelites about not returning, Moses and Aaron answer, and a local skirmish ensues. Jasher 81:17 says Israel gave the Egyptians a severe beating on that day. When Pharaoh hears the report he and all his subjects repent their decision to let Israel go, and YAHUAH strengthens the hearts of all the Egyptians to pursue the Israelites — for YAHUAH desired to overthrow the Egyptians in the Red Sea. Verse 21 is a clear statement that the hardening of the Egyptian heart at the end is YAHUAH’s hand, not simply human obduracy. Romans 9:17 draws exactly this verse into Paul’s argument — for this cause have I raised thee up, that I might show my power in thee. The institutional reading of Romans 9 has often distorted the passage into a question of individual eternal destinies. The Jasher-and-Exodus context keeps the passage in its proper frame. YAHUAH is not capriciously damning Pharaoh or Egypt. He is completing a covenant lawsuit. The hardening at the end is the signature on the indictment. Applying the Methodological Sequence for Reading Paul at Romans 9 — first establish what Paul was drawing from (Exodus 9:16 and the hardening narrative), then identify what he was arguing against (a reading that confuses ethnic descent with covenant standing, specifically among the Jews of his day who assumed their bloodline guaranteed them) — the passage clarifies. Paul is defending the same thing Jasher 81 is showing: the Father is sovereign over His own covenant lawsuit and can harden an empire for His own purposes of declaration. He is not thereby capriciously damning individuals who had no chance. Pharaoh had ten plagues of chances. The hardening at the end is the Father’s hand on a man who had already freely chosen his path nine times. Verses 25 through 35 give Jasher’s distinctive picture of the four divisions at the sea. The children of Reuben, Simeon, and Issachar resolve to cast themselves into the sea. The children of Zebulun, Benjamin, and Naphtali resolve to go back to Egypt. The children of Judah and Joseph resolve to fight. The children of Levi, Gad, and Asher resolve to rush into the Egyptians to confound them. Moses speaks to each division in turn: stand still and see the salvation of YAHUAH; fear not, as you have seen the Egyptians today so you shall see them no more; stand in your places, for YAHUAH will fight for you, and you shall remain silent; remain in your stations and fear not, only call to YAHUAH. Jasher’s detail of the four divisions is not in Exodus but is well attested in Jewish midrashic tradition and captures something important. The four responses to trial are all still among us. Suicide — cast yourself into the sea. Retreat — go back to Egypt. Fight — take up arms against the wrong enemy. Rush the enemy to confound them — try to out-argue, out-agitate, out-maneuver. Every one of the responses is wrong. The right response is in the four commands Moses issues: stand, fear not, be silent, cry out. That is the posture of covenant deliverance. It is the posture at Gethsemane. Not my will but yours be done. It is the posture at the cross. Father, forgive them. It is the posture for every awakening believer right now who is trapped between a Red Sea and a Pharaoh. Do not run. Do not drown yourself. Do not fight the wrong enemy. Be silent. Cry out. Watch what YAHUAH does. Verse 36 through 39. YAHUAH says to Moses, speak to the children of Israel that they shall proceed, and stretch out your rod upon the sea and divide it. Moses lifts up the rod and divides the sea. Jasher says the waters were divided into twelve parts, and the children of Israel passed through on foot with shoes as a man would pass through a prepared road. Twelve parts. One for each tribe. The covenant structure is baked into the miracle. The tribes do not pass through in a single anonymous mass; each tribe has its own dry corridor. The twelve-ness of the covenant people is preserved even in the middle of the deliverance. This is the same Father who tells Ezekiel to take two sticks and write on one for Judah and the children of Israel his companions, and on the other for Joseph the stick of Ephraim and for all the house of Israel his companions, and to join them into one stick in His hand (Ezekiel 37:15–19). The twelve-ness does not dissolve in the sea. The twelve-ness does not dissolve at Sinai. The twelve-ness does not dissolve at the regathering. The twelve-ness is permanent. It is why the New Jerusalem has twelve gates named for the twelve tribes (Revelation 21:12) and the 144,000 are numbered by tribe (Revelation 7:4–8). The Jasher detail of the twelve-part crossing is the physical rehearsal of a covenant fact. Verses 40 and 41 are the bomb in the chapter. When the children of Israel had entered the sea, the Egyptians came after them, and the waters of the sea resumed upon them, and they all sank in the water, and not one man was left excepting Pharaoh, who gave thanks to YAHUAH and believed in him, therefore YAHUAH did not cause him to perish at that time with the Egyptians. And YAHUAH ordered an angel to take him from amongst the Egyptians, who cast him upon the land of Ninevah and he reigned over it for a long time. Hold this tradition loosely. It is not in the canonical Torah. The Torah says Pharaoh led his army into the sea; it does not explicitly narrate whether he personally survived. Later rabbinic tradition collects this Jasher-line detail, and some of that tradition links the Pharaoh-sent-to-Nineveh with the king of Nineveh in the book of Jonah, who repents at Jonah’s preaching in sackcloth (Jonah 3:6–10). The canonical scripture does not name the Nineveh king of Jonah’s day, so the identification cannot be confirmed. What is theologically usable is this: even in the moment of His most categorical judgment on Egypt, YAHUAH spares a specific Egyptian, because the specific Egyptian in the moment of the judgment gave thanks and believed. And the spared Egyptian is sent away from Egypt to reign over a Gentile people. This is the Father’s mercy on a single confessing pagan ruler at the climax of a covenant lawsuit. The commentary does not stand on whether the Pharaoh-to-Nineveh tradition is historically exact. It stands on the pattern. The Father’s judgments are severe. The Father’s mercies within His judgments are real and specific. Nothing Gentile is thrown away without the opportunity of confession. Pharaoh, against all odds, took that opportunity in the water. Jasher records it. The record instructs the reader to hold open the possibility of late confession even among those we are sure are lost. Verses 42 through 44 are the song. Jasher compresses Exodus 15 to a single line — I will sing to YAHUAH for He is greatly exalted, the horse and his rider has He cast into the sea — and adds the note: behold it is written in the book of the law of Elohim. Jasher is self-aware. It knows that the song at the sea is fully preserved in the Torah and does not need to duplicate it. Revelation 15 will later place a recapitulation of the song of Moses in the mouths of the victorious saints standing on the sea of glass — and they sang the song of Moses the servant of Elohim and the song of the Lamb. The song of Moses and the song of the Lamb are the same song. Every generation of the covenant people sings the deliverance of Exodus with new verses as the generations give new occasions for it. Verses 45 through 49. Marah, the bitter waters made sweet by a tree cast into them. This is a rehearsal of the cross to come — a tree changes the bitterness of the water of life into sweetness, and the statutes and judgments of YAHUAH are given to the children of Israel at Marah. Elim, the twelve springs and seventy date trees (one spring per tribe, one tree per elder — the covenant’s structure encoded in palm trees). The wilderness of Sin on the fifteenth day of the second month. The manna begins. Verse 49 says the children of Israel ate the manna for forty years, all the days that they were in the wilderness, until they came to the land of Canaan. The one-day-at-a-time bread is the covenant’s economy. You cannot store up the provision. You gather what you need for today. On the sixth day a double portion for the Sabbath. The feast-calendar is already present in the manna gathering before Sinai — the Sabbath is not a later invention appended at Sinai; it is visible in the bread falling on the wilderness floor. Exodus 16:23 — tomorrow is the rest of the holy Sabbath to YAHUAH. The Sabbath is older than the Torah as a delivered text because the Sabbath is older than the Torah as a created reality. Genesis 2:2–3. Verses 50 through 62. Amalek the son of Eliphaz son of Esau, brother of Zepho, comes to fight with Israel in Rephidim with eight hundred and one thousand men, magicians and conjurors. YAHUAH delivers Amalek and his people into the hands of Moses and Joshua. Joshua the son of Nun the Ephrathite is named here — from the tribe of Ephraim — and this is his first named mission. YAHUAH tells Moses to write this thing as a memorial in a book and to place it in the hand of Joshua, and to command the children of Israel that when they come to the land of Canaan they shall utterly efface the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven. Verse 61: the king who shall have pity on Amalek or upon his memory or upon his seed will be cut off. This is the seed of 1 Samuel 15 where Saul will fail to destroy Agag the Amalekite and lose the kingdom. It is the seed of Esther where Haman the Agagite descendant of Amalek rises up to destroy the Jews and is hanged on his own gallows. Amalek is the perpetual enemy of the covenant seed, and the Torah sets a covenant hostility against Amalek that will ring through the Tanakh until the Father disposes of every Amalekite heart at the end. There is a hard pastoral note here. Amalek is Esau’s grandson. The first battle Israel fights in the wilderness is against its own cousin. The covenant people’s most persistent enemies are its own estranged relations. This is the two-house pain in miniature. The descendants of Ishmael and of Esau and the unbelieving of every later generation of scattered Hebrews carry pieces of the covenant DNA and fight the covenant people most bitterly because the nearness is most personal. Hold the victims-not-enemies posture even here. Amalek the man has been specifically hostile and specifically judged. The Amalekite people are under a Torah-command of blotting out. And even Amalek is a descendant of Esau who was loved (Malachi 1:2), and even the bitterest of enemies is made of flesh the Father formed and knows by name. The Torah’s severity toward Amalek is not racism. It is covenant surgery. The infection had to be cut out because it would not stop attacking. The surgery does not cancel the Father’s general love for every image-bearer. It just names what had to be done with a specific unrepentant infection in a specific covenant hour. Cross-references: Exodus 12:29–42; Exodus 13; Exodus 14–15; Exodus 16; Exodus 17:8–16; Numbers 11:4–6; Numbers 33:3–8; Deuteronomy 25:17–19; Joshua 4:18; 1 Samuel 15; Esther 3:1, 7:10; Psalm 78, 105, 136; Isaiah 43:16–19; Isaiah 51:10; Jeremiah 23:7–8; Ezekiel 37:15–19; Hosea 2:14–15; Micah 6:4; Jonah 3:6–10; Malachi 1:2–3; Matthew 12:40–41; Matthew 14:19–20; Luke 22:15–16; Romans 9:17; 1 Corinthians 5:7–8; 1 Corinthians 10:1–13; Hebrews 11:29; Hebrews 12:24; Revelation 7:4–8; Revelation 15:3; Revelation 21:12–13.

chapters.title: Sinai, the Ten Words, and the Golden Calf

verses.text: And the children of Israel proceeded from Rephidim and they encamped in the wilderness of Sinai, in the third month from their going forth from Egypt.

At that time came Reuel the Midianite, the father-in-law of Moses, with Zipporah his daughter and her two sons, for he had heard of the wonders of YAHUAH (the Lord) which he had done to Israel, that he had delivered them from the hand of Egypt.
And Reuel came to Moses to the wilderness where he was encamped, where was the mountain of Elohim (God).
And Moses went forth to meet his father-in-law with great honor, and all Israel was with him.
And Reuel and his children remained amongst the Israelites for many days, and Reuel knew YAHUAH from that day forward.
And in the third month from the children of Israel’s departure from Egypt, on the sixth day of it, YAHUAH gave to Israel the ten commandments on Mount Sinai.
And all Israel heard all these commandments, and all Israel rejoiced exceedingly in YAHUAH on that day.
And the glory of YAHUAH rested upon Mount Sinai, and he called to Moses, and Moses came in the midst of a cloud and ascended the mountain.
And Moses was upon the mount forty days and forty nights; he ate no bread and drank no water, and YAHUAH instructed him in the statutes and judgments in order to teach the children of Israel.
And YAHUAH wrote the ten commandments which he had commanded the children of Israel upon two tablets of stone, which he gave to Moses to command the children of Israel.
And at the end of forty days and forty nights, when YAHUAH had finished speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai, then YAHUAH gave to Moses the tablets of stone, written with the finger of Elohim.
And when the children of Israel saw that Moses tarried to come down from the mount, they gathered round Aaron, and said, As for this man Moses we know not what has become of him.
Now therefore rise up, make to us a god who shall go before us, so that you shall not die.
And Aaron was greatly afraid of the people, and he ordered them to bring him gold and he made it into a molten calf for the people.
And YAHUAH said to Moses, before he had come down from the mount, Get you down, for your people whom you did bring forth from Egypt have corrupted themselves.
They have made to themselves a molten calf, and have bowed down to it, now therefore leave me, that I may consume them from off the earth, for they are a stiffnecked people.
