And Moses besought the countenance of YAHUAH, and he prayed to YAHUAH for the people on account of the calf which they had made, and he afterward descended from the mount and in his hands were the two tablets of stone, which Elohim had given him to command the Israelites.
And when Moses approached the camp and saw the calf which the people had made, the anger of Moses was kindled and he broke the tablets under the mount.
And Moses came to the camp and he took the calf and burned it with fire, and ground it till it became fine dust, and strewed it upon the water and gave it to the Israelites to drink.
And there died of the people by the swords of each other about three thousand men who had made the calf.
And on the morrow Moses said to the people, I will go up to YAHUAH, peradventure I may make atonement for your sins which you have sinned to YAHUAH.
And Moses again went up to YAHUAH, and he remained with YAHUAH forty days and forty nights.
And during the forty days did Moses entreat YAHUAH in behalf of the children of Israel, and YAHUAH hearkened to the prayer of Moses, and YAHUAH was entreated of him in behalf of Israel.
Then spoke YAHUAH to Moses to hew two stone tablets and to bring them up to YAHUAH, who would write upon them the ten commandments.
Now Moses did so, and he came down and hewed the two tablets and went up to Mount Sinai to YAHUAH, and YAHUAH wrote the ten commandments upon the tablets.
And Moses remained yet with YAHUAH forty days and forty nights, and YAHUAH instructed him in statutes and judgments to impart to Israel.

And YAHUAH commanded him respecting the children of Israel that they should make a sanctuary for YAHUAH, that his name might rest in it, and YAHUAH showed him the likeness of the sanctuary and the likeness of all its vessels.
And at the end of the forty days, Moses came down from the mount and the two tablets were in his hand.
And Moses came to the children of Israel and spoke to them all the words of YAHUAH, and he taught them laws, statutes and judgments which YAHUAH had taught him.
And Moses told the children of Israel the word of YAHUAH, that a sanctuary should be made for him, to dwell amongst the children of Israel.
And the people rejoiced greatly at all the good which YAHUAH had spoken to them, through Moses, and they said, We will do all that YAHUAH has spoken to you.
And the people rose up like one man and they made generous offerings to the sanctuary of YAHUAH, and each man brought the offering of YAHUAH for the work of the sanctuary, and for all its service.

And all the children of Israel brought each man of all that was found in his possession for the work of the sanctuary of YAHUAH, gold, silver and brass, and every thing that was serviceable for the sanctuary.

And all the wise men who were practiced in work came and made the sanctuary of the YAHUAH, according to all that YAHUAH had commanded, every man in the work in which he had been practiced; and all the wise men in heart made the sanctuary, and its furniture and all the vessels for the holy service, as YAHUAH had commanded Moses.
And the work of the sanctuary of the tabernacle was completed at the end of five months, and the children of Israel did all that YAHUAH had commanded Moses.
And they brought the sanctuary and all its furniture to Moses; like to the representation which YAHUAH had shown to Moses, so did the children of Israel.

And Moses saw the work, and behold they did it as YAHUAH had commanded him, so Moses blessed them. « • • • Chapter 82 holds Sinai, the Torah, the calf, the second tablets, and the building of the sanctuary in a compressed span. Each of these events deserves more pages than this commentary has, but the framework can be named and held at each. Verses 1 through 11. Reuel the father-in-law comes to Moses in the wilderness, for he has heard of the wonders, with Zipporah his daughter and her two sons. Moses goes out with great honor to meet his father-in-law. Reuel remains among the Israelites for many days and knows YAHUAH from that day forward. This is a Gentile confession received with honor. Reuel’s status does not change; he is the father-in-law, a priest of Midian, a descendant of Abraham through Keturah. He is brought into the camp as a beloved participant. He is not made into an Israelite, nor is he required to be. The Cornelius-pattern is already in place at Sinai. The giving of the ten commandments follows in verses 6 through 11. Third month, sixth day. All Israel hears the commandments. All Israel rejoices in YAHUAH. The glory of YAHUAH rests upon Sinai. Moses ascends in the cloud, is forty days and forty nights on the mountain without bread or water, and YAHUAH writes the ten commandments on two tablets of stone with His finger. The ten words are the plainest application of 1 John 2:3–4 in the entire Torah. He that says he knows the Father and does not keep His commandments is a liar. Which commandments? These ten, to begin with. They are not a devotional suggestion. They are not a dispensationally outdated code. They are the permanent shape of the life that loves YAHUAH with all the heart and loves the neighbor as the self. Yahusha (Jesus) will summarize them in Matthew 22:37–40 and will say that on these two summaries hang all the Torah and the prophets. The two-summary reading does not abolish the ten words; it clarifies them. The first four words shape love of YAHUAH; the last six shape love of the neighbor. Remove any one and the love is crippled. The institutional reading that discards the fourth word (Sabbath) while keeping the other nine has already rejected the unity of the set. The Torah-observant reading that keeps all ten but applies them without the love of Matthew 22 risks the cold performance that the prophets rebuke (Isaiah 1:11–17; Amos 5:21–24). The right reading keeps all ten and holds them inside the love. Hebrews 8 and Jeremiah 31 must be read together against the institutional misreading that claims the Torah has been abolished. Jeremiah 31:33 says, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their Elohim, and they shall be my people. The Father is not abolishing the Torah. He is internalizing it. Hebrews 8:10 quotes Jeremiah exactly. The new covenant does not delete the ten words; it writes them on the heart. Any reading that treats the new covenant as a license to discard the Torah has missed the operation. The operation is transfer, not deletion. Apply the Methodological Sequence for Reading Paul. First establish what Paul drew from — Jeremiah 31, internalization of Torah. Then identify what Paul was arguing against — a Judaizing party that was requiring ritual Torah observance as a prerequisite for Gentile believers to receive the Spirit. Paul is against the Judaizers; Paul is not against the Torah. A reading that turns Paul into an abolisher of the Torah has taken Paul’s argument against the Judaizers and inflated it into an argument against the thing Paul himself kept all his life (Acts 21:20–26, Acts 28:17). Verses 12 through 23 are the calf. Moses tarries on the mountain forty days. The people gather around Aaron and say, as for this man Moses we know not what has become of him; rise up, make to us a god who shall go before us. Aaron, afraid of the people, asks for gold and makes a molten calf. The people bow down to it. YAHUAH tells Moses on the mountain that the people have corrupted themselves. Moses descends, sees the calf, breaks the tablets, burns the calf, grinds it to dust, scatters it on water, gives it to the people to drink. Three thousand men die by the swords of each other. This is the single most important hermeneutical scene in the Torah for the critique of the institutional church. Read it slowly. Exodus 32:5 — and Aaron made proclamation and said, tomorrow is a feast to YAHUAH. Aaron does not declare a feast to Baal. Aaron does not declare a feast to Apis or Hathor. Aaron declares a feast to YAHUAH. The calf is not a rival god. The calf is an image made to worship the covenant God of Israel. The sin is not polytheism. The sin is the attempt to worship the real Elohim by the pattern of the nations. Hold this tightly. Deuteronomy 12:29–32 is categorical. When YAHUAH your Elohim shall cut off the nations from before you, whither you go to possess them, and you succeed them, and dwell in their land; take heed to yourself that you be not snared by following them, after that they be destroyed from before you; and that you inquire not after their gods, saying, How did these nations serve their gods? even so will I do likewise. You shall not do so unto YAHUAH your Elohim. You shall not ask how the nations worshiped their gods and then worship the real Elohim that way. The golden calf is the rehearsal of the sin. Every pattern the nations used to worship their gods — processions, icons, ceremonial eating, sacred calendars keyed to the sun — has at some point in the last twenty centuries been adopted by the institutional church and directed toward YAHUAH. Christmas as a sanitized Saturnalia. Easter as a sanitized spring fertility festival. Sunday worship as a rebranded veneration of the day of the sun. The steeple as the descendant of the obelisk. The cross as the descendant of the crux commissa. None of these are institutional accidents. Each was consciously adopted at a specific historical juncture, and each was defended with the argument that the intent was good — we are worshiping YAHUAH with this, we are worshiping Yahusha (Jesus) with this. Aaron’s argument exactly. It is a feast to YAHUAH. The calf is just to help us worship. Three thousand die at the calf. This is the Levite sword day. Exodus 32:26–28 says Moses stood in the gate of the camp and said, who is on YAHUAH’s side? let him come to me. And all the sons of Levi gathered themselves together to him. The Levite refusal to serve Pharaoh a century earlier (Jasher 65) now receives its covenant reward. The tribe that would not serve Pharaoh becomes the tribe that stands for YAHUAH when the rest of Israel is serving a calf. The priesthood of Levi is forged in this day of sword work. Every time later scripture places the Levites at the altar, this day is what stands behind the robe. The Levites are not holy because they are genetically special. They are holy because, when the whole camp was bowed to the calf, they put the calf to the sword. At Pentecost in Acts 2, three thousand receive the Spirit (Acts 2:41). The numerical echo is not an accident. The number three thousand appears at Sinai in judgment and at Pentecost in grace. The calf-worshipers who died at Sinai were confronted and killed. The calf-worshipers’ descendants who heard Peter preach Yahusha (Jesus) were confronted and saved. Sinai and Pentecost are not two separate covenants overwriting each other. They are two movements of the same Father on the same covenant people. The same Spirit that signed the stone tablets at Sinai signed the hearts of the three thousand at Pentecost. Jeremiah 31 being kept. Verses 21 through 27. Moses entreats YAHUAH for forty more days, hews new tablets, ascends, receives the second writing of the ten commandments by the finger of Elohim. The people are not disqualified from the covenant by the calf. They are corrected and restored. This is enormously important for the awakening remnant who has discovered their own calf in their inherited tradition. The discovery of the calf does not disqualify the worshiper. The grinding of the calf and the swallowing of the grindings in humility is the road to the second tablets. Every awakening believer has to drink the dust of the idol he once bowed to before he can stand clean under the covenant again. Verses 28 through 37 close the chapter with the sanctuary. YAHUAH commands the children of Israel to make a sanctuary for Him that His name might rest in it. The people bring offerings freely. The wise-in-heart craftsmen make the sanctuary according to the pattern shown to Moses on the mountain. Five months of building. Moses sees the finished work and blesses them. The Father who has had no house among His people since Eden now has a tent. The Shekinah, the visible glory, will descend on it in chapter 83. A closing theological note. The tabernacle is a pattern of things in the heavens (Hebrews 8:5). Every element of it — the menorah, the showbread, the ark, the mercy seat, the veil, the incense altar — prefigures the work of the Messiah. The calf tried to worship YAHUAH by the pattern of the nations. The tabernacle worships YAHUAH by the pattern shown on the mountain. The difference between the two is the whole difference between faithful covenant worship and institutional idolatry. Every church service held today must answer the question: is this worship the pattern shown on the mountain, or is this worship the pattern of the nations rebranded? The Father’s rule is simple. Build by the pattern He gave. Not by the pattern the nations gave. Cross-references: Exodus 19–34; Exodus 35–40; Deuteronomy 4; Deuteronomy 5:6–21; Deuteronomy 12:29–32; Deuteronomy 18:15–18; Leviticus 23; Jeremiah 31:31–34; Ezekiel 20; Hosea 2:16–23; Micah 6:6–8; Isaiah 1:11–17; Amos 5:21–24; Matthew 5:17–20; Matthew 22:37–40; Acts 2:41; Acts 7:38–43; Acts 21:20–26; Romans 3:31; Romans 7:12; Hebrews 8; Hebrews 10:16–17; 1 John 2:3–4; 1 John 5:3; Revelation 14:12; Revelation 15:3.

chapters.title: The Priesthood, the Spies, and the Forty Years

verses.text: And in the twelfth month, in the twenty-third day of the month, Moses took Aaron and his sons, and he dressed them in their garments, and anointed them and did to them as the YAHUAH (the Lord) had commanded him, and Moses brought up all the offerings which YAHUAH had on that day commanded him.
Moses afterward took Aaron and his sons and said to them, For seven days shall you remain at the door of the tabernacle, for thus am I commanded.
And Aaron and his sons did all that YAHUAH had commanded them through Moses, and they remained for seven days at the door of the tabernacle.

And on the eighth day, being the first day of the first month, in the second year from the Israelites’ departure from Egypt, Moses erected the sanctuary, and Moses put up all the furniture of the tabernacle and all the furniture of the sanctuary, and he did all that YAHUAH had commanded him.
And Moses called to Aaron and his sons, and they brought the burnt offering and the sin offering for themselves and the children of Israel, as YAHUAH had commanded Moses.

On that day the two sons of Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, took strange fire and brought it before YAHUAH who had not commanded them, and a fire went forth from before YAHUAH, and consumed them, and they died before YAHUAH on that day.
Then on the day when Moses had completed to erect the sanctuary, the princes of the children of Israel began to bring their offerings before YAHUAH for the dedication of the altar.
And they brought up their offerings each prince for one day, a prince each day for twelve days.

And all the offerings which they brought, each man in his day, one silver charger weighing one hundred and thirty shekels, one silver bowl of seventy shekels after the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour, mingled with oil for a meat offering.
One spoon, weighing ten shekels of gold, full of incense.
One young bullock, one ram, one lamb of the first year for a burnt offering.
And one kid of the goats for a sin offering.
And for a sacrifice of peace offering, two oxen, five rams, five he-goats, five lambs of a year old.
Thus did the twelve princes of Israel day by day, each man in his day.
And it was after this, in the thirteenth day of the month, that Moses commanded the children of Israel to observe the Passover.
And the children of Israel kept the Passover in its season in the fourteenth day of the month, as YAHUAH had commanded Moses, so did the children of Israel.
And in the second month, on the first day of it, YAHUAH spoke to Moses, saying,
Number the heads of all the males of the children of Israel from twenty years old and upward, you and your brother Aaron and the twelve princes of Israel.
And Moses did so, and Aaron came with the twelve princes of Israel, and they numbered the children of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai.
And the numbers of the children of Israel by the houses of their fathers, from twenty years old and upward, were six hundred and three thousand, five hundred and fifty.
But the children of Levi were not numbered amongst their brethren the children of Israel.
And the number of all the males of the children of Israel from one month old and upward, was twenty-two thousand, two hundred and seventy-three.
And the number of the children of Levi from one month old and above, was twenty-two thousand.
And Moses placed the priests and the Levites each man to his service and to his burden to serve the sanctuary of the tabernacle, as YAHUAH had commanded Moses.
And on the twentieth day of the month, the cloud was taken away from the tabernacle of testimony.

At that time the children of Israel continued their journey from the wilderness of Sinai, and they took a journey of three days, and the cloud rested upon the wilderness of Paran; there the anger of YAHUAH was kindled against Israel, for they had provoked YAHUAH in asking him for meat, that they might eat.
And YAHUAH hearkened to their voice, and gave them meat which they ate for one month.
But after this the anger of YAHUAH was kindled against them, and he smote them with a great slaughter, and they were buried there in that place.
And the children of Israel called that place Kebroth Hattaavah, because there they buried the people that lusted flesh.
And they departed from Kebroth Hattaavah and pitched in Hazeroth, which is in the wilderness of Paran.
And whilst the children of Israel were in Hazeroth, the anger of YAHUAH was kindled against Miriam on account of Moses, and she became leprous, white as snow.
And she was confined without the camp for seven days, until she had been received again after her leprosy.
The children of Israel afterward departed from Hazeroth, and pitched in the end of the wilderness of Paran.
At that time, YAHUAH spoke to Moses to send twelve men from the children of Israel, one man to a tribe, to go and explore the land of Canaan.
And Moses sent the twelve men, and they came to the land of Canaan to search and examine it, and they explored the whole land from the wilderness of Sin to Rechob as you come to Chamoth.

And at the end of forty days they came to Moses and Aaron, and they brought him word as it was in their hearts, and ten of the men brought up an evil report to the children of Israel, of the land which they had explored, saying, It is better for us to return to Egypt than to go to this land, a land that consumes its inhabitants.
But Joshua the son of Nun, and Caleb the son of Jephuneh, who were of those that explored the land, said, The land is exceedingly good.
If YAHUAH delight in us, then he will bring us to this land and give it to us, for it is a land flowing with milk and honey.
But the children of Israel would not hearken to them, and they hearkened to the words of the ten men who had brought up an evil report of the land.
And YAHUAH heard the murmurings of the children of Israel and he was angry and swore, saying,
Surely not one man of this wicked generation shall see the land from twenty years old and upward excepting Caleb the son of Jephuneh and Joshua the son of Nun.

But surely this wicked generation shall perish in this wilderness, and their children shall come to the land and they shall possess it; so the anger of YAHUAH was kindled against Israel, and he made them wander in the wilderness for forty years until the end of that wicked generation, because they did not follow YAHUAH.

And the people dwelt in the wilderness of Paran a long time, and they afterward proceeded to the wilderness by the way of the Red Sea. « • • • Chapter 83 compresses Leviticus and Numbers. The priesthood is installed. Nadab and Abihu die for offering strange fire. The princes bring dedication offerings. The Passover is kept in the second year. The census is taken. Miriam is briefly leprous. The spies are sent, ten return with an evil report, the generation is sentenced to forty years of wandering. Verse 6 is the sharp corrective note that the institutional reading rarely sits with. Nadab and Abihu, sons of Aaron, priests themselves, enter the sanctuary with strange fire that YAHUAH had not commanded, and fire goes forth from YAHUAH and consumes them. Leviticus 10 gives the full story. The priests are held to a standard higher than the people because they stand between the people and the altar. A fire improvised by Nadab and Abihu — not the fire YAHUAH prescribed — kills them. The lesson for every institutional church is severe. The fire you are offering up to YAHUAH must be the fire He commanded. Innovation at the altar is not piety; it is idolatry waiting to happen. Every institutional church that has invented new sacraments, new liturgical fires, new worship technologies in the name of reaching the people is approaching the altar of Nadab and Abihu. The people need the commanded fire. The commanded fire is in the Torah. The new fire is exactly the disease Nadab and Abihu carried. Verses 7 through 14 give the princes’ dedication offerings and day-by-day procession of twelve tribal offerings. The Torah’s long Numbers 7 passage is compressed here. Every tribe brings identical gifts. The equality of the tribal gifts matters covenant-structurally. No tribe is elevated at the altar. Judah has the scepter, Levi has the priesthood, Joseph has the double portion, Benjamin has the Messiah’s first Pauline apostle — and at the dedication every tribe brings the same silver charger, the same silver bowl, the same golden spoon, the same bullock, ram, lamb, and goats. The tribes are distinct but equal at the altar. The covenant is one. The institutional readings that have played tribes against each other across the centuries — especially the readings that elevate Judah while despising Ephraim — do not have this equality in their imagination. Verses 15 and 16 are a single sentence that carries great weight. The children of Israel kept the Passover in its season on the fourteenth day of the month, as YAHUAH had commanded Moses, so did the children of Israel. Year two of the Exodus. The Passover is kept again. Not abolished. Not replaced. Kept. Every year it is to be kept. This is the second rehearsal of the feast, and the second rehearsal matters because it establishes the feast as a permanent practice rather than a one-time historical commemoration. Every generation of awakening believers who has rediscovered the Passover and begun keeping it again is stepping into Jasher 83:15–16 — keeping the Passover in its season as YAHUAH had commanded Moses. The season of the calf may be followed by the season of the feast. It has been before. Verses 17 through 25 are the census and the tabernacle service arrangements. Six hundred and three thousand, five hundred and fifty males from twenty years old and upward. Twenty-two thousand two hundred and seventy-three male-children from a month old. Twenty-two thousand Levites. These are covenant numbers, and they mean that the nation that came out of Egypt is mature enough and populous enough to enter Canaan immediately — no demographic excuse for the forty years that will follow. The forty years will be judgment, not necessity. Verses 31 and 32 compress Miriam’s leprosy. YAHUAH’s anger was kindled against Miriam on account of Moses. She became leprous, white as snow. She was confined without the camp for seven days. Numbers 12 preserves the fuller text. Miriam (and Aaron with her, more quietly) spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman he had married, saying, has YAHUAH indeed spoken only by Moses? Hath He not spoken also by us? The sin is a spiritual overreach — claiming equal prophetic authority with the meekest man in all the earth. The sin is judged immediately. Miriam is healed after seven days, but the lesson is not forgotten. Hebrews 3:2 places Moses as the faithful servant in all the Father’s house. Miriam and Aaron under Moses. The pattern of prophetic authority is hierarchical in scripture. YAHUAH chooses particular vessels to speak at particular times, and the speaking of other vessels must defer to the chosen one in the time of his authority. Every age has to sort out its own Miriams and Aarons. Every awakening believer has to discern whose voice is speaking the Father’s word in the hour. Verses 34 through 42 are the spies and the forty-year sentence. Twelve men are sent, one man per tribe. Ten return with an evil report, saying it is better to return to Egypt than to go to this land. Two — Joshua and Caleb — return with faith. The people side with the ten. YAHUAH’s anger is kindled, and the sentence is that not one man of that wicked generation from twenty years old and upward, except Caleb and Joshua, shall see the land. The generation will wander forty years until it is consumed. 1 Corinthians 10:11 says these things happened to them for ensamples, and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages are come. This is the hinge verse for applying the Methodological Sequence for Reading Paul to the wilderness narratives. Paul’s argument in 1 Corinthians 10 is not dispensational. It is rigorously covenant-continuity. The wilderness generation is not ancient history; it is the mirror for every believer in every generation, including Paul’s Corinthian Greeks. The wilderness is the school every believer will attend. The tests that killed the wilderness generation will test every believer. The report of the spies is a test still being given: is the promised land worth leaving the known system for, or would we rather go back to Egypt? The institutional reading that removes the wilderness generation from view treats this chapter as a curiosity. The covenant reading treats this chapter as direct address. The forty-year judgment has a mercy inside it. Verse 42: but surely this wicked generation shall perish in this wilderness, and their children shall come to the land and they shall possess it. The children of the rebels inherit what the rebels refused. The covenant promise is not broken by the generation’s failure. It is transferred to the next generation. This pattern is the Father’s covenant pattern with Israel repeatedly. The first exodus generation refuses; the second enters. The first temple builders refuse; the next generation builds. Every awakening believer today who feels they have wasted a generation in the wilderness of an institutional system can read verse 42 as a promise to their children. The children may possess what the parents only saw. The covenant is long. The Father is patient. Cross-references: Leviticus 9–10; Leviticus 23:5–8; Numbers 1; Numbers 7; Numbers 9:1–5; Numbers 12; Numbers 13–14; Deuteronomy 1:19–46; Psalm 95:7–11; Psalm 106; Hebrews 3:7–4:11; 1 Corinthians 10:1–13; Jude 5; Revelation 2:7.

chapters.title: Korah, Sihon, the Brother-Nations, and the Death of Aaron

verses.text: At that time Korah the son of Jetzer the son of Kehath the son of Levi, took many men of the children of Israel, and they rose up and quarreled with Moses and Aaron and the whole congregation.
And YAHUAH (the Lord) was angry with them, and the earth opened its mouth, and swallowed them up, with their houses and all belonging to them, and all the men belonging to Korah.
And after this Elohim (God) made the people go round by the way of Mount Seir for a long time.

At that time YAHUAH said to Moses, Provoke not a war against the children of Esau, for I will not give to you of any thing belonging to them, as much as the sole of the foot could tread upon, for I have given Mount Seir for an inheritance to Esau.

Therefore did the children of Esau fight against the children of Seir in former times, and the YAHUAH had delivered the children of Seir into the hands of the children of Esau, and destroyed them from before them, and the children of Esau dwelt in their stead to this day.

Therefore YAHUAH said to the children of Israel, Fight not against the children of Esau your brethren, for nothing in their land belongs to you, but you may buy food of them for money and eat it, and you may buy water of them for money and drink it.
And the children of Israel did according to the word of YAHUAH.

And the children of Israel went about the wilderness, going round by the way of Mount Sinai for a long time, and touched not the children of Esau, and they continued in that district for nineteen years.
At that time died Latinus king of the children of Chittim, in the forty-fifth year of his reign, which is the fourteenth year of the children of Israel’s departure from Egypt.
And they buried him in his place which he had built for himself in the land of Chittim, and Abimnas reigned in his place for thirty-eight years.
And the children of Israel passed the boundary of the children of Esau in those days, at the end of nineteen years, and they came and passed the road of the wilderness of Moab.
And YAHUAH said to Moses, besiege not Moab, and do not fight against them, for I will give you nothing of their land.
And the children of Israel passed the road of the wilderness of Moab for nineteen years, and they did not fight against them.

And in the thirty-sixth year of the children of Israel’s departing from Egypt YAHUAH smote the heart of Sihon, king of the Amorites, and he waged war, and went forth to fight against the children of Moab.

And Sihon sent messengers to Beor the son of Janeas, the son of Balaam, counsellor to the king of Egypt, and to Balaam his son, to curse Moab, in order that it might be delivered into the hand of Sihon.

And the messengers went and brought Beor the son of Janeas, and Balaam his son, from Pethor in Mesopotamia, so Beor and Balaam his son came to the city of Sihon and they cursed Moab and their king in the presence of Sihon king of the Amorites.
So Sihon went out with his whole army, and he went to Moab and fought against them, and he subdued them, and YAHUAH delivered them into his hands, and Sihon slew the king of Moab.

And Sihon took all the cities of Moab in the battle; he also took Heshbon from them, for Heshbon was one of the cities of Moab, and Sihon placed his princes and his nobles in Heshbon, and Heshbon belonged to Sihon in those days.
Therefore the parable speakers Beor and Balaam his son uttered these words, saying, Come to Heshbon, the city of Sihon will be built and established.
Woe to you Moab! you are lost, O people of Kemosh! behold it is written upon the book of the law of Elohim.

And when Sihon had conquered Moab, he placed guards in the cities which he had taken from Moab, and a considerable number of the children of Moab fell in battle into the hand of Sihon, and he made a great capture of them, sons and daughters, and he slew their king; so Sihon turned back to his own land.
And Sihon gave numerous presents of silver and gold to Beor and Balaam his son, and he dismissed them, and they went to Mesopotamia to their home and country.
At that time all the children of Israel passed from the road of the wilderness of Moab, and returned and surrounded the wilderness of Edom.

So the whole congregation came to the wilderness of Sin in the first month of the fortieth year from their departure from Egypt, and the children of Israel dwelt there in Kadesh, of the wilderness of Sin, and Miriam died there and she was buried there.

At that time Moses sent messengers to Hadad king of Edom, saying, Thus says your brother Israel, Let me pass I pray you through your land, we will not pass through field or vineyard, we will not drink the water of the well; we will walk in the king’s road.
And Edom said to him, You shall not pass through my country, and Edom went forth to meet the children of Israel with a mighty people.
And the children of Esau refused to let the children of Israel pass through their land, so the Israelites removed from them and fought not against them.
For before this YAHUAH had commanded the children of Israel, saying, You shall not fight against the children of Esau, therefore the Israelites removed from them and did not fight against them.
So the children of Israel departed from Kadesh, and all the people came to Mount Hor.
At that time YAHUAH said to Moses, Tell your brother Aaron that he shall die there, for he shall not come to the land which I have given to the children of Israel.
And Aaron went up, at the command of YAHUAH, to Mount Hor, in the fortieth year, in the fifth month, in the first day of the month.

And Aaron was one hundred and twenty-three years old when he died in Mount Hor « • • • Chapter 84 takes the thirty-eight years of wandering and compresses them to the headlines. Korah’s rebellion. The long circling of Esau’s territory. The negotiations with Moab. Sihon’s conquest of Moab (with Balaam cursing Moab for Sihon). Israel passing by Moab without fighting. Miriam’s death at Kadesh. The death of Aaron at Mount Hor. A lot of time and motion. Verses 1 and 2. Korah’s rebellion is compressed to a single sentence. Korah the son of Jetzer the son of Kehath the son of Levi took many men of the children of Israel, and they rose up and quarreled with Moses and Aaron and the whole congregation. YAHUAH was angry with them, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up with their houses and all belonging to them. Numbers 16 preserves the full story. Korah was a cousin of Moses through Levi. He led 250 princes of the congregation, men of renown, against Moses’ authority, claiming that all the congregation was holy and that Moses and Aaron were taking too much on themselves. The earth opened and swallowed Korah and his household. Fire went out from YAHUAH and consumed the 250. Jude 11 invokes Korah as a warning to the rebellious in the apostolic church: woe unto them, for they have gone in the way of Cain, and ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward, and perished in the gainsaying of Korah. The Korah pattern matters for every age. The rebellion was framed in democratic rhetoric. All the congregation is holy. Why do you lift up yourselves? It sounded like justice. It was rebellion. Every institutional church and every awakening movement has seen this pattern. A man rises up using egalitarian language to dismantle the authority the Father has placed in His chosen servants. The pattern is not always wrong — there are false shepherds who deserve to be dismantled. The discernment is in whether the critic is calling the shepherd back to the Father’s word or calling the shepherd away from the Father’s commandment. Korah was calling Moses away from the commandment. The earth opened. Every age has to discern its Korahs. Verses 3 through 13 are the long patient circling. YAHUAH tells Israel not to provoke the children of Esau, for Mount Seir is Esau’s inheritance. Israel may buy food and water for money but shall not fight. This is the Father’s severe mercy on the descendants of Esau. Esau sold his birthright for a bowl of lentils; Esau lost the blessing to Jacob; Esau made himself an enemy of Jacob. And yet YAHUAH preserves Esau’s inheritance and forbids Israel to take from it. Deuteronomy 2:4–5 is more explicit still. The Father’s love for Esau is not sentimental. It is active. The Father disciplines Esau’s descendants when they are unjust, but He does not annihilate them, and He forbids His covenant people to try. Malachi 1:2–3 famously says, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated — language that Paul will quote in Romans 9:13. The Pauline-sequence reading of that verse has to hold together with the Jasher 84:6 pattern. The Father’s “hate” of Esau is covenant-functional — Esau is not the one through whom the covenant line runs — but His actual treatment of Esau’s descendants is one of preservation, boundary, and patient waiting for their repentance. Obadiah judges Edom at length for Edom’s violence against Israel, and then closes with a picture of Zion where saviors will come up on Mount Zion to judge the mount of Esau — not to annihilate it but to set it under YAHUAH’s kingdom (Obadiah 21). Even the judged brother is eventually brought under the covenant kingdom. Moab and Ammon receive similar treatment in verses 11 through 13. YAHUAH says do not besiege Moab; do not fight them; I will give you nothing of their land. The descendants of Lot — Abraham’s nephew — are preserved like the descendants of Esau. The covenant family ties are honored even in the midst of conquest. Ruth the Moabitess will later become the great-grandmother of David. The gentle handling of Moab in Jasher 84 prepares for the grafting of Ruth into the messianic line. Nothing in the Father’s providence is accidental. Verses 14 through 22 are the Sihon-and-Balaam arc. Sihon, king of the Amorites, wages war on Moab before Israel gets there and conquers Moab’s key cities. Sihon sends to Beor son of Janeas and to Balaam son of Beor — who are in Mesopotamia, not in Egypt; Balaam has relocated — to come and curse Moab so that Moab may be delivered into Sihon’s hand. The two come. They curse Moab in Sihon’s presence. Verse 19 gives the parable they speak: “Come to Heshbon, the city of Sihon will be built and established. Woe to you Moab! you are lost, O people of Kemosh!” Jasher adds the reminder: behold it is written upon the book of the law of Elohim. This is Numbers 21:27–30 being quoted. The Torah itself quotes these parable-speakers. Here is the ugly fact of the Balaam career that modern readers often miss. Balaam curses for hire. He curses Moab in Sihon’s service in Jasher 84. He will try to curse Israel in Balak’s service in Jasher 85. He is not a neutral prophet; he is a prophet for hire. The institutional reading sometimes softens Balaam because of the donkey scene and the four beautiful oracles. Jasher does not allow the softening. Balaam is the Balaam of Cush who counseled murder of the Hebrew sons; the Balaam of Egypt who stood against Moses; the Balaam of Mesopotamia who curses Moab; the Balaam of Moab who tries to curse Israel; the Balaam who counsels the matter of Peor; and the Balaam who dies by the sword in Numbers 31. The whole career is of a piece. The four oracles in chapter 85 are beautiful not because Balaam was beautiful, but because YAHUAH overrode him. The horse can carry a beautiful rider without being itself beautiful. Verses 23 through 32 bring Israel back to the wilderness of Sin at the end of the forty years. Miriam dies and is buried at Kadesh. Moses sends to Hadad king of Edom for passage; Edom refuses; Israel turns aside rather than fight. Aaron is told to die at Mount Hor, for he shall not come into the land. Aaron was 123 years old when he died. Numbers 20 preserves the full story, including the striking of the rock that costs Moses his own entry into the land. Aaron’s death is theologically important. The high priest dies outside the land. The priesthood continues through Eleazar, but the first high priest — the one consecrated by Moses, the one who made the calf and was forgiven, the one who stood at Sinai and at the tabernacle — does not enter. This is a preview of Hebrews 4:8 — for if Joshua had given them rest, then would he not afterward have spoken of another day. The Aaronic priesthood cannot bring the people into the final rest. Aaron dies on the mountain. Moses will die on the mountain. Only the greater High Priest, after the order of Melchizedek, brings the covenant people into the rest that remains. Every high priest of Israel is a type; the fulfillment is Yahusha (Jesus). And every death of a type is a reminder that the type is not the thing itself. Miriam’s death and Aaron’s death both happen in this chapter. The older generation is passing. The two figures who stood with Moses at the Red Sea are gone. The deliverer himself has only a few years left. The transition from Moses to Joshua is coming into view. Every awakening movement that has seen its founding generation passing on knows the quiet sorrow of chapter 84. The torch has to be passed. It always has to be passed. Cross-references: Numbers 16; Numbers 20; Numbers 21:21–30; Numbers 33:37–39; Deuteronomy 2:1–9; Deuteronomy 10:6; Deuteronomy 32:50; Obadiah; Malachi 1:2–3; Romans 9:13; Jude 11; Hebrews 3:7–4:13; Hebrews 5:1–10; Hebrews 7.

chapters.title: Og, Balaam, the Matter of Peor, and Phineas

verses.text: And king Arad the Canaanite, who dwelt in the south, heard that the Israelites had come by the way of the spies, and he arranged his forces to fight against the Israelites.
And the children of Israel were greatly afraid of him, for he had a great and heavy army, so the children of Israel resolved to return to Egypt.
And the children of Israel turned back about the distance of three days’ journey to Maserath Beni Jaakon, for they were greatly afraid on account of the king Arad.
And the children of Israel would not get back to their places, so they remained in Beni Jaakon for thirty days.

And when the children of Levi saw that the children of Israel would not turn back, they were jealous for the sake of YAHUAH (the Lord), and they rose up and fought against the Israelites their brethren, and slew of them a great body, and forced them to turn back to their place, Mount Hor.
And when they returned, king Arad was still arranging his host for battle against the Israelites.
And Israel vowed a vow, saying, If you will deliver this people into my hand, then I will utterly destroy their cities.
And YAHUAH hearkened to the voice of Israel, and he delivered the Canaanites into their hand, and he utterly destroyed them and their cities, and he called the name of the place Hormah.
And the children of Israel journeyed from Mount Hor and pitched in Oboth, and they journeyed from Oboth and they pitched at Ije-abarim, in the border of Moab.

And the children of Israel sent to Moab, saying, Let us pass now through your land into our place, but the children of Moab would not suffer the children of Israel to pass through their land, for the children of Moab were greatly afraid lest the children of Israel should do to them as Sihon king of the Amorites had done to them, who had taken their land and had slain many of them.

Therefore Moab would not suffer the Israelites to pass through his land, and YAHUAH commanded the children of Israel, saying, That they should not fight against Moab, so the Israelites removed from Moab.

And the children of Israel journeyed from the border of Moab, and they came to the other side of Arnon, the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorites, and they pitched in the border of Sihon, king of the Amorites, in the wilderness of Kedemoth.
And the children of Israel sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, saying,

Let us pass through your land, we will not turn into the fields or into the vineyards, we will go along by the king’s highway until we shall have passed your border, but Sihon would not suffer the Israelites to pass.
So Sihon collected all the people of the Amorites and went forth into the wilderness to meet the children of Israel, and he fought against Israel in Jahaz.
And YAHUAH delivered Sihon king of the Amorites into the hand of the children of Israel, and Israel smote all the people of Sihon with the edge of the sword and avenged the cause of Moab.
And the children of Israel took possession of the land of Sihon from Aram to Jabuk, to the children of Ammon, and they took all the spoil of the cities.
And Israel took all these cities, and Israel dwelt in all the cities of the Amorites.
And all the children of Israel resolved to fight against the children of Ammon, to take their land also.

So YAHUAH said to the children of Israel, Do not besiege the children of Ammon, neither stir up battle against them, for I will give nothing to you of their land, and the children of Israel hearkened to the word of YAHUAH, and did not fight against the children of Ammon.

And the children of Israel turned and went up by the way of Bashan to the land of Og, king of Bashan, and Og the king of Bashan went out to meet the Israelites in battle, and he had with him many valiant men, and a very strong force from the people of the Amorites.
And Og king of Bashan was a very powerful man, but Naaron his son was exceedingly powerful, even stronger than he was.
And Og said in his heart, Behold now the whole camp of Israel takes up a space of three parsa, now will I smite them at once without sword or spear.

And Og went up Mount Jahaz, and took therefrom one large stone, the length of which was three parsa, and he placed it on his head, and resolved to throw it upon the camp of the children of Israel, to smite all the Israelites with that stone.
And the angel of YAHUAH came and pierced the stone upon the head of Og, and the stone fell upon the neck of Og that Og fell to the earth on account of the weight of the stone upon his neck.
At that time YAHUAH said to the children of Israel, Be not afraid of him, for I have given him and all his people and all his land into your hand, and you shall do to him as you did to Sihon.
And Moses went down to him with a small number of the children of Israel, and Moses smote Og with a stick at the ankles of his feet and slew him.
The children of Israel afterward pursued the children of Og and all his people, and they beat and destroyed them till there was no remnant left of them.
Moses afterward sent some of the children of Israel to spy out Jaazer, for Jaazer was a very famous city.
And the spies went to Jaazer and explored it, and the spies trusted in YAHUAH, and they fought against the men of Jaazer.
And these men took Jaazer and its villages, and YAHUAH delivered them into their hand, and they drove out the Amorites who had been there.
And the children of Israel took the land of the two kings of the Amorites, sixty cities which were on the other side of Jordan, from the brook of Arnon to Mount Herman.
And the children of Israel journeyed and came into the plain of Moab which is on this side of Jordan, by Jericho.
And the children of Moab heard all the evil which the children of Israel had done to the two kings of the Amorites, to Sihon and Og, so all the men of Moab were greatly afraid of the Israelites.

And the elders of Moab said, Behold the two kings of the Amorites, Sihon and Og, who were more powerful than all the kings of the earth, could not stand against the children of Israel, how then can we stand before them?

Surely they sent us a message before now to pass through our land on their way, and we would not suffer them, now they will turn upon us with their heavy swords and destroy us; and Moab was distressed on account of the children of Israel, and they were greatly afraid of them, and they counselled together what was to be done to the children of Israel.
And the elders of Moab resolved and took one of their men, Balak the son of Zippor the Moabite, and made him king over them at that time, and Balak was a very wise man.

And the elders of Moab rose up and sent to the children of Midian to make peace with them, for a great battle and enmity had been in those days between Moab and Midian, from the days of Hadad the son of Bedad king of Edom, who smote Midian in the field of Moab, to these days.
And the children of Moab sent to the children of Midian, and they made peace with them, and the elders of Midian came to the land of Moab to make peace in behalf of the children of Midian.
And the elders of Moab counselled with the elders of Midian what to do in order to save their lives from Israel.

And all the children of Moab said to the elders of Midian, Now therefore the children of Israel lick up all that are round about us, as the ox licks up the grass of the field, for thus did they do to the two kings of the Amorites who are stronger than we are.

And the elders of Midian said to Moab, We have heard that at the time when Sihon king of the Amorites fought against you, when he prevailed over you and took your land, he had sent to Beor the son of Janeas and to Balaam his son from Mesopotamia, and they came and cursed you; therefore did the hand of Sihon prevail over you, that he took your land.

Now therefore send you also to Balaam his son, for he still remains in his land, and give him his hire, that he may come and curse all the people of whom you are afraid; so the elders of Moab heard this thing, and it pleased them to send to Balaam the son of Beor.
So Balak the son of Zippor king of Moab sent messengers to Balaam, saying,
Behold there is a people come out from Egypt, behold they cover the face of the earth, and they abide over against me.

Now therefore come and curse this people for me, for they are too mighty for me, peradventure I shall prevail to fight against them, and drive them out, for I heard that he whom you bless is blessed, and whom you curse is cursed.
So the messengers of Balak went to Balaam and brought Balaam to curse the people to fight against Moab.
And Balaam came to Balak to curse Israel, and YAHUAH said to Balaam, Curse not this people for it is blessed.
And Balak urged Balaam day by day to curse Israel, but Balaam hearkened not to Balak on account of the word of YAHUAH which he had spoken to Balaam.
And when Balak saw that Balaam would not accede to his wish, he rose up and went home, and Balaam also returned to his land and he went from there to Midian.
And the children of Israel journeyed from the plain of Moab, and pitched by Jordan from Beth-jesimoth even to Abel-shittim, at the end of the plains of Moab.
And when the children of Israel abode in the plain of Shittim, they began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab.
And the children of Israel approached Moab, and the children of Moab pitched their tents opposite to the camp of the children of Israel.

And the children of Moab were afraid of the children of Israel, and the children of Moab took all their daughters and their wives of beautiful aspect and comely appearance, and dressed them in gold and silver and costly garments.
And the children of Moab seated those women at the door of their tents, in order that the children of Israel might see them and turn to them, and not fight against Moab.

And all the children of Moab did this thing to the children of Israel, and every man placed his wife and daughter at the door of his tent, and all the children of Israel saw the act of the children of Moab, and the children of Israel turned to the daughters of Moab and coveted them, and they went to them.

And it came to pass that when a Hebrew came to the door of the tent of Moab, and saw a daughter of Moab and desired her in his heart, and spoke with her at the door of the tent that which he desired, whilst they were speaking together the men of the tent would come out and speak to the Hebrew like to these words:

Surely you know that we are brethren, we are all the descendants of Lot and the descendants of Abraham his brother, therefore then will you not remain with us, and therefore will you not eat our bread and our sacrifice?

And when the children of Moab had thus overwhelmed him with their speeches, and enticed him by their flattering words, they seated him in the tent and cooked and sacrificed for him, and he ate of their sacrifice and of their bread.

They then gave him wine and he drank and became intoxicated, and they placed before him a beautiful damsel, and he did with her as he liked, for he knew not what he was doing, as he had drunk plentifully of wine.

Thus did the children of Moab to Israel in that place, in the plain of Shittim, and the anger of YAHUAH was kindled against Israel on account of this matter, and he sent a pestilence amongst them, and there died of the Israelites twenty-four thousand men.

Now there was a man of the children of Simeon whose name was Zimri, the son of Salu, who connected himself with the Midianite Cosbi, the daughter of Zur, king of Midian, in the sight of all the children of Israel.

And Phineas the son of Elazer, the son of Aaron the priest, saw this wicked thing which Zimri had done, and he took a spear and rose up and went after them, and pierced them both and slew them, and the pestilence ceased from the children of Israel. « • • • Chapter 85 is dense with incidents and must be read in sequence. Arad the Canaanite attacks. The Levites force the Israelites back to their place after they try to turn toward Egypt. Arad is defeated. Sihon is defeated. Og king of Bashan is defeated. Balak king of Moab hires Balaam. Balaam blesses Israel instead of cursing. The matter of Peor — Israel’s seduction by the daughters of Moab. Phineas’ zeal ends the pestilence. A fast-moving chapter that holds three of the most important Torah-narrative beats of the wilderness period. Verses 1 through 8. King Arad the Canaanite attacks. The children of Israel are afraid and resolve to return to Egypt, turning back three days’ journey. The children of Levi, jealous for the sake of YAHUAH, rise up and fight against the Israelites their brethren and force them to turn back toward Mount Hor. This is an astonishing Jasher detail. The Levites, in the thirty-ninth or fortieth year of the wandering, have to use the sword against their own covenant brothers to stop them from going back to Egypt. The same Levite sword that fell at Sinai has to fall again at the border of the land. Hold this pastorally. Every awakening movement has moments when the leadership has to exercise severe correction on its own people to prevent the movement from collapsing back into what it came out of. The Levites are not enemies of the Israelites; they are brothers using severity to save brothers. The sword in the hand of a covenant brother is not the same as the sword in the hand of an enemy. Verses 9 through 32 are the battles with Sihon and Og. Sihon is defeated. Og king of Bashan, a very powerful man with an exceedingly powerful son named Naaron, tries to throw a stone three parsa in length upon the Israelite camp to crush it all at once. The angel of YAHUAH pierces the stone upon Og’s head, the stone falls on Og’s neck, Og falls to the earth under the weight of his own stone. Moses smites Og with a stick at the ankles and slays him. The size detail is Jasher’s and should be held loosely; the theology is Torah-plain. Og was the last of the Rephaim, the remnant of the giant line that the Nephilim flood-aftermath produced (Deuteronomy 3:11 notes his iron bed-frame nine cubits long). When Og falls, a generation of giant-kings ends. Numbers 21:34 records YAHUAH saying fear him not, for I have delivered him into your hand. The pattern is that the Father’s severe enemies often look crushable only by YAHUAH’s hand, and when His hand moves, the enemy is crushed by his own weapon. Pharaoh drowned in the sea he would not let Israel cross. Og was felled by the stone he raised to crush Israel. Haman will be hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai. The pattern is permanent. The enemies of the covenant keep dying by their own devices. Verses 37 through 50 are the hiring of Balaam. Balak son of Zippor is made king of Moab, Moab sends to Midian, the elders of Moab and Midian counsel together. They remember that Sihon had hired Beor and Balaam against Moab. They resolve to hire Balaam themselves. Balaam comes to Moab, and YAHUAH speaks to him — do not curse this people, for it is blessed. Balaam refuses Balak day by day. Balak goes home; Balaam goes home. Jasher compresses the four oracles of Numbers 22 through 24 almost to nothing, which is surprising given how much theological weight they carry. The commentary has to fill in what Jasher leaves to the Torah. The four oracles of Balaam in Numbers 22 through 24 are some of the most beautiful prophecy in the Torah. The first oracle (Numbers 23:7–10): how shall I curse whom Elohim has not cursed? Who can count the dust of Jacob? The second oracle (Numbers 23:18–24): YAHUAH his Elohim is with him, and the shout of a king is among them. El brought them forth out of Egypt; he has as it were the strength of the wild ox. The third oracle (Numbers 24:3–9): how goodly are your tents, O Jacob, and your tabernacles, O Israel! As the valleys are they spread forth, as gardens by the river’s side. He shall pour the water out of his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters, and his king shall be higher than Agag, and his kingdom shall be exalted. The fourth oracle (Numbers 24:15–24): I shall see him, but not now; I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Scepter shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth. The fourth oracle is the messianic prophecy that Matthew’s magi will later follow. Numbers 24:17 is the star that rises over Bethlehem. Balaam the hired curse-slinger, who has spent his whole career trying to curse the covenant people, is forced by the hand of YAHUAH to speak the coming of the Messiah who will break every Pharaoh’s throne and lift every Star of Jacob for every nation to follow. This is the Father’s exquisite irony. The enemy is made to speak the ruin of his own system. Caiaphas will later prophesy that it is expedient for one man to die for the nation (John 11:49–52), not knowing that he is announcing the very deliverance he thinks he is stopping. The Father is always making His enemies speak the gospel. Verses 51 through 63 are the matter of Peor, the darkest hour of the wilderness and one of the most important pastoral warnings in the whole Torah. Jasher gives the mechanism in unusual detail. The daughters of Moab (and Midian) are dressed in gold and silver and costly garments and seated at the doors of their tents. When a Hebrew man comes to the door and desires a Moabite woman, the men of the tent come out and speak like brothers. We are all descendants of Abraham and Lot, they say. Why not remain with us? Why not eat our bread and our sacrifice? The Hebrew is drawn into the tent. Food is cooked. Wine is poured. The Hebrew drinks plentifully, becomes intoxicated, and is given a beautiful woman. Three features of this seduction must be named. First, the bait is not raw lust. The bait is brotherhood. The Moabites speak to the Hebrews as brothers, which — through Lot and Abraham — they are. The attack is sold as family reunion. Second, the meal is a pagan sacrificial meal. The Hebrews are not only fornicating; they are eating food sacrificed to idols at the table of another god. Paul’s 1 Corinthians 10:14–22 warning — you cannot drink the cup of YAHUAH and the cup of demons, you cannot partake of YAHUAH’s table and the table of demons — is rooted in Peor. Third, the wine is the weapon. The Hebrews consent to the full seduction only after intoxication. Drunkenness disables the will. The institutional church has replayed Peor at every century. The awakening believer who will not eat the sacrificial meal while sober can be brought to eat it drunk. Guard the cup. Twenty-four thousand die in the pestilence that follows. This is five times the death toll at the calf. Peor is worse than Sinai. Why? At Sinai, the sin was Israel’s attempt to worship YAHUAH by the pattern of the nations. At Peor, the sin was Israel’s acceptance of the nations’ worship of their own gods — eating at the tables, taking the beds. Both are catastrophic. The second is worse because it abandons the pretense of worshiping YAHUAH. Revelation 2:14 will name Peor by name as the enduring sin of the church at Pergamum: “you have there them that hold the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balak to cast a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat things sacrificed unto idols, and to commit fornication.” The apostolic word says Balaam taught Balak this tactic; Numbers 31:16 confirms Balaam’s counsel caused the matter of Peor; Jasher preserves the same. Phineas in verse 63 stops the pestilence. Zimri, a man of the tribe of Simeon, and Cosbi, a daughter of Zur king of Midian, commit the sin publicly in the sight of all the congregation. Phineas, grandson of Aaron the high priest, takes a spear, rises up, goes after them into the tent, and pierces both of them through with one spear. The pestilence ceases. Numbers 25:10–13 records YAHUAH’s covenant of an everlasting priesthood with Phineas. Phineas has been zealous for YAHUAH with the zeal of YAHUAH Himself. The institutional reading often softens Phineas because the modern ear struggles with his sword work. Do not soften him. Phineas stopped a plague that had already killed twenty-four thousand. The act of zeal was covenant-saving, not bloodthirsty. Every age needs its Phineas — the man or woman who will stop a covenant-corrupting public sin at the personal cost. In the awakening today, Phineas is the one who stands up and names the specific institutional compromise out loud, at whatever cost. The pestilence has to be stopped somewhere. A pastoral word on Peor. The man in the tent is not an enemy of YAHUAH in the simple sense. He is a Hebrew in the middle of a wilderness seduction. He is a victim of the empire’s tactic even as he is a participant in the sin. He dies in the pestilence specifically because he was a covenant son who broke the covenant. The victims-not-enemies posture here is uncomfortable. The twenty-four thousand Hebrew men who died at Peor are not the Father’s enemies in the deep sense; they are His own children who were deceived, who were seduced, who broke the covenant, and who died. This is the posture toward the awakening believer who has fallen into a Peor seduction in this generation: you are not my enemy; you are my brother; the seduction is real; the pestilence is real; come out before it kills you. Peor still kills. The wine still disables. Cross-references: Numbers 21–25; Numbers 31; Deuteronomy 2:26–37; Deuteronomy 3:1–11; Deuteronomy 4:3; Deuteronomy 23:3–6; Joshua 13:21–22; Judges 11:17–18; Psalm 106:28–31; Micah 6:5; Nehemiah 13:2; Matthew 2:1–2; 1 Corinthians 10:6–22; 2 Peter 2:15–16; Jude 11; Revelation 2:14; Revelation 22:16.

chapters.title: The Second Census and the Fall of Balaam

verses.text: At that time after the pestilence, YAHUAH (the Lord) said to Moses, and to Elazer the son of Aaron the priest, saying,
Number the heads of the whole community of the children of Israel, from twenty years old and upward, all that went forth in the army.
And Moses and Elazer numbered the children of Israel after their families, and the number of all Israel was seven hundred thousand, seven hundred and thirty.

And the number of the children of Levi, from one month old and upward, was twenty-three thousand, and amongst these there was not a man of those numbered by Moses and Aaron in the wilderness of Sinai.
For YAHUAH had told them that they would die in the wilderness, so they all died, and not one had been left of them excepting Caleb the son of Jephuneh, and Joshua the son of Nun.
And it was after this that YAHUAH said to Moses, Say to the children of Israel to avenge upon Midian the cause of their brethren the children of Israel.
And Moses did so, and the children of Israel chose from amongst them twelve thousand men, being one thousand to a tribe, and they went to Midian.
And the children of Israel warred against Midian, and they slew every male, also the five princes of Midian, and Balaam the son of Beor did they slay with the sword.
And the children of Israel took the wives of Midian captive, with their little ones and their cattle, and all belonging to them.
And they took all the spoil and all the prey, and they brought it to Moses and to Elazer to the plains of Moab.
And Moses and Elazer and all the princes of the congregation went forth to meet them with joy.

And they divided all the spoil of Midian, and the children of Israel had been revenged upon Midian for the cause of their brethren the children of Israel. « • • • Chapter 86 is brief. It records the second census after the plague of Peor and the avenging of Midian. Seven hundred thousand, seven hundred and thirty. Twenty-three thousand Levites. Not one man of the original census is left except Caleb and Joshua. The wilderness generation has been completed. The forty-year judgment is fulfilled. The next generation stands ready to cross. Verse 5 is the sobering line. They all died. The six hundred thousand men of the first census who refused to enter on the report of the ten spies all lie in the sand of the wilderness. Their wives, their children, their grandchildren stand on the east side of Jordan. The judgment was categorical. Hebrews 3:17–19 — with whom was he grieved forty years? was it not with them that had sinned, whose carcasses fell in the wilderness? And to whom sware he that they should not enter into his rest, but to them that believed not? So we see that they could not enter in because of unbelief. The wilderness generation is the negative example for every generation thereafter. The covenant promise was real. The entry was real. The unbelieving generation simply did not enter. Verses 6 through 12 are the avenging of Midian. YAHUAH commands Moses to avenge upon Midian the cause of their brethren the children of Israel — because it was Midian who cooperated with Moab in the Peor seduction, and because Midian’s daughters were in the tents. Twelve thousand Israelite men — one thousand per tribe — go to Midian. Every male is killed. The five princes of Midian are named. Balaam son of Beor — the career anti-Moses counselor — is slain by the sword. The career arc that started in Pharaoh’s court at Jasher 66 ends at an Israelite spear in Jasher 86:8. Numbers 31:8 preserves the detail. Balaam’s death is the covenant’s verdict on his whole life of hire-curse prophecy. Hold the moral shape of Midian’s judgment carefully. Not every Midianite is Midian at Peor. Reuel-Jethro, Zipporah’s father, was a Midianite priest who received Moses, blessed YAHUAH, gave counsel about the judicial system (Exodus 18), and was treated with honor. The Kenites, descendants of Jethro, were treated with ongoing favor through the Tanakh (1 Samuel 15:6; Judges 4:11). The Midian that is judged is specifically the Midian that participated in the seduction at Peor. The judgment is targeted. The victims-not-enemies posture is maintained even in a war of extermination because the extermination is against specific coverage of a specific covenant corruption, not against every Midianite everywhere. A pastoral word for the awakening believer. Ministry teams sometimes have a Balaam somewhere near them. Every awakening movement has had teachers-for-hire who have used the movement’s language while directing their gift for private profit and private compromise. The wise movement names its Balaam early, corrects, and — when correction is refused — parts ways. The careless movement lets Balaam stay and counsel Peor, and twenty-four thousand die. The Father will eventually dispose of Balaam by the sword of the covenant people. The awakening has to dispose of its Balaams before the twenty-four thousand fall. Cross-references: Numbers 26; Numbers 31; Deuteronomy 1:34–39; Joshua 13:21–22; Judges 4–5; 1 Samuel 15:6; Psalm 95:10–11; Hebrews 3:7–19; 2 Peter 2:15–16; Revelation 2:14.

chapters.title: The Commissioning of Joshua and the Death of Moses

verses.text: At that time YAHUAH (the Lord) said to Moses, Behold your days are approaching to an end, take now Joshua the son of Nun your servant and place him in the tabernacle, and I will command him, and Moses did so.
And YAHUAH appeared in the tabernacle in a pillar of cloud, and the pillar of cloud stood at the entrance of the tabernacle.
And YAHUAH commanded Joshua the son of Nun and said to him, Be strong and courageous, for you shall bring the children of Israel to the land which I swore to give them, and I will be with you.

And Moses said to Joshua, Be strong and courageous, for you will make the children of Israel inherit the land, and YAHUAH will be with you, he will not leave you nor forsake you, be not afraid nor disheartened.
And Moses called to all the children of Israel and said to them, You have seen all the good which YAHUAH your Elohim (the Lord your God) has done for you in the wilderness.
Now therefore observe all the words of this law, and walk in the way of YAHUAH your Elohim, turn not from the way which YAHUAH has commanded you, either to the right or to the left.
And Moses taught the children of Israel statutes and judgments and laws to do in the land as YAHUAH had commanded him.
And he taught them the way of YAHUAH and his laws; behold they are written upon the book of the law of Elohim (God) which he gave to the children of Israel by the hand of Moses.
And Moses finished commanding the children of Israel, and YAHUAH said to him, saying, Go up to the Mount Abarim and die there, and be gathered to your people as Aaron your brother was gathered.
And Moses went up as YAHUAH had commanded him, and he died there in the land of Moab by the order of YAHUAH, in the fortieth year from the Israelites going forth from the land of Egypt.

And the children of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab for thirty days, and the days of weeping and mourning for Moses were completed. « • • • Chapter 87 is short. Moses is told his days are ending. Joshua is placed in the tabernacle; YAHUAH appears in a pillar of cloud and commissions Joshua. Moses speaks to all Israel; teaches them the way of YAHUAH; commissions Joshua again with be strong and courageous; goes up to Mount Abarim and dies there in the land of Moab in the fortieth year. Israel weeps thirty days. The deliverer is gone. Slow for Moses. This is the servant of whom the Father said in Numbers 12:7, my servant Moses is not so, who is faithful in all my house. This is the man who has been prepared in Pharaoh’s court for forty years, in Cush on a foreign throne for forty years, in Midian as a shepherd for forty years, and in the wilderness as a prophet for forty years. One hundred twenty years of preparation and labor. He does not enter the land. He sees it from Pisgah but does not cross. He lays down his life on the mountain outside the land, at YAHUAH’s word, before the people he led for forty years go over Jordan without him. This is Moses-as-type handing off to Joshua-as-type. The name Joshua is Yehoshua. Yahusha (Jesus) is the same name. The Son bears the name of the successor. Hebrews 4:8 is explicit: for if Joshua had given them rest, then would he not afterward have spoken of another day. There remains therefore a rest to the people of Elohim. Joshua brought them into the land. Joshua did not bring them into the rest. The greater Yehoshua brings them into the rest. Every institutional reading that treats Moses and Joshua as merely historical figures has missed the typology. Moses is the servant of the old administration, whose work is law-giving and covenant-framing, who leads to the border but not in. Yahusha (Jesus) the greater is the Son of the house, who leads through the border and into the rest. Hebrews 3:1–6 puts the relationship: Moses was faithful as a servant in the house; Yahusha (Jesus) is faithful as a Son over the house. Both are faithful. One is servant; one is Son. Moses does not resent the arrangement. Moses is content to die on the mountain because Joshua is crossing. Every awakening believer content to die outside the promise so that the next generation may enter has caught the spirit of Moses’ ending. Deuteronomy 34:10–12 is the Torah’s eulogy. There arose not a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom YAHUAH knew face to face, in all the signs and the wonders which YAHUAH sent him to do in the land of Egypt. Not a prophet like Moses. Until the prophet promised in Deuteronomy 18:15–18 arose. That prophet is the greater Yehoshua. Peter knows it and cites Deuteronomy 18 at the Temple in Acts 3:22–23. Stephen knows it and cites it in his sermon in Acts 7. Moses pointed ahead. When the one pointed at comes, the pointer is honored and surpassed without shame. The thirty days of weeping. The Egyptians buried their firstborn for three days at the tenth plague. Israel weeps for Moses for thirty. The deliverer has finished. The grief is real. No rush to the crossing. The covenant people stop and mourn their servant. Hold this pastorally. Every awakening believer who has lost a teacher, a father in the faith, a founding voice of their movement should take thirty days to weep. Do not rush past the grief. The Israel that crosses Jordan after thirty days of weeping is a different Israel than the Israel that tries to rush on day three. The grief is part of the preparation. Cross-references: Numbers 27:12–23; Deuteronomy 31; Deuteronomy 32:48–52; Deuteronomy 34; Joshua 1:1–9; Acts 3:22–23; Acts 7:35–37; Hebrews 3:1–6; Hebrews 4:1–11; Matthew 17:1–8; Luke 9:28–36; Revelation 15:3.

chapters.title: The Crossing of the Jordan, the Fall of Jericho, Achan, Ai,

verses.text: And it was after the death of Moses that YAHUAH (the Lord) said to Joshua the son of Nun, saying,
Rise up and pass the Jordan to the land which I have given to the children of Israel, and you shall make the children of Israel inherit the land.
Every place upon which the sole of your feet shall tread shall belong to you, from the wilderness of Lebanon to the great river the river of Perath shall be your boundary.

No man shall stand up against you all the days of your life; as I was with Moses, so will I be with you, only be strong and of good courage to observe all the law which Moses commanded you, turn not from the way either to the right or to the left, in order that you may prosper in all that you do.

And Joshua commanded the officers of Israel, saying, Pass through the camp and command the people, saying, Prepare for yourselves provisions, for in three days more you will pass the Jordan to possess the land.
And the officers of the children of Israel did so, and they commanded the people and they did all that Joshua had commanded.
And Joshua sent two men to spy out the land of Jericho, and the men went and spied out Jericho.
And at the end of seven days they came to Joshua in the camp and said to him, YAHUAH has delivered the whole land into our hand, and the inhabitants of it are melted with fear because of us.

And it came to pass after that, that Joshua rose up in the morning and all Israel with him, and they journeyed from Shittim, and Joshua and all Israel with him passed the Jordan; and Joshua was eighty-two years old when he passed the Jordan with Israel.
And the people went up from Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and they encamped in Gilgal at the eastern corner of Jericho.
And the children of Israel kept the Passover in Gilgal, in the plains of Jericho, on the fourteenth day at the month, as it is written in the law of Moses.
And the manna ceased at that time on the morrow of the Passover, and there was no more manna for the children of Israel, and they ate of the produce of the land of Canaan.
And Jericho was entirely closed against the children of Israel, no one came out or went in.

And it was in the second month, on the first day of the month, that YAHUAH said to Joshua, Rise up, behold I have given Jericho into your hand with all the people of it; and all your fighting men shall go round the city, once each day, thus shall you do for six days.

And the priests shall blow upon trumpets, and when you shall hear the sound of the trumpet, all the people shall give a great shouting, that the walls of the city shall fall down; all the people shall go up every man against his opponent.
And Joshua did so according to all that YAHUAH had commanded him.
And on the seventh day they went round the city seven times, and the priests blew upon trumpets.
And at the seventh round, Joshua said to the people, Shout, for YAHUAH has delivered the whole city into our hands.
Only the city and all that it contains shall be accursed to YAHUAH, and keep yourselves from the accursed thing, lest you make the camp of Israel accursed and trouble it.
But all the silver and gold and brass and iron shall be consecrated to YAHUAH, they shall come into the treasury of YAHUAH.

And the people blew upon trumpets and made a great shouting, and the walls of Jericho fell down, and all the people went up, every man straight before him, and they took the city and utterly destroyed all that was in it, both man and woman, young and old, ox and sheep and ass, with the edge of the sword.
And they burned the whole city with fire; only the vessels of silver and gold, and brass and iron, they put into the treasury of YAHUAH.
And Joshua swore at that time, saying, Cursed be the man who builds Jericho; he shall lay the foundation of it in his first-born, and in his youngest son shall he set up the gates of it.

And Achan the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, son of Judah, dealt treacherously in the accursed thing, and he took of the accursed thing and hid it in the tent, and the anger of YAHUAH was kindled against Israel.
And it was after this when the children of Israel had returned from burning Jericho, Joshua sent men to spy out also Ai, and to fight against it.

And the men went up and spied out Ai, and they returned and said, Let not all the people go up with you to Ai, only let about three thousand men go up and smite the city, for the men of it are but few.
And Joshua did so, and there went up with him of the children of Israel about three thousand men, and they fought against the men of Ai.
And the battle was severe against Israel, and the men of Ai smote thirty-six men of Israel, and the children of Israel fled from before the men of Ai.
And when Joshua saw this thing, he tore his garments and fell upon his face to the ground before YAHUAH, he, with the elders of Israel, and they put dust upon their heads.
And Joshua said, Why O YAHUAH (O Lord) did you bring this people over the Jordan? what shall I say after the Israelites have turned their backs against their enemies?
Now therefore all the Canaanites, inhabitants of the land, will hear this thing, and surround us and cut off our name.

And YAHUAH said to Joshua, Why dost you fall upon your face? rise, get you off, for the Israelites have sinned, and taken of the accursed thing; I will no more be with them unless they destroy the accursed thing from amongst them.
And Joshua rose up and assembled the people, and brought the Urim by the order of the YAHUAH, and the tribe of Judah was taken, and Achan the son of Carmi was taken.

And Joshua said to Achan, Tell me my son, what have you done, and Achan said, I saw amongst the spoil a goodly garment of Shinar and two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels weight; I coveted them and took them, and behold they are all hid in the earth in the midst of the tent.
And Joshua sent men who went and took them from the tent of Achan, and they brought them to Joshua.
And Joshua took Achan and these utensils, and his sons and daughters and all belonging to him, and they brought them into the valley of Achor.

And Joshua burned them there with fire, and all the Israelites stoned Achan with stones, and they raised over him a heap of stones, therefore did he call that place the valley of Achor, so YAHUAH’s anger was appeased, and Joshua afterward came to the city and fought against it.

And YAHUAH said to Joshua, Fear not, neither be you dismayed, behold I have given into your hand Ai, her king and her people, and you shall do to them as you did to Jericho and her king, only the spoil of it and the cattle of it shall you take for a prey for yourselves; lay an ambush for the city behind it.
