So Joshua did according to the word of YAHUAH, and he chose from amongst the sons of war thirty thousand valiant men, and he sent them, and they lay in ambush for the city.
And he commanded them, saying, When you shall see us we will flee before them with cunning, and they will pursue us, you shall then rise out of the ambush and take the city, and they did so.
And Joshua fought, and the men of the city went out toward Israel, not knowing that they were lying in ambush for them behind the city.
And Joshua and all the Israelites feigned themselves wearied out before them, and they fled by the way of the wilderness with cunning.

And the men of Ai gathered all the people who were in the city to pursue the Israelites, and they went out and were drawn away from the city, not one remained, and they left the city open and pursued the Israelites.

And those who were lying in ambush rose up out of their places, and hastened to come to the city and took it and set it on fire, and the men of Ai turned back, and behold the smoke of the city ascended to the skies, and they had no means of retreating either one way or the other.
And all the men of Ai were in the midst of Israel, some on this side and some on that side, and they smote them so that not one of them remained.
And the children of Israel took Melosh king of Ai alive, and they brought him to Joshua, and Joshua hanged him on a tree and he died.
And the children of Israel returned to the city after having burned it, and they smote all those that were in it with the edge of the sword.

And the number of those that had fallen of the men of Ai, both man and woman, was twelve thousand; only the cattle and the spoil of the city they took to themselves, according to the word of YAHUAH to Joshua.

And all the kings on this side Jordan, all the kings of Canaan, heard of the evil which the children of Israel had done to Jericho and to Ai, and they gathered themselves together to fight against Israel.

Only the inhabitants of Gibeon were greatly afraid of fighting against the Israelites lest they should perish, so they acted cunningly, and they came to Joshua and to all Israel, and said to them, We have come from a distant land, now therefore make a covenant with us.

And the inhabitants of Gibeon over-reached the children of Israel, and the children of Israel made a covenant with them, and they made peace with them, and the princes of the congregation swore to them, but afterward the children of Israel knew that they were neighbors to them and were dwelling amongst them.
But the children of Israel slew them not; for they had sworn to them by YAHUAH, and they became hewers of wood and drawers of water.

And Joshua said to them, Why did you deceive me, to do this thing to us? and they answered him, saying, Because it was told to your servants all that you had done to all the kings of the Amorites, and we were greatly afraid of our lives, and we did this thing.
And Joshua appointed them on that day to hew wood and to draw water, and he divided them for slaves to all the tribes of Israel.

And when Adonizedek king of Jerusalem heard all that the children of Israel had done to Jericho and to Ai, he sent to Hoham king of Hebron and to Piram king at Jarmuth, and to Japhia king of Lachish and to Deber king of Eglon, saying,
Come up to me and help me, that we may smite the children of Israel and the inhabitants of Gibeon who have made peace with the children of Israel.
And they gathered themselves together and the five kings of the Amorites went up with all their camps, a mighty people numerous as the sand of the sea shore.

And all these kings came and encamped before Gibeon, and they began to fight against the inhabitants of Gibeon, and all the men of Gibeon sent to Joshua, saying, Come up quickly to us and help us, for all the kings of the Amorites have gathered together to fight against us.
And Joshua and all the fighting people went up from Gilgal, and Joshua came suddenly to them, and smote these five kings with a great slaughter.

And YAHUAH confounded them before the children at Israel, who smote them with a terrible slaughter in Gibeon, and pursued them along the way that goes up to Beth Horon to Makkedah, and they fled from before the children of Israel.
And whilst they were fleeing, YAHUAH sent upon them hailstones from heaven, and more of them died by the hailstones, than by the slaughter of the children of Israel.
And the children of Israel pursued them, and they still smote them in the road, going on and smiting them.

And when they were smiting, the day was declining toward evening, and Joshua said in the sight of all the people, Sun, stand you still upon Gibeon, and you moon in the valley of Ajalon, until the nation shall have revenged itself upon its enemies.

And YAHUAH hearkened to the voice of Joshua, and the sun stood still in the midst of the heavens, and it stood still six and thirty moments, and the moon also stood still and hastened not to go down a whole day.

And there was no day like that, before it or after it, that YAHUAH hearkened to the voice of a man, for YAHUAH fought for Israel. « • • • Chapter 88 is the longest chapter in this final stretch of Jasher and contains the moment that justifies this entire volume. Slow for all of it. Verses 1 through 11. Joshua is commanded to cross the Jordan. He sends two spies to Jericho. They return in seven days with the report that the inhabitants are melted with fear. Joshua and all Israel cross the Jordan. Joshua was eighty-two years old when he passed the Jordan. The people go up from the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month and encamp in Gilgal. On the fourteenth day they keep the Passover. Hold the calendar. The children of Israel exit Egypt on the fifteenth day of the first month in year one. They cross the Jordan forty years later, on the tenth day of the first month in year forty-one. They keep the Passover on the fourteenth, four days after entering the land. The crossing is calibrated to the feast calendar. The first Passover was the exodus from slavery. The first Passover in the land is the entry into the inheritance. The same feast that delivered them from Egypt is the first feast they keep in Canaan. The feasts are the shape of the covenant year across every transition. The institutional reading that has discarded the feasts has discarded the calendar-shape of the Father’s pattern. Every awakening believer who is recovering the feasts is recovering the rhythm by which the covenant actually moves through history. Verse 12. The manna ceased on the morrow of the Passover, and there was no more manna for the children of Israel, and they ate of the produce of the land of Canaan. The forty years of wilderness bread is done. The produce of the land takes over. This is a great mercy and a great transition. The covenant economy changes. In the wilderness the bread came down daily from heaven. In the land the bread comes up from the soil. Both are the Father’s provision. Neither is independent of Him. But the land-provision requires work — planting, reaping, tithing, celebrating at the feasts. The covenant is now an agricultural covenant as well as a pilgrimage covenant. The institutional reading that tries to keep the awakening believer in a permanent wilderness mentality — where every day’s bread falls miraculously and no work is required — has missed the transition. The Father gives both patterns and both are real. The wilderness is necessary; the land is the inheritance. Verses 13 through 23. Jericho is entirely closed. YAHUAH commands the march. Six days the people circle the city once. The seventh day, seven circles, then the trumpet and the shout and the wall falling. The detail in verse 19 matters — only the city and all that it contains shall be accursed to YAHUAH, and keep yourselves from the accursed thing. Verse 20 — all the silver and gold and brass and iron shall be consecrated to YAHUAH and shall come into the treasury of YAHUAH. Jericho is the firstfruits of the conquest. Firstfruits belong to YAHUAH entirely. The principle is the same as the firstfruits of the harvest (Exodus 23:19, Leviticus 23:10). The first city, like the first sheaf, is wholly His. The other cities the people will take with spoil allowed. Jericho, no. This is why Achan’s sin in verses 24 through 37 is so severe. Achan, of the tribe of Judah, coveted a goodly garment of Shinar and two hundred shekels of silver and a wedge of gold, and hid them in his tent. Israel’s first battle after Jericho — the little town of Ai — is lost, and thirty-six Israelites die, because the accursed thing is in the camp. Joshua inquires. The lot falls on Judah, then on Zabdi’s household, then on Achan. Achan confesses. Achan and his family and his cattle and his goods are burned and stoned in the valley of Achor. Anger appeased. Hold Achan carefully. The institutional reading tends either to minimize him (he only took some loot, did he really deserve to die?) or to weaponize him (see how strict the Father is). Both miss the shape. Achan was a son of Judah — the royal tribe. He was at the leading edge of the conquest. He took what belonged to YAHUAH’s treasury, and he hid it. His sin endangered the whole camp. Thirty-six Israelites died at Ai because of Achan’s tent. The covenant community is organically connected — one man’s private sin can cost the community its battles. 1 Corinthians 5:6 — a little leaven leavens the whole lump. The institutional church that has treated sin as strictly private has never understood Achan. The Father’s severity with Achan is severity on behalf of the community. The whole camp could not move forward until the accursed thing was removed. A pastoral note for the awakening believer. Every movement has Achans. People who have left the institutional system with baggage they have not fully surrendered. The baggage may look small — a grudge, an ongoing compromise, a hidden habit. The baggage is the accursed thing. If the community does not confront it, the community loses its next battle. Achan’s sin is still operating in every awakening movement that has refused to call for confession and surrender at the beginning. Verses 38 through 48. Ai is retaken with strategy and ambush. Twelve thousand men and women die. The king of Ai is hanged on a tree. Joshua burns the city. The second battle is won because the first sin was confessed. Verses 49 through 54. The inhabitants of Gibeon — Canaanites living near — deceive Israel by pretending to come from a distant land. The Israelites make a covenant with them without consulting YAHUAH. Three days later it is discovered. Joshua holds the covenant anyway — the princes of the congregation had sworn by YAHUAH — but appoints Gibeon as hewers of wood and drawers of water. The deception is met with integrity; the oath is kept; the punishment is servitude, not death. This is a covenant-integrity moment worth holding. Israel made a mistake — swore an oath on bad information. The right response is not to break the oath. The right response is to keep the oath and to correct the consequence. Every awakening believer who has made a bad promise while still in the institutional system or in the early days of the awakening faces the same question: do you break the promise, or do you keep it while correcting its terms? Joshua kept it. The Gibeonites, centuries later, will be the people Saul wrongly slaughters and David makes restitution for (2 Samuel 21). The Father’s integrity about oaths reaches across centuries. Verses 55 through 62. Five Amorite kings — Adonizedek of Jerusalem, Hoham of Hebron, Piram of Jarmuth, Japhia of Lachish, Debir of Eglon — ally to attack Gibeon for having made peace with Israel. The Gibeonites send for help. Joshua marches all night from Gilgal and falls upon them suddenly. The kings flee. YAHUAH sends hailstones on them, and more die by the hailstones than by the Israelite sword. The Father’s providence is again visible at the seam. Verses 63 through 65 are Jasher 10:13 in Joshua’s own voice — and they are the single most important reference in the entire Book of Jasher for the volume the reader is holding. Joshua said in the sight of all the people, Sun, stand you still upon Gibeon, and you moon in the valley of Ajalon, until the nation shall have revenged itself upon its enemies. And YAHUAH hearkened to the voice of Joshua, and the sun stood still in the midst of the heavens, and it stood still six and thirty moments, and the moon also stood still and hastened not to go down a whole day. And there was no day like that, before it or after it, that YAHUAH hearkened to the voice of a man, for YAHUAH fought for Israel. Joshua 10:12–14 in the canonical scripture tells the same story in nearly identical words, and at verse 13 the canonical text says: is not this written in the book of Jasher? So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down about a whole day. Stop the reader here. Let the weight settle. The Book of Jasher — this book, the volume you are holding in your hands right now, a book that has been dismissed by institutional scholarship for centuries as a curiosity, a book whose very name has been a byword for apocryphal obscurity — is cited by name in the canonical scripture of Joshua 10:13. The Holy Spirit who inspired the Torah inspired Joshua, and through Joshua cited Jasher as the reference document for the event of the sun standing still. This is not a peripheral detail. It is the canonical warrant for the book. Every reader who wonders whether Jasher matters, whether Jasher deserves their reading hours, whether Jasher belongs on the shelf next to the Torah and the prophets, has this passage as the Father’s own answer. It belongs. The Spirit cited it. Read it. Samuel will later reference Jasher again in 2 Samuel 1:18, when David’s lament over Saul and Jonathan is said to be written in the book of Jasher. Two canonical citations of the same extrabiblical book. The ancient people of Israel knew Jasher. Their prophets wrote about Jasher. Their kings’ songs were recorded in Jasher. And it has been sitting on the edge of the canon ever since, waiting for a people who would pick it up and read it. The sun stood still. The theological shape of the moment is enormous. The created order itself pauses for the covenant people to finish a battle. The Father’s agent asks for a cosmological miracle on behalf of the covenant warfare, and YAHUAH, in an act Jasher says has no equal before or after in history, does it. “Hearkened to the voice of a man” — the Father submitting the sky to Joshua’s word. Matthew 17:20 — if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove; and nothing shall be impossible unto you. The mustard seed faith that speaks and creation moves is the same faith operating in Joshua’s command. It will operate again through the Son who commands the storm (Mark 4:39) and the fig tree (Mark 11:14) and the grave (John 11:43). The covenant agent can speak to creation because the covenant agent is being backed by the covenant Creator. Hebrews 11:30 lists the fall of Jericho as a work of faith, and Hebrews 11:32–34 lists Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets as subduers of kingdoms and stoppers of the mouths of lions. The long history of covenant faith is a history of creation paused, enemies routed, walls fallen, bread multiplied, seas parted, suns held in the sky. The awakening believer in this hour is heir to all of it. The same Father who held the sun for Joshua holds the sun today. The same faith that commanded the halt is the faith by which the awakening believer moves today — not at the cosmic scale of Gibeon necessarily, but in the specific scale of the specific battle the Father has given. Joshua asked for what the battle needed. YAHUAH gave it. The awakening believer asks for what the battle needs. YAHUAH gives it. Cross-references: Joshua 1–10; Exodus 17:14–16; Deuteronomy 11:30–32; Deuteronomy 27:1–8; Joshua 10:12–14 (cites Jasher by name); Joshua 24; 2 Samuel 1:18 (cites Jasher by name); 2 Samuel 21:1–9; 1 Kings 16:34; Isaiah 28:21; Habakkuk 3:11; Matthew 17:20; Mark 4:39; Mark 11:14, 23–24; John 11:43; Hebrews 11:30–34; James 5:17–18; 1 Corinthians 5:6–7; 1 John 2:3–4; Revelation 19:11–16.

chapters.title: The Song of Joshua and the Completion of the Southern and

verses.text: Then spoke Joshua this song, on the day that YAHUAH (the Lord) had given the Amorites into the hand of Joshua and the children of Israel, and he said in the sight of all Israel,
You have done mighty things, O YAHUAH (O Lord), you have performed great deeds; who is like to you? my lips shall sing to your name.
My goodness and my fortress, my high tower, I will sing a new song to you, with thanksgiving will I sing to you, you are the strength of my salvation.
All the kings of the earth shall praise you, the princes of the world shall sing to you, the children of Israel shall rejoice in your salvation, they shall sing and praise your power.
To you, O YAHUAH, did we confide; we said you are our Elohim (God), for you were our shelter and strong tower against our enemies.

To you we cried and were not ashamed, in you we trusted and were delivered; when we cried to you, you did hear our voice, you did deliver our souls from the sword, you did show to us your grace, you did give to us your salvation, you did rejoice our hearts with your strength.
You did go forth for our salvation, with your arm you did redeem your people; you did answer us from the heavens of your holiness, you did save us from ten thousands of people.
The sun and moon stood still in heaven, and you did stand in your wrath against our oppressors and did command your judgments over them.
All the princes of the earth stood up, the kings of the nations had gathered themselves together, they were not moved at your presence, they desired your battles.
You did rise against them in your anger, and did bring down your wrath upon them; you did destroy them in your anger, and cut them off in your heart.
Nations have been consumed with your fury, kingdoms have declined because of your wrath, you did wound kings in the day of your anger.
You did pour out your fury upon them, your wrathful anger took hold of them; you did turn their iniquity upon them, and did cut them off in their wickedness.
They did spread a trap, they fell in it, in the net they hid, their foot was caught.

Your hand was ready for all your enemies who said, Through their sword they possessed the land, through their arm they dwelt in the city; you did fill their faces with shame, you did bring their horns down to the ground, you did terrify them in your wrath, and did destroy them in your anger.
The earth trembled and shook at the sound of your storm over them, you did not withhold their souls from death, and did bring down their lives to the grave.
You did pursue them in your storm, you did consume them in your whirlwind, you did turn their rain into hail, they fell in deep pits so that they could not rise.
Their carcasses were like rubbish cast out in the middle of the streets.
They were consumed and destroyed in your anger, you did save your people with your might.
Therefore our hearts rejoice in you, our souls exalt in your salvation.
Our tongues shall relate your might, we will sing and praise your wondrous works.
For you did save us from our enemies, you did deliver us from those who rose up against us, you did destroy them from before us and depress them beneath our feet.
Thus shall all your enemies perish O YAHUAH, and the wicked shall be like chaff driven by the wind, and your beloved shall be like trees planted by the waters.
So Joshua and all Israel with him returned to the camp in Gilgal, after having smitten all the kings, so that not a remnant was left of them.
And the five kings fled alone on foot from battle, and hid themselves in a cave, and Joshua sought for them in the field of battle, and did not find them.
And it was afterward told to Joshua, saying, The kings are found and behold they are hidden in a cave.
And Joshua said, Appoint men to be at the mouth of the cave, to guard them, lest they take themselves away; and the children of Israel did so.
And Joshua called to all Israel and said to the officers of battle, Place your feet upon the necks of these kings, and Joshua said, So shall YAHUAH do to all your enemies.
And Joshua commanded afterward that they should slay the kings and cast them into the cave, and to put great stones at the mouth of the cave.
And Joshua went afterward with all the people that were with him on that day to Makkedah, and he smote it with the edge of the sword.
And he utterly destroyed the souls and all belonging to the city, and he did to the king and people of it as he had done to Jericho.

And he passed from there to Libnah and he fought against it, and YAHUAH delivered it into his hand, and Joshua smote it with the edge of the sword, and all the souls of it, and he did to it and to the king of it as he had done to Jericho.
And from there he passed on to Lachish to fight against it, and Horam king of Gaza went up to assist the men of Lachish, and Joshua smote him and his people until there was none left to him.
And Joshua took Lachish and all the people of it, and he did to it as he had done to Libnah.
And Joshua passed from there to Eglon, and he took that also, and he smote it and all the people of it with the edge of the sword.

And from there he passed to Hebron and fought against it and took it and utterly destroyed it, and he returned from there with all Israel to Debir and fought against it and smote it with the edge of the sword.
And he destroyed every soul in it, he left none remaining, and he did to it and the king of it as he had done to Jericho.
And Joshua smote all the kings of the Amorites from Kadesh-barnea to Azah, and he took their country at once, for YAHUAH had fought for Israel.
And Joshua with all Israel came to the camp to Gilgal.

When at that time Jabin king of Chazor heard all that Joshua had done to the kings of the Amorites, Jabin sent to Jobat king of Midian, and to Laban king of Shimron, to Jephal king of Achshaph, and to all the kings of the Amorites, saying,
Come quickly to us and help us, that we may smite the children of Israel, before they come upon us and do to us as they have done to the other kings of the Amorites.

And all these kings hearkened to the words of Jabin, king of Chazor, and they went forth with all their camps, seventeen kings, and their people were as numerous as the sand on the sea shore, together with horses and chariots innumerable, and they came and pitched together at the waters of Merom, and they were met together to fight against Israel.
And YAHUAH said to Joshua, Fear them not, for tomorrow about this time I will deliver them up all slain before you, you shall hough their horses and burn their chariots with fire.
And Joshua with all the men of war came suddenly upon them and smote them, and they fell into their hands, for YAHUAH had delivered them into the hands of the children of Israel.
So the children of Israel pursued all these kings with their camps, and smote them until there was none left of them, and Joshua did to them as YAHUAH had spoken to him.

And Joshua returned at that time to Chazor and smote it with the sword and destroyed every soul in it and burned it with fire, and from Chazor, Joshua passed to Shimron and smote it and utterly destroyed it.
From there he passed to Achshaph and he did to it as he had done to Shimron.
From there he passed to Adulam and he smote all the people in it, and he did to Adulam as he had done to Achshaph and to Shimron.
And he passed from them to all the cities of the kings which he had smitten, and he smote all the people that were left of them and he utterly destroyed them.
Only their booty and cattle the Israelites took to themselves as a prey, but every human being they smote, they suffered not a soul to live.
As YAHUAH had commanded Moses so did Joshua and all Israel, they failed not in anything.

So Joshua and all the children of Israel smote the whole land of Canaan as YAHUAH had commanded them, and smote all their kings, being thirty and one kings, and the children of Israel took their whole country.

Besides the kingdoms of Sihon and Og which are on the other side Jordan, of which Moses had smitten many cities, and Moses gave them to the Reubenites and the Gadites and to half the tribe of Manasseh.
And Joshua smote all the kings that were on this side Jordan to the west, and gave them for an inheritance to the nine tribes and to the half tribe of Israel.

For five years did Joshua carry on the war with these kings, and he gave their cities to the Israelites, and the land became tranquil from battle throughout the cities of the Amorites and the Canaanites. « • • • Chapter 89 opens with the song Joshua sang when YAHUAH gave the Amorites into his hand. The song is Jasher-unique — the canonical Joshua does not preserve it — and it is one of the treasures this volume brings back into circulation. Verses 1 through 22 are the song. Hold a few lines. Verse 3 — my goodness and my fortress, my high tower, I will sing a new song to you, with thanksgiving will I sing to you, you are the strength of my salvation. This is the vocabulary of Psalm 18 and Psalm 144, both attributed to David. The song is older than the psalms. David inherits the vocabulary of Joshua’s song. Verse 4 — all the kings of the earth shall praise you, the princes of the world shall sing to you, the children of Israel shall rejoice in your salvation. This is already a universalist note at the heart of a conquest song. The kings of the earth — not merely Israel’s kings — will praise YAHUAH. Psalm 72:11 will later echo this. Revelation 21:24 will echo it at the end — the kings of the earth shall bring their glory and honor into the New Jerusalem. The covenant vision has always included the nations in a specific way — not as absorbed into Israel, but as brought into YAHUAH’s kingdom under Israel’s Messiah, each nation bringing its glory. Joshua’s song at the victory over five Amorite kings already sees forward to this. Verse 22 is the formal closing of the song. Thus shall all your enemies perish, O YAHUAH, and the wicked shall be like chaff driven by the wind, and your beloved shall be like trees planted by the waters. The parallelism is deep. Psalm 1 ends with the tree and the chaff; Joshua’s song ends with the tree and the chaff. The wisdom tradition of the covenant has a single core image — the obedient one is a tree planted by the waters, and the wicked is the chaff driven by the wind. Jeremiah 17:8 preserves it. Every generation of awakening believers has to decide which of these two it will be. Verses 23 through 38 are the conquest of the southern cities. The five kings flee into a cave; Joshua seals the cave and returns to finish the southern campaign; later he returns and executes the five. Makkedah. Libnah. Lachish. Horam king of Gaza coming to assist Lachish and being destroyed. Eglon. Hebron. Debir. The whole south is taken. Verses 39 through 54 are the northern campaign. Jabin king of Chazor assembles a great coalition of Amorite kings — seventeen kings — at the waters of Merom. Horses and chariots innumerable. Joshua falls on them suddenly; YAHUAH delivers them; Chazor is burned; every northern Canaanite city is taken. Thirty and one kings in total across both campaigns. Joshua’s five-year conquest is compressed here into the summary. Verse 51 is the pulse of the chapter. Joshua and all the children of Israel smote the whole land of Canaan as YAHUAH had commanded them, and smote all their kings, being thirty and one kings, and the children of Israel took their whole country. The covenant promise made to Abraham in Genesis 15 — to your seed I give this land — is now fulfilled through Joshua. Genesis 15:13 said Israel would be strangers in a land not theirs four hundred years; Jasher 75 compared the Ephraimite false exodus to this timing; Jasher 81 marked the actual exodus as two hundred and ten years from Jacob’s descent. Counting from Abraham’s own sojourning, the four hundred years are complete at Jasher 89. The promise has kept its time. Two pastoral notes on the conquest. First, the severity. Every Canaanite population is judged; every city is destroyed. The institutional reader of the twenty-first century recoils at this. The recoil is not illegitimate. It is disordered. The Father’s severity on Canaan is not racism. It is covenant surgery, the removal of a population whose sin had reached its full measure — Genesis 15:16 said the iniquity of the Amorite was not yet full, and the four hundred years of Israel’s sojourn were partly the Father’s mercy waiting for the Amorite iniquity to reach its own full measure. When it was full, the conquest came. The Canaanite sin included child sacrifice, ritual prostitution, and covenant-sorcery. The conquest was surgery on a malignant system. Rahab of Jericho was preserved because she responded to the rumor of YAHUAH with faith. The Gibeonites were preserved because they chose deception over combat. The Father had a door for every Canaanite who would take it. Most did not. The severity is real. The door was real. Second, the incompleteness. Later Judges will record that the Canaanites were not in fact all driven out — Jebusites remained in Jerusalem, Philistines on the coast, Canaanites in the valleys. The conquest under Joshua was substantial but not complete, and Judges 1 through 3 catalog the gaps. The incompleteness becomes the setup for everything that follows — the cycle of apostasy, judgment, deliverance, rest, and new apostasy through the judges; the eventual kingdom under Saul and David; the division; the exile; the regathering. The pattern of partial obedience that leads to long consequences is set here. Every awakening believer who has left the institutional system but not fully removed the institutional patterns from their own household is walking in the Judges template. The remnant of the old system left standing will trouble the next generation. The lesson is not despair. It is patience. The Father keeps working through the partial for long generations, preparing the full. Cross-references: Joshua 10–12; Judges 1–3; Psalm 1; Psalm 18; Psalm 72; Psalm 144; Jeremiah 17:7–8; Isaiah 49:6; Ephesians 2:11–22; Revelation 21:24–26.

chapters.title: The Division of the Land, the Burial of the Patriarchs, and

verses.text: At that time in the fifth year after the children of Israel had passed over Jordan, after the children of Israel had rested from their war with the Canaanites, at that time great and severe battles arose between Edom and the children of Chittim, and the children of Chittim fought against Edom.

And Abianus king of Chittim went forth in that year, that is in the thirty-first year of his reign, and a great force with him of the mighty men of the children of Chittim, and he went to Seir to fight against the children of Esau.
And Hadad the king of Edom heard of his report, and he went forth to meet him with a heavy people and strong force, and engaged in battle with him in the field of Edom.
And the hand of Chittim prevailed over the children of Esau, and the children of Chittim slew of the children of Esau, two and twenty thousand men, and all the children of Esau fled from before them.
And the children of Chittim pursued them and they reached Hadad king of Edom, who was running before them and they caught him alive, and brought him to Abianus king of Chittim.
And Abianus ordered him to be slain, and Hadad king of Edom died in the forty-eighth year of his reign.
And the children of Chittim continued their pursuit of Edom, and they smote them with a great slaughter and Edom became subject to the children of Chittim.
And the children of Chittim ruled over Edom, and Edom became under the hand of the children of Chittim and became one kingdom from that day.
And from that time they could no more lift up their heads, and their kingdom became one with the children of Chittim.
And Abianus placed officers in Edom and all the children of Edom became subject and tributary to Abianus, and Abianus turned back to his own land, Chittim.
And when he returned he renewed his government and built for himself a spacious and fortified palace for a royal residence, and reigned securely over the children of Chittim and over Edom.
In those days, after the children of Israel had driven away all the Canaanites and the Amorites, Joshua was old and advanced in years.
And YAHUAH (the Lord) said to Joshua, You are old, advanced in life, and a great part of the land remains to be possessed.
Now therefore divide this land for an inheritance to the nine tribes and to the half tribe of Manasseh, and Joshua rose up and did as YAHUAH had spoken to him.
And he divided the whole land to the tribes of Israel as an inheritance according to their divisions.
But to the tribe at Levi he gave no inheritance, the offerings of YAHUAH are their inheritance as YAHUAH had spoken of them by the hand of Moses.
And Joshua gave Mount Hebron to Caleb the son of Jephuneh, one portion above his brethren, as YAHUAH had spoken through Moses.
Therefore Hebron became an inheritance to Caleb and his children to this day.
And Joshua divided the whole land by lots to all Israel for an inheritance, as YAHUAH had commanded him.

And the children of Israel gave cities to the Levites from their own inheritance, and suburbs for their cattle, and property, as YAHUAH had commanded Moses so did the children of Israel, and they divided the land by lot whether great or small.
And they went to inherit the land according to their boundaries, and the children of Israel gave to Joshua the son of Nun an inheritance amongst them.
By the word of YAHUAH did they give to him the city which he required, Timnath-serach in Mount Ephraim, and he built the city and dwelt in it.

These are the inheritances which Elazer the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers of the tribes portioned out to the children of Israel by lot in Shiloh, before YAHUAH, at the door of the tabernacle, and they left off dividing the land.
And YAHUAH gave the land to the Israelites, and they possessed it as YAHUAH had spoken to them, and as YAHUAH had sworn to their ancestors.

And YAHUAH gave to the Israelites rest from all their enemies around them, and no man stood up against them, and YAHUAH delivered all their enemies into their hands, and not one thing failed of all the good which YAHUAH had spoken to the children of Israel, yea YAHUAH performed every thing.

And Joshua called to all the children of Israel and he blessed them, and commanded them to serve YAHUAH, and he afterward sent them away, and they went each man to his city, and each man to his inheritance.
And the children of Israel served YAHUAH all the days of Joshua, and YAHUAH gave them rest from all around them, and they dwelt securely in their cities.

And it came to pass in those days, that Abianus king of Chittim died, in the thirty-eighth year of his reign, that is the seventh year of his reign over Edom, and they buried him in his place which he had built for himself, and Latinus reigned in his stead fifty years.

And during his reign he brought forth an army, and he went and fought against the inhabitants of Britannia and Kernania, the children of Elisha son of Javan, and he prevailed over them and made them tributary.

He then heard that Edom had revolted from under the hand of Chittim, and Latinus went to them and smote them and subdued them, and placed them under the hand of the children of Chittim, and Edom became one kingdom with the children of Chittim all the days.
And for many years there was no king in Edom, and their government was with the children of Chittim and their king.

And it was in the twenty-sixth year after the children of Israel had passed the Jordan, that is the sixty-sixth year after the children of Israel had departed from Egypt, that Joshua was old, advanced in years, being one hundred and eight years old in those days.

And Joshua called to all Israel, to their elders, their judges and officers, after YAHUAH had given to all the Israelites rest from all their enemies round about, and Joshua said to the elders of Israel, and to their judges, Behold I am old, advanced in years, and you have seen what YAHUAH has done to all the nations whom he has driven away from before you, for it is YAHUAH who has fought for you.

Now therefore strengthen yourselves to keep and to do all the words of the law of Moses, not to deviate from it to the right or to the left, and not to come amongst those nations who are left in the land; neither shall you make mention of the name of their gods, but you shall cleave to YAHUAH your Elohim (the Lord your God), as you have done to this day.
And Joshua greatly exhorted the children of Israel to serve YAHUAH all their days.
And all the Israelites said, We will serve YAHUAH our Elohim (the Lord our God) all our days, we and our children, and our children’s children, and our seed for ever.
And Joshua made a covenant with the people on that day, and he sent away the children of Israel, and they went each man to his inheritance and to his city.

And it was in those days, when the children of Israel were dwelling securely in their cities, that they buried the coffins of the tribes of their ancestors, which they had brought up from Egypt, each man in the inheritance of his children, the twelve sons of Jacob did the children of Israel bury, each man in the possession of his children.
And these are the names of the cities wherein they buried the twelve sons of Jacob, whom the children of Israel had brought up from Egypt.
And they buried Reuben and Gad on this side Jordan, in Romia, which Moses had given to their children.
And Simeon and Levi they buried in the city Mauda, which he had given to the children of Simeon, and the suburb of the city was for the children of Levi.
And Judah they buried in the city of Benjamin opposite Bethlehem.
And the bones of Issachar and Zebulun they buried in Zidon, in the portion which fell to their children.
And Dan was buried in the city of his children in Eshtael, and Naphtali and Asher they buried in Kadesh-naphtali, each man in his place which he had given to his children.
And the bones of Joseph they buried in Shechem, in the part of the field which Jacob had purchased from Hamor, and which became to Joseph for an inheritance.
And they buried Benjamin in Jerusalem opposite the Jebusite, which was given to the children of Benjamin; the children of Israel buried their fathers each man in the city of his children.

And at the end of two years, Joshua the son of Nun died, one hundred and ten years old, and the time which Joshua judged Israel was twenty-eight years, and Israel served YAHUAH all the days of his life.

And the other affairs of Joshua and his battles and his reproofs with which he reproved Israel, and all which he had commanded them, and the names of the cities which the children of Israel possessed in his days, behold they are written in the book of the words of Joshua to the children of Israel, and in the book of the wars of YAHUAH, which Moses and Joshua and the children of Israel had written.
And the children of Israel buried Joshua in the border of his inheritance, in Timnath-serach, which was given to him in Mount Ephraim.

And Elazer the son of Aaron died in those days, and they buried him in a hill belonging to Phineas his son, which was given him in Mount Ephraim. « • • • Chapter 90 closes the Joshua narrative. The land is divided. The patriarchs are buried. Joshua gives his farewell covenant and dies. The elders judge for seventeen years. The Jasher-Joshua narrative is done. Verses 1 through 11 are a political aside — Abianus king of Chittim wars with Edom, prevails, kills Hadad king of Edom, subjects Edom to Chittim. This is another Jasher geopolitical tracking of the nations while Israel is settling. Hold it for the same reason as the chapter 74 interlude: the Father is watching the nations while He works on Israel. Verses 12 through 23. Joshua is old. YAHUAH tells him to divide the land to the nine tribes and the half tribe of Manasseh. Joshua divides the whole land by lot. Levi receives no inheritance — the offerings of YAHUAH are their inheritance. Caleb receives Hebron as his portion. The division takes place in Shiloh before YAHUAH at the door of the tabernacle. The lot-divisions are not random. Joshua 13 through 21 give the detailed boundaries. Each tribe receives what the Father had prepared for that tribe. Levi alone is scattered across all the cities as priestly teachers — forty-eight Levite cities across the twelve tribes. Simeon is absorbed inside Judah, fulfilling Jacob’s Genesis 49 prophecy that Simeon would be scattered in Jacob. Dan will later relocate northward, fulfilling the prophecy of Dan as a serpent by the way. The tribal blessings of Genesis 49 are now being worked out in the actual geography. The prophecy made on Jacob’s deathbed finds its shape in the surveyor’s measuring line four centuries later. The Torah is not a book of detached prophecies. The Torah is a book of prophecies that come true in time. Verses 24 through 27. YAHUAH gave the land. They possessed it. YAHUAH gave them rest from their enemies. They served YAHUAH all the days of Joshua. This is the summary verse of a generation that kept covenant. The promise kept its word. The people kept their word — this generation. The next generation, as Judges will reveal, did not know YAHUAH nor yet the works which He had done for Israel (Judges 2:10). The pattern of a faithful generation producing an unfaithful next generation is one of the hard shapes of scripture. Every awakening parent reading this has to face the question: will the next generation know? The discipleship of children is not optional. The covenant has to be handed down explicitly, taught deliberately, rehearsed annually through the feasts. The next generation does not inherit the covenant automatically. It has to be taught. Verses 38 through 46 are the detail that binds this volume to Genesis. The children of Israel bury the coffins of the tribes of their ancestors which they had brought up from Egypt. Jasher 80:63 recorded the moment Moses retrieved Joseph’s coffin and the tribes brought up their patriarchs’ coffins. Now the coffins are buried in the land of inheritance. Reuben and Gad on the east side of Jordan. Simeon and Levi in the city Mauda. Judah in the city of Benjamin opposite Bethlehem. Issachar and Zebulun in Zidon. Dan in Eshtael. Naphtali and Asher in Kadesh-naphtali. Joseph at Shechem, in the field Jacob had purchased from Hamor. Benjamin in Jerusalem opposite the Jebusite. Every patriarch is buried in the territory of his own children. This is a quiet but enormous theological moment. The covenant promise to Abraham was a promise of the land to his seed. Jacob’s twelve sons died in Egypt, and their bones were kept in coffins for four centuries waiting for this moment. Every one of the twelve is now buried in his inheritance. The Father’s word has kept itself. Joseph, embalmed in Egypt for over three hundred years, lies at last in the field at Shechem. Judah lies near Bethlehem — the town that will later give the Messiah. Benjamin lies in Jerusalem opposite the Jebusite — the city that will later become the royal city of David and the location of the Temple. The geography of the patriarchs’ burial mirrors the geography of the coming salvation story. Hold this for the two-house framework. The tribes are buried separately. There is no pan-Israelite ossuary where all twelve rest anonymously. Each patriarch is in his own tribe’s territory. The twelve-ness is preserved even in death. The dispersion that will later happen — the northern ten tribes scattered by Assyria, Judah carried away by Babylon, the remnant returning under Ezra and Nehemiah — all of it will be read against the ground of the tribes’ original named allotments. The regathering at the end will be a regathering to these original tribal geographies. Ezekiel 47 through 48 gives the eschatological division of the land; it matches the tribal structure. The New Jerusalem has twelve gates named for the twelve tribes (Revelation 21:12). The twelve-ness is permanent. The patriarchs’ coffins are the foundation stones of an enduring covenant structure. Verses 47 through 50 record Joshua’s death at one hundred and ten and his burial at Timnath-serach in Mount Ephraim. The deliverer of the land is buried in Ephraim. Eleazar the high priest dies in those days and is buried in a hill belonging to Phineas his son in Mount Ephraim. Two ends mark the transition: the prophet-successor and the priest-successor both die, and the elders take up the leadership. Cross-references: Genesis 49; Genesis 50:25; Exodus 13:19; Joshua 13–22; Joshua 23–24; Judges 2:6–10; Psalm 95:7–11; Hebrews 4:1–11; Hebrews 11:21–22; Revelation 7:4–8; Revelation 21:12–14; Ezekiel 47–48.

chapters.title: The Continuing Conquest and the Closing Blessing

verses.text: At that time, after the death of Joshua, the children of the Canaanites were still in the land, and the Israelites resolved to drive them out.
And the children of Israel asked of YAHUAH (the Lord), saying, Who shall first go up for us to the Canaanites to fight against them? and YAHUAH said, Judah shall go up.

And the children of Judah said to Simeon, Go up with us into our lot, and we will fight against the Canaanites and we likewise will go up with you, in your lot, so the children of Simeon went with the children of Judah.
And the children of Judah went up and fought against the Canaanites, so YAHUAH delivered the Canaanites into the hands of the children of Judah, and they smote them in Bezek, ten thousand men.
And they fought with Adonibezek in Bezek, and he fled from before them, and they pursued him and caught him, and they took hold of him and cut off his thumbs and great toes.

And Adonibezek said, Three score and ten kings having their thumbs and great toes cut off, gathered their meat under my table, as I have done, so Elohim (God) has requited me, and they brought him to Jerusalem and he died there.
And the children of Simeon went with the children of Judah, and they smote the Canaanites with the edge of the sword.
And YAHUAH was with the children of Judah, and they possessed the mountain, and the children of Joseph went up to Bethel, the same is Luz, and YAHUAH was with them.

And the children of Joseph spied out Bethel, and the watchmen saw a man going forth from the city, and they caught him and said to him, Show us now the entrance of the city and we will show kindness to you.
And that man showed them the entrance of the city, and the children of Joseph came and smote the City with the edge of the sword.

And the man with his family they sent away, and he went to the Hittites and he built a city, and he called the name of it Luz, so all the Israelites dwelt in their cities, and the children at Israel dwelt in their cities, and the children of Israel served YAHUAH all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders, who had lengthened their days after Joshua, and saw the great work of YAHUAH, which he had performed for Israel.
And the elders judged Israel after the death of Joshua for seventeen years.
And all the elders also fought the battles of Israel against the Canaanites and YAHUAH drove the Canaanites from before the children of Israel, in order to place the Israelites in their land.
And he accomplished all the words which he had spoken to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the oath which he had sworn, to give to them and to their children, the land of the Canaanites.

And YAHUAH gave to the children of Israel the whole land of Canaan, as he had sworn to their ancestors, and YAHUAH gave them rest from those around them, and the children of Israel dwelt securely in their cities.
Blessed be YAHUAH for ever, amen, and amen.

Strengthen yourselves, and let the hearts of all you that trust in YAHUAH be of good courage. THE END « • • • Chapter 91 is the final chapter. It records the continuation of the conquest after Joshua’s death — Judah goes first, with Simeon attached, and they smite the Canaanites. Adonibezek the tyrant of Bezek is captured; his thumbs and great toes are cut off; he recognizes in the act the covenant recompense for his own cruelty to seventy captive kings and dies in Jerusalem. The children of Joseph go up to Bethel (formerly Luz) and take the city by the help of a local informant whose family is spared and who goes to build a new Luz among the Hittites. The Israelites dwell in their cities. The elders judge Israel after Joshua for seventeen years. The elders fight the battles of Israel against the Canaanites, and YAHUAH drives the Canaanites out, and YAHUAH accomplishes all the words He spoke to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Hold the closing theological movements. Verse 2. Judah is chosen by YAHUAH to go first. This is the Genesis 49 scepter prophecy already enacted. Judah reigns over his brethren in the covenant arrangement of the land-taking. Every covenant battle from Judges forward will be led by Judah until the kingdom of David formalizes what is here informally the case. Judah first — the tribe of the scepter — goes into the battle. This will be the pattern until the greater Son of Judah comes. Verse 6. Adonibezek’s confession — three score and ten kings having their thumbs and great toes cut off, gathered their meat under my table, as I have done, so Elohim has requited me. The tyrant recognizes the covenant recompense on his own body. This is the Father’s pedagogy with the enemies of His people. Even pagan kings eventually confess the shape of His justice when it falls on them. Nebuchadnezzar will make the same confession after the seven seasons among the beasts (Daniel 4:34–37). Belshazzar will read the writing on the wall and know its meaning even as he dies (Daniel 5). The empires of the earth each receive a moment of recognition before the end. Some take it and live (Pharaoh at the sea, by Jasher 81:40; Nebuchadnezzar at Daniel 4). Most do not. Verses 11 through 16. All the Israelites dwelt in their cities, and the children of Israel served YAHUAH all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who had lengthened their days after Joshua, and saw the great work of YAHUAH which He had performed for Israel. The elders judged Israel after the death of Joshua for seventeen years. All the elders also fought the battles of Israel against the Canaanites, and YAHUAH drove the Canaanites from before the children of Israel, in order to place the Israelites in their land. And He accomplished all the words which He had spoken to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the oath which He had sworn, to give to them and to their children, the land of the Canaanites. This is the covenant completion. From Genesis 12:7 where YAHUAH tells Abraham, to your seed I will give this land, through Genesis 15:13–16 where the four hundred years of sojourning and affliction are spoken, through Genesis 22 at the binding of Isaac, through Genesis 28 at Jacob’s Bethel dream, through Exodus 3 at the burning bush, through the ten plagues, the Exodus, Sinai, the forty years of wandering, the conquest under Joshua, the five-year campaign, the seventeen-year generation after Joshua — the covenant word kept its time and kept its shape and kept its place. He accomplished all the words. The covenant’s first great horizon, from promise to inheritance, is now fulfilled. The greater horizons remain — the dispersion, the regathering, the Messiah’s first coming, the second, the New Jerusalem. But the first horizon is closed. Jasher ends at the closing of the first horizon. Verse 16 is the doxology. Blessed be YAHUAH for ever, amen, and amen. A two-fold amen. The second amen is important. Nehemiah 8:6 records Ezra blessing YAHUAH and all the people answering, amen, amen. The double amen is a liturgical confession in the covenant. It means so be it, so be it. It is the signature at the bottom of a covenant document. Jasher signs its final page with the double amen. Verse 17 is the closing exhortation. Strengthen yourselves, and let the hearts of all you that trust in YAHUAH be of good courage. This is the voice of the book turning to its reader. Not just the Israelites inside the text. The reader. You. The one who has read this volume through to the end. Strengthen yourselves. Be of good courage. The covenant kept its word to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The covenant is keeping its word to you. Cross-references: Judges 1; Judges 2:7–10; Genesis 12:7; Genesis 15:13–18; Genesis 22:15–18; Genesis 28:13–15; Exodus 3:6–8; Deuteronomy 7:6–11; Joshua 21:43–45; Joshua 23:14; Nehemiah 8:6; Psalm 105; Psalm 106; Isaiah 11:11–16; Jeremiah 23:7–8; Ezekiel 37:15–28; Hosea 11:1–11; Romans 15:8; Hebrews 6:13–18; Hebrews 11:8–16; Revelation 21:3–7. The commentary for the Book of Jasher is now complete. The Seed War Through Jasher — A Reader's Lens Two Seeds, One Ledger Genesis 3:15 opened a ledger. Every page of Jasher that the reader has just finished tracks it. Two seeds, two fathers, two fruits — running from Cain's offering rejected in Chapter 1 to Achan's stolen gold in Chapter 88. The book reads like ninety-one disconnected episodes only if the reader has not been given the lens. With the lens, it reads as one unbroken contest, with the Father keeping score and the scattered line being gathered home the whole time. This essay is the lens. It is not a new doctrine. It is not a program. It is a reading aid. When the reader closes the Cross-Reference Apparatus and puts the book down, this essay is what the reader carries. The filter sits at the top of the frame — "And hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his commandments. He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him" (1 John 2:3–4). The 1234 of Truth is the only test every subsequent claim gets submitted to. If any reading in this essay can be held against that filter and fails, the reading is wrong and must be rewritten. The Word is the last judge. What this essay does NOT do: hand the reader a practice list. It does not tell the reader to pursue genealogical research, to look in any face for signs of lineage, to decide for themselves whether they are seed of Adam or seed of Belial. The fruit reveals the tree (Matthew 7:16). The Father knows His own. The essay's job is to take the lie off — the lie that there is no seed war, or that it was settled at Golgotha, or that it is a metaphor. The Father takes it from there. Cain and Seth — The First Forked Path The seed war begins in Genesis 4, not Genesis 6. The fork is a lineage event, not a moral abstraction. Jasher's Chapter 1 opens with the story the church has softened for seventeen centuries — the first man of the first generation, born of Havah, rose up and killed his brother over an offering. "And Cain approached his brother Abel in anger, and he said to him, What is there between me and you, that you come to place yourself near my flock?" (Jasher 1:18). The question is not rhetorical. It names the thing. Cain asked the question every son of Belial has asked ever since — what is there between me and the one the Father accepted — and the answer was always the same. Envy. Blood. Ground. YAHUAH (God) had already spoken the frame before the fork opened. In the cool of the garden, after the fall, He spoke to the serpent — "And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel" (Genesis 3:15). Two seeds. Two lines. One war. The rest of the Hebrew scriptures and the writings of the apostles are the unfolding of that one sentence. The sons of Adam are the seed of the woman — the covenant lineage, the image-bearers, the line from which the Messiah (Christ) would come. Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah — the pre-flood righteous line preserved through the flood. The sons of Belial are the seed of the serpent — those of whom Yahusha (Jesus) Himself said "ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do" (John 8:44). The line is not a metaphor. It is a lineage in rebellion. Cain. Cain's line. The corrupted seed. Those whose fruit reveals whose they are. Jasher records Abel's blood going into the ground and staying there. "And the blood of Abel was absorbed in the ground, and Cain was afraid, for if he fled from there the blood would cry out to YAHUAH against him" (Jasher 1:27). The book of Hebrews lifts that ground-cry into the frame of the whole covenant — "But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God… And to Yahusha (Jesus) the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel" (Hebrews 12:22–24). Abel's blood cries judgment. The blood of Messiah cries mercy. Both are real blood. Both are heard. The seed war is the story of how the second answers the first. Jude seals the line between Cain and every son of Belial who has come since — "Woe unto them! for they have gone in the way of Cain" (Jude 1:11). John says it the plainest. "Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother's righteous" (1 John 3:12). "Of that wicked one" is not a metaphor. It is the lineage naming itself. And yet — Seth. Jasher 1:44 picks up the thread the horn has been trying to drop for seventeen centuries. "And Adam knew his wife Eve and she bore him a son, and she called his name Seth, saying, Because YAHUAH has appointed me another seed in the place of Abel, for Cain slew him" (Jasher 1:44). Another seed. Not a replacement. Not a moral do-over. A seed appointed in the place of the seed that was taken. Seth is not Abel. Seth is the line. The line continues. Genesis 5:3 is precise about it — "And Adam lived an hundred and thirty years, and begat a son in his own likeness, after his image; and called his name Seth" — the same grammar used of the Formless when He made Adam. Adam passes on what Adam was given. The image continues down the righteous line. Seth is the continuance. The two lines fork and the fork deepens. Cain's line produces Lamech — not the Methuselah-fathering Lamech of Seth's line, but the Lamech of the seventh generation in Cain's house. Genesis 4:23–24 records his boast: "And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech: for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt. If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold." The first recorded poem in scripture is a murder-ballad. Cain had been spared judgment and protected by a sevenfold curse on any who would kill him; Lamech inverts that mercy into a boast. He does not ask for protection; he claims vengeance seventy and sevenfold for his own wounds. The first human to speak in meter used the meter to celebrate blood. The sons-of-Belial posture does not simply reject the covenant; it parodies the mercy. When Yahusha was asked by Peter how many times a brother's offense should be forgiven, and Yahusha answered "until seventy times seven" (Matthew 18:22), He was speaking into Lamech's meter. The son of Adam answers Lamech's seventy-sevenfold vengeance with seventy-sevenfold forgiveness. One line counts wounds and multiplies. The other line counts mercies and multiplies. The same number in two mouths on two sides of the fork. The two lines even produced two men with the same name. Cain's line has an Enoch — Genesis 4:17 — a city-builder whose city bore his name, the first urban project in the Hebrew scriptures and already a fingerprint of the Babel impulse. Seth's line has an Enoch — Genesis 5:18–24 — the seventh from Adam, the walker with YAHUAH, the one taken. Same word. Different man. Different office. Different destiny. The seed war reached even into naming conventions, and the reader who knows the text can tell the two lines apart by the fruit each name bore. What this section dismantles: the Cain-as-symbol reading that dissolves the lineage into a generalized warning about anger or sibling rivalry. The reading that makes Genesis 4 a Sunday school fable rather than the opening page of the war the Father is winning. And the flattened "we're all one family" reading that erases the fork Genesis 4 names by name — a reading the church has grown comfortable with because it does not require any particular person to be saved out of anywhere. What this section invites: recognition that the fork is real, that the reader is not neutral in it, that some are being drawn home whose names were written in the book of life before the foundation of the world, and that the Father has already been doing the work the reader is only beginning to see. Trust the One who keeps books. Pre-Flood Corruption and the Watchers Genesis 6 has been defused for so long that the modern reader opens the chapter expecting a weather report. "And YAHUAH saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth" (Genesis 6:5) gets read as moral decline — the generalized failing of a forgetful species. The Sethite hypothesis of the early church made it worse, explaining away the sons-of-God language by downgrading the verse to "good Sethites married pretty Cainite girls" and collapsing an entire lineage war into a demographic anxiety. Jasher will not allow that reading. "And in those days the sons of men continued to rebel and transgress against Elohim (God), to provoke the anger of YAHUAH; and every man made to himself a god, and they robbed and plundered every man his neighbor as well as his relative, and they corrupted the earth, and the earth was filled with violence" (Jasher 2:19). Note the sequence. Rebellion. Idol-making. Corruption of the earth. These are not the same as bad behavior. These are the markers of the Watchers' footprint. A few verses later Jasher says the quiet part plainly. "And their judges and rulers went to the daughters of men and took their wives by force from their husbands according to their choice, and the sons of men in those days took from the cattle of the earth, the beasts of the field and the fowls of the air, and taught the mixture of animals of one species with the other, in order to provoke YAHUAH; and Elohim saw the whole earth and it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted its ways upon the earth, all men and all animals" (Jasher 4:18). The mixture of species. The corruption reaching into the animal kingdom. That is not a moral collapse; that is a genetic one. That is what the book of 1 Enoch names in chapters 6 through 16 — the Watchers descended, bound themselves to the daughters of Adam, fathered the giants, and taught humanity the technologies of destruction. The Jasher and Enoch witnesses are one witness. The Enoch commentary in the volume that precedes this one has already traced the Watchers narrative in full. This essay does not repeat that work. It only notes that Jasher's telling of pre-flood corruption is a second witness to the same event, written in the narrative register that belongs to the Torah-patterned book of the upright. The two books are not in tension. They are in conversation. The seed war sharpens here because the enemy's strategy is revealed for the first time. The serpent's initial play in the garden was a conversation — "did Elohim really say?" (Genesis 3:1) — but the Watchers' play in Genesis 6 was a genetic one. If the seed of the woman was going to bruise the serpent's head, the serpent's counter-strategy was to corrupt the seed at the source, to breed out of the human line every possibility of the promised one. The flood was the Father's surgery. "And Noah found grace in the eyes of YAHUAH… These are the generations of Noah: Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with Elohim" (Genesis 6:8–9). The word translated perfect is tamim — unblemished. It has genetic weight. Noah's line was still clean. The flood cut out the corrupted portion and preserved the line through which the promise could still run. Eight souls. One line. The covenant continues. The serpent's counter-strategy failed, and the Father's ledger kept turning. But the line was not permanently cleansed. The Watchers' strategy left traces. Numbers 13:32–33 records what the twelve spies saw in Canaan a thousand years after the flood — "There we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight." The Anakim. Deuteronomy 2:11 names the Emim, 2:20 the Zamzummim, 3:11 Og king of Bashan whose iron bedstead was thirteen cubits long. The giants reappeared. The corruption that the flood had cut out found its way back through lineages the text does not fully explain — whether through the genetic material of one of Ham's lines, through a re-emergence of the Watchers pattern after the flood, or through some other vector the prophets did not specify for us. The mechanism is hidden. The result is not. When Yashar'el came up out of Egypt, the giants were already waiting in the land of promise. The seed war had a new front. The conquest of Canaan under Joshua was not a xenophobic land-grab, as the horn's pulpit has sometimes accused. It was the Father closing a door the enemy had reopened. Deuteronomy 7:1–6's seven nations named for destruction — the Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites — were the territories where the Anakim and the giants had taken root and where the Watchers' technologies of destruction were still in circulation. Goliath of Gath in 1 Samuel 17 was one of their last survivors; David killing Goliath was the covenant line finishing what Joshua had begun. The Enoch volume traces this continuity in full. For Jasher's reader, the note to hold is that the Watchers' corruption did not end at the flood; it left a residue the covenant line was still clearing when Samuel anointed David over Yashar'el. What this section dismantles: the Sethite hypothesis and every reading of Genesis 6 that empties the Watchers material out of the text. The weather-report reading of the flood. The reverse error of making Enoch's translation a Christological event — Enoch is the pre-flood witness, not the pre-flood Messiah, and his office is to point, not to be pointed at. That distinction belongs to Yahusha alone, and the Enoch volume preserves it carefully. What this section invites: honest engagement with what the scriptures actually say happened. The horn's pulpit has been asking "did Elohim really say?" since Laodicea. The reader who has come this far into Jasher is already done with that question. The answer is yes — the scriptures say what they say, the seed war is a war of lineages, and the flood was the Father defending the line. Ham and Shem — The Branching After the Flood The curse of Ham was never about skin color. It has been used against every African, Afro-Caribbean, and Black reader who has had the verse quoted at them by a horn-trained pulpit trying to justify a hierarchy Elohim never authorized. The misuse was real, and the harm it has done is real, and no essay in this series can pretend otherwise. What this section does is hand the verse back clean. Jasher gives the post-flood episode without softening. "And the wine gave Noah drink, and he was drunken, and he uncovered himself in the midst of his tent. And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father and told it to his two brethren without" (reflecting Genesis 9:21–22; Jasher 5–6 tells the same story). When Noah awoke and learned what his youngest son had done, he pronounced a specific curse — "And Noah said, Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be unto his brethren" (Genesis 9:25). The curse names Canaan. Not Ham. Not Ham's skin. Not Ham's descendants as a category. Canaan. This distinction is not a nicety. It is load-bearing. The curse on Canaan is the explanation for why, seven centuries later, the land promised to Abraham was the land of Canaan specifically — the land that had been forfeit from the moment Canaan inherited the consequence of his father's profanation. The covenant giving the land to Abraham and his seed is the covenant revoking Canaan's claim. Joshua's conquest is the ledger being balanced. Jasher's account of Noah's blessing upon Shem and Japheth, and the curse upon Canaan, is not a racial pronouncement. It is a land allocation and a moral accounting. Then Jasher does what the ordinary Genesis Table of Nations does not — it names where each line settled. "These are the sons of Japheth according to their families… And the children of Gomer were Ascenaz, Riphath, and Tegarmah. And the children of Magog were Elichanaf and Lubal. And the children of Madai were Achon, Zeelo, Chazoni and Lot" (Jasher 7:1–3 and following). Japheth's sons became the nations of the north and the west — the isles of the gentiles of Isaiah 49:1 and Jeremiah 31:10. Ham's sons settled in the south and along the rivers. Shem's sons stayed in the covenant center. This Table is the map of where the scattered seed would later be sown. When the ten northern tribes of Yashar'el (Israel) were carried away by Assyria eight hundred years later, they went into the lands Japheth's sons had settled. The scattered seed of the house of Yashar'el grew wild among the nations Japheth had planted. Romans 11's wild olive branches are those scattered sheep — still olive, always olive, never anything else — growing in the soil of the Japhetic lands until the Father started grafting them back into their own natural root. The nations themselves — Japheth's actual descendants and Ham's and the rest — remained the nations, the stranger and sojourner of Torah, loved and provided for under the Torah stranger rules, but not made the seed. Both branches on the olive tree of Romans 11 are Yashar'el. The wild olive is the scattered line. The cultivated olive is the house that retained identity. The nations are not grafted in as a third branch. This is the distinction the Torah-observant reader who came up through evangelicalism needs to understand, and it is the distinction the Islam reader needs to understand, and it is the distinction the rabbinic-Judaism reader needs to understand. All four houses flattened it. The prophets never did. What this section dismantles: the Hamitic hypothesis that justified centuries of enslavement and apartheid; the replacement readings that treat Japheth as the "predecessor" of the church; the inclusion readings that treat Ham or Japheth as now being grafted into Yashar'el by faith. None of those readings fit the text. What this section invites: a cleaner, calmer reading of Genesis 9 and 10 — the curse falls where the text says it falls, the nations are real nations loved by Elohim, the covenant seed runs through Shem, and the scattered line has a map of where it was sown. The reader whose inheritance was poisoned by the Ham-curse weaponization is handed the text back clean. The ledger of that harm is open, and the Father knows how to close it. Nimrod and Babel — The First Covenant-Opposing Kingdom Every pulpit in Christendom has reduced Nimrod to a paragraph. Jasher gives him nine chapters. That disparity is not an accident — the horn does not want the reader to see what Nimrod was, because what Nimrod was is what the horn is. Jasher 7:30 opens the pattern. "And Nimrod strengthened himself, and he rose up from amongst his brethren, and he went to the field with his brethren to hunt for animals, and he became a hunter before YAHUAH" (compare Genesis 10:8–9). "Before YAHUAH" is not a compliment in this context. It is the Hebrew idiom for standing up against — in the face of, in defiance of. The King James rendering keeps the phrase but muffles the sense. Nimrod hunted men as well as animals. He built the first kingdom that organized humanity against the covenant. Jasher traces the ambition. "And they built the city and the tower, and they did this thing daily until many days and years were elapsed. And Elohim said to the seventy angels who stood foremost before him, to those who were near to him, saying, Come let us descend and confuse their tongues" (Jasher 9:33). The tower's purpose is the thing to see. Babel was not hubris in the abstract. Babel was an architectural assault on a specific place. The builders reached up because there was a summit they were reaching for. "How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground… For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north" (Isaiah 14:12–13). The Mount of the Assembly. Lucifer reached for it first. Nimrod reached for it second. The builders at Babel were doing what their father-in-rebellion had done. The pattern will recur. Nimrod's kingdom had all the marks of every later Babel. Organized religion in service of the state. A centralized language used to police consent. A building project to consolidate power. A strongman whose image was above scrutiny. The Watchers' technologies from before the flood, re-engineered. A hunt that treated human beings as game. Everything the horn has ever been, Nimrod was first. Jasher then does something the Genesis account does not — it shows Nimrod's kingdom in personal collision with Abram. "And Abram saw the whole earth, and all its inhabitants, and they were nothing. And Abram looked at the heaven and the earth, and the sun and the moon, and he questioned them and said, Who created all these? And Abram said in his heart, The Most High, He is the Elohim who created everything" (Jasher 9 — summarized). The young Abram reasons out the Creator. Nimrod, in the same book, is told by his astrologers that a star rising from the east is the sign that a child has been born who will inherit both worlds. Nimrod tries to kill the child. Abram is hidden. The child grows. The covenant line survives again. The pattern is unmistakable. Babel's king hunts the covenant seed. The covenant seed escapes. Centuries later, Pharaoh hunts the Hebrew infants, and Moses escapes in the basket. Centuries later, Herod hunts the Bethlehem infants, and Yahusha escapes into Egypt. The sons of Belial strategy does not change. Kill the seed. Extinguish the line. Prevent the bruise to the serpent's head. Jasher 9:26 preserves a line no church has ever had the courage to read from the pulpit. The tower's purpose was expressed in three parties of men with three different aims. "One said, We will ascend into heaven and fight against Him. The second said, We will ascend into heaven and place our own gods there and serve them. And the third party said, We will ascend into heaven and smite Him with bows and spears." Three factions. Three strategies. Military conquest of heaven, colonization of heaven with counterfeit gods, or outright assault. Every subsequent covenant-opposing system has run variations on these three — the secular state's war on the covenant, the colonizing church that plants counterfeit gods in Elohim's sanctuary, the persecuting spirit that sends armies against the saints. Babel is the catalog of every later Babylon. And Babel is where the counterfeit worship that every pulpit in the four houses would later be selling was born. The tradition that pairs Nimrod with a queen — Semiramis in one strand, Ashtoreth in another, Ishtar in another, the Queen of Heaven of Jeremiah 7:18 and 44:17 — is the beginning of the mother-and-child pagan motif that would be reproduced in Egypt as Isis and Horus, in Babylon as Ishtar and Tammuz, in Rome as Venus and Cupid, and in the pulpit's own Christmas iconography. The iconography is not innocent. It is Babel's counterfeit gods re-badged for each age. The awakening believer is not being called to burn anyone's family decorations. The believer is being shown the pedigree. The Father gave His own imagery to Yashar'el in the tabernacle, with specific and reverent bounds. The pattern humanity reaches for when it builds its own religion has never once matched what the Father asked for. What this section dismantles: the dispensational reduction of Babylon to "Rome only" or "a future literal city only" or "the apostate church only." Babylon is a spirit. It first took form at Babel. It has taken form again in every subsequent system that organized humanity against the covenant — and it will take final form at the end. Revelation 17 and

are the closing of the ledger that opened in Jasher 7 and 9. It also dismantles the Torah-observant reading that reduces Babel to a language event. The confusion of languages was real. The purpose of the tower was also real. The Father scattered the nations precisely because a consolidated humanity under Nimrod's kingdom would have been able to carry out what the Watchers had begun — corrupting the seed at the source. The scattering preserved the line. It bought the time the covenant needed to raise up Abram and his house. What this section invites: recognition of Babel's fingerprints on every system the reader has walked out of, and a patient posture toward those still inside. The Christian sitting in the service of institutional Christianity, the Jew sitting under rabbinic fences against the prophets, the Torah-observant believer sitting inside a Hebrew Roots teacher's replacement-by-Torah-keeping reading, the Muslim sitting under the transfer-of-covenant lie — every one of them is inside a system with Nimrod's fingerprints on it, and the people inside are the lost sheep. The war is with the system. It is not with the grandmother who hung the cross, or the imam who loves his neighbor, or the yeshiva student who fasts on Yom Kippur, or the Torah teacher whose heart is turned toward the Sabbath but whose frame is off. The war is with the spirit that took form at Babel and has been wearing new costumes ever since. Ishmael and Isaac — The First Abrahamic Fork The covenant line narrows here, and the narrowing is sovereign. The Father chose Isaac. He did not choose him because Ishmael was worse. He chose him because the covenant is always a choosing, and the choosing is always the Father's. The seed of promise runs where He says it runs. Jasher handles the Sarai and Hagar story without the softening a modern reader might expect. Hagar was given to Abram by Sarai herself. Ishmael was born, and Ishmael was loved by his father — the grief Abram carried over sending Ishmael away is not something Jasher hides. "And the thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight on account of his son, and Abraham rose up early in the morning and took bread and a bottle of water, and gave it to Hagar, and sent her away with her son" (Jasher 21 — echoing Genesis 21:11–14). The grief was real. The decision was still made. Elohim Himself had told Abraham to listen to Sarah — "in Isaac shall thy seed be called" (Genesis 21:12) — and Abraham, the friend of Elohim, obeyed. But Ishmael was not abandoned. "And Elohim heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of Elohim called to Hagar out of heaven… Arise, lift up the lad, and hold him in thine hand; for I will make him a great nation" (Genesis 21:17–18). And He did. Jasher 25:12–18 records the twelve princes of Ishmael and the territories they settled. Ishmael became a great nation, as YAHUAH had promised.
